BERT is an encoder-only model and differs from other decoder-style transformers (e.g., GPT-4 or Llama-2) that are capable of generating sentences, answering questions, or producing a new output in general. Thus, to re-train BERT for this specific task of response accuracy prediction, we first tokenize action sequences and add a linear output layer on the top of the BERT model for predicting the response accuracy of examinees taking PSTRE items in PIAAC 2012. This process is also known as *fine-tuning an LLM*. Next, we examine the algorithmic bias in fine-tuned BERT models when countries with different performance levels have been used as training sets. Specifically, we identify top-, average-, and low-performing countries based on the availability of the log data. The top-performing country is Finland, the average-performing country is Slovakia, and the low-performing country is the United States. We fine-tune the BERT model using the overall sample including all countries, only Finland, only Slovakia, and only the United States, and compare the response accuracy across these four different models obtained by having different countries as training and test sets. Our research questions are as follows. ## Research questions **RQ1:** To what extent do the fine-tuned BERT models with different populations predict response accuracy? The aim of this research question is to investigate the utility of a pretrained LLM for predicting response accuracy using action sequences directly. We replicate the feasibility of fine-tuning BERT across countries with different ability levels for response accuracy prediction in PSTRE items. **RQ2:** Is there a difference in model performance when BERT is fined-tuned with different populations? # Algorithmic Bias in BERT for Response Accuracy Prediction The purpose of this research question is to investigate the population validity of the fine-tuned BERT model for predicting response accuracy using three different countries with different overall performance levels. This allows us to investigate the extent of algorithmic bias present in the trained models as well as showcase the importance of examining bias in predictive models. ## Method ### Data Data for this study comes from the log files extracted from three PSTRE items administered in the 2012 PIAAC. PIAAC is a large-scale international assessment developed by the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) to assess the proficiency levels of adults in literacy, numeracy, and problem-solving. PSTRE items in the 2012 PIAAC target adults’ problem-solving skills and include 14 items in total (OECD, 2019). We selected three dichotomously scored PSTRE items—U03A, U07X, and U16X because (1) log data extracted from PSTRE items included action sequences that provided rich information about examinee behavior, and (2) we can train a binary classification model using BERT. The action sequences included human-computer interactions recorded for each PSTRE item, such as opening a folder, viewing a folder, clicking on a link, or using the help function. The log data were not publicly available for all countries that participated in the 2012 PIAAC cycle. Based on the overall country performance across all domains, we identified three countries with different performance levels¹. Based on the availability of log data, the top-performing country was Finland, followed by Slovakia located in the middle of the performance distribution, and the worse-performing country was the United States. The first dichotomously scored item, U03A—CD Tally, selected for this study was located in Booklet 1 and included $n_{Finland}$ = 1,482, $n_{Slovakia}$ = 1,096, and $n_{United States}$ = 1,337 participants. The second and third dichotomously scored items, U07X—Book Order and U16X—Reply All, selected were located in Booklet 2 and included $n_{Finland}$ = 1,445, $n_{Slovakia}$ = 1,160, and $n_{United States}$ = 1,340, and $n_{Finland}$ = 1,440, $n_{Slovakia}$ = 1,160, and $n_{United States}$ = 1,342 participants, respectively. Across all items included in the study, the distribution of participants from Finland, Slovakia, and the United States was balanced. To date, a few studies employed BERT for identifying anomalous responses in process data (e.g., Chen & Liao, 2022; Guo et al., 2021; Landauer et al., 2023; Shao et al., 2022), yet BERT has not been used for predicting response accuracy using action sequences. As emphasized, action sequences provide rich yet unstructured information about the examinee behavior. In most cases, it is difficult to directly use the action sequences data due to their high dimensionality. For this reason, researchers may use dimension reduction techniques (e.g., multidimensional scaling) or may extract useful features (e.g., number of actions, duration of actions) from action sequences to be used in machine learning models. A novelty of this study is that using BERT allows to directly use action sequences without the need of using such preprocessing approaches, permitting us to keep the rich information as is. 5 Gorgun and Yildirim-Erbash BERT is a pretrained transformer composed of token embeddings (i.e., capture the meaning and context of individual words in a text; Huang et al., 2020), segment embeddings (i.e., differentiate between sentences A and B for next sentence prediction loss; Devlin et al., 2018), and position embeddings (i.e., encode absolute positions from 1 to a maximum length with each position having a learnable vector; Huang et al., 2020). As explained, we selected only dichotomously scored items. We recoded missing values (coded as 0 in the dataset) and not-reached items (coded as 9 in the dataset) as NA, incorrect responses (coded as 7 in the dataset) as 0. The correct responses were coded as 1. For the items se- # Algorithmic Bias in BERT for Response Accuracy Prediction lected, we had only three cases with missing outcome variables, and we removed those cases from the analysis. Finally, we created a dataset for each PSTRE item, including variables Examinee ID, Country ID, action sequences, and response accuracy (i.e., target variable). Next, we split the data into training and test sets, and 20% of the data is used as the hold-out test set. We also created subsets of training and test sets based on the country to train the data with the overall sample (i.e., including all countries), Finland-only, Slovakia-only, and the United States-only samples. Following training and test set preparations, we tokenized the action sequences for each item using the BERT base cased model. During the tokenization process, we selected a max token length of 512 and padding = True, to achieve equal sequence lengths for each action sequence. Thus, examinees with action sequences longer than 512 actions were trimmed to a length of 512 tokens, and those with action sequences shorter than 512 actions were added [PAD]—a special- ized token used to adjust the token length. Concerning Item U03A, none of the action sequences were longer than 512 tokens, for Item U07X, only one case in the United States sample has action sequences longer than 512 tokens, and for Item U16X, 26 cases (0.7%) have action sequences longer than 512 tokens (Table 1). Given that no or only a very few cases have action sequences longer than 512 tokens, we expect that truncation has a minimal influence on the models developed. Based on the tokenization process, we obtained a 768-dimensional embedding vector of action sequences. The tokenization process also adds two special tokens: CLS at the beginning of each action sequence and SEP at the end of each action sequence. We fine-tuned BERT for a downstream task (i.e., classification) for pre- dicting examinees' response accuracy using the tokenized action sequences. Specif- ically, using the *AutoModelForSequenceClassification* function, we added a linear output layer for predicting the response accuracy on the top of the pooled CLS to- ken. We used a learning rate of 5e-6 and 3 epochs with a batch size of 8. We repeated the same process using the training data including overall data (i.e., including all countries), Finland, Slovakia, and the United States for all three items. We then eval- uated model performance on the hold-out test sets, including the overall data, only Finland, only Slovakia, and only the United States test sets. This yielded 16 models per item with a total of 48 models. The preprocessing steps were conducted in R (R Core Team, 2022), and the analysis was conducted in Python with NVIDIA T4 Tensor Core GPU. ## Model evaluation We evaluated the model performance of all 48 models us- ing Accuracy, Precision, Recall, F1, and Absolute Between-ROC Area (ABROCA; (Gardner et al., 2019)). Accuracy is defined as $$ Accuracy = \frac{TP + TN}{TP + TN + FP + FN} \quad (1) $$ *Gorgun and Yildirim-Erbash* where TP is true-positive rate, TN is true-negative rate, FP is false-positive rate, and FN is false-negative rate. Precision is defined as $$ Precision = \frac{TP}{TP + FP} \quad (2) $$ recall is defined as $$ Recall = \frac{TP}{TP + FN} \quad (3) $$ and F1 is defined as $$ F1 = 2 \frac{Precision \times Recall}{Precision + Recall} \quad (4) $$ ABROCA is a measure developed for evaluating algorithmic fairness across two subgroups by comparing model performance for both groups using a Receiver Operating Characteristic (ROC) Curve. Simply, ABROCA finds the difference between the areas in AUC by $$ ABROCA = AUC_b - AUC_c \quad (5) $$ and thus, it quantifies the difference between a baseline model and a comparison group (Gardner et al., 2019). # Results ## Descriptive Statistics The descriptive statistics for the items selected are given in Table 1. Except for item U07X, the other two items were relatively more difficult for the United States compared to Finland and Slovakia. Item U07X had the same difficulty for all countries included in the study. Item U16X was easiest for Finland, and Item U03A was easiest for Slovakia. DOI: 10.1111/jedm.12420 Journal of Educational Measurement # Algorithmic Bias in BERT for Response Accuracy Prediction: A Case Study for Investigating Population Validity Guher Gorgun (ID) University of Alberta Seyma N. Yildirim-Erbasli Concordia University of Edmonton Pretrained large language models (LLMs) have gained popularity in recent years due to their high performance in various educational tasks such as learner modeling, automated scoring, automatic item generation, and prediction. Nevertheless, LLMs are black box approaches where models are less interpretable, and they may carry human biases and prejudices because historical human data have been used for pretraining these large-scale models. For these reasons, the prediction tasks based on LLMs require scrutiny to ensure that the prediction models are fair and unbiased. In this study, we used BERT—a pretrained encoder-only LLM for predicting response accuracy using action sequences extracted from the 2012 PIAAC assessment. We selected three countries (i.e., Finland, Slovakia, and the United States) representing different performance levels in the overall PIAAC assessment. We found promising results for predicting response accuracy using the fine-tuned BERT model. Additionally, we examined algorithmic bias in the prediction models trained with different countries. We found differences in model performance, suggesting that some trained models are not free from bias, and thus the models are less generalizable across countries. Our results highlighted the importance of investigating algorithmic fairness in prediction models utilizing algorithmic systems to ensure models are bias-free. In the last decade, machine learning and data mining methods have become popular for analyzing assessment data to discover hidden response patterns and provide a nuanced understanding of response behavior (e.g., Goldhammer et al., 2017; He et al., 2021; Nagy et al., 2022; Ulitzsch et al., 2022). Computer-based assessments have facilitated the use of these methods by providing rich information about examinees (Jiao et al., 2023). With computer-based assessments, supplementary information, in addition to traditionally captured response accuracy, can be obtained about data, may include response time spent for each item (e.g., Gorgun & Bulut, 2021), the number of actions taken by examinees (e.g., Sahin & Colvin, 2020), hint requests (e.g., Gorgun & Bulut, 2022b), response changes (e.g., Kroehne & Goldhammer, 2018), action sequences (e.g., Ulitzsch et al., 2022), keystrokes (e.g., Conijn et al., 2019), or eye tracking data (e.g., Orange et al., 2017). --- © 2024 The Author(s). *Journal of Educational Measurement* published by Wiley Periodicals LLC on behalf of National Council on Measurement in Education. This is an open access article under the terms of the CreativeCommonsAttribution-NonCommercial-NoDerivs License, which permits use and distribution in any medium, provided the original work is properly cited, the use is non-commercial and no modifications or adaptations are made. *Gorgun and Yildirim-Erbasli* To date, researchers have leveraged log data to uncover behavioral patterns of examinees with correct and incorrect responses (e.g., Plewan *et al*., 2016), investigate problem-solving strategies (e.g., Pejic & Molcer, 2021), identify disengaged or unmotivated examinees (e.g., Yildirim-Erbasli & Bulut, 2021), and detect anomalous responses (e.g., Shao *et al*., 2022). These studies typically employed computer algorithms for modeling examinee responses. However, algorithmic systems trained with historical human data may discriminate against certain groups, leading to unwarranted inferences about examinees (Kizilcec & Lee, 2022). For example, this may include assigning unrealistically low scores to a certain group (Smith, 2020) or not selecting a certain racial group during the admission process due to the reliance on the historical data (Kleinberg *et al*., 2018). In this study, we first propose to use a pretrained encoder-only large-language model (LLM), Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers (BERT; Devlin *et al*., 2018), for predicting response accuracy using action sequences extracted from the 2012 Programme for the International Assessment of Adult Competencies (PIAAC) log data. Then, we aim to investigate algorithmic bias in fine-tuned BERT for predicting response accuracy in countries that performed well (i.e., Finland), average (i.e., Slovakia), and worse (i.e., the United States) in the 2012 PIAAC assessment. This allows us to examine the population validity of the fine-tuned BERT models across countries with different performance levels. Investigating fairness issues in LLMs is of utmost importance because LLMs are trained with historical human data and may carry human biases and prejudices (e.g., Papakyriakopoulos *et al*., 2020). Recent studies have highlighted that LLMs may hallucinate and generate incorrect information with seemingly high confidence (Zhang *et al*., 2023). Another challenge associated with using LLMs for modeling response behavior is the lack of model interpretability due to LLMs being black-box models (e.g., Lin *et al*., 2023). These models are considered less interpretable because they were trained with a deep learning-based architecture. For these reasons, this study not only proposes to use BERT for response accuracy prediction but also investigates the extent of model generalizability (i.e., algorithmic fairness) across countries with different performance levels. The contributions of this study include understanding the feasibility of using a pretrained LLM, BERT, for predicting response accuracy using action sequences and examining the extent of algorithmic fairness in LLMs for the model's generalizability across all subpopulations. ## Literature Review Process data refers to users’ actions that occurred while interacting with the computer interface stored as log files (He *et al*., 2021; Tang *et al*., 2021). Given that log files capture each action, sequences of actions, and time spent in each state, process data provide rich yet unstructured and high-dimensional information about the examinee response processes (Tang *et al*., 2020). Typically, two forms of approaches have been followed by the researcher when analyzing the process data: (1) preprocess the process data to reduce dimensionality, such as by creating aggregated features (e.g., total response time spent on each item or the total number of actions taken; Gorgun & Bulut, 2022b; Jiang *et al*., 2024) or (using a dimension reduction tech- 2 # Algorithmic Bias in BERT for Response Accuracy Prediction nique (e.g., Bulut et al., 2024; Tang et al., 2021), or (2) use raw process data as is for subsequent analysis (e.g., feature extraction or identifying aberrant responses) (e.g., He & von Davier, 2015; Ulitzsch et al., 2022; Xiong et al., 2024). Note that which approach

has elevated in recent years as more educational settings incorporate artificial intelligence to model learners. Most studies analyzed algorithmic bias in prediction models in the presence of class imbalances. An oversampling technique such as SMOTE or ADASYN helped improve algorithmic fairness (Deho et al., 2023; Jiang & Pardos, 2021; Sha et al., 2022, 2023). Even though oversampling techniques are useful for improving model accuracy across different populations, researchers also suggested that more marginalized and underrepresented populations (e.g., racial and gender groups) should be included in training sets (Baker et al., 2023). In addition to representational issues of minority groups, studies also documented biases in prediction models when individuals have different native languages, leading to the underestimation of examinee performance in assessments or learning environments (Gaskins, 2022; Loukina et al., 2019). Traditionally, studies have examined algorithmic bias in prediction models by considering groups based on factors such as gender, age, race, and religion. Yet, the list of groups or populations can be expanded to align with the specific purpose of the algorithmic system. For instance, additional factors such as school region (e.g., urban, suburban, or rural), learner speed (e.g., slow or fast learners), cultural variations (e.g., native language or home country), and socioeconomic status (e.g., low-income students) can be considered (Doroudi & Brunskill, 2019; Li et al., 2019; Loukina et al., 2019; Ocumpaugh et al., 2014; Sackett et al., 2009). In the context of international large-scale assessments, it is important to investigate algorithmic fairness in modeling student performance across countries. This ensures that valid comparisons can be made among countries participating in such assessments. ## Current Study In this study, we first investigate the utility of using an LLM, BERT, for predicting response accuracy employing action sequences extracted from the log files of Problem-Solving in Technology-Rich Environments (PSTRE). To date, a few studies employed BERT for identifying anomalous responses in process data (e.g., Chen & Liao, 2022; Guo et al., 2021; Landauer et al., 2023; Shao et al., 2022), yet BERT has not been used for predicting response accuracy using action sequences. As emphasized, action sequences provide rich yet unstructured information about the examinee behavior. In most cases, it is difficult to directly use the action sequences data due to their high dimensionality. For this reason, researchers may use dimension reduction techniques (e.g., multidimensional scaling) or may extract useful features (e.g., number of actions, duration of actions) from action sequences to be used in machine learning models. A novelty of this study is that using BERT allows to directly use action sequences without the need of using such preprocessing approaches, permitting us to keep the rich information as is. 5 Gorgun and Yildirim-Erbash BERT is a pretrained transformer composed of token embeddings (i.e., capture the meaning and context of individual words in a text; Huang et al., 2020), segment embeddings (i.e., differentiate between sentences A and B for next sentence prediction loss; Devlin et al., 2018), and position embeddings (i.e., encode absolute positions from 1 to a maximum length with each position having a learnable vector; Huang et al., 2020). For example, in the sentence "The quick brown fox jumps over the lazy dog," the token embeddings would represent each individual word as numerical vectors capturing their semantic meaning and context within the sentence. Regarding segment embeddings, for example, consider two sentences: "The cat sat on the mat" (Sentence A) and "The dog barked loudly" (Sentence B). Segment embeddings differentiate between these two sentences and enable BERT to predict the relationship between them, such as whether Sentence B follows Sentence A logically or not. Regarding the position embeddings, consider a 20-token passage where the position embeddings would assign a unique learnable vector to each token based on its position from 1 to 20. These position embeddings enable BERT to understand the sequential order of tokens and capture the contextual relationships between them, regardless of their absolute positions in the input text. BERT is an encoder-only model and differs from other decoder-style transformers (e.g., GPT-4 or Llama-2) that are capable of generating sentences, answering questions, or producing a new output in general. Thus, to re-train BERT for this specific task of response accuracy prediction, we first tokenize action sequences and add a linear output layer on the top of the BERT model for predicting the response accuracy of examinees taking PSTRE items in PIAAC 2012. This process is also known as *fine-tuning an LLM*. Next, we examine the algorithmic bias in fine-tuned BERT models when countries with different performance levels have been used as training sets. Specifically, we identify top-, average-, and low-performing countries based on the availability of the log data. The top-performing country is Finland, the average-performing country is Slovakia, and the low-performing country is the United States. We fine-tune the BERT model using the overall sample including all countries, only Finland, only Slovakia, and only the United States, and compare the response accuracy across these four different models obtained by having different countries as training and test sets. Our research questions are as follows. ## Research questions **RQ1:** To what extent do the fine-tuned BERT models with different populations predict response accuracy? The aim of this research question is to investigate the utility of a pretrained LLM for predicting response accuracy using action sequences directly. We replicate the feasibility of fine-tuning BERT across countries with different ability levels for response accuracy prediction in PSTRE items. **RQ2:** Is there a difference in model performance when BERT is fined-tuned with different populations? # Algorithmic Bias in BERT for Response Accuracy Prediction The purpose of this research question is to investigate the population validity of the fine-tuned BERT model for predicting response accuracy using three different countries with different overall performance levels. This allows us to investigate the extent of algorithmic bias present in the trained models as well as showcase the importance of examining bias in predictive models. ## Method ### Data Data for this study comes from the log files extracted from three PSTRE items administered in the 2012 PIAAC.

For example, in the sentence "The quick brown fox jumps over the lazy dog," the token embeddings would represent each individual word as numerical vectors capturing their semantic meaning and context within the sentence. Regarding segment embeddings, for example, consider two sentences: "The cat sat on the mat" (Sentence A) and "The dog barked loudly" (Sentence B). Segment embeddings differentiate between these two sentences and enable BERT to predict the relationship between them, such as whether Sentence B follows Sentence A logically or not. Regarding the position embeddings, consider a 20-token passage where the position embeddings would assign a unique learnable vector to each token based on its position from 1 to 20. These position embeddings enable BERT to understand the sequential order of tokens and capture the contextual relationships between them, regardless of their absolute positions in the input text. BERT is an encoder-only model and differs from other decoder-style transformers (e.g., GPT-4 or Llama-2) that are capable of generating sentences, answering questions, or producing a new output in general. Thus, to re-train BERT for this specific task of response accuracy prediction, we first tokenize action sequences and add a linear output layer on the top of the BERT model for predicting the response accuracy of examinees taking PSTRE items in PIAAC 2012. This process is also known as *fine-tuning an LLM*. Next, we examine the algorithmic bias in fine-tuned BERT models when countries with different performance levels have been used as training sets. Specifically, we identify top-, average-, and low-performing countries based on the availability of the log data. The top-performing country is Finland, the average-performing country is Slovakia, and the low-performing country is the United States. We fine-tune the BERT model using the overall sample including all countries, only Finland, only Slovakia, and only the United States, and compare the response accuracy across these four different models obtained by having different countries as training and test sets. Our research questions are as follows. ## Research questions **RQ1:** To what extent do the fine-tuned BERT models with different populations predict response accuracy? The aim of this research question is to investigate the utility of a pretrained LLM for predicting response accuracy using action sequences directly. We replicate the feasibility of fine-tuning BERT across countries with different ability levels for response accuracy prediction in PSTRE items. **RQ2:** Is there a difference in model performance when BERT is fined-tuned with different populations? # Algorithmic Bias in BERT for Response Accuracy Prediction The purpose of this research question is to investigate the population validity of the fine-tuned BERT model for predicting response accuracy using three different countries with different overall performance levels. This allows us to investigate the extent of algorithmic bias present in the trained models as well as showcase the importance of examining bias in predictive models. ## Method ### Data Data for this study comes from the log files extracted from three PSTRE items administered in the 2012 PIAAC. PIAAC is a large-scale international assessment developed by the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) to assess the proficiency levels of adults in literacy, numeracy, and problem-solving. PSTRE items in the 2012 PIAAC target adults’ problem-solving skills and include 14 items in total (OECD, 2019). We selected three dichotomously scored PSTRE items—U03A, U07X, and U16X because (1) log data extracted from PSTRE items included action sequences that provided rich information about examinee behavior, and (2) we can train a binary classification model using BERT. The action sequences included human-computer interactions recorded for each PSTRE item, such as opening a folder, viewing a folder, clicking on a link, or using the help function. The log data were not publicly available for all countries that participated in the 2012 PIAAC cycle. Based on the overall country performance across all domains, we identified three countries with different performance levels¹. Based on the availability of log data, the top-performing country was Finland, followed by Slovakia located in the middle of the performance distribution, and the worse-performing country was the United States. The first dichotomously scored item, U03A—CD Tally, selected for this study was located in Booklet 1 and included $n_{Finland}$ = 1,482, $n_{Slovakia}$ = 1,096, and $n_{United States}$ = 1,337 participants. The second and third dichotomously scored items, U07X—Book Order and U16X—Reply All, selected were located in Booklet 2 and included $n_{Finland}$ = 1,445, $n_{Slovakia}$ = 1,160, and $n_{United States}$ = 1,340, and $n_{Finland}$ = 1,440, $n_{Slovakia}$ = 1,160, and $n_{United States}$ = 1,342 participants, respectively. Across all items included in the study, the distribution of participants from Finland, Slovakia, and the United States was balanced. The descriptive statistics, including the number of participants, min, max, mean, standard deviation of item length, the number of cases with action sequences longer than 512 tokens, and the proportion-correct scores across all countries are given in Table 1. ### Data Analysis We provided a flowchart presenting the preprocessing and data analysis steps adopted in this study (Figure 1). We first extracted the log data for the selected countries and items using the software program, LogDataAnalyzer available on the PIAAC website. This process created the individual log files for Finland, Slovakia, and the United States. We replaced the underscore separating action descriptions with a space to facilitate the tokenization process with BERT—breaking down the text into words or subwords based on predefined rules (Devlin et al., 2018). After preprocessing the action sequences, an example action sequence for the item U03A is given as: ``` START-COMBOBOX-BUTTON-DOACTION-NEXT INQUIRY-NEXT BUTTON- CONFIRMATION OPENED-BUTTON-DOACTION-BUTTON-CONFIRMATION CLOSED-NEXT ITEM-END. ``` We also merged response data with log data files to obtain response accuracy for each participant for the selected PSTRE items. As explained, we selected only dichotomously scored items. We recoded missing values (coded as 0 in the dataset) and not-reached items (coded as 9 in the dataset) as NA, incorrect responses (coded as 7 in the dataset) as 0. The correct responses were coded as 1. For the items se- # Algorithmic Bias in BERT for Response Accuracy Prediction lected, we had only three cases with missing outcome variables, and we removed those cases from the analysis. Finally, we created a dataset for each PSTRE item, including variables Examinee ID, Country ID, action sequences, and response accuracy (i.e., target variable). Next, we split the data into training and test sets, and 20% of the data is used as the hold-out test set. We also created subsets of training and test sets based on the country to train the data with the overall sample (i.e., including all countries), Finland-only, Slovakia-only, and the United States-only samples. Following training and test set preparations, we tokenized the action sequences for each item using the BERT base cased model. During the tokenization process, we selected a max token length of 512 and padding = True, to achieve equal sequence lengths for each action sequence. Thus, examinees with action sequences longer than 512 actions were trimmed to a length of 512 tokens, and those with action sequences shorter than 512 actions were added [PAD]—a special- ized token used to adjust the token length. Concerning Item U03A, none of the action sequences were longer than 512 tokens, for Item U07X, only one case in the United States sample has action sequences longer than 512 tokens, and for Item U16X, 26 cases (0.7%) have action sequences longer than 512 tokens (Table 1). Given that no or only a very few cases have action sequences longer than 512 tokens, we expect that truncation has a minimal influence on the models developed. Based on the tokenization process, we obtained a 768-dimensional embedding vector of action sequences. The tokenization process also adds two special tokens: CLS at the beginning of each action sequence and SEP at the end of each action sequence. We fine-tuned BERT for a downstream task (i.e., classification) for pre- dicting examinees' response accuracy using the tokenized action sequences. Specif- ically, using the *AutoModelForSequenceClassification* function, we added a linear output layer for predicting the response accuracy on the top of the pooled CLS to- ken. We used a learning rate of 5e-6 and 3 epochs with a batch size of 8. We repeated the same process using the training data including overall data (i.e., including all countries), Finland, Slovakia, and the United States for all three items. We then eval- uated model performance on the hold-out test sets, including the overall data, only Finland, only Slovakia, and only the United States test sets. This yielded 16 models per item with a total of 48 models. The preprocessing steps were conducted in R (R Core Team, 2022), and the analysis was conducted in Python with NVIDIA T4 Tensor Core GPU. ## Model evaluation We evaluated the model performance of all 48 models us- ing Accuracy, Precision, Recall, F1, and Absolute Between-ROC Area (ABROCA; (Gardner et al., 2019)). Accuracy is defined as $$ Accuracy = \frac{TP + TN}{TP + TN + FP + FN} \quad (1) $$ *Gorgun and Yildirim-Erbash* where TP is true-positive rate, TN is true-negative rate, FP is false-positive rate, and FN is false-negative rate. Precision is defined as $$ Precision = \frac{TP}{TP + FP} \quad (2) $$ recall is defined as $$ Recall = \frac{TP}{TP + FN} \quad (3) $$ and F1 is defined as $$ F1 = 2 \frac{Precision \times Recall}{Precision + Recall} \quad (4) $$ ABROCA is a measure developed for evaluating algorithmic fairness across two subgroups by comparing model performance for both groups using a Receiver Operating Characteristic (ROC) Curve. Simply, ABROCA finds the difference between the areas in AUC by $$ ABROCA = AUC_b - AUC_c \quad (5) $$ and thus, it quantifies the difference between a baseline model and a comparison group (Gardner et al., 2019). # Results ## Descriptive Statistics The descriptive statistics for the items selected are given in Table 1. PIAAC is a large-scale international assessment developed by the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) to assess the proficiency levels of adults in literacy, numeracy, and problem-solving. PSTRE items in the 2012 PIAAC target adults’ problem-solving skills and include 14 items in total (OECD, 2019). We selected three dichotomously scored PSTRE items—U03A, U07X, and U16X because (1) log data extracted from PSTRE items included action sequences that provided rich information about examinee behavior, and (2) we can train a binary classification model using BERT. The action sequences included human-computer interactions recorded for each PSTRE item, such as opening a folder, viewing a folder, clicking on a link, or using the help function. The log data were not publicly available for all countries that participated in the 2012 PIAAC cycle. Based on the overall country performance across all domains, we identified three countries with different performance levels¹. Based on the availability of log data, the top-performing country was Finland, followed by Slovakia located in the middle of the performance distribution, and the worse-performing country was the United States. The first dichotomously scored item, U03A—CD Tally, selected for this study was located in Booklet 1 and included $n_{Finland}$ = 1,482, $n_{Slovakia}$ = 1,096, and $n_{United States}$ = 1,337 participants. The second and third dichotomously scored items, U07X—Book Order and U16X—Reply All, selected were located in Booklet 2 and included $n_{Finland}$ = 1,445, $n_{Slovakia}$ = 1,160, and $n_{United States}$ = 1,340, and $n_{Finland}$ = 1,440, $n_{Slovakia}$ = 1,160, and $n_{United States}$ = 1,342 participants, respectively. Across all items included in the study, the distribution of participants from Finland, Slovakia, and the United States was balanced. The descriptive statistics, including the number of participants, min, max, mean, standard deviation of item length, the number of cases with action sequences longer than 512 tokens, and the proportion-correct scores across all countries are given in Table 1. ### Data Analysis We provided a flowchart presenting the preprocessing and data analysis steps adopted in this study (Figure 1). We first extracted the log data for the selected countries and items using the software program, LogDataAnalyzer available on the PIAAC website. This process created the individual log files for Finland, Slovakia, and the United States. position having a learnable vector; Huang et al., 2020). For example, in the sentence "The quick brown fox jumps over the lazy dog," the token embeddings would represent each individual word as numerical vectors capturing their semantic meaning and context within the sentence. Regarding segment embeddings, for example, consider two sentences: "The cat sat on the mat" (Sentence A) and "The dog barked loudly" (Sentence B). Segment embeddings differentiate between these two sentences and enable BERT to predict the relationship between them, such as whether Sentence B follows Sentence A logically or not. Regarding the position embeddings, consider a 20-token passage where the position embeddings would assign a unique learnable vector to each token based on its position from 1 to 20. These position embeddings enable BERT to understand the sequential order of tokens and capture the contextual relationships between them, regardless of their absolute positions in the input text. BERT is an encoder-only model and differs from other decoder-style transformers (e.g., GPT-4 or Llama-2) that are capable of generating sentences, answering questions, or producing a new output in general. Thus, to re-train BERT for this specific task of response accuracy prediction, we first tokenize action sequences and add a linear output layer on the top of the BERT model for predicting the response accuracy of examinees taking PSTRE items in PIAAC 2012. This process is also known as *fine-tuning an LLM*. Next, we examine the algorithmic bias in fine-tuned BERT models when countries with different performance levels have been used as training sets. Specifically, we identify top-, average-, and low-performing countries based on the availability of the log data. The top-performing country is Finland, the average-performing country is Slovakia, and the low-performing country is the United States. We fine-tune the BERT model using the overall sample including all countries, only Finland, only Slovakia, and only the United States, and compare the response accuracy across these four different models obtained by having different countries as training and test sets. Our research questions are as follows. ## Research questions **RQ1:** To what extent do the fine-tuned BERT models with different populations predict response accuracy? The aim of this research question is to investigate the utility of a pretrained LLM for predicting response accuracy using action sequences directly. We replicate the feasibility of fine-tuning BERT across countries with different ability levels for response accuracy prediction in PSTRE items. **RQ2:** Is there a difference in model performance when BERT is fined-tuned with different populations? # Algorithmic Bias in BERT for Response Accuracy Prediction The purpose of this research question is to investigate the population validity of the fine-tuned BERT model for predicting response accuracy using three different countries with different overall performance levels. This allows us to investigate the extent of algorithmic bias present in the trained models as well as showcase the importance of examining bias in predictive models. ## Method ### Data Data for this study comes from the log files extracted from three PSTRE items administered in the 2012 PIAAC. PIAAC is a large-scale international assessment developed by the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) to assess the proficiency levels of adults in literacy, numeracy, and problem-solving. We selected three dichotomously scored PSTRE items—U03A, U07X, and U16X because (1) log data extracted from PSTRE items included action sequences that provided rich information about examinee behavior, and (2) we can train a binary classification model using BERT. The action sequences included human-computer interactions recorded for each PSTRE item, such as opening a folder, viewing a folder, clicking on a link, or using the help function. The log data were not publicly available for all countries that participated in the 2012 PIAAC cycle. Based on the overall country performance across all domains, we identified three countries with different performance levels¹. Based on the availability of log data, the top-performing country was Finland, followed by Slovakia located in the middle of the performance distribution, and the worse-performing country was the United States. Yildirim-Erbasli Concordia University of Edmonton Pretrained large language models (LLMs) have gained popularity in recent years due to their high performance in various educational tasks such as learner modeling, automated scoring, automatic item generation, and prediction. Nevertheless, LLMs are black box approaches where models are less interpretable, and they may carry human biases and prejudices because historical human data have been used for pretraining these large-scale models. For these reasons, the prediction tasks based on LLMs require scrutiny to ensure that the prediction models are fair and unbiased. In this study, we used BERT—a pretrained encoder-only LLM for predicting response accuracy using action sequences extracted from the 2012 PIAAC assessment. We selected three countries (i.e., Finland, Slovakia, and the United States) representing different performance levels in the overall PIAAC assessment. We found promising results for predicting response accuracy using the fine-tuned BERT model. Additionally, we examined algorithmic bias in the prediction models trained with different countries. We found differences in model performance, suggesting that some trained models are not free from bias, and thus the models are less generalizable across countries. Our results highlighted the importance of investigating algorithmic fairness in prediction models utilizing algorithmic systems to ensure models are bias-free. In the last decade, machine learning and data mining methods have become popular for analyzing assessment data to discover hidden response patterns and provide a nuanced understanding of response behavior (e.g., Goldhammer et al., 2017; He et al., 2021; Nagy et al., 2022; Ulitzsch et al., 2022). Computer-based assessments have facilitated the use of these methods by providing rich information about examinees (Jiao et al., 2023). With computer-based assessments, supplementary information, in addition to traditionally captured response accuracy, can be obtained about data, may include response time spent for each item (e.g., Gorgun & Bulut, 2021), the number of actions taken by examinees (e.g., Sahin & Colvin, 2020), hint requests (e.g., Gorgun & Bulut, 2022b), response changes (e.g., Kroehne & Goldhammer, 2018), action sequences (e.g., Ulitzsch et al., 2022), keystrokes (e.g., Conijn et al., 2019), or eye tracking data (e.g., Orange et al., 2017). --- © 2024 The Author(s). *Journal of Educational Measurement* published by Wiley Periodicals LLC on behalf of National Council on Measurement in Education. This is an open access article under the terms of the CreativeCommonsAttribution-NonCommercial-NoDerivs License, which permits use and distribution in any medium, provided the original work is properly cited, the use is non-commercial and no modifications or adaptations are made. *Gorgun and Yildirim-Erbasli* To date, researchers have leveraged log data to uncover behavioral patterns of examinees with correct and incorrect responses (e.g., Plewan *et al*., 2016), investigate problem-solving strategies (e.g., Pejic & Molcer, 2021), identify disengaged or unmotivated examinees (e.g., Yildirim-Erbasli & Bulut, 2021), and detect anomalous responses (e.g., Shao *et al*., 2022). These studies typically employed computer algorithms for modeling examinee responses. However, algorithmic systems trained with historical human data may discriminate against certain groups, leading to unwarranted inferences about examinees (Kizilcec & Lee, 2022). For example, this may include assigning unrealistically low scores to a certain group (Smith, 2020) or not selecting a certain racial group during the admission process due to the reliance on the historical data (Kleinberg *et al*., 2018). In this study, we first propose to use a pretrained encoder-only large-language model (LLM), Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers (BERT; Devlin *et al*., 2018), for predicting response accuracy using action sequences extracted from the 2012 Programme for the International Assessment of Adult Competencies (PIAAC) log data. Then, we aim to investigate algorithmic bias in fine-tuned BERT for predicting response accuracy in countries that performed well (i.e., Finland), average (i.e., Slovakia), and worse (i.e., the United States) in the 2012 PIAAC assessment. This allows us to examine the population validity of the fine-tuned BERT models across countries with different performance levels. Investigating fairness issues in LLMs is of utmost importance because LLMs are trained with historical human data and may carry human biases and prejudices (e.g., Papakyriakopoulos *et al*., 2020). Recent studies have highlighted that LLMs may hallucinate and generate incorrect information with seemingly high confidence (Zhang *et al*., 2023). Another challenge associated with using LLMs for modeling response behavior is the lack of model interpretability due to LLMs being black-box models (e.g., Lin *et al*., 2023). These models are considered less interpretable because they were trained with a deep learning-based architecture. For these reasons, this study not only proposes to use BERT for response accuracy prediction but also investigates the extent of model generalizability (i.e., algorithmic fairness) across countries with different performance levels. The contributions of this study include understanding the feasibility of using a pretrained LLM, BERT, for predicting response accuracy using action sequences and examining the extent of algorithmic fairness in LLMs for the model's generalizability across all subpopulations. ## Literature Review Process data refers to users’ actions that occurred while interacting with the computer interface stored as log files (He *et al*., 2021; Tang *et al*., 2021). Given that log files capture each action, sequences of actions, and time spent in each state, process data provide rich yet unstructured and high-dimensional information about the examinee response processes (Tang *et al*., 2020). Typically, two forms of approaches have been followed by the researcher when analyzing the process data: (1) preprocess the process data to reduce dimensionality, such as by creating aggregated features (e.g., total response time spent on each item or the total number of actions taken; Gorgun & Bulut, 2022b; Jiang *et al*., 2024) or (using a dimension reduction tech- 2 # Algorithmic Bias in BERT for Response Accuracy Prediction nique (e.g., Bulut et al., 2024; Tang et al., 2021), or (2) use raw process data as is for subsequent analysis (e.g., feature extraction or identifying aberrant responses) (e.g., He & von Davier, 2015; Ulitzsch et al., 2022; Xiong et al., 2024). For example, in the sentence "The quick brown fox jumps over the lazy dog," the token embeddings would represent each individual word as numerical vectors capturing their semantic meaning and context within the sentence. Regarding segment embeddings, for example, consider two sentences: "The cat sat on the mat" (Sentence A) and "The dog barked loudly" (Sentence B). Segment embeddings differentiate between these two sentences and enable BERT to predict the relationship between them, such as whether Sentence B follows Sentence A logically or not. Regarding the position embeddings, consider a 20-token passage where the position embeddings would assign a unique learnable vector to each token based on its position from 1 to 20. These position embeddings enable BERT to understand the sequential order of tokens and capture the contextual relationships between them, regardless of their absolute positions in the input text. BERT is an encoder-only model and differs from other decoder-style transformers (e.g., GPT-4 or Llama-2) that are capable of generating sentences, answering questions, or producing a new output in general. Thus, to re-train BERT for this specific task of response accuracy prediction, we first tokenize action sequences and add a linear output layer on the top of the BERT model for predicting the response accuracy of examinees taking PSTRE items in PIAAC 2012. This process is also known as *fine-tuning an LLM*. Next, we examine the algorithmic bias in fine-tuned BERT models when countries with different performance levels have been used as training sets. Specifically, we identify top-, average-, and low-performing countries based on the availability of the log data. The top-performing country is Finland, the average-performing country is Slovakia, and the low-performing country is the United States. We fine-tune the BERT model using the overall sample including all countries, only Finland, only Slovakia, and only the United States, and compare the response accuracy across these four different models obtained by having different countries as training and test sets. Our research questions are as follows. ## Research questions **RQ1:** To what extent do the fine-tuned BERT models with different populations predict response accuracy? The aim of this research question is to investigate the utility of a pretrained LLM for predicting response accuracy using action sequences directly. PSTRE items in the 2012 PIAAC target adults’ problem-solving skills and include 14 items in total (OECD, 2019). We selected three dichotomously scored PSTRE items—U03A, U07X, and U16X because (1) log data extracted from PSTRE items included action sequences that provided rich information about examinee behavior, and (2) we can train a binary classification model using BERT. The log data were not publicly available for all countries that participated in the 2012 PIAAC cycle. Her primary research interests include learner modeling, automatic item generation and evaluation, and learning analytics. For example, in the sentence "The quick brown fox jumps over the lazy dog," the token embeddings would represent each individual word as numerical vectors capturing their semantic meaning and context within the sentence. Regarding segment embeddings, for example, consider two sentences: "The cat sat on the mat" (Sentence A) and "The dog barked loudly" (Sentence B). Segment embeddings differentiate between these two sentences and enable BERT to predict the relationship between them, such as whether Sentence B follows Sentence A logically or not. Regarding the position embeddings, consider a 20-token passage where the position embeddings would assign a unique learnable vector to each token based on its position from 1 to 20. These position embeddings enable BERT to understand the sequential order of tokens and capture the contextual relationships between them, regardless of their absolute positions in the input text. BERT is an encoder-only model and differs from other decoder-style transformers (e.g., GPT-4 or Llama-2) that are capable of generating sentences, answering questions, or producing a new output in general. Thus, to re-train BERT for this specific task of response accuracy prediction, we first tokenize action sequences and add a linear output layer on the top of the BERT model for predicting the response accuracy of examinees taking PSTRE items in PIAAC 2012. This process is also known as *fine-tuning an LLM*. Next, we examine the algorithmic bias in fine-tuned BERT models when countries with different performance levels have been used as training sets. Specifically, we identify top-, average-, and low-performing countries based on the availability of the log data. The top-performing country is Finland, the average-performing country is Slovakia, and the low-performing country is the United States. We fine-tune the BERT model using the overall sample including all countries, only Finland, only Slovakia, and only the United States, and compare the response accuracy across these four different models obtained by having different countries as training and test sets. Our research questions are as follows. ## Research questions **RQ1:** To what extent do the fine-tuned BERT models with different populations predict response accuracy? The aim of this research question is to investigate the utility of a pretrained LLM for predicting response accuracy using action sequences directly. We replicate the feasibility of fine-tuning BERT across countries with different ability levels for response accuracy prediction in PSTRE items. **RQ2:** Is there a difference in model performance when BERT is fined-tuned with different populations? # Algorithmic Bias in BERT for Response Accuracy Prediction The purpose of this research question is to investigate the population validity of the fine-tuned BERT model for predicting response accuracy using three different countries with different overall performance levels. This allows us to investigate the extent of algorithmic bias present in the trained models as well as showcase the importance of examining bias in predictive models. ## Method ### Data Data for this study comes from the log files extracted from three PSTRE items administered in the 2012 PIAAC. PIAAC is a large-scale international assessment developed by the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) to assess the proficiency levels of adults in literacy, numeracy, and problem-solving. PSTRE items in the 2012 PIAAC target adults’ problem-solving skills and include 14 items in total (OECD, 2019). We selected three dichotomously scored PSTRE items—U03A, U07X, and U16X because (1) log data extracted from PSTRE items included action sequences that provided rich information about examinee behavior, and (2) we can train a binary classification model using BERT. The action sequences included human-computer interactions recorded for each PSTRE item, such as opening a folder, viewing a folder, clicking on a link, or using the help function. The log data were not publicly available for all countries that participated in the 2012 PIAAC cycle. Based on the overall country performance across all domains, we identified three countries with different performance levels¹. Based on the availability of log data, the top-performing country was Finland, followed by Slovakia located in the middle of the performance distribution, and the worse-performing country was the United States. The first dichotomously scored item, U03A—CD Tally, selected for this study was located in Booklet 1 and included $n_{Finland}$ = 1,482, $n_{Slovakia}$ = 1,096, and $n_{United States}$ = 1,337 participants. The second and third dichotomously scored items, U07X—Book Order and U16X—Reply All, selected were located in Booklet 2 and included $n_{Finland}$ = 1,445, $n_{Slovakia}$ = 1,160, and $n_{United States}$ = 1,340, and $n_{Finland}$ = 1,440, $n_{Slovakia}$ = 1,160, and $n_{United States}$ = 1,342 participants, respectively. Across all items included in the study, the distribution of participants from Finland, Slovakia, and the United States was balanced. The descriptive statistics, including the number of participants, min, max, mean, standard deviation of item length, the number of cases with action sequences longer than 512 tokens, and the proportion-correct scores across all countries are given in Table 1. ### Data Analysis We provided a flowchart presenting the preprocessing and data analysis steps adopted in this study (Figure 1). We first extracted the log data for the selected countries and items using the software program, LogDataAnalyzer available on the PIAAC website. This process created the individual log files for Finland, Slovakia, and the United States. We replaced the underscore separating action descriptions with a space to facilitate the tokenization process with BERT—breaking down the text into words or subwords based on predefined rules (Devlin et al., 2018). As emphasized, action sequences provide rich yet unstructured information about the examinee behavior. In most cases, it is difficult to directly use the action sequences data due to their high dimensionality. For this reason, researchers may use dimension reduction techniques (e.g., multidimensional scaling) or may extract useful features (e.g., number of actions, duration of actions) from action sequences to be used in machine learning models. A novelty of this study is that using BERT allows to directly use action sequences without the need of using such preprocessing approaches, permitting us to keep the rich information as is. 5 Gorgun and Yildirim-Erbash BERT is a pretrained transformer composed of token embeddings (i.e., capture the meaning and context of individual words in a text; Huang et al., 2020), segment embeddings (i.e., differentiate between sentences A and B for next sentence prediction loss; Devlin et al., 2018), and position embeddings (i.e., encode absolute positions from 1 to a maximum length with each position having a learnable vector; Huang et al., 2020). For example, in the sentence "The quick brown fox jumps over the lazy dog," the token embeddings would represent each individual word as numerical vectors capturing their semantic meaning and context within the sentence. Regarding segment embeddings, for example, consider two sentences: "The cat sat on the mat" (Sentence A) and "The dog barked loudly" (Sentence B). Segment embeddings differentiate between these two sentences and enable BERT to predict the relationship between them, such as whether Sentence B follows Sentence A logically or not. Regarding the position embeddings, consider a 20-token passage where the position embeddings would assign a unique learnable vector to each token based on its position from 1 to 20. These position embeddings enable BERT to understand the sequential order of tokens and capture the contextual relationships between them, regardless of their absolute positions in the input text. BERT is an encoder-only model and differs from other decoder-style transformers (e.g., GPT-4 or Llama-2) that are capable of generating sentences, answering questions, or producing a new output in general. context: DOI: 10.1111/jedm.12420 Journal of Educational Measurement # Algorithmic Bias in BERT for Response Accuracy Prediction: A Case Study for Investigating Population Validity Guher Gorgun (ID) University of Alberta Seyma N. Yildirim-Erbasli Concordia University of Edmonton Pretrained large language models (LLMs) have gained popularity in recent years due to their high performance in various educational tasks such as learner modeling, automated scoring, automatic item generation, and prediction. Nevertheless, LLMs are black box approaches where models are less interpretable, and they may carry human biases and prejudices because historical human data have been used for pretraining these large-scale models. For these reasons, the prediction tasks based on LLMs require scrutiny to ensure that the prediction models are fair and unbiased. In this study, we used BERT—a pretrained encoder-only LLM for predicting response accuracy using action sequences extracted from the 2012 PIAAC assessment. We selected three countries (i.e., Finland, Slovakia, and the United States) representing different performance levels in the overall PIAAC assessment. We found promising results for predicting response accuracy using the fine-tuned BERT model. Additionally, we examined algorithmic bias in the prediction models trained with different countries. We found differences in model performance, suggesting that some trained models are not free from bias, and thus the models are less generalizable across countries. Our results highlighted the importance of investigating algorithmic fairness in prediction models utilizing algorithmic systems to ensure models are bias-free. In the last decade, machine learning and data mining methods have become popular for analyzing assessment data to discover hidden response patterns and provide a nuanced understanding of response behavior (e.g., Goldhammer et al., 2017; He et al., 2021; Nagy et al., 2022; Ulitzsch et al., 2022). Computer-based assessments have facilitated the use of these methods by providing rich information about examinees (Jiao et al., 2023). With computer-based assessments, supplementary information, in addition to traditionally captured response accuracy, can be obtained about data, may include response time spent for each item (e.g., Gorgun & Bulut, 2021), the number of actions taken by examinees (e.g., Sahin & Colvin, 2020), hint requests (e.g., Gorgun & Bulut, 2022b), response changes (e.g., Kroehne & Goldhammer, 2018), action sequences (e.g., Ulitzsch et al., 2022), keystrokes (e.g., Conijn et al., 2019), or eye tracking data (e.g., Orange et al., 2017). --- © 2024 The Author(s). *Journal of Educational Measurement* published by Wiley Periodicals LLC on behalf of National Council on Measurement in Education. This is an open access article under the terms of the CreativeCommonsAttribution-NonCommercial-NoDerivs License, which permits use and distribution in any medium, provided the original work is properly cited, the use is non-commercial and no modifications or adaptations are made. *Gorgun and Yildirim-Erbasli* To date, researchers have leveraged log data to uncover behavioral patterns of examinees with correct and incorrect responses (e.g., Plewan *et al*., 2016), investigate problem-solving strategies (e.g., Pejic & Molcer, 2021), identify disengaged or unmotivated examinees (e.g., Yildirim-Erbasli & Bulut, 2021), and detect anomalous responses (e.g., Shao *et al*., 2022). These studies typically employed computer algorithms for modeling examinee responses. However, algorithmic systems trained with historical human data may discriminate against certain groups, leading to unwarranted inferences about examinees (Kizilcec & Lee, 2022). For example, this may include assigning unrealistically low scores to a certain group (Smith, 2020) or not selecting a certain racial group during the admission process due to the reliance on the historical data (Kleinberg *et al*., 2018). In this study, we first propose to use a pretrained encoder-only large-language model (LLM), Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers (BERT; Devlin *et al*., 2018), for predicting response accuracy using action sequences extracted from the 2012 Programme for the International Assessment of Adult Competencies (PIAAC) log data. Then, we aim to investigate algorithmic bias in fine-tuned BERT for predicting response accuracy in countries that performed well (i.e., Finland), average (i.e., Slovakia), and worse (i.e., the United States) in the 2012 PIAAC assessment. This allows us to examine the population validity of the fine-tuned BERT models across countries with different performance levels. Investigating fairness issues in LLMs is of utmost importance because LLMs are trained with historical human data and may carry human biases and prejudices (e.g., Papakyriakopoulos *et al*., 2020). Recent studies have highlighted that LLMs may hallucinate and generate incorrect information with seemingly high confidence (Zhang *et al*., 2023). Another challenge associated with using LLMs for modeling response behavior is the lack of model interpretability due to LLMs being black-box models (e.g., Lin *et al*., 2023). These models are considered less interpretable because they were trained with a deep learning-based architecture. For these reasons, this study not only proposes to use BERT for response accuracy prediction but also investigates the extent of model generalizability (i.e., algorithmic fairness) across countries with different performance levels. The contributions of this study include understanding the feasibility of using a pretrained LLM, BERT, for predicting response accuracy using action sequences and examining the extent of algorithmic fairness in LLMs for the model's generalizability across all subpopulations. ## Literature Review Process data refers to users’ actions that occurred while interacting with the computer interface stored as log files (He *et al*., 2021; Tang *et al*., 2021). BERT is an encoder-only model and differs from other decoder-style transformers (e.g., GPT-4 or Llama-2) that are capable of generating sentences, answering questions, or producing a new output in general. Thus, to re-train BERT for this specific task of response accuracy prediction, we first tokenize action sequences and add a linear output layer on the top of the BERT model for predicting the response accuracy of examinees taking PSTRE items in PIAAC 2012. BERT is an encoder-only model and differs from other decoder-style transformers (e.g., GPT-4 or Llama-2) that are capable of generating sentences, answering questions, or producing a new output in general. Thus, to re-train BERT for this specific task of response accuracy prediction, we first tokenize action sequences and add a linear output layer on the top of the BERT model for predicting the response accuracy of examinees taking PSTRE items in PIAAC 2012. This process is also known as *fine-tuning an LLM*. Next, we examine the algorithmic bias in fine-tuned BERT models when countries with different performance levels have been used as training sets. Specifically, we identify top-, average-, and low-performing countries based on the availability of the log data. The top-performing country is Finland, the average-performing country is Slovakia, and the low-performing country is the United States. We fine-tune the BERT model using the overall sample including all countries, only Finland, only Slovakia, and only the United States, and compare the response accuracy across these four different models obtained by having different countries as training and test sets. The aim of this research question is to investigate the utility of a pretrained LLM for predicting response accuracy using action sequences directly. has elevated in recent years as more educational settings incorporate artificial intelligence to model learners. Most studies analyzed algorithmic bias in prediction models in the presence of class imbalances. An oversampling technique such as SMOTE or ADASYN helped improve algorithmic fairness (Deho et al., 2023; Jiang & Pardos, 2021; Sha et al., 2022, 2023). Even though oversampling techniques are useful for improving model accuracy across different populations, researchers also suggested that more marginalized and underrepresented populations (e.g., racial and gender groups) should be included in training sets (Baker et al., 2023). In addition to representational issues of minority groups, studies also documented biases in prediction models when individuals have different native languages, leading to the underestimation of examinee performance in assessments or learning environments (Gaskins, 2022; Loukina et al., 2019). Traditionally, studies have examined algorithmic bias in prediction models by considering groups based on factors such as gender, age, race, and religion. Yet, the list of groups or populations can be expanded to align with the specific purpose of the algorithmic system. For instance, additional factors such as school region (e.g., urban, suburban, or rural), learner speed (e.g., slow or fast learners), cultural variations (e.g., native language or home country), and socioeconomic status (e.g., low-income students) can be considered (Doroudi & Brunskill, 2019; Li et al., 2019; Loukina et al., 2019; Ocumpaugh et al., 2014; Sackett et al., 2009). In the context of international large-scale assessments, it is important to investigate algorithmic fairness in modeling student performance across countries. This ensures that valid comparisons can be made among countries participating in such assessments. ## Current Study In this study, we first investigate the utility of using an LLM, BERT, for predicting response accuracy employing action sequences extracted from the log files of Problem-Solving in Technology-Rich Environments (PSTRE). To date, a few studies employed BERT for identifying anomalous responses in process data (e.g., Chen & Liao, 2022; Guo et al., 2021; Landauer et al., 2023; Shao et al., 2022), yet BERT has not been used for predicting response accuracy using action sequences. As emphasized, action sequences provide rich yet unstructured information about the examinee behavior. In most cases, it is difficult to directly use the action sequences data due to their high dimensionality. For this reason, researchers may use dimension reduction techniques (e.g., multidimensional scaling) or may extract useful features (e.g., number of actions, duration of actions) from action sequences to be used in machine learning models. A novelty of this study is that using BERT allows to directly use action sequences without the need of using such preprocessing approaches, permitting us to keep the rich information as is. 5 Gorgun and Yildirim-Erbash BERT is a pretrained transformer composed of token embeddings (i.e., capture the meaning and context of individual words in a text; Huang et al., 2020), segment embeddings (i.e., differentiate between sentences A and B for next sentence prediction loss; Devlin et al., 2018), and position embeddings (i.e., encode absolute positions from 1 to a maximum length with each position having a learnable vector; Huang et al., 2020). These position embeddings enable BERT to understand the sequential order of tokens and capture the contextual relationships between them, regardless of their absolute positions in the input text. BERT is an encoder-only model and differs from other decoder-style transformers (e.g., GPT-4 or Llama-2) that are capable of generating sentences, answering questions, or producing a new output in general. Thus, to re-train BERT for this specific task of response accuracy prediction, we first tokenize action sequences and add a linear output layer on the top of the BERT model for predicting the response accuracy of examinees taking PSTRE items in PIAAC 2012. This process is also known as *fine-tuning an LLM*. Next, we examine the algorithmic bias in fine-tuned BERT models when countries with different performance levels have been used as training sets. Specifically, we identify top-, average-, and low-performing countries based on the availability of the log data. The top-performing country is Finland, the average-performing country is Slovakia, and the low-performing country is the United States. We fine-tune the BERT model using the overall sample including all countries, only Finland, only Slovakia, and only the United States, and compare the response accuracy across these four different models obtained by having different countries as training and test sets. Our research questions are as follows. ## Research questions **RQ1:** To what extent do the fine-tuned BERT models with different populations predict response accuracy? The aim of this research question is to investigate the utility of a pretrained LLM for predicting response accuracy using action sequences directly. We replicate the feasibility of fine-tuning BERT across countries with different ability levels for response accuracy prediction in PSTRE items. **RQ2:** Is there a difference in model performance when BERT is fined-tuned with different populations? # Algorithmic Bias in BERT for Response Accuracy Prediction The purpose of this research question is to investigate the population validity of the fine-tuned BERT model for predicting response accuracy using three different countries with different overall performance levels. This allows us to investigate the extent of algorithmic bias present in the trained models as well as showcase the importance of examining bias in predictive models. ## Method ### Data Data for this study comes from the log files extracted from three PSTRE items administered in the 2012 PIAAC. PIAAC is a large-scale international assessment developed by the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) to assess the proficiency levels of adults in literacy, numeracy, and problem-solving. PSTRE items in the 2012 PIAAC target adults’ problem-solving skills and include 14 items in total (OECD, 2019). Use 20% as test set dataset_train, dataset_test = train_test_split(data_U16x000S, test_size = .2) # Remove unnecessary columns dataset_train = dataset_train.remove_columns('__index_level_0__') dataset_test = dataset_test.remove_columns('__index_level_0__') # Save datasets as data dict to be used for tokenization and model training data_dict = datasets.DatasetDict({'train': dataset_train, "test": dataset_test}) # Tokenize the action sequences tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained("bert-base-cased") def tokenize_function(examples): return tokenizer(examples['text'], padding = "max_length", truncation = True, max_length = 512) tokenized_datasets = data_dict.map(tokenize_function, batched = True) # Initialize the model for fine-tuning device = torch.device('cuda' if torch.cuda.is_available() else 'cpu') from transformers import AutoModelForSequenceClassification model = AutoModelForSequenceClassification.from_pretrained("bert-base-cased", num_labels = 2).to(device) # Fine-tune the model for response accuracy prediction training_args = TrainingArguments(output_dir = 'test_trainer', evaluation_strategy = 'epoch', learning_rate = 5e-6, prediction_loss_only = False) def compute_metrics(eval_pred): logits, labels = eval_pred predictions = np.argmax(logits, axis = -1) return evaluate.load("confusion_matrix").compute(predictions = predictions, references = labels) trainer = Trainer( model = model, args = training_args, train_dataset = train_dataset, eval_dataset = test_dataset, compute_metrics = compute_metrics ) trainer.train() # Predict the response accuracy new_predictions = trainer.predict(test_dataset) ``` # Algorithmic Bias in BERT for Response Accuracy Prediction ## Authors GUHER GORGUN, PhD is a postdoctoral research associate at the University of Alberta, Edmonton, Alberta, Canada T6G 2E8; gorgun@ualberta.ca. To date, a few studies employed BERT for identifying anomalous responses in process data (e.g., Chen & Liao, 2022; Guo et al., 2021; Landauer et al., 2023; Shao et al., 2022), yet BERT has not been used for predicting response accuracy using action sequences. As emphasized, action sequences provide rich yet unstructured information about the examinee behavior. In most cases, it is difficult to directly use the action sequences data due to their high dimensionality. For this reason, researchers may use dimension reduction techniques (e.g., multidimensional scaling) or may extract useful features (e.g., number of actions, duration of actions) from action sequences to be used in machine learning models. A novelty of this study is that using BERT allows to directly use action sequences without the need of using such preprocessing approaches, permitting us to keep the rich information as is. 5 Gorgun and Yildirim-Erbash BERT is a pretrained transformer composed of token embeddings (i.e., capture the meaning and context of individual words in a text; Huang et al., 2020), segment embeddings (i.e., differentiate between sentences A and B for next sentence prediction loss; Devlin et al., 2018), and position embeddings (i.e., encode absolute positions from 1 to a maximum length with each position having a learnable vector; Huang et al., 2020). For example, in the sentence "The quick brown fox jumps over the lazy dog," the token embeddings would represent each individual word as numerical vectors capturing their semantic meaning and context within the sentence. Regarding segment embeddings, for example, consider two sentences: "The cat sat on the mat" (Sentence A) and "The dog barked loudly" (Sentence B). Segment embeddings differentiate between these two sentences and enable BERT to predict the relationship between them, such as whether Sentence B follows Sentence A logically or not. Regarding the position embeddings, consider a 20-token passage where the position embeddings would assign a unique learnable vector to each token based on its position from 1 to 20. These position embeddings enable BERT to understand the sequential order of tokens and capture the contextual relationships between them, regardless of their absolute positions in the input text. BERT is an encoder-only model and differs from other decoder-style transformers (e.g., GPT-4 or Llama-2) that are capable of generating sentences, answering questions, or producing a new output in general. Thus, to re-train BERT for this specific task of response accuracy prediction, we first tokenize action sequences and add a linear output layer on the top of the BERT model for predicting the response accuracy of examinees taking PSTRE items in PIAAC 2012. This process is also known as *fine-tuning an LLM*. Next, we examine the algorithmic bias in fine-tuned BERT models when countries with different performance levels have been used as training sets. We used a learning rate of 5e-6 and 3 epochs with a batch size of 8. We repeated the same process using the training data including overall data (i.e., including all countries), Finland, Slovakia, and the United States for all three items. We then eval- uated model performance on the hold-out test sets, including the overall data, only Finland, only Slovakia, and only the United States test sets. This yielded 16 models per item with a total of 48 models. Accuracy is defined as $$ Accuracy = \frac{TP + TN}{TP + TN + FP + FN} \quad (1) $$ *Gorgun and Yildirim-Erbash* where TP is true-positive rate, TN is true-negative rate, FP is false-positive rate, and FN is false-negative rate. Precision is defined as $$ Precision = \frac{TP}{TP + FP} \quad (2) $$ recall is defined as $$ Recall = \frac{TP}{TP + FN} \quad (3) $$ and F1 is defined as $$ F1 = 2 \frac{Precision \times Recall}{Precision + Recall} \quad (4) $$ ABROCA is a measure developed for evaluating algorithmic fairness across two subgroups by comparing model performance for both groups using a Receiver Operating Characteristic (ROC) Curve. Simply, ABROCA finds the difference between the areas in AUC by $$ ABROCA = AUC_b - AUC_c \quad (5) $$ and thus, it quantifies the difference between a baseline model and a comparison group (Gardner et al., 2019). # Results ## Descriptive Statistics The descriptive statistics for the items selected are given in Table 1.
