Accuracy is defined as $$ Accuracy = \frac{TP + TN}{TP + TN + FP + FN} \quad (1) $$ *Gorgun and Yildirim-Erbash* where TP is true-positive rate, TN is true-negative rate, FP is false-positive rate, and FN is false-negative rate. Precision is defined as $$ Precision = \frac{TP}{TP + FP} \quad (2) $$ recall is defined as $$ Recall = \frac{TP}{TP + FN} \quad (3) $$ and F1 is defined as $$ F1 = 2 \frac{Precision \times Recall}{Precision + Recall} \quad (4) $$ ABROCA is a measure developed for evaluating algorithmic fairness across two subgroups by comparing model performance for both groups using a Receiver Operating Characteristic (ROC) Curve. To date, a few studies employed BERT for identifying anomalous responses in process data (e.g., Chen & Liao, 2022; Guo et al., 2021; Landauer et al., 2023; Shao et al., 2022), yet BERT has not been used for predicting response accuracy using action sequences. As emphasized, action sequences provide rich yet unstructured information about the examinee behavior. In most cases, it is difficult to directly use the action sequences data due to their high dimensionality. For this reason, researchers may use dimension reduction techniques (e.g., multidimensional scaling) or may extract useful features (e.g., number of actions, duration of actions) from action sequences to be used in machine learning models. A novelty of this study is that using BERT allows to directly use action sequences without the need of using such preprocessing approaches, permitting us to keep the rich information as is. 5 Gorgun and Yildirim-Erbash BERT is a pretrained transformer composed of token embeddings (i.e., capture the meaning and context of individual words in a text; Huang et al., 2020), segment embeddings (i.e., differentiate between sentences A and B for next sentence prediction loss; Devlin et al., 2018), and position embeddings (i.e., encode absolute positions from 1 to a maximum length with each position having a learnable vector; Huang et al., 2020). For example, in the sentence "The quick brown fox jumps over the lazy dog," the token embeddings would represent each individual word as numerical vectors capturing their semantic meaning and context within the sentence. Regarding segment embeddings, for example, consider two sentences: "The cat sat on the mat" (Sentence A) and "The dog barked loudly" (Sentence B). Segment embeddings differentiate between these two sentences and enable BERT to predict the relationship between them, such as whether Sentence B follows Sentence A logically or not. Regarding the position embeddings, consider a 20-token passage where the position embeddings would assign a unique learnable vector to each token based on its position from 1 to 20. These position embeddings enable BERT to understand the sequential order of tokens and capture the contextual relationships between them, regardless of their absolute positions in the input text. BERT is an encoder-only model and differs from other decoder-style transformers (e.g., GPT-4 or Llama-2) that are capable of generating sentences, answering questions, or producing a new output in general. Thus, to re-train BERT for this specific task of response accuracy prediction, we first tokenize action sequences and add a linear output layer on the top of the BERT model for predicting the response accuracy of examinees taking PSTRE items in PIAAC 2012. This process is also known as *fine-tuning an LLM*. Next, we examine the algorithmic bias in fine-tuned BERT models when countries with different performance levels have been used as training sets. Specifically, we identify top-, average-, and low-performing countries based on the availability of the log data. The top-performing country is Finland, the average-performing country is Slovakia, and the low-performing country is the United States. We fine-tune the BERT model using the overall sample including all countries, only Finland, only Slovakia, and only the United States, and compare the response accuracy across these four different models obtained by having different countries as training and test sets. Our research questions are as follows. ## Research questions **RQ1:** To what extent do the fine-tuned BERT models with different populations predict response accuracy? The aim of this research question is to investigate the utility of a pretrained LLM for predicting response accuracy using action sequences directly. We replicate the feasibility of fine-tuning BERT across countries with different ability levels for response accuracy prediction in PSTRE items. **RQ2:** Is there a difference in model performance when BERT is fined-tuned with different populations? # Algorithmic Bias in BERT for Response Accuracy Prediction The purpose of this research question is to investigate the population validity of the fine-tuned BERT model for predicting response accuracy using three different countries with different overall performance levels. Finally, we created a dataset for each PSTRE item, including variables Examinee ID, Country ID, action sequences, and response accuracy (i.e., target variable). Next, we split the data into training and test sets, and 20% of the data is used as the hold-out test set. We also created subsets of training and test sets based on the country to train the data with the overall sample (i.e., including all countries), Finland-only, Slovakia-only, and the United States-only samples. Following training and test set preparations, we tokenized the action sequences for each item using the BERT base cased model. During the tokenization process, we selected a max token length of 512 and padding = True, to achieve equal sequence lengths for each action sequence. Thus, examinees with action sequences longer than 512 actions were trimmed to a length of 512 tokens, and those with action sequences shorter than 512 actions were added [PAD]—a special- ized token used to adjust the token length. Concerning Item U03A, none of the action sequences were longer than 512 tokens, for Item U07X, only one case in the United States sample has action sequences longer than 512 tokens, and for Item U16X, 26 cases (0.7%) have action sequences longer than 512 tokens (Table 1). Given that no or only a very few cases have action sequences longer than 512 tokens, we expect that truncation has a minimal influence on the models developed. Based on the tokenization process, we obtained a 768-dimensional embedding vector of action sequences. The tokenization process also adds two special tokens: CLS at the beginning of each action sequence and SEP at the end of each action sequence. We fine-tuned BERT for a downstream task (i.e., classification) for pre- dicting examinees' response accuracy using the tokenized action sequences. Specif- ically, using the *AutoModelForSequenceClassification* function, we added a linear output layer for predicting the response accuracy on the top of the pooled CLS to- ken. We used a learning rate of 5e-6 and 3 epochs with a batch size of 8. We repeated the same process using the training data including overall data (i.e., including all countries), Finland, Slovakia, and the United States for all three items. We then eval- uated model performance on the hold-out test sets, including the overall data, only Finland, only Slovakia, and only the United States test sets. This yielded 16 models per item with a total of 48 models. The preprocessing steps were conducted in R (R Core Team, 2022), and the analysis was conducted in Python with NVIDIA T4 Tensor Core GPU. ## Model evaluation We evaluated the model performance of all 48 models us- ing Accuracy, Precision, Recall, F1, and Absolute Between-ROC Area (ABROCA; (Gardner et al., 2019)). Accuracy is defined as $$ Accuracy = \frac{TP + TN}{TP + TN + FP + FN} \quad (1) $$ *Gorgun and Yildirim-Erbash* where TP is true-positive rate, TN is true-negative rate, FP is false-positive rate, and FN is false-negative rate. Precision is defined as $$ Precision = \frac{TP}{TP + FP} \quad (2) $$ recall is defined as $$ Recall = \frac{TP}{TP + FN} \quad (3) $$ and F1 is defined as $$ F1 = 2 \frac{Precision \times Recall}{Precision + Recall} \quad (4) $$ ABROCA is a measure developed for evaluating algorithmic fairness across two subgroups by comparing model performance for both groups using a Receiver Operating Characteristic (ROC) Curve. Yildirim-Erbasli Concordia University of Edmonton Pretrained large language models (LLMs) have gained popularity in recent years due to their high performance in various educational tasks such as learner modeling, automated scoring, automatic item generation, and prediction. Nevertheless, LLMs are black box approaches where models are less interpretable, and they may carry human biases and prejudices because historical human data have been used for pretraining these large-scale models. For these reasons, the prediction tasks based on LLMs require scrutiny to ensure that the prediction models are fair and unbiased. In this study, we used BERT—a pretrained encoder-only LLM for predicting response accuracy using action sequences extracted from the 2012 PIAAC assessment. We selected three countries (i.e., Finland, Slovakia, and the United States) representing different performance levels in the overall PIAAC assessment. We found promising results for predicting response accuracy using the fine-tuned BERT model. Additionally, we examined algorithmic bias in the prediction models trained with different countries. We found differences in model performance, suggesting that some trained models are not free from bias, and thus the models are less generalizable across countries. Our results highlighted the importance of investigating algorithmic fairness in prediction models utilizing algorithmic systems to ensure models are bias-free. In the last decade, machine learning and data mining methods have become popular for analyzing assessment data to discover hidden response patterns and provide a nuanced understanding of response behavior (e.g., Goldhammer et al., 2017; He et al., 2021; Nagy et al., 2022; Ulitzsch et al., 2022). Computer-based assessments have facilitated the use of these methods by providing rich information about examinees (Jiao et al., 2023). These studies typically employed computer algorithms for modeling examinee responses. However, algorithmic systems trained with historical human data may discriminate against certain groups, leading to unwarranted inferences about examinees (Kizilcec & Lee, 2022). For example, this may include assigning unrealistically low scores to a certain group (Smith, 2020) or not selecting a certain racial group during the admission process due to the reliance on the historical data (Kleinberg *et al*., 2018). In this study, we first propose to use a pretrained encoder-only large-language model (LLM), Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers (BERT; Devlin *et al*., 2018), for predicting response accuracy using action sequences extracted from the 2012 Programme for the International Assessment of Adult Competencies (PIAAC) log data. Then, we aim to investigate algorithmic bias in fine-tuned BERT for predicting response accuracy in countries that performed well (i.e., Finland), average (i.e., Slovakia), and worse (i.e., the United States) in the 2012 PIAAC assessment. This allows us to examine the population validity of the fine-tuned BERT models across countries with different performance levels. Investigating fairness issues in LLMs is of utmost importance because LLMs are trained with historical human data and may carry human biases and prejudices (e.g., Papakyriakopoulos *et al*., 2020). Another challenge associated with using LLMs for modeling response behavior is the lack of model interpretability due to LLMs being black-box models (e.g., Lin *et al*., 2023). These models are considered less interpretable because they were trained with a deep learning-based architecture. For these reasons, this study not only proposes to use BERT for response accuracy prediction but also investigates the extent of model generalizability (i.e., algorithmic fairness) across countries with different performance levels. Recently, students in the UK have been assigned final grades using an algorithm because students could not take the final exam due to the COVID-19 pandemic. They found that some students received unrealistically lower grades which led to public pressure for re-evaluating students' grades (Smith, 2020). This further highlights the importance of scrutinizing the algorithm's performance for different groups to ensure the validity of inferences made. Two broad families of algorithmic bias have been adopted in the literature (Awasthi et al., 2020): group fairness and individual fairness. Group fairness is often operationalized by delineating protected subgroups based on attributes like race, gender, ethnicity, or sexual orientation. Metrics such as the false-positive rate, falsenegative rate, or accuracy are then employed to gauge fairness, aiming for uniformity in these metrics across all identified subgroups. In contrast, individual fairness demands that the model treats similar individuals similarly, regardless of their characteristics. This principle emphasizes a more granular approach to fairness within algorithmic systems. For example, group fairness would involve ensuring that the predicted performance outcomes of students from different demographic backgrounds # Algorithmic Bias in BERT for Response Accuracy Prediction are similar, indicating a lack of algorithmic bias. Individual fairness, on the other hand, would involve ensuring that students with similar predicted learning needs and preferences receive comparable recommendations for educational resources, tutoring, or intervention strategies. The focus on fairness in algorithms has elevated in recent years as more educational settings incorporate artificial intelligence to model learners. Most studies analyzed algorithmic bias in prediction models in the presence of class imbalances. An oversampling technique such as SMOTE or ADASYN helped improve algorithmic fairness (Deho et al., 2023; Jiang & Pardos, 2021; Sha et al., 2022, 2023). Even though oversampling techniques are useful for improving model accuracy across different populations, researchers also suggested that more marginalized and underrepresented populations (e.g., racial and gender groups) should be included in training sets (Baker et al., 2023). In addition to representational issues of minority groups, studies also documented biases in prediction models when individuals have different native languages, leading to the underestimation of examinee performance in assessments or learning environments (Gaskins, 2022; Loukina et al., 2019). Traditionally, studies have examined algorithmic bias in prediction models by considering groups based on factors such as gender, age, race, and religion. Yet, the list of groups or populations can be expanded to align with the specific purpose of the algorithmic system. For instance, additional factors such as school region (e.g., urban, suburban, or rural), learner speed (e.g., slow or fast learners), cultural variations (e.g., native language or home country), and socioeconomic status (e.g., low-income students) can be considered (Doroudi & Brunskill, 2019; Li et al., 2019; Loukina et al., 2019; Ocumpaugh et al., 2014; Sackett et al., 2009). In the context of international large-scale assessments, it is important to investigate algorithmic fairness in modeling student performance across countries. This ensures that valid comparisons can be made among countries participating in such assessments. ## Current Study In this study, we first investigate the utility of using an LLM, BERT, for predicting response accuracy employing action sequences extracted from the log files of Problem-Solving in Technology-Rich Environments (PSTRE). As emphasized, action sequences provide rich yet unstructured information about the examinee behavior. In most cases, it is difficult to directly use the action sequences data due to their high dimensionality. For this reason, researchers may use dimension reduction techniques (e.g., multidimensional scaling) or may extract useful features (e.g., number of actions, duration of actions) from action sequences to be used in machine learning models. For example, in the sentence "The quick brown fox jumps over the lazy dog," the token embeddings would represent each individual word as numerical vectors capturing their semantic meaning and context within the sentence. These position embeddings enable BERT to understand the sequential order of tokens and capture the contextual relationships between them, regardless of their absolute positions in the input text. Accuracy is defined as $$ Accuracy = \frac{TP + TN}{TP + TN + FP + FN} \quad (1) $$ *Gorgun and Yildirim-Erbash* where TP is true-positive rate, TN is true-negative rate, FP is false-positive rate, and FN is false-negative rate. Precision is defined as $$ Precision = \frac{TP}{TP + FP} \quad (2) $$ recall is defined as $$ Recall = \frac{TP}{TP + FN} \quad (3) $$ and F1 is defined as $$ F1 = 2 \frac{Precision \times Recall}{Precision + Recall} \quad (4) $$ ABROCA is a measure developed for evaluating algorithmic fairness across two subgroups by comparing model performance for both groups using a Receiver Operating Characteristic (ROC) Curve. Simply, ABROCA finds the difference between the areas in AUC by $$ ABROCA = AUC_b - AUC_c \quad (5) $$ and thus, it quantifies the difference between a baseline model and a comparison group (Gardner et al., 2019). # Results ## Descriptive Statistics The descriptive statistics for the items selected are given in Table 1. All items selected had moderate difficulty (.36 < proportion-correct < .67), yet the easiest item was U16X. Except for item U07X, the other two items were relatively more difficult for the United States compared to Finland and Slovakia. Item U07X had the same difficulty for all countries included in the study. Item U16X was easiest for Finland, and Item U03A was easiest for Slovakia. Regarding the length of action sequences, for Item U03A, the min sequence lengths were similar across Finland, Slovakia, and the United States, whereas the average sequence and max sequence lengths were longer for the United States and Finland when compared to Slovakia. Regarding Item U07X, the min sequence length was the shortest for Finland, and the max sequence length was the longest for the United States. Interestingly, although the max sequence length was drastically longer for the United States compared to Slovakia and Finland, the average sequence length was the longest for Finland. Although sequence lengths were dissimilar across the countries, the proportion-correct scores were almost identical. Concerning the final item, Item U16X, the average and max sequence lengths were longer for Finland compared to the other countries, yet the proportion-correct score was also relatively higher for Finland. The descriptive statistics suggested that the difficulty of the items across countries was more or less the same, yet the sequence length for some items was dissimilar across the countries selected. # Algorithmic Bias in BERT for Response Accuracy Prediction ## Model Performance across Different Training and Test Sets We evaluated the model performance when different training and test sets were used by accuracy, precision, recall, and $F_1$ measures. Tables 2–4 provide results of model performance when trained with Finland-only, Slovakia-only, the United States-only, and overall data using all countries in the dataset. Item U03A. The performance of models trained with Finland, Slovakia, and the United States, and the overall data were similar for predicting Finland or Slovakia-only test sets (Table 2). However, we observed different model performances for predicting the United States and overall test sets. Specifically, the precision was significantly low when Slovakia was used for predicting response accuracy for the United States test set, yet recall was significantly higher for the same training-test set pair. Additionally, precision and accuracy were relatively low when Finland was used as the training set to predict response accuracy in the overall test set. Overall, for Item U03A, the models trained were performed similarly across different test sets used. Item U07X. For Item U07X, we did not have similar results to Item U03A, and we observed differences in model performance when different training and test sets were used (Table 3). For predicting response accuracy in the Finland test set, we found that Finland, the United States, and the overall data performed relatively similar (Precision was between .75 and .78. Recall was between .80 and .87, and Accuracy was between .82 and .84); however, when Slovakia was used as the training set, precision (Precision = .62) and accuracy (Accuracy = .75) dropped while recall increased (Recall = .93) significantly. For predicting response accuracy in Slovakia only test set, we observed that Finland performed the worst (Precision = .86, Recall = .26, $F_1$ = .42, and Accuracy = .64) compared to other models trained with Slovakia, the United States, and overall data. The same trend was observed for the United States and the overall test sets where Finland was used as the training set. Specifically, the recall values were lower when Finland was used for training the model. Overall, there were more differences among the models trained, and specifically with the Finland only training set performed worse for predicting other test sets except for Finland. Item U16X. An interesting pattern emerged for Item U16X (Table 4). For all test sets, the model trained with the overall dataset including all countries performed better than using a single country as the training set. Specifically, the accuracy of the overall dataset for predicting response accuracy in Finland, Slovakia, the United States, and overall data was .91, .93, .86, and .86, respectively, whereas the accuracy ranged between .73 and .83 when Finland, Slovakia, or the United States was used as a training set. Therefore, using the overall dataset was better for predicting response accuracy in Item U16X, suggesting that researchers may benefit from using the total datasets when training prediction models for different countries. Yet, we need to underscore that this is not a uniform observation, highlighting the importance of the trial-error process in data-driven approaches. context: DOI: 10.1111/jedm.12420 Journal of Educational Measurement # Algorithmic Bias in BERT for Response Accuracy Prediction: A Case Study for Investigating Population Validity Guher Gorgun (ID) University of Alberta Seyma N. Yildirim-Erbasli Concordia University of Edmonton Pretrained large language models (LLMs) have gained popularity in recent years due to their high performance in various educational tasks such as learner modeling, automated scoring, automatic item generation, and prediction. Nevertheless, LLMs are black box approaches where models are less interpretable, and they may carry human biases and prejudices because historical human data have been used for pretraining these large-scale models. For these reasons, the prediction tasks based on LLMs require scrutiny to ensure that the prediction models are fair and unbiased. In this study, we used BERT—a pretrained encoder-only LLM for predicting response accuracy using action sequences extracted from the 2012 PIAAC assessment. We selected three countries (i.e., Finland, Slovakia, and the United States) representing different performance levels in the overall PIAAC assessment. We found promising results for predicting response accuracy using the fine-tuned BERT model. Additionally, we examined algorithmic bias in the prediction models trained with different countries. We found differences in model performance, suggesting that some trained models are not free from bias, and thus the models are less generalizable across countries. Our results highlighted the importance of investigating algorithmic fairness in prediction models utilizing algorithmic systems to ensure models are bias-free. In the last decade, machine learning and data mining methods have become popular for analyzing assessment data to discover hidden response patterns and provide a nuanced understanding of response behavior (e.g., Goldhammer et al., 2017; He et al., 2021; Nagy et al., 2022; Ulitzsch et al., 2022). Computer-based assessments have facilitated the use of these methods by providing rich information about examinees (Jiao et al., 2023). With computer-based assessments, supplementary information, in addition to traditionally captured response accuracy, can be obtained about data, may include response time spent for each item (e.g., Gorgun & Bulut, 2021), the number of actions taken by examinees (e.g., Sahin & Colvin, 2020), hint requests (e.g., Gorgun & Bulut, 2022b), response changes (e.g., Kroehne & Goldhammer, 2018), action sequences (e.g., Ulitzsch et al., 2022), keystrokes (e.g., Conijn et al., 2019), or eye tracking data (e.g., Orange et al., 2017). --- © 2024 The Author(s). *Journal of Educational Measurement* published by Wiley Periodicals LLC on behalf of National Council on Measurement in Education. This is an open access article under the terms of the CreativeCommonsAttribution-NonCommercial-NoDerivs License, which permits use and distribution in any medium, provided the original work is properly cited, the use is non-commercial and no modifications or adaptations are made. *Gorgun and Yildirim-Erbasli* To date, researchers have leveraged log data to uncover behavioral patterns of examinees with correct and incorrect responses (e.g., Plewan *et al*., 2016), investigate problem-solving strategies (e.g., Pejic & Molcer, 2021), identify disengaged or unmotivated examinees (e.g., Yildirim-Erbasli & Bulut, 2021), and detect anomalous responses (e.g., Shao *et al*., 2022). These studies typically employed computer algorithms for modeling examinee responses. However, algorithmic systems trained with historical human data may discriminate against certain groups, leading to unwarranted inferences about examinees (Kizilcec & Lee, 2022). For example, this may include assigning unrealistically low scores to a certain group (Smith, 2020) or not selecting a certain racial group during the admission process due to the reliance on the historical data (Kleinberg *et al*., 2018). In this study, we first propose to use a pretrained encoder-only large-language model (LLM), Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers (BERT; Devlin *et al*., 2018), for predicting response accuracy using action sequences extracted from the 2012 Programme for the International Assessment of Adult Competencies (PIAAC) log data. Then, we aim to investigate algorithmic bias in fine-tuned BERT for predicting response accuracy in countries that performed well (i.e., Finland), average (i.e., Slovakia), and worse (i.e., the United States) in the 2012 PIAAC assessment. This allows us to examine the population validity of the fine-tuned BERT models across countries with different performance levels. Investigating fairness issues in LLMs is of utmost importance because LLMs are trained with historical human data and may carry human biases and prejudices (e.g., Papakyriakopoulos *et al*., 2020). Recent studies have highlighted that LLMs may hallucinate and generate incorrect information with seemingly high confidence (Zhang *et al*., 2023). Another challenge associated with using LLMs for modeling response behavior is the lack of model interpretability due to LLMs being black-box models (e.g., Lin *et al*., 2023). These models are considered less interpretable because they were trained with a deep learning-based architecture. For these reasons, this study not only proposes to use BERT for response accuracy prediction but also investigates the extent of model generalizability (i.e., algorithmic fairness) across countries with different performance levels. Whereas those with incorrect responses showed deviance in their action sequences compared with those who answered the task correctly, and their action sequences were more heterogeneous (Ulitzsch et al., 2022). For instance, Liao and colleagues (2021) identified examinees with aberrant test-taking behavior by determining common test-taking processes by employing the *k*-means clustering technique and flagging those deviating from the common test-taking processes as aberrant. In a similar study, researchers employed unsupervised anomaly detection methods (e.g., isolation forest, elliptic envelope) to identify responses deviating from normal response behavior using the aggregated features extracted from the log files of a learning platform (Gorgun & Bulut, 2022b). Despite the increased use of algorithmic systems for identifying aberrances and problem-solving strategies of examinees using log files, studies have not considered the algorithmic fairness of models developed for assessing generalizability across different populations. Nonetheless, the population validity of algorithmic models is fundamental for analyzing examinee responses to ensure that predictive models are generalizable across different populations. Gorgun and Yildirim-Erbash ## Algorithmic Bias The development of algorithms often neglects a crucial aspect: their potential to perpetuate biased outcomes, thus conserving historical and societal inequalities. Despite the wealth of accessible data and advanced analytical techniques, there is a prevalent misconception that these systems inherently guarantee fairness. However, similar to human decision-making, algorithms constructed using individual-collected data are susceptible to biases influenced by prior experiences and personal beliefs (Timmons et al., 2023). Definitions of algorithmic bias may differ depending on the context, stakeholders involved, and goals of the analysis. A common definition includes the existence of discrimination and unfairness in an algorithmic system that results in disproportionate outcomes for certain groups or individuals (Hutchinson & Mitchell, 2019; Kizilcec & Lee, 2022). An algorithm is fair when discrimination or inequity based on group membership is absent. This entails that the algorithm's decision is independent of group membership. Many prediction models are trained with historical data and may carry biases and societal injustices that may be reflected while predicting outcomes about learners or examinees (Gándara et al., 2023). Especially, when algorithmic systems are used to make high-stakes decisions about different actors of education (e.g., examinees, teachers), researchers and practitioners need to scrutinize whether components of the decision-making pipeline are free from bias, discrimination, or inequity (Kizilcec & Lee, 2022; von Winckelmann, 2023). Assume that an algorithmic system has been used to detect cheating behavior using process data. If there is bias in the algorithm toward a certain group of individuals, wrong inferences and conclusions could be made about this group. For example, if the algorithm suggests that members of a certain group are more likely to cheat, we may mistakenly remove the answers of these individuals leading to erroneous performance estimations. Continuing in this vein, Xiang et al. (2022) found differences in model performance across subgroups of learners when two machine learning models were trained to predict learner success and retention. Recently, students in the UK have been assigned final grades using an algorithm because students could not take the final exam due to the COVID-19 pandemic. They found that some students received unrealistically lower grades which led to public pressure for re-evaluating students' grades (Smith, 2020). This further highlights the importance of scrutinizing the algorithm's performance for different groups to ensure the validity of inferences made. Two broad families of algorithmic bias have been adopted in the literature (Awasthi et al., 2020): group fairness and individual fairness. Group fairness is often operationalized by delineating protected subgroups based on attributes like race, gender, ethnicity, or sexual orientation. Metrics such as the false-positive rate, falsenegative rate, or accuracy are then employed to gauge fairness, aiming for uniformity in these metrics across all identified subgroups. In contrast, individual fairness demands that the model treats similar individuals similarly, regardless of their characteristics. This principle emphasizes a more granular approach to fairness within algorithmic systems. For example, group fairness would involve ensuring that the predicted performance outcomes of students from different demographic backgrounds # Algorithmic Bias in BERT for Response Accuracy Prediction are similar, indicating a lack of algorithmic bias. Individual fairness, on the other hand, would involve ensuring that students with similar predicted learning needs and preferences receive comparable recommendations for educational resources, tutoring, or intervention strategies. The focus on fairness in algorithms has elevated in recent years as more educational settings incorporate artificial intelligence to model learners. Most studies analyzed algorithmic bias in prediction models in the presence of class imbalances. An oversampling technique such as SMOTE or ADASYN helped improve algorithmic fairness (Deho et al., 2023; Jiang & Pardos, 2021; Sha et al., 2022, 2023). Even though oversampling techniques are useful for improving model accuracy across different populations, researchers also suggested that more marginalized and underrepresented populations (e.g., racial and gender groups) should be included in training sets (Baker et al., 2023). In addition to representational issues of minority groups, studies also documented biases in prediction models when individuals have different native languages, leading to the underestimation of examinee performance in assessments or learning environments (Gaskins, 2022; Loukina et al., 2019). Traditionally, studies have examined algorithmic bias in prediction models by considering groups based on factors such as gender, age, race, and religion. Yet, the list of groups or populations can be expanded to align with the specific purpose of the algorithmic system. For instance, additional factors such as school region (e.g., urban, suburban, or rural), learner speed (e.g., slow or fast learners), cultural variations (e.g., native language or home country), and socioeconomic status (e.g., low-income students) can be considered (Doroudi & Brunskill, 2019; Li et al., 2019; Loukina et al., 2019; Ocumpaugh et al., 2014; Sackett et al., 2009). In the context of international large-scale assessments, it is important to investigate algorithmic fairness in modeling student performance across countries. This

We fine-tune the BERT model using the overall sample including all countries, only Finland, only Slovakia, and only the United States, and compare the response accuracy across these four different models obtained by having different countries as training and test sets. Our research questions are as follows. ## Research questions **RQ1:** To what extent do the fine-tuned BERT models with different populations predict response accuracy? The aim of this research question is to investigate the utility of a pretrained LLM for predicting response accuracy using action sequences directly. We replicate the feasibility of fine-tuning BERT across countries with different ability levels for response accuracy prediction in PSTRE items. **RQ2:** Is there a difference in model performance when BERT is fined-tuned with different populations? # Algorithmic Bias in BERT for Response Accuracy Prediction The purpose of this research question is to investigate the population validity of the fine-tuned BERT model for predicting response accuracy using three different countries with different overall performance levels. This allows us to investigate the extent of algorithmic bias present in the trained models as well as showcase the importance of examining bias in predictive models. ## Method ### Data Data for this study comes from the log files extracted from three PSTRE items administered in the 2012 PIAAC. PIAAC is a large-scale international assessment developed by the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) to assess the proficiency levels of adults in literacy, numeracy, and problem-solving. PSTRE items in the 2012 PIAAC target adults’ problem-solving skills and include 14 items in total (OECD, 2019). We selected three dichotomously scored PSTRE items—U03A, U07X, and U16X because (1) log data extracted from PSTRE items included action sequences that provided rich information about examinee behavior, and (2) we can train a binary classification model using BERT. The action sequences included human-computer interactions recorded for each PSTRE item, such as opening a folder, viewing a folder, clicking on a link, or using the help function. The log data were not publicly available for all countries that participated in the 2012 PIAAC cycle. Based on the overall country performance across all domains, we identified three countries with different performance levels¹. Based on the availability of log data, the top-performing country was Finland, followed by Slovakia located in the middle of the performance distribution, and the worse-performing country was the United States. The first dichotomously scored item, U03A—CD Tally, selected for this study was located in Booklet 1 and included $n_{Finland}$ = 1,482, $n_{Slovakia}$ = 1,096, and $n_{United States}$ = 1,337 participants. The second and third dichotomously scored items, U07X—Book Order and U16X—Reply All, selected were located in Booklet 2 and included $n_{Finland}$ = 1,445, $n_{Slovakia}$ = 1,160, and $n_{United States}$ = 1,340, and $n_{Finland}$ = 1,440, $n_{Slovakia}$ = 1,160, and $n_{United States}$ = 1,342 participants, respectively. Across all items included in the study, the distribution of participants from Finland, Slovakia, and the United States was balanced. Yildirim-Erbasli Concordia University of Edmonton Pretrained large language models (LLMs) have gained popularity in recent years due to their high performance in various educational tasks such as learner modeling, automated scoring, automatic item generation, and prediction. Nevertheless, LLMs are black box approaches where models are less interpretable, and they may carry human biases and prejudices because historical human data have been used for pretraining these large-scale models. For these reasons, the prediction tasks based on LLMs require scrutiny to ensure that the prediction models are fair and unbiased. In this study, we used BERT—a pretrained encoder-only LLM for predicting response accuracy using action sequences extracted from the 2012 PIAAC assessment. We selected three countries (i.e., Finland, Slovakia, and the United States) representing different performance levels in the overall PIAAC assessment. We found promising results for predicting response accuracy using the fine-tuned BERT model. Additionally, we examined algorithmic bias in the prediction models trained with different countries. We found differences in model performance, suggesting that some trained models are not free from bias, and thus the models are less generalizable across countries. Our results highlighted the importance of investigating algorithmic fairness in prediction models utilizing algorithmic systems to ensure models are bias-free. The top-performing country is Finland, the average-performing country is Slovakia, and the low-performing country is the United States. We fine-tune the BERT model using the overall sample including all countries, only Finland, only Slovakia, and only the United States, and compare the response accuracy across these four different models obtained by having different countries as training and test sets. Our research questions are as follows. ## Research questions **RQ1:** To what extent do the fine-tuned BERT models with different populations predict response accuracy? The aim of this research question is to investigate the utility of a pretrained LLM for predicting response accuracy using action sequences directly. We replicate the feasibility of fine-tuning BERT across countries with different ability levels for response accuracy prediction in PSTRE items. **RQ2:** Is there a difference in model performance when BERT is fined-tuned with different populations? # Algorithmic Bias in BERT for Response Accuracy Prediction The purpose of this research question is to investigate the population validity of the fine-tuned BERT model for predicting response accuracy using three different countries with different overall performance levels. This allows us to investigate the extent of algorithmic bias present in the trained models as well as showcase the importance of examining bias in predictive models. ## Method ### Data Data for this study comes from the log files extracted from three PSTRE items administered in the 2012 PIAAC. PIAAC is a large-scale international assessment developed by the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) to assess the proficiency levels of adults in literacy, numeracy, and problem-solving. PSTRE items in the 2012 PIAAC target adults’ problem-solving skills and include 14 items in total (OECD, 2019). We selected three dichotomously scored PSTRE items—U03A, U07X, and U16X because (1) log data extracted from PSTRE items included action sequences that provided rich information about examinee behavior, and (2) we can train a binary classification model using BERT. The action sequences included human-computer interactions recorded for each PSTRE item, such as opening a folder, viewing a folder, clicking on a link, or using the help function. The log data were not publicly available for all countries that participated in the 2012 PIAAC cycle. Based on the overall country performance across all domains, we identified three countries with different performance levels¹. Based on the availability of log data, the top-performing country was Finland, followed by Slovakia located in the middle of the performance distribution, and the worse-performing country was the United States. The first dichotomously scored item, U03A—CD Tally, selected for this study was located in Booklet 1 and included $n_{Finland}$ = 1,482, $n_{Slovakia}$ = 1,096, and $n_{United States}$ = 1,337 participants. The second and third dichotomously scored items, U07X—Book Order and U16X—Reply All, selected were located in Booklet 2 and included $n_{Finland}$ = 1,445, $n_{Slovakia}$ = 1,160, and $n_{United States}$ = 1,340, and $n_{Finland}$ = 1,440, $n_{Slovakia}$ = 1,160, and $n_{United States}$ = 1,342 participants, respectively. Across all items included in the study, the distribution of participants from Finland, Slovakia, and the United States was balanced. Gorgun and Yildirim-Erbash ## Algorithmic Bias The development of algorithms often neglects a crucial aspect: their potential to perpetuate biased outcomes, thus conserving historical and societal inequalities. Despite the wealth of accessible data and advanced analytical techniques, there is a prevalent misconception that these systems inherently guarantee fairness. However, similar to human decision-making, algorithms constructed using individual-collected data are susceptible to biases influenced by prior experiences and personal beliefs (Timmons et al., 2023). Definitions of algorithmic bias may differ depending on the context, stakeholders involved, and goals of the analysis. A common definition includes the existence of discrimination and unfairness in an algorithmic system that results in disproportionate outcomes for certain groups or individuals (Hutchinson & Mitchell, 2019; Kizilcec & Lee, 2022). An algorithm is fair when discrimination or inequity based on group membership is absent. This entails that the algorithm's decision is independent of group membership. Many prediction models are trained with historical data and may carry biases and societal injustices that may be reflected while predicting outcomes about learners or examinees (Gándara et al., 2023). Especially, when algorithmic systems are used to make high-stakes decisions about different actors of education (e.g., examinees, teachers), researchers and practitioners need to scrutinize whether components of the decision-making pipeline are free from bias, discrimination, or inequity (Kizilcec & Lee, 2022; von Winckelmann, 2023). Assume that an algorithmic system has been used to detect cheating behavior using process data. If there is bias in the algorithm toward a certain group of individuals, wrong inferences and conclusions could be made about this group. For example, if the algorithm suggests that members of a certain group are more likely to cheat, we may mistakenly remove the answers of these individuals leading to erroneous performance estimations. Continuing in this vein, Xiang et al. (2022) found differences in model performance across subgroups of learners when two machine learning models were trained to predict learner success and retention. Recently, students in the UK have been assigned final grades using an algorithm because students could not take the final exam due to the COVID-19 pandemic. They found that some students received unrealistically lower grades which led to public pressure for re-evaluating students' grades (Smith, 2020). This further highlights the importance of scrutinizing the algorithm's performance for different groups to ensure the validity of inferences made. Two broad families of algorithmic bias have been adopted in the literature (Awasthi et al., 2020): group fairness and individual fairness. Group fairness is often operationalized by delineating protected subgroups based on attributes like race, gender, ethnicity, or sexual orientation. Metrics such as the false-positive rate, falsenegative rate, or accuracy are then employed to gauge fairness, aiming for uniformity in these metrics across all identified subgroups. In contrast, individual fairness demands that the model treats similar individuals similarly, regardless of their characteristics. This principle emphasizes a more granular approach to fairness within algorithmic systems. For example, group fairness would involve ensuring that the predicted performance outcomes of students from different demographic backgrounds # Algorithmic Bias in BERT for Response Accuracy Prediction are similar, indicating a lack of algorithmic bias. Individual fairness, on the other hand, would involve ensuring that students with similar predicted learning needs and preferences receive comparable recommendations for educational resources, tutoring, or intervention strategies. The focus on fairness in algorithms has elevated in recent years as more educational settings incorporate artificial intelligence to model learners. Most studies analyzed algorithmic bias in prediction models in the presence of class imbalances. An oversampling technique such as SMOTE or ADASYN helped improve algorithmic fairness (Deho et al., 2023; Jiang & Pardos, 2021; Sha et al., 2022, 2023). Even though oversampling techniques are useful for improving model accuracy across different populations, researchers also suggested that more marginalized and underrepresented populations (e.g., racial and gender groups) should be included in training sets (Baker et al., 2023). In addition to representational issues of minority groups, studies also documented biases in prediction models when individuals have different native languages, leading to the underestimation of examinee performance in assessments or learning environments (Gaskins, 2022; Loukina et al., 2019). Traditionally, studies have examined algorithmic bias in prediction models by considering groups based on factors such as gender, age, race, and religion. Yet, the list of groups or populations can be expanded to align with the specific purpose of the algorithmic system. For instance, additional factors such as school region (e.g., urban, suburban, or rural), learner speed (e.g., slow or fast learners), cultural variations (e.g., native language or home country), and socioeconomic status (e.g., low-income students) can be considered (Doroudi & Brunskill, 2019; Li et al., 2019; Loukina et al., 2019; Ocumpaugh et al., 2014; Sackett et al., 2009). In the context of international large-scale assessments, it is important to investigate algorithmic fairness in modeling student performance across countries. This

An algorithm is fair when discrimination or inequity based on group membership is absent. This entails that the algorithm's decision is independent of group membership. Many prediction models are trained with historical data and may carry biases and societal injustices that may be reflected while predicting outcomes about learners or examinees (Gándara et al., 2023). Especially, when algorithmic systems are used to make high-stakes decisions about different actors of education (e.g., examinees, teachers), researchers and practitioners need to scrutinize whether components of the decision-making pipeline are free from bias, discrimination, or inequity (Kizilcec & Lee, 2022; von Winckelmann, 2023). Assume that an algorithmic system has been used to detect cheating behavior using process data. If there is bias in the algorithm toward a certain group of individuals, wrong inferences and conclusions could be made about this group. For example, if the algorithm suggests that members of a certain group are more likely to cheat, we may mistakenly remove the answers of these individuals leading to erroneous performance estimations. Continuing in this vein, Xiang et al. (2022) found differences in model performance across subgroups of learners when two machine learning models were trained to predict learner success and retention. Recently, students in the UK have been assigned final grades using an algorithm because students could not take the final exam due to the COVID-19 pandemic. They found that some students received unrealistically lower grades which led to public pressure for re-evaluating students' grades (Smith, 2020). This further highlights the importance of scrutinizing the algorithm's performance for different groups to ensure the validity of inferences made. Two broad families of algorithmic bias have been adopted in the literature (Awasthi et al., 2020): group fairness and individual fairness. Group fairness is often operationalized by delineating protected subgroups based on attributes like race, gender, ethnicity, or sexual orientation. Metrics such as the false-positive rate, falsenegative rate, or accuracy are then employed to gauge fairness, aiming for uniformity in these metrics across all identified subgroups. In contrast, individual fairness demands that the model treats similar individuals similarly, regardless of their characteristics. This principle emphasizes a more granular approach to fairness within algorithmic systems. For example, group fairness would involve ensuring that the predicted performance outcomes of students from different demographic backgrounds # Algorithmic Bias in BERT for Response Accuracy Prediction are similar, indicating a lack of algorithmic bias. Individual fairness, on the other hand, would involve ensuring that students with similar predicted learning needs and preferences receive comparable recommendations for educational resources, tutoring, or intervention strategies. For example, in the sentence "The quick brown fox jumps over the lazy dog," the token embeddings would represent each individual word as numerical vectors capturing their semantic meaning and context within the sentence. Regarding segment embeddings, for example, consider two sentences: "The cat sat on the mat" (Sentence A) and "The dog barked loudly" (Sentence B). Segment embeddings differentiate between these two sentences and enable BERT to predict the relationship between them, such as whether Sentence B follows Sentence A logically or not. Regarding the position embeddings, consider a 20-token passage where the position embeddings would assign a unique learnable vector to each token based on its position from 1 to 20. These position embeddings enable BERT to understand the sequential order of tokens and capture the contextual relationships between them, regardless of their absolute positions in the input text. BERT is an encoder-only model and differs from other decoder-style transformers (e.g., GPT-4 or Llama-2) that are capable of generating sentences, answering questions, or producing a new output in general. Thus, to re-train BERT for this specific task of response accuracy prediction, we first tokenize action sequences and add a linear output layer on the top of the BERT model for predicting the response accuracy of examinees taking PSTRE items in PIAAC 2012. This process is also known as *fine-tuning an LLM*. Next, we examine the algorithmic bias in fine-tuned BERT models when countries with different performance levels have been used as training sets. Specifically, we identify top-, average-, and low-performing countries based on the availability of the log data. The top-performing country is Finland, the average-performing country is Slovakia, and the low-performing country is the United States. We fine-tune the BERT model using the overall sample including all countries, only Finland, only Slovakia, and only the United States, and compare the response accuracy across these four different models obtained by having different countries as training and test sets. Our research questions are as follows. ## Research questions **RQ1:** To what extent do the fine-tuned BERT models with different populations predict response accuracy? The aim of this research question is to investigate the utility of a pretrained LLM for predicting response accuracy using action sequences directly. We replicate the feasibility of fine-tuning BERT across countries with different ability levels for response accuracy prediction in PSTRE items. **RQ2:** Is there a difference in model performance when BERT is fined-tuned with different populations? # Algorithmic Bias in BERT for Response Accuracy Prediction The purpose of this research question is to investigate the population validity of the fine-tuned BERT model for predicting response accuracy using three different countries with different overall performance levels. This allows us to investigate the extent of algorithmic bias present in the trained models as well as showcase the importance of examining bias in predictive models. ## Method ### Data Data for this study comes from the log files extracted from three PSTRE items administered in the 2012 PIAAC. PIAAC is a large-scale international assessment developed by the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) to assess the proficiency levels of adults in literacy, numeracy, and problem-solving. PSTRE items in the 2012 PIAAC target adults’ problem-solving skills and include 14 items in total (OECD, 2019). We selected three dichotomously scored PSTRE items—U03A, U07X, and U16X because (1) log data extracted from PSTRE items included action sequences that provided rich information about examinee behavior, and (2) we can train a binary classification model using BERT. The action sequences included human-computer interactions recorded for each PSTRE item, such as opening a folder, viewing a folder, clicking on a link, or using the help function. The log data were not publicly available for all countries that participated in the 2012 PIAAC cycle. Based on the overall country performance across all domains, we identified three countries with different performance levels¹. Based on the availability of log data, the top-performing country was Finland, followed by Slovakia located in the middle of the performance distribution, and the worse-performing country was the United States. The first dichotomously scored item, U03A—CD Tally, selected for this study was located in Booklet 1 and included $n_{Finland}$ = 1,482, $n_{Slovakia}$ = 1,096, and $n_{United States}$ = 1,337 participants. The second and third dichotomously scored items, U07X—Book Order and U16X—Reply All, selected were located in Booklet 2 and included $n_{Finland}$ = 1,445, $n_{Slovakia}$ = 1,160, and $n_{United States}$ = 1,340, and $n_{Finland}$ = 1,440, $n_{Slovakia}$ = 1,160, and $n_{United States}$ = 1,342 participants, respectively. Across all items included in the study, the distribution of participants from Finland, Slovakia, and the United States was balanced. The descriptive statistics, including the number of participants, min, max, mean, standard deviation of item length, the number of cases with action sequences longer than 512 tokens, and the proportion-correct scores across all countries are given in Table 1. ### Data Analysis We provided a flowchart presenting the preprocessing and data analysis steps adopted in this study (Figure 1). We first extracted the log data for the selected countries and items using the software program, LogDataAnalyzer available on the PIAAC website. This process created the individual log files for Finland, Slovakia, and the United States. We replaced the underscore separating action descriptions with a space to facilitate the tokenization process with BERT—breaking down the text into words or subwords based on predefined rules (Devlin et al., 2018). DOI: 10.1111/jedm.12420 Journal of Educational Measurement # Algorithmic Bias in BERT for Response Accuracy Prediction: A Case Study for Investigating Population Validity Guher Gorgun (ID) University of Alberta Seyma N. Yildirim-Erbasli Concordia University of Edmonton Pretrained large language models (LLMs) have gained popularity in recent years due to their high performance in various educational tasks such as learner modeling, automated scoring, automatic item generation, and prediction. Nevertheless, LLMs are black box approaches where models are less interpretable, and they may carry human biases and prejudices because historical human data have been used for pretraining these large-scale models. For these reasons, the prediction tasks based on LLMs require scrutiny to ensure that the prediction models are fair and unbiased. In this study, we used BERT—a pretrained encoder-only LLM for predicting response accuracy using action sequences extracted from the 2012 PIAAC assessment. We selected three countries (i.e., Finland, Slovakia, and the United States) representing different performance levels in the overall PIAAC assessment. We found promising results for predicting response accuracy using the fine-tuned BERT model. Additionally, we examined algorithmic bias in the prediction models trained with different countries. We found differences in model performance, suggesting that some trained models are not free from bias, and thus the models are less generalizable across countries. Our results highlighted the importance of investigating algorithmic fairness in prediction models utilizing algorithmic systems to ensure models are bias-free. In the last decade, machine learning and data mining methods have become popular for analyzing assessment data to discover hidden response patterns and provide a nuanced understanding of response behavior (e.g., Goldhammer et al., 2017; He et al., 2021; Nagy et al., 2022; Ulitzsch et al., 2022). Computer-based assessments have facilitated the use of these methods by providing rich information about examinees (Jiao et al., 2023). With computer-based assessments, supplementary information, in addition to traditionally captured response accuracy, can be obtained about data, may include response time spent for each item (e.g., Gorgun & Bulut, 2021), the number of actions taken by examinees (e.g., Sahin & Colvin, 2020), hint requests (e.g., Gorgun & Bulut, 2022b), response changes (e.g., Kroehne & Goldhammer, 2018), action sequences (e.g., Ulitzsch et al., 2022), keystrokes (e.g., Conijn et al., 2019), or eye tracking data (e.g., Orange et al., 2017). --- © 2024 The Author(s). *Journal of Educational Measurement* published by Wiley Periodicals LLC on behalf of National Council on Measurement in Education. This is an open access article under the terms of the CreativeCommonsAttribution-NonCommercial-NoDerivs License, which permits use and distribution in any medium, provided the original work is properly cited, the use is non-commercial and no modifications or adaptations are made. *Gorgun and Yildirim-Erbasli* To date, researchers have leveraged log data to uncover behavioral patterns of examinees with correct and incorrect responses (e.g., Plewan *et al*., 2016), investigate problem-solving strategies (e.g., Pejic & Molcer, 2021), identify disengaged or unmotivated examinees (e.g., Yildirim-Erbasli & Bulut, 2021), and detect anomalous responses (e.g., Shao *et al*., 2022). These studies typically employed computer algorithms for modeling examinee responses. However, algorithmic systems trained with historical human data may discriminate against certain groups, leading to unwarranted inferences about examinees (Kizilcec & Lee, 2022). For example, this may include assigning unrealistically low scores to a certain group (Smith, 2020) or not selecting a certain racial group during the admission process due to the reliance on the historical data (Kleinberg *et al*., 2018). In this study, we first propose to use a pretrained encoder-only large-language model (LLM), Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers (BERT; Devlin *et al*., 2018), for predicting response accuracy using action sequences extracted from the 2012 Programme for the International Assessment of Adult Competencies (PIAAC) log data. Then, we aim to investigate algorithmic bias in fine-tuned BERT for predicting response accuracy in countries that performed well (i.e., Finland), average (i.e., Slovakia), and worse (i.e., the United States) in the 2012 PIAAC assessment. This allows us to examine the population validity of the fine-tuned BERT models across countries with different performance levels. Investigating fairness issues in LLMs is of utmost importance because LLMs are trained with historical human data and may carry human biases and prejudices (e.g., Papakyriakopoulos *et al*., 2020). Recent studies have highlighted that LLMs may hallucinate and generate incorrect information with seemingly high confidence (Zhang *et al*., 2023). Another challenge associated with using LLMs for modeling response behavior is the lack of model interpretability due to LLMs being black-box models (e.g., Lin *et al*., 2023). These models are considered less interpretable because they were trained with a deep learning-based architecture. For these reasons, this study not only proposes to use BERT for response accuracy prediction but also investigates the extent of model generalizability (i.e., algorithmic fairness) across countries with different performance levels. The contributions of this study include understanding the feasibility of using a pretrained LLM, BERT, for predicting response accuracy using action sequences and examining the extent of algorithmic fairness in LLMs for the model's generalizability across all subpopulations. ## Literature Review Process data refers to users’ actions that occurred while interacting with the computer interface stored as log files (He *et al*., 2021; Tang *et al*., 2021). Next, we split the data into training and test sets, and 20% of the data is used as the hold-out test set. We also created subsets of training and test sets based on the country to train the data with the overall sample (i.e., including all countries), Finland-only, Slovakia-only, and the United States-only samples. Following training and test set preparations, we tokenized the action sequences for each item using the BERT base cased model. During the tokenization process, we selected a max token length of 512 and padding = True, to achieve equal sequence lengths for each action sequence. Thus, examinees with action sequences longer than 512 actions were trimmed to a length of 512 tokens, and those with action sequences shorter than 512 actions were added [PAD]—a special- ized token used to adjust the token length. Concerning Item U03A, none of the action sequences were longer than 512 tokens, for Item U07X, only one case in the United States sample has action sequences longer than 512 tokens, and for Item U16X, 26 cases (0.7%) have action sequences longer than 512 tokens (Table 1). Given that no or only a very few cases have action sequences longer than 512 tokens, we expect that truncation has a minimal influence on the models developed. Based on the tokenization process, we obtained a 768-dimensional embedding vector of action sequences. The tokenization process also adds two special tokens: CLS at the beginning of each action sequence and SEP at the end of each action sequence. We fine-tuned BERT for a downstream task (i.e., classification) for pre- dicting examinees' response accuracy using the tokenized action sequences. Specif- ically, using the *AutoModelForSequenceClassification* function, we added a linear output layer for predicting the response accuracy on the top of the pooled CLS to- ken. We used a learning rate of 5e-6 and 3 epochs with a batch size of 8. We repeated the same process using the training data including overall data (i.e., including all countries), Finland, Slovakia, and the United States for all three items. We then eval- uated model performance on the hold-out test sets, including the overall data, only Finland, only Slovakia, and only the United States test sets. This yielded 16 models per item with a total of 48 models. Recently, students in the UK have been assigned final grades using an algorithm because students could not take the final exam due to the COVID-19 pandemic. They found that some students received unrealistically lower grades which led to public pressure for re-evaluating students' grades (Smith, 2020). This further highlights the importance of scrutinizing the algorithm's performance for different groups to ensure the validity of inferences made. Two broad families of algorithmic bias have been adopted in the literature (Awasthi et al., 2020): group fairness and individual fairness. Group fairness is often operationalized by delineating protected subgroups based on attributes like race, gender, ethnicity, or sexual orientation. Metrics such as the false-positive rate, falsenegative rate, or accuracy are then employed to gauge fairness, aiming for uniformity in these metrics across all identified subgroups. In contrast, individual fairness demands that the model treats similar individuals similarly, regardless of their characteristics. This principle emphasizes a more granular approach to fairness within algorithmic systems. For example, group fairness would involve ensuring that the predicted performance outcomes of students from different demographic backgrounds # Algorithmic Bias in BERT for Response Accuracy Prediction are similar, indicating a lack of algorithmic bias. Individual fairness, on the other hand, would involve ensuring that students with similar predicted learning needs and preferences receive comparable recommendations for educational resources, tutoring, or intervention strategies. The focus on fairness in algorithms has elevated in recent years as more educational settings incorporate artificial intelligence to model learners. Most studies analyzed algorithmic bias in prediction models in the presence of class imbalances. An oversampling technique such as SMOTE or ADASYN helped improve algorithmic fairness (Deho et al., 2023; Jiang & Pardos, 2021; Sha et al., 2022, 2023). Even though oversampling techniques are useful for improving model accuracy across different populations, researchers also suggested that more marginalized and underrepresented populations (e.g., racial and gender groups) should be included in training sets (Baker et al., 2023). In addition to representational issues of minority groups, studies also documented biases in prediction models when individuals have different native languages, leading to the underestimation of examinee performance in assessments or learning environments (Gaskins, 2022; Loukina et al., 2019). Traditionally, studies have examined algorithmic bias in prediction models by considering groups based on factors such as gender, age, race, and religion. Yet, the list of groups or populations can be expanded to align with the specific purpose of the algorithmic system. For instance, additional factors such as school region (e.g., urban, suburban, or rural), learner speed (e.g., slow or fast learners), cultural variations (e.g., native language or home country), and socioeconomic status (e.g., low-income students) can be considered (Doroudi & Brunskill, 2019; Li et al., 2019; Loukina et al., 2019; Ocumpaugh et al., 2014; Sackett et al., 2009). In the context of international large-scale assessments, it is important to investigate algorithmic fairness in modeling student performance across countries. This ensures that valid comparisons can be made among countries participating in such assessments. ## Current Study In this study, we first investigate the utility of using an LLM, BERT, for predicting response accuracy employing action sequences extracted from the log files of Problem-Solving in Technology-Rich Environments (PSTRE). To date, a few studies employed BERT for identifying anomalous responses in process data (e.g., Chen & Liao, 2022; Guo et al., 2021; Landauer et al., 2023; Shao et al., 2022), yet BERT has not been used for predicting response accuracy using action sequences. As emphasized, action sequences provide rich yet unstructured information about the examinee behavior. In most cases, it is difficult to directly use the action sequences data due to their high dimensionality. For this reason, researchers may use dimension reduction techniques (e.g., multidimensional scaling) or may extract useful features (e.g., number of actions, duration of actions) from action sequences to be used in machine learning models. A novelty of this study is that using BERT allows to directly use action sequences without the need of using such preprocessing approaches, permitting us to keep the rich information as is. 5 Gorgun and Yildirim-Erbash BERT is a pretrained transformer composed of token embeddings (i.e., capture the meaning and context of individual words in a text; Huang et al., 2020), segment embeddings (i.e., differentiate between sentences A and B for next sentence prediction loss; Devlin et al., 2018), and position embeddings (i.e., encode absolute positions from 1 to a maximum length with each position having a learnable vector; Huang et al., 2020). For example, in the sentence "The quick brown fox jumps over the lazy dog," the token embeddings would represent each individual word as numerical vectors capturing their semantic meaning and context within the sentence. Regarding segment embeddings, for example, consider two sentences: "The cat sat on the mat" (Sentence A) and "The dog barked loudly" (Sentence B). Segment embeddings differentiate between these two sentences and enable BERT to predict the relationship between them, such as whether Sentence B follows Sentence A logically or not. Regarding the position embeddings, consider a 20-token passage where the position embeddings would assign a unique learnable vector to each token based on its position from 1 to 20. These position embeddings enable BERT to understand the sequential order of tokens and capture the contextual relationships between them, regardless of their absolute positions in the input text. BERT is an encoder-only model and differs from other decoder-style transformers (e.g., GPT-4 or Llama-2) that are capable of generating sentences, answering questions, or producing a new output in general. Thus, to re-train BERT for this specific task of response accuracy prediction, we first tokenize action sequences and add a linear output layer on the top of the BERT model for predicting the response accuracy of examinees taking PSTRE items in PIAAC 2012. This process is also known as *fine-tuning an LLM*. Next, we examine the algorithmic bias in fine-tuned BERT models when countries with different performance levels have been

This allows us to investigate the extent of algorithmic bias present in the trained models as well as showcase the importance of examining bias in predictive models. ## Method ### Data Data for this study comes from the log files extracted from three PSTRE items administered in the 2012 PIAAC. PIAAC is a large-scale international assessment developed by the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) to assess the proficiency levels of adults in literacy, numeracy, and problem-solving. PSTRE items in the 2012 PIAAC target adults’ problem-solving skills and include 14 items in total (OECD, 2019). We selected three dichotomously scored PSTRE items—U03A, U07X, and U16X because (1) log data extracted from PSTRE items included action sequences that provided rich information about examinee behavior, and (2) we can train a binary classification model using BERT. The action sequences included human-computer interactions recorded for each PSTRE item, such as opening a folder, viewing a folder, clicking on a link, or using the help function. The log data were not publicly available for all countries that participated in the 2012 PIAAC cycle. Based on the overall country performance across all domains, we identified three countries with different performance levels¹. Based on the availability of log data, the top-performing country was Finland, followed by Slovakia located in the middle of the performance distribution, and the worse-performing country was the United States.
