For conviction history, participants were asked if they had ever been convicted of a crime or pled guilty to any charges other than minor traffic violations (0 = “no” and 1 = “yes”). For incarceration history, participants were asked if they had ever spent time in a jail, prison, juvenile detention center, or other correctional facility (0 = “no” and 1 = “yes”). ## Sociodemographic variables Sociodemographic variables included gender, race, high school dropout status, and level of educational difficulty. For gender and race, binary variables (0 = “no” and 1 = “yes”) were created using female and White, respectively, as reference categories. High school dropout status was a single binary variable (0 = “no” and 1 = “yes”). Educational difficulty was calculated as the sum (range: 0–3) of the scores of three dichotomously measured items (0 = “no” and 1 = “yes”) assessing respondents’ experiences of repeated grades, suspension, and expulsion from school. ## Behavioral/situational risk variables Behavioral and situational risk variables included violent behavior, violence victimization experience, minor delinquency, drug use, alcohol use, cigarette smoking, immature sexual intercourse, romantic relationships, and time spent with peers. Violent behavior comprised seven items assessing involvement in a serious physical fight, hurting someone badly, shooting or stabbing someone, using or threatening to use a weapon to get something from someone, taking part in a group fight, using a weapon in a fight, and pulling a knife or gun on someone in the past 12 months (α = .75). Violent victimization (0 = “no” and 1 = “yes”) experience comprised three items assessing whether someone pulled a knife or gun on the participant, shot or stabbed the participant, and cut or stabbed the participant in the past 12 months. Minor delinquency was assessed with 10 items about asking about painting graffiti or signs on someone else’s property or in a public place, damaging someone else’s property, lying to one’s parents or guardians about where and whom one was with, taking something from a store without paying for it, running away from home, driving a car without a license, stealing something worth more than 50, USD going into a house or building to steal something, stealing something worth less than 50, USD and being loud, rowdy, or unruly in a public place (α = .78). Drug use was assessed by asking participants whether they had used marijuana, cocaine, inhalants, or any other drugs including LSD, PCP, ecstasy, mushrooms, speed, ice, heroin, or pills (0 = “no” and 1 = “yes”). As for alcohol use, participants were asked whether they had consumed beer, wine, or liquor – not just a sip or taste of someone else’s drink – more than two or three times in their lives (0 = “no” and 1 = “yes”). To measure cigarette use, participants were asked whether they had ever smoked cigarettes regularly – that is, at least one cigarette every day for 30 days (0 = “no” and 1 = “yes”). To measure immature sexual intercourse, participants were asked whether they had ever had sexual intercourse before the age of adulthood (0 = “no” and 1 = “yes”). Participants were also asked whether they had had a special romantic relationship with anyone in the last 18 months (0 = “no” and 1 = “yes”). Finally, time spent with peers was measured by asking participants how many times they had been “just hung out” with friends during the past week (range: 0–3). ## Emotional/environmental variables Emotional/environmental variables included hopelessness, depression, suicide attempts, physical abuse, neglect, religion, neighborhood collective efficacy, and evaluation of one’s neighborhood. Second, we build nested models with additive predictive factors to examine the relative predictive abilities of RF and LR models according to the type and number of predictors. Given that an ML-based predictive model would be more suitable to capture the small effects of additional variables than would LR (Rosenfeld and Lewis, 2005; Yang, Liu, and Coid, 2010), we sequentially add three different sets of risk factors to both the RF and LR models. The first set of factors comprises nine sociodemographic variables, the second set comprises nine behavioral and situational risk factors, and the third set comprises eight emotional and environmental risk factors. Consequently, the first model includes six predicting factors, the second model includes 15 factors, and the third model includes 23 factors. We designate criminal involvement of young adults as the outcome variable for all models. On the surface, the experience of arrest seems adequate to capture individuals’ criminality; however, not all arrestees actually committed the crime, and not all criminal activities result in arrest. More complex external factors intervene when deciding conviction and incarceration. Throughout the process from criminal activity to incarceration, decision-makers can be more influential than the nature of criminal involvement itself. Although not all outcome variables in this study (arrest, conviction, and incarceration) are ideal measures to capture individuals' behavioral problems, it is enough to reflect the tendency of antisocial behavior. Accordingly, the current study forecasts arrest, conviction, and incarceration exclusively, using the same sets of risk factors for each. # Method ## Data The current study used the National Longitudinal Study of Adolescent Health (Add Health) data derived from a nationally representative sample of U.S. adolescents in grades 7–12 from 1994–1995. We utilized public-use data from Wave 1 for risk factors and data from Wave 4 for the outcome variables. The Wave 1 data consists of a randomly selected half of the core sample, as well as one half of the oversample of African American adolescents with at least one parent holding a college degree. Wave 4 was designed to study trajectories from adolescence to young adulthood (age 24–32). There were a total of 6,504 respondents in this dataset. Of the total cases, 5,067 cases had valid data for the arrest outcome, 4,290 cases had valid data for the conviction outcome, and 4,935 cases had valid data for the incarceration outcome. # Measures ## Outcome variables To measure arrest history, participants were asked during the last follow-up interview conducted in Wave 4 if they had ever been arrested (0 = “no” and 1 = “yes”). For conviction history, participants were asked if they had ever been convicted of a crime or pled guilty to any charges other than minor traffic violations (0 = “no” and 1 = “yes”). For incarceration history, participants were asked if they had ever spent time in a jail, prison, juvenile detention center, or other correctional facility (0 = “no” and 1 = “yes”). ## Sociodemographic variables Sociodemographic variables included gender, race, high school dropout status, and level of educational difficulty. For gender and race, binary variables (0 = “no” and 1 = “yes”) were created using female and White, respectively, as reference categories. High school dropout status was a single binary variable (0 = “no” and 1 = “yes”). Educational difficulty was calculated as the sum (range: 0–3) of the scores of three dichotomously measured items (0 = “no” and 1 = “yes”) assessing respondents’ experiences of repeated grades, suspension, and expulsion from school. ## Behavioral/situational risk variables Behavioral and situational risk variables included violent behavior, violence victimization experience, minor delinquency, drug use, alcohol use, cigarette smoking, immature sexual intercourse, romantic relationships, and time spent with peers. Violent behavior comprised seven items assessing involvement in a serious physical fight, hurting someone badly, shooting or stabbing someone, using or threatening to use a weapon to get something from someone, taking part in a group fight, using a weapon in a fight, and pulling a knife or gun on someone in the past 12 months (α = .75). Violent victimization (0 = “no” and 1 = “yes”) experience comprised three items assessing whether someone pulled a knife or gun on the participant, shot or stabbed the participant, and cut or stabbed the participant in the past 12 months. Minor delinquency was assessed with 10 items about asking about painting graffiti or signs on someone else’s property or in a public place, damaging someone else’s property, lying to one’s parents or guardians about where and whom one was with, taking something from a store without paying for it, running away from home, driving a car without a license, stealing something worth more than 50, USD going into a house or building to steal something, stealing something worth less than 50, USD and being loud, rowdy, or unruly in a public place (α = .78). Drug use was assessed by asking participants whether they had used marijuana, cocaine, inhalants, or any other drugs including LSD, PCP, ecstasy, mushrooms, speed, ice, heroin, or pills (0 = “no” and 1 = “yes”). As for alcohol use, participants were asked whether they had consumed beer, wine, or liquor – not just a sip or taste of someone else’s drink – more than two or three times in their lives (0 = “no” and 1 = “yes”). To measure cigarette use, participants were asked whether they had ever smoked cigarettes regularly – that is, at least one cigarette every day for 30 days (0 = “no” and 1 = “yes”). To measure immature sexual intercourse, participants were asked whether they had ever had sexual intercourse before the age of adulthood (0 = “no” and 1 = “yes”). Participants were also asked whether they had had a special romantic relationship with anyone in the last 18 months (0 = “no” and 1 = “yes”). Despite the mixed results of using ML to forecast individual criminal involvement, Berk, Azusa, and Hickman (2005; 2009) have highlighted the benefits of the random forest method in forecasting recidivism and antisocial behaviors. Berk (2012) consistently argues that the costs to the community of overlooking high-risk releasees should not be considered equivalent to the costs of monitoring low-risk releasees resulting from the misclassification of risk assessment tools. Considering that misclassifying risky individuals into a non-risk group is more harmful to communities than misclassifying non-risky individuals into a risk group, Berk, Azusa, and Hickman (2005) built the balanced predictive model to intentionally decrease 'false negative' cases – the individuals who actually engaged in offending behaviors although they were not predicted to be offenders. Previous studies (Berk, Azusa, and Hickman, 2005; Berk et al., 2009) applied the balanced random forest (RF) modeling approach by making the cost ratio of false negatives to false positives 10 to 1, improving prediction of offenders' actual risk after release. Although these studies arbitrarily presumed that missing future criminals is ten times more costly than detaining offenders who would not recidivate in the future, the balanced RF approach can provide administrators and practitioners with less precarious predictions of individual reoffending behavior compared to conventional statistical models with 1-to-1 cost ratios. While the RF model has been applied primarily to forecasting recidivism and violent behaviors of patients with mental disorders, no attempts have been made to forecast juvenile criminal offenses. A few decades ago, the risk factor prevention paradigm began to emerge, which highlighted the importance of early identification of risky juveniles and early intervention to prevent persistent criminal involvement (Farrington, 2000). Several longitudinal studies have strengthened this argument by revealing that most delinquent juveniles stop engaging in criminal behavior by their early twenties (Moffitt, 1993). From the developmental perspective of criminal behaviors, the development and validation of assessment tools to identify high-risk individuals is fundamental. However, crime is a rare event in the general youth population and its prediction is inherently difficult – especially when there is a limited number of predictors available to increase the predictive accuracy. In this context, the current study intends to apply the ML-based classification model in forecasting criminal offenses of juveniles and young adults using different sets of theoretically grounded risk/preventive factors. We expect that ML-based classification will be an attractive method if the advanced forecasting model of future criminal involvement proves effective under various conditions (e.g., even when predictions must be made with limited numbers and types of predictors). ## Literature Review Since the 1980s, the importance of predicting antisocial behaviors using risk assessment tools has been highlighted by scholars in behavioral science and criminal justice (see Gottfredson, 1987; see also Andrews and Bonta, 2010). Over 150 structured risk assessment tools have been developed in the past decades to predict violent and deviant behaviors (Fazel et al., 2012). Based on the concrete evidence on the efficiency of risk assessment tools, the actuarial Risk-Need-Responsivity (RNR) models are now widely applied to classify high-risk offenders and youths, especially in the juvenile criminal justice system (e.g., Hamilton et al., 2020; Ho, Lesneskie, and Hsu, 2018; Schmidt et al., 2017). For instance, the Positive Achievement Change Tool (PACT) was implemented in several states of the United States and found to be effective in predicting offenders who are more likely to recidivate (Hamilton et al., 2020). Recently, coupled with the development of ML techniques, several empirical studies have attempted to apply ML algorithms in forecasting behavioral problems using risk assessment tools to maximize the predictive accuracy. Scholars have gained confidence that problematic behaviors can be forecasted by ## C. NA ET AL. artificial intelligence relying on robust tree-based classification methods (Berk, Azusa, and Hickman 2005; Berk and Bleich 2014; Berk et al. 2009; Holleran and Stout 2017; Neuilly et al. 2011; Pflueger et al. 2015; Rosenfeld and Lewis 2005; Silver, Smith, and Banks 2000; Steadman et al. 2000). ML algorithms yield more accurate classification of individuals into non-risk and risk groups, especially when risk assessment tools for evaluating the hazard of problematic behaviors are predetermined. In earlier stages, psychiatrists devoted their attention to forecasting violent behaviors of patients with mental disorders (Gardner et al. 1996; Steadman et al. 2000). For practical reasons, clinicians focused on screening high-risk patients before discharging them to the community. Consequently, research has examined whether tree-based ML methods would improve the prediction of violence compared to conventional regression-based, actuarial prediction methods. Furthermore, some researchers have used RF modeling to forecast recidivism (Berk and Bleich 2014; Berk et al. 2009; Rosenfeld and Lewis 2005), capital charges and death sentences (Berk, Azusa, and Hickman 2005), and inmate misconduct (Berk, Kriegler, and Baek 2006). This study examined the predictive ability of a balanced RF model (one of the most popular ML algorithms applied in prevention science) when predicting future criminal involvement of juveniles. Our findings make a significant contribution to the risk factor prevention paradigm by providing advanced tools to identify high-risk juveniles drawing on theory-based risk factors. Recently, coupled with the development of ML techniques, several empirical studies have attempted to apply ML algorithms in forecasting behavioral problems using risk assessment tools to maximize the predictive accuracy. ML algorithms yield more accurate classification of individuals into non-risk and risk groups, especially when risk assessment tools for evaluating the hazard of problematic behaviors are predetermined. In earlier stages, psychiatrists devoted their attention to forecasting violent behaviors of patients with mental disorders (Gardner et al. 1996; Steadman et al. 2000). For practical reasons, clinicians focused on screening high-risk patients before discharging them to the community. Consequently, research has examined whether tree-based ML methods would improve the prediction of violence compared to conventional regression-based, actuarial prediction methods. Furthermore, some researchers have used RF modeling to forecast recidivism (Berk and Bleich 2014; Berk et al. 2009; Rosenfeld and Lewis 2005), capital charges and death sentences (Berk, Azusa, and Hickman 2005), and inmate misconduct (Berk, Kriegler, and Baek 2006). Thus, the current study applies advanced forecasting methods and a statistical learning approach to identify individuals at high risk for becoming criminal offenders. Among several types of ML algorithms, the tree-based algorithm is one of the most widely applied techniques in forecasting recidivism and other antisocial behaviors. Such models are built on single or multiple decision trees, each composed of multiple nodes and branches to classify cases with homogeneous characteristics (Berk and Bleich 2014). The current study focuses on the RF model, which has several benefits over other tree-based models. RF is an ensemble model that generates several classifiers and aggregates results to make a final decision (Breiman 2001). The ensemble model refers to the technique generating multiple models instead of a single model and then combining the results of each model to yield conclusions. Because RF builds several classification trees using randomly selected subsamples and predictors, the model is less vulnerable to overfitting issues (Berk 2012). RF has been used to forecast various types of antisocial behavior, including inmate misconduct (Berk, Kriegler, and Baek 2006), violence (Pflueger et al. 2015), and recidivism (Berk et al. 2009; Duwe and Kim 2017; Hamilton et al. 2015). Specifically, Hamilton et al. (2015) created separate predictive models based on RF, neural networks, and logistic regression (LR) using a large sample ($N = 297,600$) drawn from Washington state offenders. They reported that there were no differences in predictive accuracy or overall performance among the three models. Another recent study (Duwe and Kim 2017) revealed that, overall, RF outperformed LR and other ML-based classification methods, although the difference was marginal. Consistent with these results, others have reported that the forecasting accuracy and overall performance of the RF model are nearly identical to or slightly better than the performance of conventional statistical analyses such as LR (Ozkan 2017). Despite RF's similar performance relative to other statistical learning methods, there is a significant benefit when using RF to build a forecasting model: differentiating the cost ratio between false negatives and false positives. As argued by Berk, Kriegler, and Baek (2006), the model's predictive accuracy is not meaningful if the outcome variable is highly unbalanced. For instance, the forecasting model may provide low classification error rates by classifying all cases into negative or positive cases if there are only a few negative or positive cases. To remedy this issue, Berk, Kriegler, and Baek (2006) suggest that the costs of false negatives and false positives should be predetermined instead of using the default 1-to-1 cost ratio. In their study, they determined that misclassifying actually risky individuals (false negative) is 10 times more harmful than misclassifying actually non-risky individuals (false positive); as a result, the error rate of misclassifying actually risky individuals into the non-risky group decreases significantly. Following this argument, Holleran and Stout (2017) applied a balanced RF model approach to forecast juvenile incarceration. The results of their study revealed that, relative to the unbalanced RF model with a 1-to-1 cost ratio, the balanced RF model dramatically decreased the misclassification of non-commitment cases as non-commitment cases. The current study adopts the balanced RF model to decrease rates of misclassifying risky juveniles into the non-risky group. Meanwhile, recent studies using ML-based predictive models have explored the benefits of statistical learning approaches that address the shortcomings of parametric statistical analyses such as LR. In particular, Yang, Liu, and Coid (2010) called into question the predictive ability of LR when using with relatively small sample sizes due to the potential shrinkage of interaction effects among predictors. To remedy this issue, Berk, Kriegler, and Baek (2006) suggest that the costs of false negatives and false positives should be predetermined instead of using the default 1-to-1 cost ratio. In their study, they determined that misclassifying actually risky individuals (false negative) is 10 times more harmful than misclassifying actually non-risky individuals (false positive); as a result, the error rate of misclassifying actually risky individuals into the non-risky group decreases significantly. Following this argument, Holleran and Stout (2017) applied a balanced RF model approach to forecast juvenile incarceration. The results of their study revealed that, relative to the unbalanced RF model with a 1-to-1 cost ratio, the balanced RF model dramatically decreased the misclassification of non-commitment cases as non-commitment cases. The current study adopts the balanced RF model to decrease rates of misclassifying risky juveniles into the non-risky group. Meanwhile, recent studies using ML-based predictive models have explored the benefits of statistical learning approaches that address the shortcomings of parametric statistical analyses such as LR. In particular, Yang, Liu, and Coid (2010) called into question the predictive ability of LR when using with relatively small sample sizes due to the potential shrinkage of interaction effects among predictors. To examine relative predictive abilities of LR, neural networks, and classification trees, the researchers built several nested models by sequentially adding dynamic risk factors of prison inmates to predetermined risk assessment tools. Expanding the number of risk factors did not improve the LR model, whereas the neural network model including additional risk factors demonstrated significantly improved predictive ability. Rosenfeld and Lewis (2005) found similar results when using a series of nested models with additive based predictive model, a classification and regression tree (CART), and an LR model to forecast violent offenses. Consistent with Yang, Liu, and Coid (2010) results, the overall accuracy of the CART model significantly improved as predictors were added, while the LR model showed no significant changes when adding risk factors. In sum, more work is needed to assess the utility of ML methods in crime prediction and explore the contingencies in which their predictive power is enhanced. ## Current Study Taking lessons from the studies outlined above, the current study aims to examine the predictive accuracy of balanced RF models using two schemes. First, following the argument of Berk, Kriegler, and Baek (2006), we apply a balanced RF approach to build models forecasting arrests, convictions, and incarcerations. As mentioned above, the balanced approach refers to the model that intentionally increases the cost of false negatives in the prediction. Although the optimal cost ratio can vary depending on various factors decision-makers must consider, we apply a 10-to-1 cost ratio following the suggestion of previous studies to make the results of the current study comparable to those of extant studies (Berk, Kriegler, and Baek, 2006; Holleran and Stout, 2017). To assess balanced RF models' predictive ability, we compare their criminal offense forecasting results with those of LR models. Second, we build nested models with additive predictive factors to examine the relative predictive abilities of RF and LR models according to the type and number of predictors. Given that an ML-based predictive model would be more suitable to capture the small effects of additional variables than would LR (Rosenfeld and Lewis, 2005; Yang, Liu, and Coid, 2010), we sequentially add three different sets of risk factors to both the RF and LR models. The first set of factors comprises nine sociodemographic variables, the second set comprises nine behavioral and situational risk factors, and the third set comprises eight emotional and environmental risk factors. Consequently, the first model includes six predicting factors, the second model includes 15 factors, and the third model includes 23 factors. We designate criminal involvement of young adults as the outcome variable for all models. On the surface, the experience of arrest seems adequate to capture individuals’ criminality; however, not all arrestees actually committed the crime, and not all criminal activities result in arrest. More complex external factors intervene when deciding conviction and incarceration. Throughout the process from criminal activity to incarceration, decision-makers can be more influential than the nature of criminal involvement itself. Although not all outcome variables in this study (arrest, conviction, and incarceration) are ideal measures to capture individuals' behavioral problems, it is enough to reflect the tendency of antisocial behavior. Accordingly, the current study forecasts arrest, conviction, and incarceration exclusively, using the same sets of risk factors for each. # Method ## Data The current study used the National Longitudinal Study of Adolescent Health (Add Health) data derived from a nationally representative sample of U.S. adolescents in grades 7–12 from 1994–1995. We utilized public-use data from Wave 1 for risk factors and data from Wave 4 for the outcome variables. The Wave 1 data consists of a randomly selected half of the core sample, as well as one half of the oversample of African American adolescents with at least one parent holding a college degree. Wave 4 was designed to study trajectories from adolescence to young adulthood (age 24–32). There were a total of 6,504 respondents in this dataset. Of the total cases, 5,067 cases had valid data for the arrest outcome, 4,290 cases had valid data for the conviction outcome, and 4,935 cases had valid data for the incarceration outcome. # Measures ## Outcome variables To measure arrest history, participants were asked during the last follow-up interview conducted in Wave 4 if they had ever been arrested (0 = “no” and 1 = “yes”). For conviction history, participants were asked if they had ever been convicted of a crime or pled guilty to any charges other than minor traffic violations (0 = “no” and 1 = “yes”). For incarceration history, participants were asked if they had ever spent time in a jail, prison, juvenile detention center, or other correctional facility (0 = “no” and 1

stopped on the street to talk with someone who lives in their neighborhood (0 = “no” and 1 = “yes”), whether people in their neighborhood look out for each other (0 = “no” and 1 = “yes”), whether they use a physical fitness or recreation center in their neighborhood (0 = “no” and 1 = “yes”), and whether they usually feel safe in their neighborhood (0 = “no” and 1 = “yes”). In a similar vein, the evaluation of neighborhood items asked participants how happy they are with living in their neighborhood (range: 1–5) and how happy they would be if they had to move to some other neighborhood (range: 1–5). ## Results Table 2 shows the descriptive statistics for the variables used in the LR and RF models. As expected, ML (RF in the current study) was moderately superior to LR in predicting the judicial decisions and criminal involvement based almost exclusively on the concrete data and evidence available to the decision-makers (i.e., conviction and incarceration), while the superiority of ML was not found in predicting arrest. The current study focuses on the RF model, which has several benefits over other tree-based models. RF is an ensemble model that generates several classifiers and aggregates results to make a final decision (Breiman 2001). The ensemble model refers to the technique generating multiple models instead of a single model and then combining the results of each model to yield conclusions. Because RF builds several classification trees using randomly selected subsamples and predictors, the model is less vulnerable to overfitting issues (Berk 2012). RF has been used to forecast various types of antisocial behavior, including inmate misconduct (Berk, Kriegler, and Baek 2006), violence (Pflueger et al. 2015), and recidivism (Berk et al. 2009; Duwe and Kim 2017; Hamilton et al. 2015). Specifically, Hamilton et al. (2015) created separate predictive models based on RF, neural networks, and logistic regression (LR) using a large sample ($N = 297,600$) drawn from Washington state offenders. They reported that there were no differences in predictive accuracy or overall performance among the three models. Another recent study (Duwe and Kim 2017) revealed that, overall, RF outperformed LR and other ML-based classification methods, although the difference was marginal. Consistent with these results, others have reported that the forecasting accuracy and overall performance of the RF model are nearly identical to or slightly better than the performance of conventional statistical analyses such as LR (Ozkan 2017). As argued by Berk, Kriegler, and Baek (2006), the model's predictive accuracy is not meaningful if the outcome variable is highly unbalanced. For instance, the forecasting model may provide low classification error rates by classifying all cases into negative or positive cases if there are only a few negative or positive cases. Following this argument, Holleran and Stout (2017) applied a balanced RF model approach to forecast juvenile incarceration. The results of their study revealed that, relative to the unbalanced RF model with a 1-to-1 cost ratio, the balanced RF model dramatically decreased the misclassification of non-commitment cases as non-commitment cases. The current study adopts the balanced RF model to decrease rates of misclassifying risky juveniles into the non-risky group. This study examined the predictive ability of a balanced RF model (one of the most popular ML algorithms applied in prevention science) when predicting future criminal involvement of juveniles. Our findings make a significant contribution to the risk factor prevention paradigm by providing advanced tools to identify high-risk juveniles drawing on theory-based risk factors. Rosenfeld and Lewis (2005) found similar results when using a series of nested models with additive based predictive model, a classification and regression tree (CART), and an LR model to forecast violent offenses. Consistent with Yang, Liu, and Coid (2010) results, the overall accuracy of the CART model significantly improved as predictors were added, while the LR model showed no significant changes when adding risk factors. In sum, more work is needed to assess the utility of ML methods in crime prediction and explore the contingencies in which their predictive power is enhanced. ## Current Study Taking lessons from the studies outlined above, the current study aims to examine the predictive accuracy of balanced RF models using two schemes. First, following the argument of Berk, Kriegler, and Baek (2006), we apply a balanced RF approach to build models forecasting arrests, convictions, and incarcerations. As mentioned above, the balanced approach refers to the model that intentionally increases the cost of false negatives in the prediction. Although the optimal cost ratio can vary depending on various factors decision-makers must consider, we apply a 10-to-1 cost ratio following the suggestion of previous studies to make the results of the current study comparable to those of extant studies (Berk, Kriegler, and Baek, 2006; Holleran and Stout, 2017). To assess balanced RF models' predictive ability, we compare their criminal offense forecasting results with those of LR models. Second, we build nested models with additive predictive factors to examine the relative predictive abilities of RF and LR models according to the type and number of predictors. Given that an ML-based predictive model would be more suitable to capture the small effects of additional variables than would LR (Rosenfeld and Lewis, 2005; Yang, Liu, and Coid, 2010), we sequentially add three different sets of risk factors to both the RF and LR models. The first set of factors comprises nine sociodemographic variables, the second set comprises nine behavioral and situational risk factors, and the third set comprises eight emotional and environmental risk factors. Consequently, the first model includes six predicting factors, the second model includes 15 factors, and the third model includes 23 factors. We designate criminal involvement of young adults as the outcome variable for all models. On the surface, the experience of arrest seems adequate to capture individuals’ criminality; however, not all arrestees actually committed the crime, and not all criminal activities result in arrest. More complex external factors intervene when deciding conviction and incarceration. Throughout the process from criminal activity to incarceration, decision-makers can be more influential than the nature of criminal involvement itself. Although not all outcome variables in this study (arrest, conviction, and incarceration) are ideal measures to capture individuals' behavioral problems, it is enough to reflect the tendency of antisocial behavior. Accordingly, the current study forecasts arrest, conviction, and incarceration exclusively, using the same sets of risk factors for each. # Method ## Data The current study used the National Longitudinal Study of Adolescent Health (Add Health) data derived from a nationally representative sample of U.S. adolescents in grades 7–12 from 1994–1995. We utilized public-use data from Wave 1 for risk factors and data from Wave 4 for the outcome variables. The Wave 1 data consists of a randomly selected half of the core sample, as well as one half of the oversample of African American adolescents with at least one parent holding a college degree. Wave 4 was designed to study trajectories from adolescence to young adulthood (age 24–32). There were a total of 6,504 respondents in this dataset. Of the total cases, 5,067 cases had valid data for the arrest outcome, 4,290 cases had valid data for the conviction outcome, and 4,935 cases had valid data for the incarceration outcome. # Measures ## Outcome variables To measure arrest history, participants were asked during the last follow-up interview conducted in Wave 4 if they had ever been arrested (0 = “no” and 1 = “yes”). For conviction history, participants were asked if they had ever been convicted of a crime or pled guilty to any charges other than minor traffic violations (0 = “no” and 1 = “yes”). For incarceration history, participants were asked if they had ever spent time in a jail, prison, juvenile detention center, or other correctional facility (0 = “no” and 1 = “yes”). ## Sociodemographic variables Sociodemographic variables included gender, race, high school dropout status, and level of educational difficulty. For gender and race, binary variables (0 = “no” and 1 = “yes”) were created using female and White, respectively, as reference categories. High school dropout status was a single binary variable (0 = “no” and 1 = “yes”). Educational difficulty was calculated as the sum (range: 0–3) of the scores of three dichotomously measured items (0 = “no” and 1 = “yes”) assessing respondents’ experiences of repeated grades, suspension, and expulsion from school. ## Behavioral/situational risk variables Behavioral and situational risk variables included violent behavior, violence victimization experience, minor delinquency, drug use, alcohol use, cigarette smoking, immature sexual intercourse, romantic relationships, and time spent with peers. Violent victimization (0 = “no” and 1 = “yes”) experience comprised three items assessing whether someone pulled a knife or gun on the participant, shot or stabbed the participant, and cut or stabbed the participant in the past 12 months. Although a considerable number of studies have applied ML to forecast recidivism (Berk and Bleich 2014; Berk et al. 2009; Rosenfeld and Lewis 2005) and violent behaviors of patients with mental disorders (Gardner et al. 1996; Steadman et al. 2000), no attempt has been made to use ML to forecast the criminal involvement of young adults based on their behavioral, emotional, and environmental status measured in earlier life stages. This study examined the predictive ability of a balanced RF model (one of the most popular ML algorithms applied in prevention science) when predicting future criminal involvement of juveniles. Our findings make a significant contribution to the risk factor prevention paradigm by providing advanced tools to identify high-risk juveniles drawing on theory-based risk factors. Two noteworthy findings emerged from this study. First, the balanced RF model results show that young adults' criminal involvement can be predicted by risk/protective factors measured during earlier life stages. Furthermore, compared with the forecasting results of the LR model, the balanced RF model yields higher hit rates of criminal involvement, while the AUCs of two models showed no substantial differences. Put simply, forecasting criminal involvement (true positives) using the balanced RF model is more efficient than using the LR model while avoiding diminishing overall predictive accuracy. Tables 3 and 4 suggest that, although the overall accuracy of the LR model is slightly better than that of the balanced RF model, the hit rates of the balanced RF model - of primary interest for both researchers and practitioners - are significantly higher with the RF model than with 1046 C. Specifically, when predicting the arrest outcome, our study's LR model missed 64% of actual arrest cases (280/437), whereas the balanced RF model missed only 13% of actual arrest cases (58/437). We found analogous patterns when predicting conviction and incarceration. Although the balanced RF model yields lower overall accuracy and precision ($\text{TP}/(\text{TP} + \text{FP})$), it misses considerably lower numbers of high-risk individuals than does the LR model. Considering the inherent tradeoff between precision and specificity, practitioners and administrators who oversee crime prevention should determine the most suitable cost ratio according to their capability (see Berk, 2012 for more details). Meanwhile, it should also be noted that the LR model is still an applicative method that provides higher levels of overall accuracy and precision unless the practitioners are highly concerned about the relativeness of the costs between false negative and false positive. These results may provide practitioners and agency administrators with more localized prediction of criminal involvement. For local agencies, ML-based forecasting models can be built upon their records of youths' criminal involvement, and the prediction of individual criminality could be more fitting to their local environments. For instance, research has demonstrated that the patterns and causes of crime in rural areas are not equivalent to those in urban areas (Weisheit and Edward Wells, 1996; Wells and Weisheit, 2004). Considering the discrete criminogenic risk factors in rural areas, forecasting individual criminal involvement should not rely on universal assessment tools. We expect that ML-based forecasting tools that are trained with local datasets will provide not only less costly but also more precise identification of high-risk individuals in their early life stages. Inconsistent with the results of previous studies Figure 3. In Table 3, the overall predictive ability of the LR model for all three outcome variables consistently increased as more predictors were added. However, as shown in Table 4, the AUC of the balanced RF model with all predictors (Model 3) was not always greater than those of the previous levels of RF models (Models 1 and 2). Specifically, in terms of arrest and conviction, the AUC of Model 2 is greater than those of the model including all risk factors (Model 3). Indeed, the results are plausible because the RF model is an ensemble model that does not encompass the variances of all predicting factors in a single predicting model. While growing several trees using randomly selected factors, the pruning process of the RF model may discard trees with certain predicting factors. Consequently, the effects of certain variables tend not to be reflected in the final decision, especially when their effect sizes are small. We found several other interesting patterns in the analysis. In general, both the balanced RF and the LR predictive models more accurately predicted conviction and incarceration than they did arrest. Although the type of offense was not included as a predictor, the machine-learned classifier yields better performance when forecasting judges’ and juries’ decisions. We speculate that the defendants’ backgrounds significantly influence judges’ and juries’ decisions; thus, the models more accurately predicted their decisions than they did an individual’s experience of arrest. Meanwhile, the variable importance plots present interesting findings regarding the relative effect size of each variable on the outcome. In Figures 1 and 2, the most influential factor in forecasting arrest and conviction was history of delinquent behavior. On the contrary, individuals’ neighborhood conditions were most influential in forecasting incarceration using the balanced RF model. The results lead us to speculate that judges consider the potential harm to the community when determining the physical custody of defendants. Despite the noteworthy findings of the present study, the results should be interpreted in light of some limitations. First, the data used for this study were a subsample of Add Health that is available to the public. Although the entire survey dataset comprises more than 15,000 individual cases at Wave 1, the current study utilized only 6,504 cases. Moreover, the subsamples used in the current study consist of one half of the oversample of African American individuals with a parent holding a college degree. It should be noted that the oversample of African American individuals may yield algorithmic bias. Future studies should consider using entire samples that are more representative of adolescents in the U.S. Second, as the type of offense for the arrest, conviction, and incarceration was not taken into account in the analyses, it is possible that the varying importance of the three outcome models might be explained by the seriousness of the alleged offense. ## Disclosure statement No potential conflict of interest was reported by the author(s). ## Notes on contributors Gyeongseok Oh received his Ph.D. from the College of Criminal Justice at Sam Houston State University. Despite the mixed results of using ML to forecast individual criminal involvement, Berk, Azusa, and Hickman (2005; 2009) have highlighted the benefits of the random forest method in forecasting recidivism and antisocial behaviors. Berk (2012) consistently argues that the costs to the community of overlooking high-risk releasees should not be considered equivalent to the costs of monitoring low-risk releasees resulting from the misclassification of risk assessment tools. Considering that misclassifying risky individuals into a non-risk group is more harmful to communities than misclassifying non-risky individuals into a risk group, Berk, Azusa, and Hickman (2005) built the balanced predictive model to intentionally decrease 'false negative' cases – the individuals who actually engaged in offending behaviors although they were not predicted to be offenders. Previous studies (Berk, Azusa, and Hickman, 2005; Berk et al., 2009) applied the balanced random forest (RF) modeling approach by making the cost ratio of false negatives to false positives 10 to 1, improving prediction of offenders' actual risk after release. Although these studies arbitrarily presumed that missing future criminals is ten times more costly than detaining offenders who would not recidivate in the future, the balanced RF approach can provide administrators and practitioners with less precarious predictions of individual reoffending behavior compared to conventional statistical models with 1-to-1 cost ratios. While the RF model has been applied primarily to forecasting recidivism and violent behaviors of patients with mental disorders, no attempts have been made to forecast juvenile criminal offenses. A few decades ago, the risk factor prevention paradigm began to emerge, which highlighted the importance of early identification of risky juveniles and early intervention to prevent persistent criminal involvement (Farrington, 2000). Several longitudinal studies have strengthened this argument by revealing that most delinquent juveniles stop engaging in criminal behavior by their early twenties (Moffitt, 1993). From the developmental perspective of criminal behaviors, the development and validation of assessment tools to identify high-risk individuals is fundamental. However, crime is a rare event in the general youth population and its prediction is inherently difficult – especially when there is a limited number of predictors available to increase the predictive accuracy. In this context, the current study intends to apply the ML-based classification model in forecasting criminal offenses of juveniles and young adults using different sets of theoretically grounded risk/preventive factors. We expect that ML-based classification will be an attractive method if the advanced forecasting model of future criminal involvement proves effective under various conditions (e.g., even when predictions must be made with limited numbers and types of predictors). ## Literature Review Since the 1980s, the importance of predicting antisocial behaviors using risk assessment tools has been highlighted by scholars in behavioral science and criminal justice (see Gottfredson, 1987; see also Andrews and Bonta, 2010). Over 150 structured risk assessment tools have been developed in the past decades to predict violent and deviant behaviors (Fazel et al., 2012). Based on the concrete evidence on the efficiency of risk assessment tools, the actuarial Risk-Need-Responsivity (RNR) models are now widely applied to classify high-risk offenders and youths, especially in the juvenile criminal justice system (e.g., Hamilton et al., 2020; Ho, Lesneskie, and Hsu, 2018; Schmidt et al., 2017). For instance, the Positive Achievement Change Tool (PACT) was implemented in several states of the United States and found to be effective in predicting offenders who are more likely to recidivate (Hamilton et al., 2020). Recently, coupled with the development of ML techniques, several empirical studies have attempted to apply ML algorithms in forecasting behavioral problems using risk assessment tools to maximize the predictive accuracy. Scholars have gained confidence that problematic behaviors can be forecasted by ## C. NA ET AL. artificial intelligence relying on robust tree-based classification methods (Berk, Azusa, and Hickman 2005; Berk and Bleich 2014; Berk et al. 2009; Holleran and Stout 2017; Neuilly et al. 2011; Pflueger et al. 2015; Rosenfeld and Lewis 2005; Silver, Smith, and Banks 2000; Steadman et al. 2000). ML algorithms yield more accurate classification of individuals into non-risk and risk groups, especially when risk assessment tools for evaluating the hazard of problematic behaviors are predetermined. In earlier stages, psychiatrists devoted their attention to forecasting violent behaviors of patients with mental disorders (Gardner et al. 1996; Steadman et al. 2000). For practical reasons, clinicians focused on screening high-risk patients before discharging them to the community. Consequently, research has examined whether tree-based ML methods would improve the prediction of violence compared to conventional regression-based, actuarial prediction methods. Furthermore, some researchers have used RF modeling to forecast recidivism (Berk and Bleich 2014; Berk et al. 2009; Rosenfeld and Lewis 2005), capital charges and death sentences (Berk, Azusa, and Hickman 2005), and inmate misconduct (Berk, Kriegler, and Baek 2006). While studies using ML-based algorithms to forecast antisocial behaviors have focused on recidivism or violent behaviors of individuals with mental health problems, no attempt has yet been made to forecast juveniles' first criminal involvement measured by official arrest, conviction, and incarceration. Nonetheless, risk factors shown to be related to reoffending behaviors and adolescents' first criminal involvement. Other theoretically deduced and empirically verified risk factors for antisocial behaviors in the general youth population could also be utilized when forecasting future criminal acts. According to the risk factor prevention paradigm, the importance of identifying such high-risk juveniles should not be overlooked, as this could prevent them from developing into life-course-persistent offenders (Farrington 2000). Thus, the current study applies advanced forecasting methods and a statistical learning approach to identify individuals at high risk for becoming criminal offenders. Among several types of ML algorithms, the tree-based algorithm is one of the most widely applied techniques in forecasting recidivism and other antisocial behaviors. Such models are built on single or multiple decision trees, each composed of multiple nodes and branches to classify cases with homogeneous characteristics (Berk and Bleich 2014). The current study focuses on the RF model, which has several benefits over other tree-based models. To remedy this issue, Berk, Kriegler, and Baek (2006) suggest that the costs of false negatives and false positives should be predetermined instead of using the default 1-to-1 cost ratio. In their study, they determined that misclassifying actually risky individuals (false negative) is 10 times more harmful than misclassifying actually non-risky individuals (false positive); as a result, the error rate of misclassifying actually risky individuals into the non-risky group decreases significantly. Following this argument, Holleran and Stout (2017) applied a balanced RF model approach to forecast juvenile incarceration. The results of their study revealed that, relative to the unbalanced RF model with a 1-to-1 cost ratio, the balanced RF model dramatically decreased the misclassification of non-commitment cases as non-commitment cases. The current study adopts the balanced RF model to decrease rates of misclassifying risky juveniles into the non-risky group. Meanwhile, recent studies using ML-based predictive models have explored the benefits of statistical learning approaches that address the shortcomings of parametric statistical analyses such as LR. In particular, Yang, Liu, and Coid (2010) called into question the predictive ability of LR when using with relatively small sample sizes due to the potential shrinkage of interaction effects among predictors. To examine relative predictive abilities of LR, neural networks, and classification trees, the researchers built several nested models by sequentially adding dynamic risk factors of prison inmates to predetermined risk assessment tools. Expanding the number of risk factors did not improve the LR model, whereas the neural network model including additional risk factors demonstrated significantly improved predictive ability. Rosenfeld and Lewis (2005) found similar results when using a series of nested models with additive based predictive model, a classification and regression tree (CART), and an LR model to forecast violent offenses. For conviction history, participants were asked if they had ever been convicted of a crime or pled guilty to any charges other than minor traffic violations (0 = “no” and 1 = “yes”). For incarceration history, participants were asked if they had ever spent time in a jail, prison, juvenile detention center, or other correctional facility (0 = “no” and 1 = “yes”). ## Sociodemographic variables Sociodemographic variables included gender, race, high school dropout status, and level of educational difficulty. To remedy this issue, Berk, Kriegler, and Baek (2006) suggest that the costs of false negatives and false positives should be predetermined instead of using the default 1-to-1 cost ratio. In their study, they determined that misclassifying actually risky individuals (false negative) is 10 times more harmful than misclassifying actually non-risky individuals (false positive); as a result, the error rate of misclassifying actually risky individuals into the non-risky group decreases significantly. Following this argument, Holleran and Stout (2017) applied a balanced RF model approach to forecast juvenile incarceration. The results of their study revealed that, relative to the unbalanced RF model with a 1-to-1 cost ratio, the balanced RF model dramatically decreased the misclassification of non-commitment cases as non-commitment cases. In particular, Yang, Liu, and Coid (2010) called into question the predictive ability of LR when using with relatively small sample sizes due to the potential shrinkage of interaction effects among predictors. To examine relative predictive abilities of LR, neural networks, and classification trees, the researchers built several nested models by sequentially adding dynamic risk factors of prison inmates to predetermined risk assessment tools. Expanding the number of risk factors did not improve the LR model, whereas the neural network model including additional risk factors demonstrated significantly improved predictive ability. Second, we build nested models with additive predictive factors to examine the relative predictive abilities of RF and LR models according to the type and number of predictors. Given that an ML-based predictive model would be more suitable to capture the small effects of additional variables than would LR (Rosenfeld and Lewis, 2005; Yang, Liu, and Coid, 2010), we sequentially add three different sets of risk factors to both the RF and LR models. The first set of factors comprises nine sociodemographic variables, the second set comprises nine behavioral and situational risk factors, and the third set comprises eight emotional and environmental risk factors. Consequently, the first model includes six predicting factors, the second model includes 15 factors, and the third model includes 23 factors. We designate criminal involvement of young adults as the outcome variable for all models. On the surface, the experience of arrest seems adequate to capture individuals’ criminality; however, not all arrestees actually committed the crime, and not all criminal activities result in arrest. More complex external factors intervene when deciding conviction and incarceration. Throughout the process from criminal activity to incarceration, decision-makers can be more influential than the nature of criminal involvement itself. Although not all outcome variables in this study (arrest, conviction, and incarceration) are ideal measures to capture individuals' behavioral problems, it is enough to reflect the tendency of antisocial behavior. Accordingly, the current study forecasts arrest, conviction, and incarceration exclusively, using the same sets of risk factors for each. # Method ## Data The current study used the National Longitudinal Study of Adolescent Health (Add Health) data derived from a nationally representative sample of U.S. adolescents in grades 7–12 from 1994–1995. We utilized public-use data from Wave 1 for risk factors and data from Wave 4 for the outcome variables. The Wave 1 data consists of a randomly selected half of the core sample, as well as one half of the oversample of African American adolescents with at least one parent holding a college degree. Wave 4 was designed to study trajectories from adolescence to young adulthood (age 24–32). There were a total of 6,504 respondents in this dataset. Of the total cases, 5,067 cases had valid data for the arrest outcome, 4,290 cases had valid data for the conviction outcome, and 4,935 cases had valid data for the incarceration outcome. # Measures ## Outcome variables To measure arrest history, participants were asked during the last follow-up interview conducted in Wave 4 if they had ever been arrested (0 = “no” and 1 = “yes”). For conviction history, participants were asked if they had ever been convicted of a crime or pled guilty to any charges other than minor traffic violations (0 = “no” and 1 = “yes”). For incarceration history, participants were asked if they had ever spent time in a jail, prison, juvenile detention center, or other correctional facility (0 = “no” and 1 = “yes”). ## Sociodemographic variables Sociodemographic variables included gender, race, high school dropout status, and level of educational difficulty. For gender and race, binary variables (0 = “no” and 1 = “yes”) were created using female and White, respectively, as reference categories. High school dropout status was a single binary variable (0 = “no” and 1 = “yes”). Educational difficulty was calculated as the sum (range: 0–3) of the scores of three dichotomously measured items (0 = “no” and 1 = “yes”) assessing respondents’ experiences of repeated grades, suspension, and expulsion from school. ## Behavioral/situational risk variables Behavioral and situational risk variables included violent behavior, violence victimization experience, minor delinquency, drug use, alcohol use, cigarette smoking, immature sexual intercourse, romantic relationships, and time spent with peers. Violent behavior comprised seven items assessing involvement in a serious physical fight, hurting someone badly, shooting or stabbing someone, using or threatening to use a weapon to get something from someone, taking part in a group fight, using a weapon in a fight, and pulling a knife or gun on someone in the past 12 months (α = .75). Violent victimization (0 = “no” and 1 = “yes”) experience comprised three items assessing whether someone pulled a knife or gun on the participant, shot or stabbed the participant, and cut or stabbed the participant in the past 12 months. Minor delinquency was assessed with 10 items about asking about painting graffiti or signs on someone else’s property or in a public place, damaging someone else’s property, lying to one’s parents or guardians about where and whom one was with, taking something from a store without paying for it, running away from home, driving a car without a license, stealing something worth more than 50, USD going into a house or building to steal something, stealing something worth less than 50, USD and being loud, rowdy, or unruly in a public place (α = .78). Drug use was assessed by asking participants whether they had used marijuana, cocaine, inhalants, or any other drugs including LSD, PCP, ecstasy, mushrooms, speed, ice, heroin, or pills (0 = “no” and 1 = “yes”). As for alcohol use, participants were asked whether they had consumed beer, wine, or liquor – not just a sip or taste of someone else’s drink – more than two or three times in their lives (0 = “no” and 1 = “yes”). To measure cigarette use, participants were asked whether they had ever smoked cigarettes regularly – that is, at least one cigarette every day for 30 days (0 = “no” and 1 = “yes”). To measure immature sexual intercourse, participants were asked whether they had ever had sexual intercourse before the age of adulthood (0 = “no” and 1 = “yes”). Participants were also asked whether they had had a special romantic relationship with anyone in the last 18 months (0 = “no” and 1 = “yes”). Finally, time spent with peers was measured by asking participants how many times they had been

stopped on the street to talk with someone who lives in their neighborhood (0 = “no” and 1 = “yes”), whether people in their neighborhood look out for each other (0 = “no” and 1 = “yes”), whether they use a physical fitness or recreation center in their neighborhood (0 = “no” and 1 = “yes”), and whether they usually feel safe in their neighborhood (0 = “no” and 1 = “yes”). In a similar vein, the evaluation of neighborhood items asked participants how happy they are with living in their neighborhood (range: 1–5) and how happy they would be if they had to move to some other neighborhood (range: 1–5). ## Results Table 2 shows the descriptive statistics for the variables used in the LR and RF models. To remedy this issue, Berk, Kriegler, and Baek (2006) suggest that the costs of false negatives and false positives should be predetermined instead of using the default 1-to-1 cost ratio. In their study, they determined that misclassifying actually risky individuals (false negative) is 10 times more harmful than misclassifying actually non-risky individuals (false positive); as a result, the error rate of misclassifying actually risky individuals into the non-risky group decreases significantly. Following this argument, Holleran and Stout (2017) applied a balanced RF model approach to forecast juvenile incarceration. The results of their study revealed that, relative to the unbalanced RF model with a 1-to-1 cost ratio, the balanced RF model dramatically decreased the misclassification of non-commitment cases as non-commitment cases. Meanwhile, recent studies using ML-based predictive models have explored the benefits of statistical learning approaches that address the shortcomings of parametric statistical analyses such as LR. In particular, Yang, Liu, and Coid (2010) called into question the predictive ability of LR when using with relatively small sample sizes due to the potential shrinkage of interaction effects among predictors. To examine relative predictive abilities of LR, neural networks, and classification trees, the researchers built several nested models by sequentially adding dynamic risk factors of prison inmates to predetermined risk assessment tools. Expanding the number of risk factors did not improve the LR model, whereas the neural network model including additional risk factors demonstrated significantly improved predictive ability. To remedy this issue, Berk, Kriegler, and Baek (2006) suggest that the costs of false negatives and false positives should be predetermined instead of using the default 1-to-1 cost ratio. Given that an ML-based predictive model would be more suitable to capture the small effects of additional variables than would LR (Rosenfeld and Lewis, 2005; Yang, Liu, and Coid, 2010), we sequentially add three different sets of risk factors to both the RF and LR models. The first set of factors comprises nine sociodemographic variables, the second set comprises nine behavioral and situational risk factors, and the third set comprises eight emotional and environmental risk factors. Consequently, the first model includes six predicting factors, the second model includes 15 factors, and the third model includes 23 factors. We designate criminal involvement of young adults as the outcome variable for all models. On the surface, the experience of arrest seems adequate to capture individuals’ criminality; however, not all arrestees actually committed the crime, and not all criminal activities result in arrest. More complex external factors intervene when deciding conviction and incarceration. Throughout the process from criminal activity to incarceration, decision-makers can be more influential than the nature of criminal involvement itself. Although not all outcome variables in this study (arrest, conviction, and incarceration) are ideal measures to capture individuals' behavioral problems, it is enough to reflect the tendency of antisocial behavior. Accordingly, the current study forecasts arrest, conviction, and incarceration exclusively, using the same sets of risk factors for each. # Method ## Data The current study used the National Longitudinal Study of Adolescent Health (Add Health) data derived from a nationally representative sample of U.S. adolescents in grades 7–12 from 1994–1995. We utilized public-use data from Wave 1 for risk factors and data from Wave 4 for the outcome variables. The Wave 1 data consists of a randomly selected half of the core sample, as well as one half of the oversample of African American adolescents with at least one parent holding a college degree. Wave 4 was designed to study trajectories from adolescence to young adulthood (age 24–32). There were a total of 6,504 respondents in this dataset. Of the total cases, 5,067 cases had valid data for the arrest outcome, 4,290 cases had valid data for the conviction outcome, and 4,935 cases had valid data for the incarceration outcome. # Measures ## Outcome variables To measure arrest history, participants were asked during the last follow-up interview conducted in Wave 4 if they had ever been arrested (0 = “no” and 1 = “yes”). For conviction history, participants were asked if they had ever been convicted of a crime or pled guilty to any charges other than minor traffic violations (0 = “no” and 1 = “yes”). For incarceration history, participants were asked if they had ever spent time in a jail, prison, juvenile detention center, or other correctional facility (0 = “no” and 1 = “yes”). ## Sociodemographic variables Sociodemographic variables included gender, race, high school dropout status, and level of educational difficulty. For gender and race, binary variables (0 = “no” and 1 = “yes”) were created using female and White, respectively, as reference categories. High school dropout status was a single binary variable (0 = “no” and 1 = “yes”). Educational difficulty was calculated as the sum (range: 0–3) of the scores of three dichotomously measured items (0 = “no” and 1 = “yes”) assessing respondents’ experiences of repeated grades, suspension, and expulsion from school. ## Behavioral/situational risk variables Behavioral and situational risk variables included violent behavior, violence victimization experience, minor delinquency, drug use, alcohol use, cigarette smoking, immature sexual intercourse, romantic relationships, and time spent with peers. Violent behavior comprised seven items assessing involvement in a serious physical fight, hurting someone badly, shooting or stabbing someone, using or threatening to use a weapon to get something from someone, taking part in a group fight, using a weapon in a fight, and pulling a knife or gun on someone in the past 12 months (α = .75). Violent victimization (0 = “no” and 1 = “yes”) experience comprised three items assessing whether someone pulled a knife or gun on the participant, shot or stabbed the participant, and cut or stabbed the participant in the past 12 months. Minor delinquency was assessed with 10 items about asking about painting graffiti or signs on someone else’s property or in a public place, damaging someone else’s property, lying to one’s parents or guardians about where and whom one was with, taking something from a store without paying for it, running away from home, driving a car without a license, stealing something worth more than 50, USD going into a house or building to steal something, stealing something worth less than 50, USD and being loud, rowdy, or unruly in a public place (α = .78). Drug use was assessed by asking participants whether they had used marijuana, cocaine, inhalants, or any other drugs including LSD, PCP, ecstasy, mushrooms, speed, ice, heroin, or pills (0 = “no” and 1 = “yes”). As for alcohol use, participants were asked whether they had consumed beer, wine, or liquor – not just a sip or taste of someone else’s drink – more than two or three times in their lives (0 = “no” and 1 = “yes”). To measure cigarette use, participants were asked whether they had ever smoked cigarettes regularly – that is, at least one cigarette every day for 30 days (0 = “no” and 1 = “yes”). To measure immature sexual intercourse, participants were asked whether they had ever had sexual intercourse before the age of adulthood (0 = “no” and 1 = “yes”). Participants were also asked whether they had had a special romantic relationship with anyone in the last 18 months (0 = “no” and 1 = “yes”). Finally, time spent with peers was measured by asking participants how many times they had been

“just hung out” with friends during the past week (range: 0–3). ## Emotional/environmental variables Emotional/environmental variables included hopelessness, depression, suicide attempts, physical abuse, neglect, religion, neighborhood collective efficacy, and evaluation of one’s neighborhood. Hopelessness was assessed with items asking participants how often during the past week that they felt hopeful about the future (reverse-coded), felt their life had been a failure, and felt life was not worth living. To measure physical abuse, participants were asked how often their parents or other adult caregivers slapped, hit, or kicked them (range: 0–5). For neglect, participants were asked about how often (range: 0–5), by the time they had started sixth grade, that their parents or other adult caregivers had left them home alone when an adult should have been with them, as well as about parents or other adult caregivers not taking care of their basic needs (e.g., hygiene, food, clothing). One item asked participants about the importance of religion in their lives (range: 0–5). Second, we build nested models with additive predictive factors to examine the relative predictive abilities of RF and LR models according to the type and number of predictors. Given that an ML-based predictive model would be more suitable to capture the small effects of additional variables than would LR (Rosenfeld and Lewis, 2005; Yang, Liu, and Coid, 2010), we sequentially add three different sets of risk factors to both the RF and LR models. The first set of factors comprises nine sociodemographic variables, the second set comprises nine behavioral and situational risk factors, and the third set comprises eight emotional and environmental risk factors. Consequently, the first model includes six predicting factors, the second model includes 15 factors, and the third model includes 23 factors. We designate criminal involvement of young adults as the outcome variable for all models. On the surface, the experience of arrest seems adequate to capture individuals’ criminality; however, not all arrestees actually committed the crime, and not all criminal activities result in arrest. More complex external factors intervene when deciding conviction and incarceration. Throughout the process from criminal activity to incarceration, decision-makers can be more influential than the nature of criminal involvement itself. Although not all outcome variables in this study (arrest, conviction, and incarceration) are ideal measures to capture individuals' behavioral problems, it is enough to reflect the tendency of antisocial behavior. Accordingly, the current study forecasts arrest, conviction, and incarceration exclusively, using the same sets of risk factors for each. # Method ## Data The current study used the National Longitudinal Study of Adolescent Health (Add Health) data derived from a nationally representative sample of U.S. adolescents in grades 7–12 from 1994–1995. We utilized public-use data from Wave 1 for risk factors and data from Wave 4 for the outcome variables. The Wave 1 data consists of a randomly selected half of the core sample, as well as one half of the oversample of African American adolescents with at least one parent holding a college degree. Wave 4 was designed to study trajectories from adolescence to young adulthood (age 24–32). There were a total of 6,504 respondents in this dataset. Of the total cases, 5,067 cases had valid data for the arrest outcome, 4,290 cases had valid data for the conviction outcome, and 4,935 cases had valid data for the incarceration outcome. # Measures ## Outcome variables To measure arrest history, participants were asked during the last follow-up interview conducted in Wave 4 if they had ever been arrested (0 = “no” and 1 = “yes”). The Wave 1 data consists of a randomly selected half of the core sample, as well as one half of the oversample of African American adolescents with at least one parent holding a college degree. Wave 4 was designed to study trajectories from adolescence to young adulthood (age 24–32). There were a total of 6,504 respondents in this dataset. Of the total cases, 5,067 cases had valid data for the arrest outcome, 4,290 cases had valid data for the conviction outcome, and 4,935 cases had valid data for the incarceration outcome. # Measures ## Outcome variables To measure arrest history, participants were asked during the last follow-up interview conducted in Wave 4 if they had ever been arrested (0 = “no” and 1 = “yes”). For conviction history, participants were asked if they had ever been convicted of a crime or pled guilty to any charges other than minor traffic violations (0 = “no” and 1 = “yes”). High school dropout status was a single binary variable (0 = “no” and 1 = “yes”). To remedy this issue, Berk, Kriegler, and Baek (2006) suggest that the costs of false negatives and false positives should be predetermined instead of using the default 1-to-1 cost ratio. In their study, they determined that misclassifying actually risky individuals (false negative) is 10 times more harmful than misclassifying actually non-risky individuals (false positive); as a result, the error rate of misclassifying actually risky individuals into the non-risky group decreases significantly. Following this argument, Holleran and Stout (2017) applied a balanced RF model approach to forecast juvenile incarceration. The results of their study revealed that, relative to the unbalanced RF model with a 1-to-1 cost ratio, the balanced RF model dramatically decreased the misclassification of non-commitment cases as non-commitment cases. The current study adopts the balanced RF model to decrease rates of misclassifying risky juveniles into the non-risky group. Meanwhile, recent studies using ML-based predictive models have explored the benefits of statistical learning approaches that address the shortcomings of parametric statistical analyses such as LR. In particular, Yang, Liu, and Coid (2010) called into question the predictive ability of LR when using with relatively small sample sizes due to the potential shrinkage of interaction effects among predictors. To examine relative predictive abilities of LR, neural networks, and classification trees, the researchers built several nested models by sequentially adding dynamic risk factors of prison inmates to predetermined risk assessment tools. Expanding the number of risk factors did not improve the LR model, whereas the neural network model including additional risk factors demonstrated significantly improved predictive ability. Rosenfeld and Lewis (2005) found similar results when using a series of nested models with additive based predictive model, a classification and regression tree (CART), and an LR model to forecast violent offenses. Consistent with Yang, Liu, and Coid (2010) results, the overall accuracy of the CART model significantly improved as predictors were added, while the LR model showed no significant changes when adding risk factors. In sum, more work is needed to assess the utility of ML methods in crime prediction and explore the contingencies in which their predictive power is enhanced. ## Current Study Taking lessons from the studies outlined above, the current study aims to examine the predictive accuracy of balanced RF models using two schemes. To improve the predictive accuracy of individual behaviors in the future, a series of Machine Learning (ML) methods have emerged and are being widely applied in various fields of behavioral science (Berk et al. 2009; Samuel 1959). Especially in the 1990s, some advanced ML techniques attracted the attention of psychiatrists for their ability to screen individuals for risky mental disorders (Gardner et al. 1996; Pflueger et al. 2015; Steadman et al. 2000). For clinical practitioners, results forecasted by ML are more effective in identifying high-risk patients compared to conventional risk assessment processes, such as summing item scores on a risk assessment tool. Similarly, researchers have attempted to apply ML in forecasting offending behaviors and recidivism.
