AI Models The built model was developed under the machine learning approach in which Random Forest (RF), Support Vector Machines (SVM), and K-Nearest Neighbors (KNN) classifiers were selected. Additionally, a cross-validation strategy was employed to determine the model’s efficiency and proper parameterization. Regarding the cross-validation process, the original dataset was initially partitioned into a 70-30 scheme, where 30 % of the data was reserved for final validation and the remaining 70 % for cross-validation. The data was partitioned into 4 subsets for cross-validation. The selection of the number of subsets was determined based on the quantity of data in the moderate and severe classes, ensuring that each validation set contained at least 3 data points from each class. RF, or Random Forest, is a model composed of multiple individual decision trees, each of which is trained with a slightly different sample of the training data, generated using a technique known as bootstrapping (Louppe, 2014). Then, to make predictions on new observations, the predictions of all the trees that make up the model are combined. SVM, Support Vector Machine, is a supervised learning technique that requires labeled data and is based on the principles of statistical learning and convex optimization. In the training process, the algorithm analyzes the input data and identifies patterns in a multidimensional feature space called a hyperplane (Betancourt, 2005). Its central objective is to efficiently find a hyperplane that can separate the different categories present in the data, thereby enabling the effective classification of new data. It has also been associated with different mental disorders present among the Colombian population, such as mixed anxiety and depression disorder, unspecified anxiety, and generalized anxiety (Procuraduría General de la Nación de Colombia, 2023). Anxiety has been linked bi-directionally with the consumption of psychoactive substances. Continuous consumption of these substances can trigger affective symptoms or anxiety disorders. Conversely, it has been determined that in individuals with anxiety, the higher the intensity of the symptoms, the greater the likelihood of substance consumption (Contreras-Olive et al., 2020). A study conducted with the young population reports how substance abuse and consumption not only generate anxiety disorders but also depression and these disorders are directly related to dependency (Encina et al., 2023). The highlights highlighted underscore the need to strengthen actions for the promotion, prevention, and early detection of anxiety. These actions work by identifying individual, social, and structural determinants and then intervening to reduce risks, promote resilience, and establish conducive environments for mental health (WHO, 2022b). One of the innovative tools supporting these interventions is Artificial Intelligence (AI). This refers to the ability of computer systems to predict outcomes that have been conceived by humans in comparable situations (El-Sherif et al., 2022). Artificial Intelligence (AI) models in healthcare are currently contributing to the field known as predictive medicine, which seeks to identify patients at risk and support decision-making in the healthcare system for their benefit and that of communities (Ruiz & Velásquez, 2023; Tigga, Garg, 2022a). As an example, studies such as those conducted by Kumar et al. (2020), Albagmi et al. (2022), and Wei et al. (2023) have used AI models to classify anxiety, yielding good results. Another way AI is applied for anxiety detection is through biolinguistic markers identified and classified with AI, as used by Wang et al. (2023). AI has also been utilized to identify and classify electroencephalographic (EEG) signals to detect and classify anxiety (Tigga, Garg, 2022b; Al-Ezzi et al., 2022). Method ## 2.1. Participants The minimum sample size was determined using the formula appropriate for the known sampling frame, taking into consideration the young population of the municipality where the study was conducted, which totals 3843 individuals, with a prevalence of anxiety symptoms of 23.3 % within this demographic (Ministerio de Salud y Protección Social de Colombia, 2015). Based on these parameters, the required minimum sample size was calculated to be 156 individuals. To accommodate potential attrition or non-response, an additional 10 % was added to this initial estimate, resulting in a minimum sample size of 172 individuals. A total of 234 young individuals were surveyed, who met the inclusion criteria defined for the study, who were aged between 18 and 28 years, residing in the department of Caldas-Colombia, agreeing to participate in the research, and signing the informed consent. As exclusion criteria, a cognitive impairment that prevented the understanding of the informed consent or acute decompensation of any ## 2.2. Materials The database was constructed from information collected during field visits, where trained personnel administered a questionnaire developed by the research team. This team comprises three professionals in psychiatry, two in public health, and three in computer science. The questionnaire included sixteen sociodemographic questions (Table 1), six from the Penn Alcohol Craving Scale (PACS), nine from the Patient Health Questionnaire (PHQ-9), seven from the Generalized Anxiety Disorder (GAD-7) questionnaire, and the Severity of Dependence Scale (SDS). The Penn Alcohol Craving Scale (PACS) is a widely recognized assessment tool designed to measure the intensity of alcohol craving in individuals experiencing issues related to alcohol consumption. Developed at the University of Pennsylvania, the PACS has become a fundamental instrument in both clinical settings and research related to alcoholism and alcohol use disorders. Comprising a series of carefully selected items, this scale allows healthcare professionals and researchers to subjectively evaluate the intensity of alcohol cravings at a given moment. In

Additionally, Castro-Pérez Vargas et al. (2022) reported that the most influential factor in the development of depression and anxiety was a history of mental illness. However, these findings contradict other studies that have reported no association between psychiatric history and increased anxiety, particularly during the pandemic (Murphy et al., 2023). They found that individuals with psychiatric histories did not worsen during this period, whereas those most affected were those without such histories (Pan et al., 2021). It is possible to infer that these contradictory results are related to studies that did not find a higher risk of anxiety in individuals with personal histories of mental illness conducted during the COVID-19 pandemic. During this period, cases of acute anxiety likely increased in individuals without psychiatric histories due to factors such as COVID-19 illness, social distancing policies, mandatory lockdowns, and other psychosocial factors, all of which were identified as risk factors for mental health problems in individuals without psychiatric histories (Zhu et al., 2023). Additionally, in the present study, having a family history of mental illness behaved as a risk factor for anxiety. This finding aligns with what was reported by Brummelhuis et al. (2024), who conducted a cross-sectional study of the general population and reported that being the child of parents with a mental illness was associated with higher levels of anxiety and depressive symptoms. Moreover, dysfunctional family relationships during childhood were associated with the severity of mental health problems in adults who grew up with a parent with a mental illness. Similarly, Serrano et al. (2023) reported that having a family history of depression was positively associated with depression, anxiety, and stress. The authors mention that this result may be explained by hereditary factors and the difficulties of caring for a family member with a mental illness. As evidenced in the analysis called SHAP values, the question PHQ9.6: "Feeling bad about yourself, or that you are a failure, or have let yourself or your family down?" while being part of the instrument to assess depression, shows characteristics that could well be associated with states of anxiety in the evaluated subject. This characteristic is relevant to the model and contributes significantly, as this information is external to the instrument itself for supporting the detection of GAD7 anxiety. This result is consistent with what Serrano et al. (2023) expressed in terms of the relationship between both disorders. Another relevant finding is the relationship between anxiety and positive responses to the questions in the GAD-7 instrument, which detects symptoms of depression. This result aligns with what has been reported by other authors who have determined that in adolescents and young people, anxiety and depression often exhibit a pattern of comorbidity. In this regard, Wang, Mou, et al. (2023) reported a comorbidity rate of anxiety and depression among adolescents at 31.6 % in their study. Similarly, Choi et al. (2020) reported how comorbidity between anxiety and depression corresponds to a common syndrome and is not only associated with immense personal and familial suffering but also leads to other adverse outcomes such as academic failure, cognitive function deterioration, poor interpersonal relationships, and even suicide. In the present study, three machine learning models were tested: SVM, KNN, and RF. Superior results were obtained compared to other studies with similar methodologies. For instance, Nemesure et al. (2021) reported a sensitivity of 70 %, whereas in the present study, the best model achieved 91 %. Similarly, Qusrawi et al. (2022) reported an accuracy, sensitivity, and F1 score of 82.9 %, compared to 91 % for the same values in the present study. When observing the results obtained with the RF model, there is a significant improvement compared to previous studies. For example, Zhou et al. (2023) used an RF model on a population of 319 individuals, obtaining an excellent F1-score metric of 96.6 %, but with accuracy, precision, and recall values of 87.4 %. , and 87.6 %, respectively, which could indicate overfitting. Another case of improved results can be seen in Bhatnagar et al. (2023), where on a population of 127 students, they applied an RF model and SVM, showing accuracies of 75.5 % and 78.9 %, respectively. Another precedent demonstrating improved results is Priya et al. (2020), in which they used the RF model on a population of 348 participants, obtaining the following metrics: accuracy of 71.4 %, precision of 43.1 %, recall of 51 %, and an F1-score of 47 %. Other studies report higher efficiency percentages; however, these have been conducted under different methodologies, which include the use of data sources such as medical images, video recordings, and EEG signals, among others. An example of this is the work of Xie et al. (2022), where they achieved a 94.6 % accuracy using video recordings and convolutional neural networks. It is worth noting that the present study exclusively requires the application of a questionnaire battery, making it more cost-effective than those employing other data sources. With the above, it is relevant to affirm that traditional machine learning techniques remain efficient in terms of determining the anxiety condition. This is particularly valuable as these models can be trained with a reduced number of variables, without requiring large volumes of information and with modest computational support by current standards. Additionally, data collection is low-cost and can be implemented without the need for expensive technologies. In coherence, the present model can be efficiently deployed across communities and contribute timely to anxiety detection efforts. ## 5. Once the best model among the three has been chosen, an analysis of the features with the greatest contribution to the construction of the RF model is conducted. For this purpose, SHAP approach is used, which provides a way to assign contributions to each feature in the classification of a model (Hamilton & Papadopoulos, 2024). SHAP values indicate how each feature contributes to the change in classification compared to the average classification of the model. A high SHAP value for a feature means that the feature had a significant influence on the classification. As shown in Fig. 7, the features that contribute the most are the questions from the GAD7 test, which is coherent with reality, as the test is a way to measure the risk of anxiety in a person. Additionally, the PHQ9 test makes a significant contribution, which continues to positively contrast with reality, as (Choi et al., 2020) explain the relationship between anxiety and depression, where depressed patients often exhibit symptoms of anxiety such as difficulty relaxing, which corresponds to GAD7_4. In the analyses conducted, the SHAP and feature importance techniques were applied, which provide a visual associated with the contribution that each feature makes to the classification models. In the case of SHAP, the most relevant features were GAD7_2, GAD7_3, GAD7_1, GAD7_5, GAD7_6, and the question PHQ9_6. For the feature importance analysis Fig. 8, the most significant questions were 37(GAD7_2), 41 (GAD7_6), 38(GAD7_3), 42(GAD7_7), and 39(GAD7_4). AI Models The built model was developed under the machine learning approach in which Random Forest (RF), Support Vector Machines (SVM), and K-Nearest Neighbors (KNN) classifiers were selected. The data was partitioned into 4 subsets for cross-validation. The selection of the number of subsets was determined based on the quantity of data in the moderate and severe classes, ensuring that each validation set contained at least 3 data points from each class. RF, or Random Forest, is a model composed of multiple individual decision trees, each of which is trained with a slightly different sample of the training data, generated using a technique known as bootstrapping (Louppe, 2014). Then, to make predictions on new observations, the predictions of all the trees that make up the model are combined. SVM, Support Vector Machine, is a supervised learning technique that requires labeled data and is based on the principles of statistical learning and convex optimization. In the training process, the algorithm analyzes the input data and identifies patterns in a multidimensional feature space called a hyperplane (Betancourt, 2005). Its central objective is to efficiently find a hyperplane that can separate the different categories present in the data, thereby enabling the effective classification of new data. addition to providing a quantitative measure of alcohol craving, the PACS has also proven useful in identifying triggers for alcohol consumption and assessing the risk of relapse in individuals undergoing recovery. Its systematic and validated use has significantly contributed to the understanding and treatment of alcohol addiction, offering a valuable tool for addressing this public health issue more effectively (Flannery et al., 1999). The Patient Health Questionnaire 9 (PHQ-9) is a Likert-type scale used to measure depression symptoms. It consists of 9 items or questions directly related to the symptoms of depression described in the DSM-V, the guide for clinical diagnosis. These questions are classified from 0 to 3. When observing the questions of the PHQ-9 Test, the direct correlation of each one with a specific symptom of depression is highlighted. For example, the question "Have you felt bad about yourself, or feel like you're a failure, or have let yourself or your family down?" clearly reflects the presence of low self-esteem. Similarly, the question "Have you had thoughts of being better off dead, or of hurting yourself in some way?" evidences the presence of intrusive or self-harming thoughts. This direct link between the questions and the symptoms underscores the usefulness of the PHQ-9 Test as a tool to assess and understand the presence of depression (Cassiani-Miranda et al., 2021). The Generalized Anxiety Disorder 7 (GAD-7) questionnaire measures generalized anxiety disorder and consist of 7 multiple-choice questions, each with four options ("Not at all", scored: 0, "Several days", scored: 1, "More than half the days", scored: 2, "Nearly every day", scored: 3) (Table 2). This questionnaire is evaluated by summing the scores of each question, classifying each individual into the following ranges: 0-4 no anxiety, 5-9 mild, 10-14 moderate, 15-21 severe (Snijders et al., 2021; Zhao, 2023). The GAD-7 rating scale is used as the target variable for model training, along with other variables collected in the data collection instrument (Spitzer et al., 2006). The Severity of Dependence Scale (SDS) is a tool designed to assess users’ dependence on narcotics, consisting of five questions. Through this tool, the user is asked about the most consumed narcotic, while the following four questions focus on assessing their dependence on that specific substance. This tool has been developed to provide an accurate measure of narcotic dependence. The relationship between drug use and depression has been reported by previous studies (Pinelo-Camacho et al., 2022), highlighting a cyclical relationship between alcohol consumption, cannabis, and the development of severe depressive symptoms (Gossop et al., 1995). K-Nearest-Neighbor (KNN) is a supervised instance-based machine learning algorithm. It can be used to classify new samples (discrete values) or to predict (regression, continuous values). Essentially, it serves to classify values by seeking the “most similar” data points (by proximity) learned in the training stage and making predictions of new points based on that classification (Cunningham & Delany, 2021). ## 2.4. Data analysis To initiate processing, a method was applied to search for NaN-type data or empty values (Null). Good practices in AI development (Tubares-Soto et al., 2022) and the framework for ethical data management from the IDB (Denis et al., 2021) indicate that applying this initial filter provides transparency and credibility to the information used in AI development. Subsequently, one-hot encoding was carried out using the scikit-learn library, allowing all character-type responses to be converted to numeric values. This will facilitate the use of data in ML model testing. The KNN method represents a non-parametric classification model. To assign a category to a given data point, the algorithm examines the information of its k nearest neighbors. This process helps determine which group the data point belongs to. In the specific context of depression classification, the KNN model uses features extracted from the data. As a supervised learning approach, the KNN model starts with training using existing data. This allows the algorithm to develop an understanding of the relationships between the features and the corresponding classes. The data analysis was conducted by merging all the questionnaires into a single database. Specifically, we integrated sociodemographic data, the Penn Alcohol Craving Scale, the GAD-7, the PHQ-9, and the SDS. All these data points were combined into one comprehensive dataset for analysis. It is important to note, however, that the dependent variable in our model is the total score of the GAD-7 test, which is calculated as described in Table 2. Additionally, the GAD-7 SCORE feature was created, representing the sum of the test questions’ results. Subsequently, the target variable was generated, which is multinomial, as it responds to the four possible groups in which a person can be found, as explained earlier in the generalities. Finally, the sociodemographic and clinical characteristics were analyzed using the SPSS program licensed by the University of Caldas. For the calculation of Odds Ratios (OR), the variables predicting anxiety were dichotomized, and from this, it was sought to identify whether they were protective or risk factors for the studied event. ## 2.5.

Artificial Intelligence (AI) models in healthcare are currently contributing to the field known as predictive medicine, which seeks to identify patients at risk and support decision-making in the healthcare system for their benefit and that of communities (Ruiz & Velásquez, 2023; Tigga, Garg, 2022a). As an example, studies such as those conducted by Kumar et al. (2020), Albagmi et al. (2022), and Wei et al. (2023) have used AI models to classify anxiety, yielding good results. Another way AI is applied for anxiety detection is through biolinguistic markers identified and classified with AI, as used by Wang et al. (2023). AI has also been utilized to identify and classify electroencephalographic (EEG) signals to detect and classify anxiety (Tigga, Garg, 2022b; Al-Ezzi et al., 2022). In this context, the objective of this study is to develop a model that identifies the factors associated with anxiety symptoms in young people, based on sociodemographic, clinical, and lifestyle information, supported by artificial intelligence (AI). psychiatric condition was established; however, no participants with these characteristics were found. # 2. Method ## 2.1. Participants The minimum sample size was determined using the formula appropriate for the known sampling frame, taking into consideration the young population of the municipality where the study was conducted, which totals 3843 individuals, with a prevalence of anxiety symptoms of 23.3 % within this demographic (Ministerio de Salud y Protección Social de Colombia, 2015). Based on these parameters, the required minimum sample size was calculated to be 156 individuals. To accommodate potential attrition or non-response, an additional 10 % was added to this initial estimate, resulting in a minimum sample size of 172 individuals. A total of 234 young individuals were surveyed, who met the inclusion criteria defined for the study, who were aged between 18 and 28 years, residing in the department of Caldas-Colombia, agreeing to participate in the research, and signing the informed consent. As exclusion criteria, a cognitive impairment that prevented the understanding of the informed consent or acute decompensation of any ## 2.2. Materials The database was constructed from information collected during field visits, where trained personnel administered a questionnaire developed by the research team. This team comprises three professionals in psychiatry, two in public health, and three in computer science. The questionnaire included sixteen sociodemographic questions (Table 1), six from the Penn Alcohol Craving Scale (PACS), nine from the Patient Health Questionnaire (PHQ-9), seven from the Generalized Anxiety Disorder (GAD-7) questionnaire, and the Severity of Dependence Scale (SDS). The Penn Alcohol Craving Scale (PACS) is a widely recognized assessment tool designed to measure the intensity of alcohol craving in individuals experiencing issues related to alcohol consumption. Developed at the University of Pennsylvania, the PACS has become a fundamental instrument in both clinical settings and research related to alcoholism and alcohol use disorders. Comprising a series of carefully selected items, this scale allows healthcare professionals and researchers to subjectively evaluate the intensity of alcohol cravings at a given moment. In addition to providing a quantitative measure of alcohol craving, the PACS has also proven useful in identifying triggers for alcohol consumption and assessing the risk of relapse in individuals undergoing recovery. Its systematic and validated use has significantly contributed to the understanding and treatment of alcohol addiction, offering a valuable tool for addressing this public health issue more effectively (Flannery et al., 1999). The Patient Health Questionnaire 9 (PHQ-9) is a Likert-type scale used to measure depression symptoms. It consists of 9 items or questions directly related to the symptoms of depression described in the DSM-V, the guide for clinical diagnosis. These questions are classified from 0 to 3. When observing the questions of the PHQ-9 Test, the direct correlation of each one with a specific symptom of depression is highlighted. For example, the question "Have you felt bad about yourself, or feel like you're a failure, or have let yourself or your family down?" clearly reflects the presence of low self-esteem. Similarly, the question "Have you had thoughts of being better off dead, or of hurting yourself in some way?" evidences the presence of intrusive or self-harming thoughts. This direct link between the questions and the symptoms underscores the usefulness of the PHQ-9 Test as a tool to assess and understand the presence of depression (Cassiani-Miranda et al., 2021). The Generalized Anxiety Disorder 7 (GAD-7) questionnaire measures generalized anxiety disorder and consist of 7 multiple-choice questions, each with four options ("Not at all", scored: 0, "Several days", scored: 1, "More than half the days", scored: 2, "Nearly every day", scored: 3) (Table 2). This questionnaire is evaluated by summing the scores of each question, classifying each individual into the following ranges: 0-4 no anxiety, 5-9 mild, 10-14 moderate, 15-21 severe (Snijders et al., 2021; Zhao, 2023). The GAD-7 rating scale is used as the target variable for model training, along with other variables collected in the data collection instrument (Spitzer et al., 2006). The Severity of Dependence Scale (SDS) is a tool designed to assess users’ dependence on narcotics, consisting of five questions. Materials The database was constructed from information collected during field visits, where trained personnel administered a questionnaire developed by the research team. This team comprises three professionals in psychiatry, two in public health, and three in computer science. The questionnaire included sixteen sociodemographic questions (Table 1), six from the Penn Alcohol Craving Scale (PACS), nine from the Patient Health Questionnaire (PHQ-9), seven from the Generalized Anxiety Disorder (GAD-7) questionnaire, and the Severity of Dependence Scale (SDS). The Penn Alcohol Craving Scale (PACS) is a widely recognized assessment tool designed to measure the intensity of alcohol craving in individuals experiencing issues related to alcohol consumption. Developed at the University of Pennsylvania, the PACS has become a fundamental instrument in both clinical settings and research related to alcoholism and alcohol use disorders. Comprising a series of carefully selected items, this scale allows healthcare professionals and researchers to subjectively evaluate the intensity of alcohol cravings at a given moment. In addition to providing a quantitative measure of alcohol craving, the PACS has also proven useful in identifying triggers for alcohol consumption and assessing the risk of relapse in individuals undergoing recovery. Its systematic and validated use has significantly contributed to the understanding and treatment of alcohol addiction, offering a valuable tool for addressing this public health issue more effectively (Flannery et al., 1999). The Patient Health Questionnaire 9 (PHQ-9) is a Likert-type scale used to measure depression symptoms. It consists of 9 items or questions directly related to the symptoms of depression described in the DSM-V, the guide for clinical diagnosis. These questions are classified from 0 to 3. When observing the questions of the PHQ-9 Test, the direct correlation of each one with a specific symptom of depression is highlighted. For example, the question "Have you felt bad about yourself, or feel like you're a failure, or have let yourself or your family down?" clearly reflects the presence of low self-esteem. Similarly, the question "Have you had thoughts of being better off dead, or of hurting yourself in some way?" evidences the presence of intrusive or self-harming thoughts. This direct link between the questions and the symptoms underscores the usefulness of the PHQ-9 Test as a tool to assess and understand the presence of depression (Cassiani-Miranda et al., 2021). The Generalized Anxiety Disorder 7 (GAD-7) questionnaire measures generalized anxiety disorder and consist of 7 multiple-choice questions, each with four options ("Not at all", scored: 0, "Several days", scored: 1, "More than half the days", scored: 2, "Nearly every day", scored: 3) (Table 2). This questionnaire is evaluated by summing the scores of each question, classifying each individual into the following ranges: 0-4 no anxiety, 5-9 mild, 10-14 moderate, 15-21 severe (Snijders et al., 2021; Zhao, 2023). The GAD-7 rating scale is used as the target variable for model training, along with other variables collected in the data collection instrument (Spitzer et al., 2006). The Severity of Dependence Scale (SDS) is a tool designed to assess users’ dependence on narcotics, consisting of five questions. Through this tool, the user is asked about the most consumed narcotic, while the following four questions focus on assessing their dependence on that specific substance. This tool has been developed to provide an accurate measure of narcotic dependence. The relationship between drug use and depression has been reported by previous studies (Pinelo-Camacho et al., 2022), highlighting a cyclical relationship between alcohol consumption, cannabis, and the development of severe depressive symptoms (Gossop et al., 1995). Once the best model among the three has been chosen, an analysis of the features with the greatest contribution to the construction of the RF model is conducted. For this purpose, SHAP approach is used, which provides a way to assign contributions to each feature in the classification of a model (Hamilton & Papadopoulos, 2024). SHAP values indicate how each feature contributes to the change in classification compared to the average classification of the model. A high SHAP value for a feature means that the feature had a significant influence on the classification. As shown in Fig. 7, the features that contribute the most are the questions from the GAD7 test, which is coherent with reality, as the test is a way to measure the risk of anxiety in a person. Additionally, the PHQ9 test makes a significant contribution, which continues to positively contrast with reality, as (Choi et al., 2020) explain the relationship between anxiety and depression, where depressed patients often exhibit symptoms of anxiety such as difficulty relaxing, which corresponds to GAD7_4. In the analyses conducted, the SHAP and feature importance techniques were applied, which provide a visual associated with the contribution that each feature makes to the classification models. In the case of SHAP, the most relevant features were GAD7_2, GAD7_3, GAD7_1, GAD7_5, GAD7_6, and the question PHQ9_6. For the feature importance analysis Fig. 8, the most significant questions were 37(GAD7_2), 41 (GAD7_6), 38(GAD7_3), 42(GAD7_7), and 39(GAD7_4). The relevance of the questions associated with GAD7 is evident since this form focuses on anxiety disorder-related questions; however, it is relevant that the characteristic PHQ9_6 is significant in this analysis as it focuses on depression symptoms. It was found that characteristics such as the educational level of parents and the frequency of alcohol consumption make a significant contribution to the construction of the model and the respective classification of anxiety. In line with the above, an analysis of the association of the most relevant characteristics found in the contrast method with feature importances from the scikit-learn library was conducted, as well as external characteristics such as affiliation to social security, since according to (Ruiz-Rodríguez et al., 2017), there is a protective relationship with health coverage, educational levels, and different types of occupations, as evidenced by (WHO, 2022) where the level of education and occupation of an individual are differentiating characteristics when it comes to experiencing anxiety. Lastly, personal and family history, according to (Dueñas-Amaya, 2019), anxiety and depression are mental disorders of potentially genetic origin, and their comorbidity is evidenced in a close bidirectional relationship. As observed in Table 4, when analyzing the OR values, it is possible to conclude that age acts as a protective factor for anxiety with a p-value of 0.0020. Note how having a family history of depression marks a 5 times higher probability of having anxiety, and when having a family history of anxiety, this probability increases, meaning there is a 13 times higher probability of suffering from anxiety in those with a family history of this pathology. For both variables, the difference was statistically significant with a p-value of 0.0000. Regarding the behavior of GAD7 responses, in the model, factors that predict anxiety with the strongest association include question 2 (in the last 15 days, have you been unable to control or avoid worrying), wherein those who have experienced this situation are 159 times more likely to suffer from anxiety. Additionally, individuals who have experienced excessive worry about different things or situations in the last 15 days have 100 times more risk of anxiety than those who do not have this sensation. Materials The database was constructed from information collected during field visits, where trained personnel administered a questionnaire developed by the research team. This team comprises three professionals in psychiatry, two in public health, and three in computer science. The questionnaire included sixteen sociodemographic questions (Table 1), six from the Penn Alcohol Craving Scale (PACS), nine from the Patient Health Questionnaire (PHQ-9), seven from the Generalized Anxiety Disorder (GAD-7) questionnaire, and the Severity of Dependence Scale (SDS). The Penn Alcohol Craving Scale (PACS) is a widely recognized assessment tool designed to measure the intensity of alcohol craving in individuals experiencing issues related to alcohol consumption. Developed at the University of Pennsylvania, the PACS has become a fundamental instrument in both clinical settings and research related to alcoholism and alcohol use disorders. Comprising a series of carefully selected items, this scale allows healthcare professionals and researchers to subjectively evaluate the intensity of alcohol cravings at a given moment. In addition to providing a quantitative measure of alcohol craving, the PACS has also proven useful in identifying triggers for alcohol consumption and assessing the risk of relapse in individuals undergoing recovery. Its systematic and validated use has significantly contributed to the understanding and treatment of alcohol addiction, offering a valuable tool for addressing this public health issue more effectively (Flannery et al., 1999). The Patient Health Questionnaire 9 (PHQ-9) is a Likert-type scale used to measure depression symptoms. It consists of 9 items or questions directly related to the symptoms of depression described in the DSM-V, the guide for clinical diagnosis. These questions are classified from 0 to 3. When observing the questions of the PHQ-9 Test, the direct correlation of each one with a specific symptom of depression is highlighted. For example, the question "Have you felt bad about yourself, or feel like you're a failure, or have let yourself or your family down?" clearly reflects the presence of low self-esteem. Similarly, the question "Have you had thoughts of being better off dead, or of hurting yourself in some way?" evidences the presence of intrusive or self-harming thoughts. This direct link between the questions and the symptoms underscores the usefulness of the PHQ-9 Test as a tool to assess and understand the presence of depression (Cassiani-Miranda et al., 2021). The Generalized Anxiety Disorder 7 (GAD-7) questionnaire measures generalized anxiety disorder and consist of 7 multiple-choice questions, each with four options ("Not at all", scored: 0, "Several days", scored: 1, "More than half the days", scored: 2, "Nearly every day", scored: 3) (Table 2). This questionnaire is evaluated by summing the scores of each question, classifying each individual into the following ranges: 0-4 no anxiety, 5-9 mild, 10-14 moderate, 15-21 severe (Snijders et al., 2021; Zhao, 2023). The GAD-7 rating scale is used as the target variable for model training, along with other variables collected in the data collection instrument (Spitzer et al., 2006). The Severity of Dependence Scale (SDS) is a tool designed to assess users’ dependence on narcotics, consisting of five questions. Through this tool, the user is asked about the most consumed narcotic, while the following four questions focus on assessing their dependence on that specific substance. This tool has been developed to provide an accurate measure of narcotic dependence. The relationship between drug use and depression has been reported by previous studies (Pinelo-Camacho et al., 2022), highlighting a cyclical relationship between alcohol consumption, cannabis, and the development of severe depressive symptoms (Gossop et al., 1995). AI Models The built model was developed under the machine learning approach in which Random Forest (RF), Support Vector Machines (SVM), and K-Nearest Neighbors (KNN) classifiers were selected. Additionally, a cross-validation strategy was employed to determine the model’s efficiency and proper parameterization. Regarding the cross-validation process, the original dataset was initially partitioned into a 70-30 scheme, where 30 % of the data was reserved for final validation and the remaining 70 % for cross-validation. The data was partitioned into 4 subsets for cross-validation. The selection of the number of subsets was determined based on the quantity of data in the moderate and severe classes, ensuring that each validation set contained at least 3 data points from each class. RF, or Random Forest, is a model composed of multiple individual decision trees, each of which is trained with a slightly different sample of the training data, generated using a technique known as bootstrapping (Louppe, 2014). Then, to make predictions on new observations, the predictions of all the trees that make up the model are combined. SVM, Support Vector Machine, is a supervised learning technique that requires labeled data and is based on the principles of statistical learning and convex optimization. In the training process, the algorithm analyzes the input data and identifies patterns in a multidimensional feature space called a hyperplane (Betancourt, 2005). Its central objective is to efficiently find a hyperplane that can separate the different categories present in the data, thereby enabling the effective classification of new data. A high SHAP value for a feature means that the feature had a significant influence on the classification. As shown in Fig. 7, the features that contribute the most are the questions from the GAD7 test, which is coherent with reality, as the test is a way to measure the risk of anxiety in a person. Additionally, Castro-Pérez Vargas et al. (2022) reported that the most influential factor in the development of depression and anxiety was a history of mental illness. However, these findings contradict other studies that have reported no association between psychiatric history and increased anxiety, particularly during the pandemic (Murphy et al., 2023). They found that individuals with psychiatric histories did not worsen during this period, whereas those most affected were those without such histories (Pan et al., 2021). It is possible to infer that these contradictory results are related to studies that did not find a higher risk of anxiety in individuals with personal histories of mental illness conducted during the COVID-19 pandemic. During this period, cases of acute anxiety likely increased in individuals without psychiatric histories due to factors such as COVID-19 illness, social distancing policies, mandatory lockdowns, and other psychosocial factors, all of which were identified as risk factors for mental health problems in individuals without psychiatric histories (Zhu et al., 2023). Additionally, in the present study, having a family history of mental illness behaved as a risk factor for anxiety. This finding aligns with what was reported by Brummelhuis et al. (2024), who conducted a cross-sectional study of the general population and reported that being the child of parents with a mental illness was associated with higher levels of anxiety and depressive symptoms. Moreover, dysfunctional family relationships during childhood were associated with the severity of mental health problems in adults who grew up with a parent with a mental illness. Similarly, Serrano et al. (2023) reported that having a family history of depression was positively associated with depression, anxiety, and stress. The authors mention that this result may be explained by hereditary factors and the difficulties of caring for a family member with a mental illness. As evidenced in the analysis called SHAP values, the question PHQ9.6: "Feeling bad about yourself, or that you are a failure, or have let yourself or your family down?" while being part of the instrument to assess depression, shows characteristics that could well be associated with states of anxiety in the evaluated subject. This characteristic is relevant to the model and contributes significantly, as this information is external to the instrument itself for supporting the detection of GAD7 anxiety. This result is consistent with what Serrano et al. (2023) expressed in terms of the relationship between both disorders. Another way AI is applied for anxiety detection is through biolinguistic markers identified and classified with AI, as used by Wang et al. (2023). AI has also been utilized to identify and classify electroencephalographic (EEG) signals to detect and classify anxiety (Tigga, Garg, 2022b; Al-Ezzi et al., 2022). In this context, the objective of this study is to develop a model that identifies the factors associated with anxiety symptoms in young people, based on sociodemographic, clinical, and lifestyle information, supported by artificial intelligence (AI). psychiatric condition was established; however, no participants with these characteristics were found. # 2. Participants The minimum sample size was determined using the formula appropriate for the known sampling frame, taking into consideration the young population of the municipality where the study was conducted, which totals 3843 individuals, with a prevalence of anxiety symptoms of 23.3 % within this demographic (Ministerio de Salud y Protección Social de Colombia, 2015). Based on these parameters, the required minimum sample size was calculated to be 156 individuals. To accommodate potential attrition or non-response, an additional 10 % was added to this initial estimate, resulting in a minimum sample size of 172 individuals. A total of 234 young individuals were surveyed, who met the inclusion criteria defined for the study, who were aged between 18 and 28 years, residing in the department of Caldas-Colombia, agreeing to participate in the research, and signing the informed consent. Materials The database was constructed from information collected during field visits, where trained personnel administered a questionnaire developed by the research team. This team comprises three professionals in psychiatry, two in public health, and three in computer science. The questionnaire included sixteen sociodemographic questions (Table 1), six from the Penn Alcohol Craving Scale (PACS), nine from the Patient Health Questionnaire (PHQ-9), seven from the Generalized Anxiety Disorder (GAD-7) questionnaire, and the Severity of Dependence Scale (SDS). The Penn Alcohol Craving Scale (PACS) is a widely recognized assessment tool designed to measure the intensity of alcohol craving in individuals experiencing issues related to alcohol consumption. Developed at the University of Pennsylvania, the PACS has become a fundamental instrument in both clinical settings and research related to alcoholism and alcohol use disorders. Comprising a series of carefully selected items, this scale allows healthcare professionals and researchers to subjectively evaluate the intensity of alcohol cravings at a given moment. In addition to providing a quantitative measure of alcohol craving, the PACS has also proven useful in identifying triggers for alcohol consumption and assessing the risk of relapse in individuals undergoing recovery. Its systematic and validated use has significantly contributed to the understanding and treatment of alcohol addiction, offering a valuable tool for addressing this public health issue more effectively (Flannery et al., 1999). The Patient Health Questionnaire 9 (PHQ-9) is a Likert-type scale used to measure depression symptoms. It consists of 9 items or questions directly related to the symptoms of depression described in the DSM-V, the guide for clinical diagnosis. These questions are classified from 0 to 3. When observing the questions of the PHQ-9 Test, the direct correlation of each one with a specific symptom of depression is highlighted. For example, the question "Have you felt bad about yourself, or feel like you're a failure, or have let yourself or your family down?" clearly reflects the presence of low self-esteem. Similarly, the question "Have you had thoughts of being better off dead, or of hurting yourself in some way?" evidences the presence of intrusive or self-harming thoughts. This direct link between the questions and the symptoms underscores the usefulness of the PHQ-9 Test as a tool to assess and understand the presence of depression (Cassiani-Miranda et al., 2021). Once the best model among the three has been chosen, an analysis of the features with the greatest contribution to the construction of the RF model is conducted. For this purpose, SHAP approach is used, which provides a way to assign contributions to each feature in the classification of a model (Hamilton & Papadopoulos, 2024). SHAP values indicate how each feature contributes to the change in classification compared to the average classification of the model. A high SHAP value for a feature means that the feature had a significant influence on the classification. As shown in Fig. 7, the features that contribute the most are the questions from the GAD7 test, which is coherent with reality, as the test is a way to measure the risk of anxiety in a person. Additionally, the PHQ9 test makes a significant contribution, which continues to positively contrast with reality, as (Choi et al., 2020) explain the relationship between anxiety and depression, where depressed patients often exhibit symptoms of anxiety such as difficulty relaxing, which corresponds to GAD7_4. In the analyses conducted, the SHAP and feature importance techniques were applied, which provide a visual associated with the contribution that each feature makes to the classification models. In the case of SHAP, the most relevant features were GAD7_2, GAD7_3, GAD7_1, GAD7_5, GAD7_6, and the question PHQ9_6. For the feature importance analysis Fig. 8, the most significant questions were 37(GAD7_2), 41 (GAD7_6), 38(GAD7_3), 42(GAD7_7), and 39(GAD7_4). The relevance of the questions associated with GAD7 is evident since this form focuses on anxiety disorder-related questions; however, it is relevant that the characteristic PHQ9_6 is significant in this analysis as it focuses on depression symptoms. It was found that characteristics such as the educational level of parents and the frequency of alcohol consumption make a significant contribution to the construction of the model and the respective classification of anxiety. In line with the above, an analysis of the association of the most relevant characteristics found in the contrast method with feature importances from the scikit-learn library was conducted, as well as external characteristics such as affiliation to social security, since according to (Ruiz-Rodríguez et al., 2017), there is a protective relationship with health coverage, educational levels, and different types of occupations, as evidenced by (WHO, 2022) where the level of education and occupation of an individual are differentiating characteristics when it comes to experiencing anxiety. Lastly, personal and family history, according to (Dueñas-Amaya, 2019), anxiety and depression are mental disorders of potentially genetic origin, and their comorbidity is evidenced in a close bidirectional relationship. As observed in Table 4, when analyzing the OR values, it is possible to conclude that age acts as a protective factor for anxiety with a p-value of 0.0020. Note how having a family history of depression marks a 5 times higher probability of having anxiety, and when having a family history of anxiety, this probability increases, meaning there is a 13 times higher probability of suffering from anxiety in those with a family history of this pathology. For both variables, the difference was statistically significant with a p-value of 0.0000. Regarding the behavior of GAD7 responses, in the model, factors that predict anxiety with the strongest association include question 2 (in the last 15 days, have you been unable to control or avoid worrying), wherein those who have experienced this situation are 159 times more likely to suffer from anxiety. Sociodemographic characterization 234 young individuals participated from the department of Caldas, where efforts were made to ensure that protected variables such as gender and age were as balanced as possible. A total of 113 males (48.29 %) and 121 females (51.71 %) were obtained. However, there is an imbalance in ages, with a tendency towards the extremes. The largest population of respondents is divided between 18 years and 28 years, representing 50 % of the data, followed by ages 19, 20, and 23. The average age is 22.95 ± 0.27 years. In terms of education, 40 % of the respondents reported having completed secondary education, while the next equivalent group, comprising 32 %, reported completing primary education. Regarding higher education, 18 % indicated having completed technical or technological studies, 6.52 % stated having completed university studies, and 0.48 % reported having postgraduate education. Regarding the activities they engage in during their free time, the most prominent ones are: listening to music, using social media, practicing sports, sleeping, and watching television. Regarding substance use, 50 % reported not consuming any substances. (2023) found that the prevalence of general mental health problems was higher in the group of abandoned adolescents, and poorer family functioning and school climate were also negatively associated with mental health. Additionally, Castro-Pérez Vargas et al. (2022) reported that the most influential factor in the development of depression and anxiety was a history of mental illness. However, these findings contradict other studies that have reported no association between psychiatric history and increased anxiety, particularly during the pandemic (Murphy et al., 2023). They found that individuals with psychiatric histories did not worsen during this period, whereas those most affected were those without such histories (Pan et al., 2021). It is possible to infer that these contradictory results are related to studies that did not find a higher risk of anxiety in individuals with personal histories of mental illness conducted during the COVID-19 pandemic. During this period, cases of acute anxiety likely increased in individuals without psychiatric histories due to factors such as COVID-19 illness, social distancing policies, mandatory lockdowns, and other psychosocial factors, all of which were identified as risk factors for mental health problems in individuals without psychiatric histories (Zhu et al., 2023). Additionally, in the present study, having a family history of mental illness behaved as a risk factor for anxiety. This finding aligns with what was reported by Brummelhuis et al. (2024), who conducted a cross-sectional study of the general population and reported that being the child of parents with a mental illness was associated with higher levels of anxiety and depressive symptoms. Moreover, dysfunctional family relationships during childhood were associated with the severity of mental health problems in adults who grew up with a parent with a mental illness. Similarly, Serrano et al. (2023) reported that having a family history of depression was positively associated with depression, anxiety, and stress. The authors mention that this result may be explained by hereditary factors and the difficulties of caring for a family member with a mental illness. As evidenced in the analysis called SHAP values, the question PHQ9.6: "Feeling bad about yourself, or that you are a failure, or have let yourself or your family down?" while being part of the instrument to assess depression, shows characteristics that could well be associated with states of anxiety in the evaluated subject. This characteristic is relevant to the model and contributes significantly, as this information is external to the instrument itself for supporting the detection of GAD7 anxiety. This result is consistent with what Serrano et al. (2023) expressed in terms of the relationship between both disorders. Another relevant finding is the relationship between anxiety and positive responses to the questions in the GAD-7 instrument, which detects symptoms of depression. This result aligns with what has been reported by other authors who have determined that in adolescents and young people, anxiety and depression often exhibit a pattern of comorbidity. In this regard, Wang, Mou, et al. (2023) reported a comorbidity rate of anxiety and depression among adolescents at 31.6 % in their study. Similarly, Choi et al. (2020) reported how comorbidity between anxiety and depression corresponds to a common syndrome and is not only associated with immense personal and familial suffering but also leads to other adverse outcomes such as academic failure, cognitive function deterioration, poor interpersonal relationships, and even suicide. (2022) reported an accuracy, sensitivity, and F1 score of 82.9 %, compared to 91 % for the same values in the present study. (2023) used an RF model on a population of 319 individuals, obtaining an excellent F1-score metric of 96.6 %, but with accuracy, precision, and recall values of 87.4 %. , and 87.6 %, respectively, which could indicate overfitting. Another case of improved results can be seen in Bhatnagar et al. (2023), where on a population of 127 students, they applied an RF model and SVM, showing accuracies of 75.5 % and 78.9 %, respectively. Another precedent demonstrating improved results is Priya et al. (2020), in which they used the RF model on a population of 348 participants, obtaining the following metrics: accuracy of 71.4 %, precision of 43.1 %, recall of 51 %, and an F1-score of 47 %. Other studies report higher efficiency percentages; however, these have been conducted under different methodologies, which include the use of data sources such as medical images, video recordings, and EEG signals, among others. An example of this is the work of Xie et al. (2022), where they achieved a 94.6 % accuracy using video recordings and convolutional neural networks. It is worth noting that the present study exclusively requires the application of a questionnaire battery, making it more cost-effective than those employing other data sources. With the above, it is relevant to affirm that traditional machine learning techniques remain efficient in terms of determining the anxiety condition. This is particularly valuable as these models can be trained with a reduced number of variables, without requiring large volumes of information and with modest computational support by current standards. Additionally, data collection is low-cost and can be implemented without the need for expensive technologies. In coherence, the present model can be efficiently deployed across communities and contribute timely to anxiety detection efforts. ## 5. A total of 113 males (48.29 %) and 121 females (51.71 %) were obtained. However, there is an imbalance in ages, with a tendency towards the extremes. The remaining individuals had no basic education, accounting for 3 %. Regarding the activities they engage in during their free time, the most prominent ones are: listening to music, using social media, practicing sports, sleeping, and watching television. The mentioned increase in the incidence of suicide rates and suicide attempts has been related to the presence of conditions such as economic vulnerability, job instability, various types of violence, lack of access to basic services, decent housing, and adequate incomes. It has also been associated with different mental disorders present among the Colombian population, such as mixed anxiety and depression disorder, unspecified anxiety, and generalized anxiety (Procuraduría General de la Nación de Colombia, 2023). Anxiety has been linked bi-directionally with the consumption of psychoactive substances. Continuous consumption of these substances can trigger affective symptoms or anxiety disorders. Conversely, it has been determined that in individuals with anxiety, the higher the intensity of the symptoms, the greater the likelihood of substance consumption (Contreras-Olive et al., 2020). A study conducted with the young population reports how substance abuse and consumption not only generate anxiety disorders but also depression and these disorders are directly related to dependency (Encina et al., 2023). The highlights highlighted underscore the need to strengthen actions for the promotion, prevention, and early detection of anxiety. These actions work by identifying individual, social, and structural determinants and then intervening to reduce risks, promote resilience, and establish conducive environments for mental health (WHO, 2022b). One of the innovative tools supporting these interventions is Artificial Intelligence (AI). This refers to the ability of computer systems to predict outcomes that have been conceived by humans in comparable situations (El-Sherif et al., 2022). Artificial Intelligence (AI) models in healthcare are currently contributing to the field known as predictive medicine, which seeks to identify patients at risk and support decision-making in the healthcare system for their benefit and that of communities (Ruiz & Velásquez, 2023; Tigga, Garg, 2022a). As an example, studies such as those conducted by Kumar et al. (2020), Albagmi et al. (2022), and Wei et al. (2023) have used AI models to classify anxiety, yielding good results. Another way AI is applied for anxiety detection is through biolinguistic markers identified and classified with AI, as used by Wang et al. (2023). AI has also been utilized to identify and classify electroencephalographic (EEG) signals to detect and classify anxiety (Tigga, Garg, 2022b; Al-Ezzi et al., 2022). A total of 234 young individuals were surveyed, who met the inclusion criteria defined for the study, who were aged between 18 and 28 years, residing in the department of Caldas-Colombia, agreeing to participate in the research, and signing the informed consent. Materials The database was constructed from information collected during field visits, where trained personnel administered a questionnaire developed by the research team. This team comprises three professionals in psychiatry, two in public health, and three in computer science. The questionnaire included sixteen sociodemographic questions (Table 1), six from the Penn Alcohol Craving Scale (PACS), nine from the Patient Health Questionnaire (PHQ-9), seven from the Generalized Anxiety Disorder (GAD-7) questionnaire, and the Severity of Dependence Scale (SDS). The Penn Alcohol Craving Scale (PACS) is a widely recognized assessment tool designed to measure the intensity of alcohol craving in individuals experiencing issues related to alcohol consumption. Developed at the University of Pennsylvania, the PACS has become a fundamental instrument in both clinical settings and research related to alcoholism and alcohol use disorders. Comprising a series of carefully selected items, this scale allows healthcare professionals and researchers to subjectively evaluate the intensity of alcohol cravings at a given moment. In addition to providing a quantitative measure of alcohol craving, the PACS has also proven useful in identifying triggers for alcohol consumption and assessing the risk of relapse in individuals undergoing recovery. Its systematic and validated use has significantly contributed to the understanding and treatment of alcohol addiction, offering a valuable tool for addressing this public health issue more effectively (Flannery et al., 1999). The Patient Health Questionnaire 9 (PHQ-9) is a Likert-type scale used to measure depression symptoms. It consists of 9 items or questions directly related to the symptoms of depression described in the DSM-V, the guide for clinical diagnosis. These questions are classified from 0 to 3. When observing the questions of the PHQ-9 Test, the direct correlation of each one with a specific symptom of depression is highlighted. For example, the question "Have you felt bad about yourself, or feel like you're a failure, or have let yourself or your family down?" clearly reflects the presence of low self-esteem. Similarly, the question "Have you had thoughts of being better off dead, or of hurting yourself in some way?" evidences the presence of intrusive or self-harming thoughts. This direct link between the questions and the symptoms underscores the usefulness of the PHQ-9 Test as a tool to assess and understand the presence of depression (Cassiani-Miranda et al., 2021). Once the best model among the three has been chosen, an analysis of the features with the greatest contribution to the construction of the RF model is conducted. For this purpose, SHAP approach is used, which provides a way to assign contributions to each feature in the classification of a model (Hamilton & Papadopoulos, 2024). SHAP values indicate how each feature contributes to the change in classification compared to the average classification of the model. A high SHAP value for a feature means that the feature had a significant influence on the classification. As shown in Fig. 7, the features that contribute the most are the questions from the GAD7 test, which is coherent with reality, as the test is a way to measure the risk of anxiety in a person. Additionally, the PHQ9 test makes a significant contribution, which continues to positively contrast with reality, as (Choi et al., 2020) explain the relationship between anxiety and depression, where depressed patients often exhibit symptoms of anxiety such as difficulty relaxing, which corresponds to GAD7_4. In the analyses conducted, the SHAP and feature importance techniques were applied, which provide a visual associated with the contribution that each feature makes to the classification models. In the case of SHAP, the most relevant features were GAD7_2, GAD7_3, GAD7_1, GAD7_5, GAD7_6, and the question PHQ9_6. For the feature importance analysis Fig. 8, the most significant questions were 37(GAD7_2), 41 (GAD7_6), 38(GAD7_3), 42(GAD7_7), and 39(GAD7_4). The relevance of the questions associated with GAD7 is evident since this form focuses on anxiety disorder-related questions; however, it is relevant that the characteristic PHQ9_6 is significant in this analysis as it focuses on depression symptoms. It was found that characteristics such as the educational level of parents and the frequency of alcohol consumption make a significant contribution to the construction of the model and the respective classification of anxiety. In line with the above, an analysis of the association of the most relevant characteristics found in the contrast method with feature importances from the scikit-learn library was conducted, as well as external characteristics such as affiliation to social security, since according to (Ruiz-Rodríguez et al., 2017), there is a protective relationship with health coverage, educational levels, and different types of occupations, as evidenced by (WHO, 2022) where the level of education and occupation of an individual are differentiating characteristics when it comes to experiencing anxiety. Lastly, personal and family history, according to (Dueñas-Amaya, 2019), anxiety and depression are mental disorders of potentially genetic origin, and their comorbidity is evidenced in a close bidirectional relationship. As observed in Table 4, when analyzing the OR values, it is possible to conclude that age acts as a protective factor for anxiety with a p-value of 0.0020. Note how having a family history of depression marks a 5 times higher probability of having anxiety, and when having a family history of anxiety, this probability increases, meaning there is a 13 times higher probability of suffering from anxiety in those with a family history of this pathology. For both variables, the difference was statistically significant with a p-value of 0.0000. Regarding the behavior of GAD7 responses, in the model, factors that predict anxiety with the strongest association include question 2 (in the last 15 days, have you been unable to control or avoid worrying), wherein those who have experienced this situation are 159 times more likely to suffer from anxiety. To understand in depth the metrics used, we briefly explain the formulas and the interpretation of the metrics extracted from (Borja-Robalino et al., 2020). * TP (True Positive) - Values that the algorithm classifies as positive and are actually positive. * TN (True Negative) - Values that the algorithm classifies as negative (0 in this case) and that are actually negative. * FP (False Positive) - Values that the algorithm classifies as positive when they are actually negative. * FN (False Negative) - False negatives, i.e. values that the algorithm classifies as negative when they are actually positive. $$ \text{Accuracy} = \frac{TP + TN}{TP + FP + TN + FN} $$ $$ \text{Precision} = \frac{TP}{TP + FP} $$ $$ \text{F1-Score} = 2 * \frac{(\text{Recall} * \text{Precision})}{(\text{Recall} + \text{Precision})} $$ $$ \text{Recall} = \frac{TP}{TP + FN} $$ The confusion matrix in Fig. 5 of the Random Forest model shows a good classification of the different categories of anxiety, with only a small difficulty in the Mild category. Further analysis of the RF model was performed using the ROC curve in which the contrast between true positives and false positives extracted from the confusion matrix Fig. 5 can be seen. The multinomial ROC curve compares the true positive rate (sensitivity) with the false positive rate of each class compared to all other classes grouped as a single negative class. The area under the multinomial ROC curve (AUC-ROC multinomial) provides an overall measure of the model's performance in terms of multiclass classification. An AUC-ROC multinomial of 1.0 would indicate perfect performance, while a value of 0.5 would indicate random performance. According to Fig. 6, the RF graph shows the best overall performance across all four features, while SVM exhibits similar performance to RF but shows random behavior when working on the second and third. Materials The database was constructed from information collected during field visits, where trained personnel administered a questionnaire developed by the research team. This team comprises three professionals in psychiatry, two in public health, and three in computer science. The questionnaire included sixteen sociodemographic questions (Table 1), six from the Penn Alcohol Craving Scale (PACS), nine from the Patient Health Questionnaire (PHQ-9), seven from the Generalized Anxiety Disorder (GAD-7) questionnaire, and the Severity of Dependence Scale (SDS). The Penn Alcohol Craving Scale (PACS) is a widely recognized assessment tool designed to measure the intensity of alcohol craving in individuals experiencing issues related to alcohol consumption. Developed at the University of Pennsylvania, the PACS has become a fundamental instrument in both clinical settings and research related to alcoholism and alcohol use disorders. Comprising a series of carefully selected items, this scale allows healthcare professionals and researchers to subjectively evaluate the intensity of alcohol cravings at a given moment. In addition to providing a quantitative measure of alcohol craving, the PACS has also proven useful in identifying triggers for alcohol consumption and assessing the risk of relapse in individuals undergoing recovery. Its systematic and validated use has significantly contributed to the understanding and treatment of alcohol addiction, offering a valuable tool for addressing this public health issue more effectively (Flannery et al., 1999). The Patient Health Questionnaire 9 (PHQ-9) is a Likert-type scale used to measure depression symptoms. It consists of 9 items or questions directly related to the symptoms of depression described in the DSM-V, the guide for clinical diagnosis. These questions are classified from 0 to 3. When observing the questions of the PHQ-9 Test, the direct correlation of each one with a specific symptom of depression is highlighted. For example, the question "Have you felt bad about yourself, or feel like you're a failure, or have let yourself or your family down?" clearly reflects the presence of low self-esteem. Similarly, the question "Have you had thoughts of being better off dead, or of hurting yourself in some way?" evidences the presence of intrusive or self-harming thoughts. This direct link between the questions and the symptoms underscores the usefulness of the PHQ-9 Test as a tool to assess and understand the presence of depression (Cassiani-Miranda et al., 2021). The Generalized Anxiety Disorder 7 (GAD-7) questionnaire measures generalized anxiety disorder and consist of 7 multiple-choice questions, each with four options ("Not at all", scored: 0, "Several days", scored: 1, "More than half the days", scored: 2, "Nearly every day", scored: 3) (Table 2). This questionnaire is evaluated by summing the scores of each question, classifying each individual into the following ranges: 0-4 no anxiety, 5-9 mild, 10-14 moderate, 15-21 severe (Snijders et al., 2021; Zhao, 2023). The GAD-7 rating scale is used as the target variable for model training, along with other variables collected in the data collection instrument (Spitzer et al., 2006). The Severity of Dependence Scale (SDS) is a tool designed to assess users’ dependence on narcotics, consisting of five questions. Regarding other sociodemographic factors, age was determined to be related to anxiety. This finding aligns with reports from other authors such as (Zhu et al., 2023), who mention in their review that age had a significant effect on anxiety risk levels, particularly during the pandemic. Specifically, in the present study, age acted as a protective factor, with individuals in the younger age range, i.e., 18 to 23 years old, exhibiting a lower risk of anxiety. This contradicts the findings reported by other authors such as (Gao et al., 2020), who stated that younger individuals had a higher vulnerability to mental illnesses. Additionally, (Ahmed et al., 2020) determined that young people were in a more vulnerable position in terms of their mental health conditions. It is important to note that part of the sample in the present study resides in the municipality of Samaná in the department of Caldas, which is considered a municipality affected by armed conflict. This could explain why older individuals showed greater mental health impact due to the violence they were exposed to in previous decades. In the present study, it was determined that personal history of mental illness acts as a risk factor for anxiety, a finding that coincides with reports from other authors. For example, (Klinger-Konig et al., 2023) reported that childhood trauma is associated with somatic and mental illnesses in adulthood, with this association being stronger in younger individuals, regardless of the nature of the childhood trauma. K-Nearest-Neighbor (KNN) is a supervised instance-based machine learning algorithm. It can be used to classify new samples (discrete values) or to predict (regression, continuous values). Essentially, it serves to classify values by seeking the “most similar” data points (by proximity) learned in the training stage and making predictions of new points based on that classification (Cunningham & Delany, 2021). ## 2.4. Data analysis To initiate processing, a method was applied to search for NaN-type data or empty values (Null). Good practices in AI development (Tubares-Soto et al., 2022) and the framework for ethical data management from the IDB (Denis et al., 2021) indicate that applying this initial filter provides transparency and credibility to the information used in AI development. Subsequently, one-hot encoding was carried out using the scikit-learn library, allowing all character-type responses to be converted to numeric values. This will facilitate the use of data in ML model testing. The KNN method represents a non-parametric classification model. To assign a category to a given data point, the algorithm examines the information of its k nearest neighbors. This process helps determine which group the data point belongs to. In the specific context of depression classification, the KNN model uses features extracted from the data. As a supervised learning approach, the KNN model starts with training using existing data. This allows the algorithm to develop an understanding of the relationships between the features and the corresponding classes. The data analysis was conducted by merging all the questionnaires into a single database. Specifically, we integrated sociodemographic data, the Penn Alcohol Craving Scale, the GAD-7, the PHQ-9, and the SDS. All these data points were combined into one comprehensive dataset for analysis. It is important to note, however, that the dependent variable in our model is the total score of the GAD-7 test, which is calculated as described in Table 2. Additionally, the GAD-7 SCORE feature was created, representing the sum of the test questions’ results. Subsequently, the target variable was generated, which is multinomial, as it responds to the four possible groups in which a person can be found, as explained earlier in the generalities. Finally, the sociodemographic and clinical characteristics were analyzed using the SPSS program licensed by the University of Caldas. AI Models The built model was developed under the machine learning approach in which Random Forest (RF), Support Vector Machines (SVM), and K-Nearest Neighbors (KNN) classifiers were selected. Additionally, a cross-validation strategy was employed to determine the model’s efficiency and proper parameterization. Regarding the cross-validation process, the original dataset was initially partitioned into a 70-30 scheme, where 30 % of the data was reserved for final validation and the remaining 70 % for cross-validation. The data was partitioned into 4 subsets for cross-validation. The selection of the number of subsets was determined based on the quantity of data in the moderate and severe classes, ensuring that each validation set contained at least 3 data points from each class. RF, or Random Forest, is a model composed of multiple individual decision trees, each of which is trained with a slightly different sample of the training data, generated using a technique known as bootstrapping (Louppe, 2014). Then, to make predictions on new observations, the predictions of all the trees that make up the model are combined. SVM, Support Vector Machine, is a supervised learning technique that requires labeled data and is based on the principles of statistical learning and convex optimization. In the training process, the algorithm analyzes the input data and identifies patterns in a multidimensional feature space called a hyperplane (Betancourt, 2005). Its central objective is to efficiently find a hyperplane that can separate the different categories present in the data, thereby enabling the effective classification of new data.
