Efforts are needed to reduce risk factors through administrative and policy interventions to manage workers' health by early screening. --- ## 1. Introduction ### 1.1. Shift work and health Shift work is defined as working outside the normal working hours of 7:00 am to 6:00 pm, with 15–25% of global workers working in shifts (Wickwire et al., 2017). Shift workers are exposed to artificial light at night, which causes their circadian rhythm to be disturbed (Fonken et al., 2013; Stevens et al., 2007). Light exposure at night can impair learning and memory abilities (Fonken et al., 2012) and may lead to neurodegeneration associated with Alzheimer's disease (Kim et al., 2018). Shift workers often complain of sleep disturbances or drowsiness during waking hours due to disturbances of the normal sleep-wake cycle. According to the Korean National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey (KHANES), 37.6% of workers get less than seven hours of sleep. Among them, sleep deprivation impacts 61.8% of shift workers (Yong et al., 2017). In addition, light pollution negatively impacts overall human health, including aging, metabolic processes, heart disease, diabetes, and mood disorders (Gangwisch, 2014; Hood et al., 2004; Stevens et al., 2007). Sleep is essential for humans to maintain physical and mental homeostasis by providing rest and stability. However, shift workers have no choice but to sleep at a different time than the body's circadian rhythm, resulting in poor sleep quality and sleep deprivation (Niu et al., 2011). Workers who complained of sleep disturbance were 2.8 times more likely to receive treatment (Daley et al., 2009) or prescription drugs for various health problems, including mental health problems, compared to those who did not (Haus and Smolensky, 2013; Kecklund and Axelsson, 2016). In the case of nurses, it can impact patient safety by reducing concentration and increasing fatigue during work, thus increasing the risk of various in-hospital accidents such as medication errors or malfunctions of medical devices (Wickwire et al., 2017; Yuan et al., 2011). This study attempted to predict suicidal ideation according to shift work by using machine learning techniques. Methods: We analyzed a total of 43,095 data conducted by using the 10-year Korean National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey (KHANES). Shift workers and daytime workers were categorized and analyzed using random forest (RF) and decision tree (DT) techniques of machine learning techniques. Results: Shift workers were more than twice as likely to have suicidal ideation as daytime workers. The RF model showed an accuracy of 91.6% for shift workers and 98% for daytime workers. In the DT technique, the rate of suicidal ideation was the highest among shift workers (82.7%) when they were depressed and had an EuroQol-5 Dimension (EQ-5D) score of less than 0.71. Limitations: Shift work type was evaluated questionnaire and based on screening data, it was not possible to reflect recent changes in the work type and we evaluated for only suicidal ideation for suicide risk factors. Conclusion: The variables influencing the suicide risk of shift workers and daytime workers differ. In the case of shift workers, negative factors such as depression and low quality of life are risk factors for suicide. Journal of Affective Disorders 307 (2022) 125–132 Contents lists available at ScienceDirect Journal of Affective Disorders journal homepage: www.elsevier.com/locate/jad ## Research paper # Prediction of suicidal ideation in shift workers compared to non-shift workers using machine learning techniques Hwanjin Park^a, Kounseok Lee^b,* ^a Department of Occupational & Environmental Medicine, Kangbuk Samsung Hospital, Sungkyunkwan University School of Medicine, Seoul, Republic of Korea ^b Department of Psychiatry, Hanyang University Medical Center, Seoul, Republic of Korea --- ## ARTICLE INFO Keywords: - Shift workers - Daytime workers - Suicide - Depression - Machine learning ## ABSTRACT Background: Shift work can affect sleep and increase the risk of suicide. This study attempted to predict suicidal ideation according to shift work by using machine learning techniques. Methods: We analyzed a total of 43,095 data conducted by using the 10-year Korean National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey (KHANES). Shift workers and daytime workers were categorized and analyzed using random forest (RF) and decision tree (DT) techniques of machine learning techniques. Results: Shift workers were more than twice as likely to have suicidal ideation as daytime workers. The RF model showed an accuracy of 91.6% for shift workers and 98% for daytime workers. In the DT technique, the rate of suicidal ideation was the highest among shift workers (82.7%) when they were depressed and had an EuroQol-5 Dimension (EQ-5D) score of less than 0.71. Limitations: Shift work type was evaluated questionnaire and based on screening data, it was not possible to reflect recent changes in the work type and we evaluated for only suicidal ideation for suicide risk factors. Conclusion: The variables influencing the suicide risk of shift workers and daytime workers differ. In the case of shift workers, negative factors such as depression and low quality of life are risk factors for suicide. Efforts are needed to reduce risk factors through administrative and policy interventions to manage workers' health by early screening. --- ## 1. Introduction ### 1.1. Shift work and health Shift work is defined as working outside the normal working hours of 7:00 am to 6:00 pm, with 15–25% of global workers working in shifts (Wickwire et al., 2017). Shift workers are exposed to artificial light at night, which causes their circadian rhythm to be disturbed (Fonken et al., 2013; Stevens et al., 2007). Light exposure at night can impair learning and memory abilities (Fonken et al., 2012) and may lead to neurodegeneration associated with Alzheimer's disease (Kim et al., 2018). Shift workers often complain of sleep disturbances or drowsiness during waking hours due to disturbances of the normal sleep-wake cycle. According to the Korean National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey (KHANES), 37.6% of workers get less than seven hours of sleep. Among them, sleep deprivation impacts 61.8% of shift workers (Yong et al., 2017). In addition, light pollution negatively impacts overall human health, including aging, metabolic processes, heart disease, diabetes, and mood disorders (Gangwisch, 2014; Hood et al., 2004; Stevens et al., 2007). Sleep is essential for humans to maintain physical and mental homeostasis by providing rest and stability. However, shift workers have no choice but to sleep at a different time than the body's circadian rhythm, resulting in poor sleep quality and sleep deprivation (Niu et al., 2011). Workers who complained of sleep disturbance were 2.8 times more likely to receive treatment (Daley et al., 2009) or prescription drugs for various health problems, including mental health problems, compared to those who did not (Haus and Smolensky, 2013; Kecklund and Axelsson, 2016). In the case of nurses, it can impact patient safety by reducing concentration and increasing fatigue during work, thus increasing the risk of various in-hospital accidents such as medication errors or malfunctions of medical devices (Wickwire et al., 2017; Yuan et al., 2011). As chronic circadian misalignment occurs, this social jet lag is known to have a negative effect on individual health, such as unhealthy eating habits, personality changes, metabolic disorders, and increased depression (Roenneberg et al., 2019). --- * Corresponding author at: Department of Psychiatry, Hanyang University Medical Center, 222-1, Wangsimni-ro, Seongdong-gu, Seoul 04763, Republic of Korea. Shift work and suicide A study of police officers discovered that depression, PTSD symptoms, and the type of work all increased suicidal ideation in female police officers (Violanti et al., 2008). Shift work was identified as a risk factor for workplace suicide (Stack, 2001; Tiesman et al., 2015). These results considered shift work as one of the major risk factors, but the question of which of the various factors affects the risk of suicide was not adequately addressed. ## 1.3. Participants This study used data from KHANES. The KHANES is a nationwide health and nutrition survey based on Article 16 of the National Health Promotion Act enacted in 1995. The health level, health behavior, and food and nutritional intake are representative and reliable statistics at the national level and through these data, help to establish health policy, such as setting and evaluating the goals of the National Health Promotion Plan and developing health promotion programs. Data for a span of 10 years were used: 2007–2013, 2015, 2017, and 2019. The 2014, 2016, and 2018 surveys did not include adult suicidal ideation, so they were excluded. All participants in KHANES provided written consent prior to the investigation so that their personal information could be used. This study included 45,386 adults aged 20 years or older who had been working for at least one year out of 10 years of survey data. Among them, a total of 43,095 people were analyzed, excluding 1391 people who did not answer their work type and 919 people who did not respond to questions related to suicidal ideation (Fig. 1). The Institutional Review Board of the Korea Disease Control and Prevention Agency approved this study (2018-01-03-P-A). ## 2.2. Measurements ### 2.2.1. Assessment of work patterns We divided work types into day work and shift work. Shift work included evening work (14:00–24:00), night shift (21:00–08:00), regular day and night shift work, 24-h shift work, split work (more than two working hours per day), irregular shift work, and other forms of shift work. ### 2.2.2. Assessment for suicide Suicide was evaluated by asking questions about suicidal ideation over the past year. The evaluative question presented to study participants asked, “*During the past year, have you ever felt that you were willing to die?*” They were classified as having suicidal ideation if they answered yes, and if they answered no, they were classified as having no suicidal ideation. ### 2.2.3. Assessment for quality of life Quality of life can be divided into health-related quality of life (HRQOL) and non-health-related quality of life (NHRQOL) (Spilker, 1996). Health-related quality of life refers to areas of life that are directly affected by changes in health. Health, as defined by the WHO, is not simply the absence of disease, but complete physical, mental, and social well-being. In this study, EuroQol-5 Dimension (EQ-5D) was used as an HRQOL measurement tool. EQ-5D is a tool that can measure HRQOL as a utility and consists of five items which include mobility, self-care, normal activities, pain/discomfort, and anxiety/depression. The higher the total score, the higher the quality of life. ### 2.2.4. Assessment for stress The stress level is evaluated with close-ended questions on a four points Likert scale (How much stress do you feel in your daily life?). The participants answered four type of stress level; extremely, stressful, moderately and minimally. ## 2.3. Among machine learning algorithms, RF is a method used to identify an optimal result by randomly combining the results by constructing multiple decision trees; RF is widely used because it is more accurate than decision trees. However, RF also has the disadvantage of losing the explanatory power of the variables included in the decision trees. A decision tree (DT) is one of the most widely used machine learning techniques for the purpose of classifying high-risk subjects. A decision tree is composed of decision nodes, branches, and leaves. It is divided into yes and no from the first question (Root Node), and the variable area is divided into two for each node, leading to the last terminal node. Finally, each divided tree is a set with the same tendency. Separation at each node can be said to have the highest explanatory, predictive power. Therefore, in this study, RF, a method with higher explanatory power, was performed first to evaluate the model suitability, followed by DT to present the explanatory power of each variable relative to suicidal ideation. In 10-fold cross-validation, the training data is divided into 10 folds of the same size; one-fold is used as a validation set, and the remaining nine folds are used as a training set (Fig. 2). This step is repeated five times to avoid overfitting and generalizing the model. context: work was identified as a risk factor for workplace suicide (Stack, 2001; Tiesman et al., 2015). In our previous study, we confirmed that major emotional problems like depression, anxiety, and suicidal ideation were common among shift workers (Park et al., 2020). Another study reported that shift work increased work stress and that the risk of suicide was significantly increased when the quality of sleep was poor (Son and Lee, 2021). These results considered shift work as one of the major risk factors, but the question of which of the various factors affects the risk of suicide was not adequately addressed. ## 1.3. Purpose of this study With the continued development of machine learning, research using it is diversifying. Machine learning is useful when analyzing multiple predictors when there are nonlinear observation and interaction terms that are difficult to conceptualize theoretically and model in practice. This study attempted to predict suicidal ideation based on shift work patterns using machine learning techniques. For this purpose, a variety of variables from national health surveys conducted over several years were used as predictive variables. # 2. Methods ## 2.1. Participants This study used data from KHANES. The KHANES is a nationwide health and nutrition survey based on Article 16 of the National Health Promotion Act enacted in 1995. The health level, health behavior, and food and nutritional intake are representative and reliable statistics at the national level and through these data, help to establish health policy, such as setting and evaluating the goals of the National Health Promotion Plan and developing health promotion programs. Data for a span of 10 years were used: 2007–2013, 2015, 2017, and 2019. The 2014, 2016, and 2018 surveys did not include adult suicidal ideation, so they were excluded. All participants in KHANES provided written consent prior to the investigation so that their personal information could be used. This study included 45,386 adults aged 20 years or older who had been working for at least one year out of 10 years of survey data. Among them, a total of 43,095 people were analyzed, excluding 1391 people who did not answer their work type and 919 people who did not respond to questions related to suicidal ideation (Fig. 1). The Institutional Review Board of the Korea Disease Control and Prevention Agency approved this study (2018-01-03-P-A). ## 2.2. Measurements ### 2.2.1. Assessment of work patterns We divided work types into day work and shift work. Shift work included evening work (14:00–24:00), night shift (21:00–08:00), regular day and night shift work, 24-h shift work, split work (more than two working hours per day), irregular shift work, and other forms of shift work. ### 2.2.2. Assessment for suicide Suicide was evaluated by asking questions about suicidal ideation over the past year. The evaluative question presented to study participants asked, “*During the past year, have you ever felt that you were willing to die?*” They were classified as having suicidal ideation if they answered yes, and if they answered no, they were classified as having no suicidal ideation. ### 2.2.3. Assessment for quality of life Quality of life can be divided into health-related quality of life (HRQOL) and non-health-related quality of life (NHRQOL) (Spilker, 1996). Health-related quality of life refers to areas of life that are directly affected by changes in health. Health, as defined by the WHO, is not simply the absence of disease, but complete physical, mental, and social well-being. In this study, EuroQol-5 Dimension (EQ-5D) was used as an HRQOL measurement tool. EQ-5D is a tool that can measure HRQOL as a utility and consists of five items which include mobility, self-care, normal activities, pain/discomfort, and anxiety/depression. The higher the total score, the higher the quality of life. ### 2.2.4. Assessment for stress The stress level is evaluated with close-ended questions on a four points Likert scale (How much stress do you feel in your daily life?). The participants answered four type of stress level; extremely, stressful, moderately and minimally. ## 2.3. Statistical analysis In this study, 19 analyzable variables thought to be related to suicidal ideation were selected and used. Missing values in some data were filled in using Predictive Mean Matching (PMM) from the Multiple Imputation by Chained Equations (MICE) package of R statistical software. However, RF also has the disadvantage of losing the explanatory power of the variables included in the decision trees. A decision tree (DT) is one of the most widely used machine learning techniques for the purpose of classifying high-risk subjects. A decision tree is composed of decision nodes, branches, and leaves. It is divided into yes and no from the first question (Root Node), and the variable area is divided into two for each node, leading to the last terminal node. Finally, each divided tree is a set with the same tendency. Separation at each node can be said to have the highest explanatory, predictive power. Assessment of work patterns We divided work types into day work and shift work. Shift work included evening work (14:00–24:00), night shift (21:00–08:00), regular day and night shift work, 24-h shift work, split work (more than two working hours per day), irregular shift work, and other forms of shift work. ### 2.2.2. Assessment for suicide Suicide was evaluated by asking questions about suicidal ideation over the past year. The evaluative question presented to study participants asked, “*During the past year, have you ever felt that you were willing to die?*” They were classified as having suicidal ideation if they answered yes, and if they answered no, they were classified as having no suicidal ideation. ### 2.2.3. Assessment for quality of life Quality of life can be divided into health-related quality of life (HRQOL) and non-health-related quality of life (NHRQOL) (Spilker, 1996). Health-related quality of life refers to areas of life that are directly affected by changes in health. Health, as defined by the WHO, is not simply the absence of disease, but complete physical, mental, and social well-being. In this study, EuroQol-5 Dimension (EQ-5D) was used as an HRQOL measurement tool. EQ-5D is a tool that can measure HRQOL as a utility and consists of five items which include mobility, self-care, normal activities, pain/discomfort, and anxiety/depression. The higher the total score, the higher the quality of life. ### 2.2.4. Assessment for stress The stress level is evaluated with close-ended questions on a four points Likert scale (How much stress do you feel in your daily life?). The participants answered four type of stress level; extremely, stressful, moderately and minimally. ## 2.3. Journal of Affective Disorders 307 (2022) 125–132 Contents lists available at ScienceDirect Journal of Affective Disorders journal homepage: www.elsevier.com/locate/jad ## Research paper # Prediction of suicidal ideation in shift workers compared to non-shift workers using machine learning techniques Hwanjin Park^a, Kounseok Lee^b,* ^a Department of Occupational & Environmental Medicine, Kangbuk Samsung Hospital, Sungkyunkwan University School of Medicine, Seoul, Republic of Korea ^b Department of Psychiatry, Hanyang University Medical Center, Seoul, Republic of Korea --- ## ARTICLE INFO Keywords: - Shift workers - Daytime workers - Suicide - Depression - Machine learning ## ABSTRACT Background: Shift work can affect sleep and increase the risk of suicide. This study attempted to predict suicidal ideation according to shift work by using machine learning techniques. Methods: We analyzed a total of 43,095 data conducted by using the 10-year Korean National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey (KHANES). Shift workers and daytime workers were categorized and analyzed using random forest (RF) and decision tree (DT) techniques of machine learning techniques. Results: Shift workers were more than twice as likely to have suicidal ideation as daytime workers. The RF model showed an accuracy of 91.6% for shift workers and 98% for daytime workers. In the DT technique, the rate of suicidal ideation was the highest among shift workers (82.7%) when they were depressed and had an EuroQol-5 Dimension (EQ-5D) score of less than 0.71. Limitations: Shift work type was evaluated questionnaire and based on screening data, it was not possible to reflect recent changes in the work type and we evaluated for only suicidal ideation for suicide risk factors. Conclusion: The variables influencing the suicide risk of shift workers and daytime workers differ. In the case of shift workers, negative factors such as depression and low quality of life are risk factors for suicide. Efforts are needed to reduce risk factors through administrative and policy interventions to manage workers' health by early screening. --- ## 1. Introduction ### 1.1. Shift work and health Shift work is defined as working outside the normal working hours of 7:00 am to 6:00 pm, with 15–25% of global workers working in shifts (Wickwire et al., 2017). Shift workers are exposed to artificial light at night, which causes their circadian rhythm to be disturbed (Fonken et al., 2013; Stevens et al., 2007). Light exposure at night can impair learning and memory abilities (Fonken et al., 2012) and may lead to neurodegeneration associated with Alzheimer's disease (Kim et al., 2018). Shift workers often complain of sleep disturbances or drowsiness during waking hours due to disturbances of the normal sleep-wake cycle. According to the Korean National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey (KHANES), 37.6% of workers get less than seven hours of sleep. Among them, sleep deprivation impacts 61.8% of shift workers (Yong et al., 2017). In addition, light pollution negatively impacts overall human health, including aging, metabolic processes, heart disease, diabetes, and mood disorders (Gangwisch, 2014; Hood et al., 2004; Stevens et al., 2007). Sleep is essential for humans to maintain physical and mental homeostasis by providing rest and stability. However, shift workers have no choice but to sleep at a different time than the body's circadian rhythm, resulting in poor sleep quality and sleep deprivation (Niu et al., 2011). Workers who complained of sleep disturbance were 2.8 times more likely to receive treatment (Daley et al., 2009) or prescription drugs for various health problems, including mental health problems, compared to those who did not (Haus and Smolensky, 2013; Kecklund and Axelsson, 2016). In the case of nurses, it can impact patient safety by reducing concentration and increasing fatigue during work, thus increasing the risk of various in-hospital accidents such as medication errors or malfunctions of medical devices (Wickwire et al., 2017; Yuan et al., 2011). As chronic circadian misalignment occurs, this social jet lag is known to have a negative effect on individual health, such as unhealthy eating habits, personality changes, metabolic disorders, and increased depression (Roenneberg et al., 2019). --- * Corresponding author at: Department of Psychiatry, Hanyang University Medical Center, 222-1, Wangsimni-ro, Seongdong-gu, Seoul 04763, Republic of Korea. Shift work and suicide A study of police officers discovered that depression, PTSD symptoms, and the type of work all increased suicidal ideation in female police officers (Violanti et al., 2008). Shift work was identified as a risk factor for workplace suicide (Stack, 2001; Tiesman et al., 2015). In our previous study, we confirmed that major emotional problems like depression, anxiety, and suicidal ideation were common among shift workers (Park et al., 2020). Another study reported that shift work increased work stress and that the risk of suicide was significantly increased when the quality of sleep was poor (Son and Lee, 2021). These results considered shift work as one of the major risk factors, but the question of which of the various factors affects the risk of suicide was not adequately addressed. ## 1.3. context: Journal of Affective Disorders 307 (2022) 125–132 Contents lists available at ScienceDirect Journal of Affective Disorders journal homepage: www.elsevier.com/locate/jad ## Research paper # Prediction of suicidal ideation in shift workers compared to non-shift workers using machine learning techniques Hwanjin Park^a, Kounseok Lee^b,* ^a Department of Occupational & Environmental Medicine, Kangbuk Samsung Hospital, Sungkyunkwan University School of Medicine, Seoul, Republic of Korea ^b Department of Psychiatry, Hanyang University Medical Center, Seoul, Republic of Korea --- ## ARTICLE INFO Keywords: - Shift workers - Daytime workers - Suicide - Depression - Machine learning ## ABSTRACT Background: Shift work can affect sleep and increase the risk of suicide. This study attempted to predict suicidal ideation according to shift work by using machine learning techniques. Methods: We analyzed a total of 43,095 data conducted by using the 10-year Korean National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey (KHANES). Shift workers and daytime workers were categorized and analyzed using random forest (RF) and decision tree (DT) techniques of machine learning techniques. Results: Shift workers were more than twice as likely to have suicidal ideation as daytime workers. The RF model showed an accuracy of 91.6% for shift workers and 98% for daytime workers. In the DT technique, the rate of suicidal ideation was the highest among shift workers (82.7%) when they were depressed and had an EuroQol-5 Dimension (EQ-5D) score of less than 0.71. Limitations: Shift work type was evaluated questionnaire and based on screening data, it was not possible to reflect recent changes in the work type and we evaluated for only suicidal ideation for suicide risk factors. Conclusion: The variables influencing the suicide risk of shift workers and daytime workers differ. In the case of shift workers, negative factors such as depression and low quality of life are risk factors for suicide. Efforts are needed to reduce risk factors through administrative and policy interventions to manage workers' health by early screening. --- ## 1. Introduction ### 1.1. Shift work and health Shift work is defined as working outside the normal working hours of 7:00 am to 6:00 pm, with 15–25% of global workers working in shifts (Wickwire et al., 2017). Shift workers are exposed to artificial light at night, which causes their circadian rhythm to be disturbed (Fonken et al., 2013; Stevens et al., 2007). Light exposure at night can impair learning and memory abilities (Fonken et al., 2012) and may lead to neurodegeneration associated with Alzheimer's disease (Kim et al., 2018). Shift workers often complain of sleep disturbances or drowsiness during waking hours due to disturbances of the normal sleep-wake cycle. According to the Korean National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey (KHANES), 37.6% of workers get less than seven hours of sleep. Among them, sleep deprivation impacts 61.8% of shift workers (Yong et al., 2017). In addition, light pollution negatively impacts overall human health, including aging, metabolic processes, heart disease, diabetes, and mood disorders (Gangwisch, 2014; Hood et al., 2004; Stevens et al., 2007). Sleep is essential for humans to maintain physical and mental homeostasis by providing rest and stability. However, shift workers have no choice but to sleep at a different time than the body's circadian rhythm, resulting in poor sleep quality and sleep deprivation (Niu et al., 2011). Workers who complained of sleep disturbance were 2.8 times more likely to receive treatment (Daley et al., 2009) or prescription drugs for various health problems, including mental health problems, compared to those who did not (Haus and Smolensky, 2013; Kecklund and Axelsson, 2016). In the case of nurses, it can impact patient safety by reducing concentration and increasing fatigue during work, thus increasing the risk of various in-hospital accidents such as medication errors or malfunctions of medical devices (Wickwire et al., 2017; Yuan et al., 2011). As chronic circadian misalignment occurs, this social jet lag is known to have a negative effect on individual health, such as unhealthy eating habits, personality changes, metabolic disorders, and increased depression (Roenneberg et al., 2019). --- * Corresponding author at: Department of Psychiatry, Hanyang University Medical Center, 222-1, Wangsimni-ro, Seongdong-gu, Seoul 04763, Republic of Korea. Shift work and suicide A study of police officers discovered that depression, PTSD symptoms, and the type of work all increased suicidal ideation in female police officers (Violanti et al., 2008). Shift work was identified as a risk factor for workplace suicide (Stack, 2001; Tiesman et al., 2015). In our previous study, we confirmed that major emotional problems like depression, anxiety, and suicidal ideation were common among shift workers (Park et al., 2020). Another study reported that shift work increased work stress and that the risk of suicide was significantly increased when the quality of sleep was poor (Son and Lee, 2021). These results considered shift work as one of the major risk factors, but the question of which of the various factors affects the risk of suicide was not adequately addressed. ## 1.3. Discussion In this study, suicidal ideation was predicted according to daytime or shift work using machine learning techniques. To predict this, variables such as depressive symptoms, quality of life scores, and stress perception, all of which are known risk factors for suicide, were used. We used RF for establish higher explanatory power to evaluate the model suitability, followed by DT to present the explanatory power of variables relative to suicidal ideation. The RF technique was found to select suicidal ideation with high specificity in both shift workers and daytime workers. In the DT model, it was confirmed that depressive symptoms, quality of life, and stress level were variables affecting suicidal ideation in both shift workers and daytime workers. When all three risk factors were present, the model results confirmed that there was a suicide risk of 54.0% for daytime workers and 82.7% for shift workers. These findings indicate that more delicate emotional management is required because shift workers who have all three risk factors may have a higher suicide risk. On the other hand, in the case of daytime workers, the research also suggests that other risk factors are affecting suicide risk in addition to the three risk factors. The next predictor variable was BMI, and a lower BMI was found to be a better predictor of suicidal ideation. This is consistent with the results of previous studies that low BMI is correlated with high suicide risk (Magnusson et al., 2006; Perera et al.,

In our previous study, we confirmed that major emotional problems like depression, anxiety, and suicidal ideation were common among shift workers (Park et al., 2020). Another study reported that shift work increased work stress and that the risk of suicide was significantly increased when the quality of sleep was poor (Son and Lee, 2021). These results considered shift work as one of the major risk factors, but the question of which of the various factors affects the risk of suicide was not adequately addressed. ## 1.3. Purpose of this study With the continued development of machine learning, research using it is diversifying. Machine learning is useful when analyzing multiple predictors when there are nonlinear observation and interaction terms that are difficult to conceptualize theoretically and model in practice. This study attempted to predict suicidal ideation based on shift work patterns using machine learning techniques. For this purpose, a variety of variables from national health surveys conducted over several years were used as predictive variables. # 2. Methods ## 2.1. Participants This study used data from KHANES. The KHANES is a nationwide health and nutrition survey based on Article 16 of the National Health Promotion Act enacted in 1995. The health level, health behavior, and food and nutritional intake are representative and reliable statistics at the national level and through these data, help to establish health policy, such as setting and evaluating the goals of the National Health Promotion Plan and developing health promotion programs. Data for a span of 10 years were used: 2007–2013, 2015, 2017, and 2019. The 2014, 2016, and 2018 surveys did not include adult suicidal ideation, so they were excluded. All participants in KHANES provided written consent prior to the investigation so that their personal information could be used. This study included 45,386 adults aged 20 years or older who had been working for at least one year out of 10 years of survey data. Among them, a total of 43,095 people were analyzed, excluding 1391 people who did not answer their work type and 919 people who did not respond to questions related to suicidal ideation (Fig. 1). The Institutional Review Board of the Korea Disease Control and Prevention Agency approved this study (2018-01-03-P-A). ## 2.2. Measurements ### 2.2.1. Assessment of work patterns We divided work types into day work and shift work. Shift work included evening work (14:00–24:00), night shift (21:00–08:00), regular day and night shift work, 24-h shift work, split work (more than two working hours per day), irregular shift work, and other forms of shift work. ### 2.2.2. Assessment for suicide Suicide was evaluated by asking questions about suicidal ideation over the past year. The evaluative question presented to study participants asked, “*During the past year, have you ever felt that you were willing to die?*” They were classified as having suicidal ideation if they answered yes, and if they answered no, they were classified as having no suicidal ideation. ### 2.2.3. Assessment for quality of life Quality of life can be divided into health-related quality of life (HRQOL) and non-health-related quality of life (NHRQOL) (Spilker, 1996). Health-related quality of life refers to areas of life that are directly affected by changes in health. Health, as defined by the WHO, is not simply the absence of disease, but complete physical, mental, and social well-being. In this study, EuroQol-5 Dimension (EQ-5D) was used as an HRQOL measurement tool. EQ-5D is a tool that can measure HRQOL as a utility and consists of five items which include mobility, self-care, normal activities, pain/discomfort, and anxiety/depression. The higher the total score, the higher the quality of life. ### 2.2.4. Assessment for stress The stress level is evaluated with close-ended questions on a four points Likert scale (How much stress do you feel in your daily life?). The participants answered four type of stress level; extremely, stressful, moderately and minimally. ## 2.3. Statistical analysis In this study, 19 analyzable variables thought to be related to suicidal ideation were selected and used. Missing values in some data were filled in using Predictive Mean Matching (PMM) from the Multiple Imputation by Chained Equations (MICE) package of R statistical software. Among machine learning algorithms, RF is a method used to identify an optimal result by randomly combining the results by constructing multiple decision trees; RF is widely used because it is more accurate than decision trees. However, RF also has the disadvantage of losing the explanatory power of the variables included in the decision trees. A decision tree (DT) is one of the most widely used machine learning techniques for the purpose of classifying high-risk subjects. A decision tree is composed of decision nodes, branches, and leaves. It is divided into yes and no from the first question (Root Node), and the variable area is divided into two for each node, leading to the last terminal node. Finally, each divided tree is a set with the same tendency. Separation at each node can be said to have the highest explanatory, predictive power. Therefore, in this study, RF, a method with higher explanatory power, was performed first to evaluate the model suitability, followed by DT to present the explanatory power of each variable relative to suicidal ideation. All ML analyses were conducted including all variables in Table 1. Daytime workers and shift workers were analyzed by dividing the sample into training data and test data by 70% and 30%, respectively. For the development of the analysis model, repeated 10-fold cross-validation was used. In 10-fold cross-validation, the training data is divided into 10 folds of the same size; one-fold is used as a validation set, and the remaining nine folds are used as a training set (Fig. 2). This step is repeated five times to avoid overfitting and generalizing the model. For RF to find the optimal mtry value and DT to find the optimal cp value, both the grid search method and random search method were analyzed to find the optimized hyperparameter value of each model to used to predict suicidal ideation in the training and test sets using a confusion matrix, resulting in predicted suicidal ideation that was compared with the actual suicidal ideation variables. The performance of the predictive model was evaluated using the area under the receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve (AUC), and the accuracy, sensitivity, specificity, positive predictive value, and negative predictive value were calculated using the confusion matrix. For all analyses, JASP v0.16.1 and R Statistical Software version 4.1.2 was used, and the MICE package of R was used for processing missing data, the “caret” package for cross validation, and the “Epi” package for the ROC curve. suicidal ideation ($p < 0.001$) reported by 13.7% of divorced daytime workers and 14.9% of divorced or widowed daytime workers. Among occupational classifications, agricultural, forestry, and fishery workers had the highest rates of suicidal ideation in daytime workers (13.2%, $p < 0.001$) and shift workers (18.6%, $p < 0.001$). The suicidal ideation rate of the groups who thought their subjective health status was bad or very bad was 16.8% and 28.3% in daytime workers, respectively, which was significantly higher ($p < 0.001$). The suicidal ideation rate of the groups who thought their subjective health status was bad or very bad was 28.6% and 51.5% in shift workers, respectively, which was significantly higher ($p < 0.001$). Daytime workers with suicidal ideation had higher hypertension (10.2%, $p < 0.001$), hyperlipidemia (9.2%, $p = 0.010$), stroke (14.3%, $p < 0.001$), myocardial infarction or angina (12.2%, $p < 0.001$), and diabetes (10.1%, $p < 0.001$). A history of cancer did not differ significantly from suicidal ideation in daytime workers ($p = 0.576$). Shift workers with suicidal ideation had higher hypertension (20.7%, $p < 0.001$), stroke (34.1%, $p < 0.001$), myocardial infarction or angina (30.5%, $p < 0.001$), diabetes (23.6%, $p < 0.001$) and cancer (23.1%, $p < 0.001$). A history of hyperlipidemia did not differ significantly from suicidal ideation in shift workers ($p = 0.869$). As for drinking, the group who drank more than four times a week had the highest rate of suicidal ideation (11.8%) in daytime workers and the group who don't drink had the highest rate of suicidal ideation (22.3%) in shift workers. The group who smoked daily had the highest rate of suicidal ideation (8.8%) and smoking overall was significantly associated with suicidal ideation ($p < 0.040$) in daytime workers and the group who don't smoke had the highest rate of suicidal ideation (17.1%) in shift workers. The suicidal ideation rate of the group who felt extreme stress in daily life was 29.3%, which was significantly high ($p < 0.001$) in daytime workers and shift workers (47.9%, $p < 0.001$) too. Those who suffered from depressive symptoms lasting for 2 weeks or longer had an overwhelmingly higher rate of suicidal ideation than those who did not in daytime workers (36.6%, $p < 0.001$) and shift workers (53.3%, $p < 0.001$). Similarly, the lower the EQ-5D score, the higher the rate of suicidal ideation in both daytime workers and shift workers ($p < 0.001$). To predict this, variables such as depressive symptoms, quality of life scores, and stress perception, all of which are known risk factors for suicide, were used. We used RF for establish higher explanatory power to evaluate the model suitability, followed by DT to present the explanatory power of variables relative to suicidal ideation. The RF technique was found to select suicidal ideation with high specificity in both shift workers and daytime workers. In the DT model, it was confirmed that depressive symptoms, quality of life, and stress level were variables affecting suicidal ideation in both shift workers and daytime workers. In our previous study, we confirmed that major emotional problems like depression, anxiety, and suicidal ideation were common among shift workers (Park et al., 2020). Another study reported that shift work increased work stress and that the risk of suicide was significantly increased when the quality of sleep was poor (Son and Lee, 2021). These results considered shift work as one of the major risk factors, but the question of which of the various factors affects the risk of suicide was not adequately addressed. ## 1.3. Purpose of this study With the continued development of machine learning, research using it is diversifying. Machine learning is useful when analyzing multiple predictors when there are nonlinear observation and interaction terms that are difficult to conceptualize theoretically and model in practice. This study attempted to predict suicidal ideation based on shift work patterns using machine learning techniques. For this purpose, a variety of variables from national health surveys conducted over several years were used as predictive variables. # 2. Methods ## 2.1. Participants This study used data from KHANES. The KHANES is a nationwide health and nutrition survey based on Article 16 of the National Health Promotion Act enacted in 1995. The health level, health behavior, and food and nutritional intake are representative and reliable statistics at the national level and through these data, help to establish health policy, such as setting and evaluating the goals of the National Health Promotion Plan and developing health promotion programs. Data for a span of 10 years were used: 2007–2013, 2015, 2017, and 2019. The 2014, 2016, and 2018 surveys did not include adult suicidal ideation, so they were excluded. All participants in KHANES provided written consent prior to the investigation so that their personal information could be used. This study included 45,386 adults aged 20 years or older who had been working for at least one year out of 10 years of survey data. Among them, a total of 43,095 people were analyzed, excluding 1391 people who did not answer their work type and 919 people who did not respond to questions related to suicidal ideation (Fig. 1). The Institutional Review Board of the Korea Disease Control and Prevention Agency approved this study (2018-01-03-P-A). ## 2.2. Measurements ### 2.2.1. Assessment of work patterns We divided work types into day work and shift work. Shift work included evening work (14:00–24:00), night shift (21:00–08:00), regular day and night shift work, 24-h shift work, split work (more than two working hours per day), irregular shift work, and other forms of shift work. ### 2.2.2. Assessment for suicide Suicide was evaluated by asking questions about suicidal ideation over the past year. The evaluative question presented to study participants asked, “*During the past year, have you ever felt that you were willing to die?*” They were classified as having suicidal ideation if they answered yes, and if they answered no, they were classified as having no suicidal ideation. ### 2.2.3. Assessment for quality of life Quality of life can be divided into health-related quality of life (HRQOL) and non-health-related quality of life (NHRQOL) (Spilker, 1996). Health-related quality of life refers to areas of life that are directly affected by changes in health. Health, as defined by the WHO, is not simply the absence of disease, but complete physical, mental, and social well-being. In this study, EuroQol-5 Dimension (EQ-5D) was used as an HRQOL measurement tool. EQ-5D is a tool that can measure HRQOL as a utility and consists of five items which include mobility, self-care, normal activities, pain/discomfort, and anxiety/depression. The higher the total score, the higher the quality of life. ### 2.2.4. Assessment for stress The stress level is evaluated with close-ended questions on a four points Likert scale (How much stress do you feel in your daily life?). The participants answered four type of stress level; extremely, stressful, moderately and minimally. ## 2.3. Statistical analysis In this study, 19 analyzable variables thought to be related to suicidal ideation were selected and used. Missing values in some data were filled in using Predictive Mean Matching (PMM) from the Multiple Imputation by Chained Equations (MICE) package of R statistical software. Among machine learning algorithms, RF is a method used to identify an optimal result by randomly combining the results by constructing multiple decision trees; RF is widely used because it is more accurate than decision trees. However, RF also has the disadvantage of losing the explanatory power of the variables included in the decision trees. A decision tree (DT) is one of the most widely used machine learning techniques for the purpose of classifying high-risk subjects. A decision tree is composed of decision nodes, branches, and leaves. It is divided into yes and no from the first question (Root Node), and the variable area is divided into two for each node, leading to the last terminal node. Finally, each divided tree is a set with the same tendency. Separation at each node can be said to have the highest explanatory, predictive power. Therefore, in this study, RF, a method with higher explanatory power, was performed first to evaluate the model suitability, followed by DT to present the explanatory power of each variable relative to suicidal ideation. Discussion In this study, suicidal ideation was predicted according to daytime or shift work using machine learning techniques. To predict this, variables such as depressive symptoms, quality of life scores, and stress perception, all of which are known risk factors for suicide, were used. We used RF for establish higher explanatory power to evaluate the model suitability, followed by DT to present the explanatory power of variables relative to suicidal ideation. The RF technique was found to select suicidal ideation with high specificity in both shift workers and daytime workers. In the DT model, it was confirmed that depressive symptoms, quality of life, and stress level were variables affecting suicidal ideation in both shift workers and daytime workers. When all three risk factors were present, the model results confirmed that there was a suicide risk of 54.0% for daytime workers and 82.7% for shift workers. These findings indicate that more delicate emotional management is required because shift workers who have all three risk factors may have a higher suicide risk. On the other hand, in the case of daytime workers, the research also suggests that other risk factors are affecting suicide risk in addition to the three risk factors. The next predictor variable was BMI, and a lower BMI was found to be a better predictor of suicidal ideation. This is consistent with the results of previous studies that low BMI is correlated with high suicide risk (Magnusson et al., 2006; Perera et al., 2010). Also, the low SES as a predictor is consistent with the results of previous studies (Daley et al., 2009; Taylor et al., 2005). This seems to be because SES is a factor that is mainly related to a person's living environment and quality of life. Machine learning methods for suicide research are useful for identifying risk factors using large-scale data (Fazel and O'Reilly, 2020). This research method is useful for identifying new risk factors from existing data, as well as known risk factors (de la Garza et al., 2021; Kim et al., 2021). In this study, it was confirmed that known variables act differently according to the characteristics of the group through the machine learning technique, and it was confirmed that the risk of suicide can be greatly increased by the group. A major risk factor for suicide is depression (Isometsa et al., 1994). In both types of work analyzed in this study, depression was the biggest risk factor for suicide. Shift workers have more emotional problems such as depression, suicidal ideation, and stress than daytime workers (Park et al., 2016). In addition, shift workers work at times that do not match with the physiological and social circadian rhythms, so their quality of sleep is poor. Assessment of work patterns We divided work types into day work and shift work. Shift work included evening work (14:00–24:00), night shift (21:00–08:00), regular day and night shift work, 24-h shift work, split work (more than two working hours per day), irregular shift work, and other forms of shift work. ### 2.2.2. Assessment for suicide Suicide was evaluated by asking questions about suicidal ideation over the past year. The evaluative question presented to study participants asked, “*During the past year, have you ever felt that you were willing to die?*” They were classified as having suicidal ideation if they answered yes, and if they answered no, they were classified as having no suicidal ideation. ### 2.2.3. Assessment for quality of life Quality of life can be divided into health-related quality of life (HRQOL) and non-health-related quality of life (NHRQOL) (Spilker, 1996). Health-related quality of life refers to areas of life that are directly affected by changes in health. Health, as defined by the WHO, is not simply the absence of disease, but complete physical, mental, and social well-being. In this study, EuroQol-5 Dimension (EQ-5D) was used as an HRQOL measurement tool. EQ-5D is a tool that can measure HRQOL as a utility and consists of five items which include mobility, self-care, normal activities, pain/discomfort, and anxiety/depression. The higher the total score, the higher the quality of life. ### 2.2.4. Assessment for stress The stress level is evaluated with close-ended questions on a four points Likert scale (How much stress do you feel in your daily life?). The participants answered four type of stress level; extremely, stressful, moderately and minimally. ## 2.3. In the case of shift workers, negative factors such as depression and low quality of life are risk factors for suicide. Efforts are needed to reduce risk factors through administrative and policy interventions to manage workers' health by early screening. --- ## 1. Introduction ### 1.1. Shift work and health Shift work is defined as working outside the normal working hours of 7:00 am to 6:00 pm, with 15–25% of global workers working in shifts (Wickwire et al., 2017). Shift workers are exposed to artificial light at night, which causes their circadian rhythm to be disturbed (Fonken et al., 2013; Stevens et al., 2007). Light exposure at night can impair learning and memory abilities (Fonken et al., 2012) and may lead to neurodegeneration associated with Alzheimer's disease (Kim et al., 2018). Shift workers often complain of sleep disturbances or drowsiness during waking hours due to disturbances of the normal sleep-wake cycle. According to the Korean National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey (KHANES), 37.6% of workers get less than seven hours of sleep. Among them, sleep deprivation impacts 61.8% of shift workers (Yong et al., 2017). In addition, light pollution negatively impacts overall human health, including aging, metabolic processes, heart disease, diabetes, and mood disorders (Gangwisch, 2014; Hood et al., 2004; Stevens et al., 2007). Sleep is essential for humans to maintain physical and mental homeostasis by providing rest and stability. However, shift workers have no choice but to sleep at a different time than the body's circadian rhythm, resulting in poor sleep quality and sleep deprivation (Niu et al., 2011). Workers who complained of sleep disturbance were 2.8 times more likely to receive treatment (Daley et al., 2009) or prescription drugs for various health problems, including mental health problems, compared to those who did not (Haus and Smolensky, 2013; Kecklund and Axelsson, 2016). In the case of nurses, it can impact patient safety by reducing concentration and increasing fatigue during work, thus increasing the risk of various in-hospital accidents such as medication errors or malfunctions of medical devices (Wickwire et al., 2017; Yuan et al., 2011). As chronic circadian misalignment occurs, this social jet lag is known to have a negative effect on individual health, such as unhealthy eating habits, personality changes, metabolic disorders, and increased depression (Roenneberg et al., 2019). --- * Corresponding author at: Department of Psychiatry, Hanyang University Medical Center, 222-1, Wangsimni-ro, Seongdong-gu, Seoul 04763, Republic of Korea. Shift work and suicide A study of police officers discovered that depression, PTSD symptoms, and the type of work all increased suicidal ideation in female police officers (Violanti et al., 2008). Shift work was identified as a risk factor for workplace suicide (Stack, 2001; Tiesman et al., 2015). In our previous study, we confirmed that major emotional problems like depression, anxiety, and suicidal ideation were common among shift workers (Park et al., 2020). Another study reported that shift work increased work stress and that the risk of suicide was significantly increased when the quality of sleep was poor (Son and Lee, 2021). These results considered shift work as one of the major risk factors, but the question of which of the various factors affects the risk of suicide was not adequately addressed. ## 1.3. Purpose of this study With the continued development of machine learning, research using it is diversifying. Machine learning is useful when analyzing multiple predictors when there are nonlinear observation and interaction terms that are difficult to conceptualize theoretically and model in practice. This study attempted to predict suicidal ideation based on shift work patterns using machine learning techniques. Discussion In this study, suicidal ideation was predicted according to daytime or shift work using machine learning techniques. To predict this, variables such as depressive symptoms, quality of life scores, and stress perception, all of which are known risk factors for suicide, were used. We used RF for establish higher explanatory power to evaluate the model suitability, followed by DT to present the explanatory power of variables relative to suicidal ideation. The RF technique was found to select suicidal ideation with high specificity in both shift workers and daytime workers. In the DT model, it was confirmed that depressive symptoms, quality of life, and stress level were variables affecting suicidal ideation in both shift workers and daytime workers. When all three risk factors were present, the model results confirmed that there was a suicide risk of 54.0% for daytime workers and 82.7% for shift workers. These findings indicate that more delicate emotional management is required because shift workers who have all three risk factors may have a higher suicide risk. On the other hand, in the case of daytime workers, the research also suggests that other risk factors are affecting suicide risk in addition to the three risk factors. The next predictor variable was BMI, and a lower BMI was found to be a better predictor of suicidal ideation. This is consistent with the results of previous studies that low BMI is correlated with high suicide risk (Magnusson et al., 2006; Perera et al.,

70% and 30%, respectively. For the development of the analysis model, repeated 10-fold cross-validation was used. In 10-fold cross-validation, the training data is divided into 10 folds of the same size; one-fold is used as a validation set, and the remaining nine folds are used as a training set (Fig. 2). This step is repeated five times to avoid overfitting and generalizing the model. Daytime workers with suicidal ideation had higher hypertension (10.2%, $p < 0.001$), hyperlipidemia (9.2%, $p = 0.010$), stroke (14.3%, $p < 0.001$), myocardial infarction or angina (12.2%, $p < 0.001$), and diabetes (10.1%, $p < 0.001$). A history of cancer did not differ significantly from suicidal ideation in daytime workers ($p = 0.576$). Purpose of this study With the continued development of machine learning, research using it is diversifying. Machine learning is useful when analyzing multiple predictors when there are nonlinear observation and interaction terms that are difficult to conceptualize theoretically and model in practice. This study attempted to predict suicidal ideation based on shift work patterns using machine learning techniques. For this purpose, a variety of variables from national health surveys conducted over several years were used as predictive variables. # 2. Methods ## 2.1. Participants This study used data from KHANES. The KHANES is a nationwide health and nutrition survey based on Article 16 of the National Health Promotion Act enacted in 1995. The health level, health behavior, and food and nutritional intake are representative and reliable statistics at the national level and through these data, help to establish health policy, such as setting and evaluating the goals of the National Health Promotion Plan and developing health promotion programs. Data for a span of 10 years were used: 2007–2013, 2015, 2017, and 2019. The 2014, 2016, and 2018 surveys did not include adult suicidal ideation, so they were excluded. All participants in KHANES provided written consent prior to the investigation so that their personal information could be used. This study included 45,386 adults aged 20 years or older who had been working for at least one year out of 10 years of survey data. Among them, a total of 43,095 people were analyzed, excluding 1391 people who did not answer their work type and 919 people who did not respond to questions related to suicidal ideation (Fig. 1). The Institutional Review Board of the Korea Disease Control and Prevention Agency approved this study (2018-01-03-P-A). ## 2.2. Measurements ### 2.2.1. Assessment of work patterns We divided work types into day work and shift work. Shift work included evening work (14:00–24:00), night shift (21:00–08:00), regular day and night shift work, 24-h shift work, split work (more than two working hours per day), irregular shift work, and other forms of shift work. ### 2.2.2. Assessment for suicide Suicide was evaluated by asking questions about suicidal ideation over the past year. The evaluative question presented to study participants asked, “*During the past year, have you ever felt that you were willing to die?*” They were classified as having suicidal ideation if they answered yes, and if they answered no, they were classified as having no suicidal ideation. ### 2.2.3. Assessment for quality of life Quality of life can be divided into health-related quality of life (HRQOL) and non-health-related quality of life (NHRQOL) (Spilker, 1996). Health-related quality of life refers to areas of life that are directly affected by changes in health. Health, as defined by the WHO, is not simply the absence of disease, but complete physical, mental, and social well-being. In this study, EuroQol-5 Dimension (EQ-5D) was used as an HRQOL measurement tool. EQ-5D is a tool that can measure HRQOL as a utility and consists of five items which include mobility, self-care, normal activities, pain/discomfort, and anxiety/depression. The higher the total score, the higher the quality of life. ### 2.2.4. Assessment for stress The stress level is evaluated with close-ended questions on a four points Likert scale (How much stress do you feel in your daily life?). The participants answered four type of stress level; extremely, stressful, moderately and minimally. ## 2.3. In our previous study, we confirmed that major emotional problems like depression, anxiety, and suicidal ideation were common among shift workers (Park et al., 2020). Machine learning is useful when analyzing multiple predictors when there are nonlinear observation and interaction terms that are difficult to conceptualize theoretically and model in practice. This study attempted to predict suicidal ideation based on shift work patterns using machine learning techniques. For this purpose, a variety of variables from national health surveys conducted over several years were used as predictive variables. # 2. Methods ## 2.1. Participants This study used data from KHANES. The KHANES is a nationwide health and nutrition survey based on Article 16 of the National Health Promotion Act enacted in 1995. The health level, health behavior, and food and nutritional intake are representative and reliable statistics at the national level and through these data, help to establish health policy, such as setting and evaluating the goals of the National Health Promotion Plan and developing health promotion programs. Data for a span of 10 years were used: 2007–2013, 2015, 2017, and 2019. The 2014, 2016, and 2018 surveys did not include adult suicidal ideation, so they were excluded. All participants in KHANES provided written consent prior to the investigation so that their personal information could be used. This study included 45,386 adults aged 20 years or older who had been working for at least one year out of 10 years of survey data. Among them, a total of 43,095 people were analyzed, excluding 1391 people who did not answer their work type and 919 people who did not respond to questions related to suicidal ideation (Fig. 1). Discussion In this study, suicidal ideation was predicted according to daytime or shift work using machine learning techniques. To predict this, variables such as depressive symptoms, quality of life scores, and stress perception, all of which are known risk factors for suicide, were used. We used RF for establish higher explanatory power to evaluate the model suitability, followed by DT to present the explanatory power of variables relative to suicidal ideation. The RF technique was found to select suicidal ideation with high specificity in both shift workers and daytime workers. In the DT model, it was confirmed that depressive symptoms, quality of life, and stress level were variables affecting suicidal ideation in both shift workers and daytime workers. When all three risk factors were present, the model results confirmed that there was a suicide risk of 54.0% for daytime workers and 82.7% for shift workers. These findings indicate that more delicate emotional management is required because shift workers who have all three risk factors may have a higher suicide risk. On the other hand, in the case of daytime workers, the research also suggests that other risk factors are affecting suicide risk in addition to the three risk factors. The next predictor variable was BMI, and a lower BMI was found to be a better predictor of suicidal ideation. Purpose of this study With the continued development of machine learning, research using it is diversifying. Machine learning is useful when analyzing multiple predictors when there are nonlinear observation and interaction terms that are difficult to conceptualize theoretically and model in practice. This study attempted to predict suicidal ideation based on shift work patterns using machine learning techniques. For this purpose, a variety of variables from national health surveys conducted over several years were used as predictive variables. # 2. Methods ## 2.1. Participants This study used data from KHANES. The KHANES is a nationwide health and nutrition survey based on Article 16 of the National Health Promotion Act enacted in 1995. The health level, health behavior, and food and nutritional intake are representative and reliable statistics at the national level and through these data, help to establish health policy, such as setting and evaluating the goals of the National Health Promotion Plan and developing health promotion programs. Data for a span of 10 years were used: 2007–2013, 2015, 2017, and 2019. The 2014, 2016, and 2018 surveys did not include adult suicidal ideation, so they were excluded. All participants in KHANES provided written consent prior to the investigation so that their personal information could be used. This study included 45,386 adults aged 20 years or older who had been working for at least one year out of 10 years of survey data. Among them, a total of 43,095 people were analyzed, excluding 1391 people who did not answer their work type and 919 people who did not respond to questions related to suicidal ideation (Fig. 1). The Institutional Review Board of the Korea Disease Control and Prevention Agency approved this study (2018-01-03-P-A). ## 2.2. Measurements ### 2.2.1. Assessment of work patterns We divided work types into day work and shift work. Shift work included evening work (14:00–24:00), night shift (21:00–08:00), regular day and night shift work, 24-h shift work, split work (more than two working hours per day), irregular shift work, and other forms of shift work. ### 2.2.2. Assessment for suicide Suicide was evaluated by asking questions about suicidal ideation over the past year. The evaluative question presented to study participants asked, “*During the past year, have you ever felt that you were willing to die?*” They were classified as having suicidal ideation if they answered yes, and if they answered no, they were classified as having no suicidal ideation. ### 2.2.3. Assessment for quality of life Quality of life can be divided into health-related quality of life (HRQOL) and non-health-related quality of life (NHRQOL) (Spilker, 1996). Health-related quality of life refers to areas of life that are directly affected by changes in health. Health, as defined by the WHO, is not simply the absence of disease, but complete physical, mental, and social well-being. In this study, EuroQol-5 Dimension (EQ-5D) was used as an HRQOL measurement tool. EQ-5D is a tool that can measure HRQOL as a utility and consists of five items which include mobility, self-care, normal activities, pain/discomfort, and anxiety/depression. The higher the total score, the higher the quality of life. ### 2.2.4. Assessment for stress The stress level is evaluated with close-ended questions on a four points Likert scale (How much stress do you feel in your daily life?). The participants answered four type of stress level; extremely, stressful, moderately and minimally. ## 2.3. Purpose of this study With the continued development of machine learning, research using it is diversifying. Machine learning is useful when analyzing multiple predictors when there are nonlinear observation and interaction terms that are difficult to conceptualize theoretically and model in practice. This study attempted to predict suicidal ideation based on shift work patterns using machine learning techniques. For this purpose, a variety of variables from national health surveys conducted over several years were used as predictive variables. # 2. Methods ## 2.1. Participants This study used data from KHANES. The KHANES is a nationwide health and nutrition survey based on Article 16 of the National Health Promotion Act enacted in 1995. The health level, health behavior, and food and nutritional intake are representative and reliable statistics at the national level and through these data, help to establish health policy, such as setting and evaluating the goals of the National Health Promotion Plan and developing health promotion programs. Data for a span of 10 years were used: 2007–2013, 2015, 2017, and 2019. The 2014, 2016, and 2018 surveys did not include adult suicidal ideation, so they were excluded. All participants in KHANES provided written consent prior to the investigation so that their personal information could be used. This study included 45,386 adults aged 20 years or older who had been working for at least one year out of 10 years of survey data. Among them, a total of 43,095 people were analyzed, excluding 1391 people who did not answer their work type and 919 people who did not respond to questions related to suicidal ideation (Fig. 1). The Institutional Review Board of the Korea Disease Control and Prevention Agency approved this study (2018-01-03-P-A). ## 2.2. Measurements ### 2.2.1. Assessment of work patterns We divided work types into day work and shift work. Shift work included evening work (14:00–24:00), night shift (21:00–08:00), regular day and night shift work, 24-h shift work, split work (more than two working hours per day), irregular shift work, and other forms of shift work. ### 2.2.2. Assessment for suicide Suicide was evaluated by asking questions about suicidal ideation over the past year. The evaluative question presented to study participants asked, “*During the past year, have you ever felt that you were willing to die?*” They were classified as having suicidal ideation if they answered yes, and if they answered no, they were classified as having no suicidal ideation. ### 2.2.3. Assessment for quality of life Quality of life can be divided into health-related quality of life (HRQOL) and non-health-related quality of life (NHRQOL) (Spilker, 1996). Health-related quality of life refers to areas of life that are directly affected by changes in health. Health, as defined by the WHO, is not simply the absence of disease, but complete physical, mental, and social well-being. In this study, EuroQol-5 Dimension (EQ-5D) was used as an HRQOL measurement tool. EQ-5D is a tool that can measure HRQOL as a utility and consists of five items which include mobility, self-care, normal activities, pain/discomfort, and anxiety/depression. The higher the total score, the higher the quality of life. ### 2.2.4. Assessment for stress The stress level is evaluated with close-ended questions on a four points Likert scale (How much stress do you feel in your daily life?). The participants answered four type of stress level; extremely, stressful, moderately and minimally. ## 2.3. Shift work and suicide A study of police officers discovered that depression, PTSD symptoms, and the type of work all increased suicidal ideation in female police officers (Violanti et al., 2008). Shift work was identified as a risk factor for workplace suicide (Stack, 2001; Tiesman et al., 2015). In our previous study, we confirmed that major emotional problems like depression, anxiety, and suicidal ideation were common among shift workers (Park et al., 2020). Another study reported that shift work increased work stress and that the risk of suicide was significantly increased when the quality of sleep was poor (Son and Lee, 2021). These results considered shift work as one of the major risk factors, but the question of which of the various factors affects the risk of suicide was not adequately addressed. ## 1.3. Purpose of this study With the continued development of machine learning, research using it is diversifying. Machine learning is useful when analyzing multiple predictors when there are nonlinear observation and interaction terms that are difficult to conceptualize theoretically and model in practice. This study attempted to predict suicidal ideation based on shift work patterns using machine learning techniques. For this purpose, a variety of variables from national health surveys conducted over several years were used as predictive variables. # 2. Methods ## 2.1. Participants This study used data from KHANES. The KHANES is a nationwide health and nutrition survey based on Article 16 of the National Health Promotion Act enacted in 1995. The health level, health behavior, and food and nutritional intake are representative and reliable statistics at the national level and through these data, help to establish health policy, such as setting and evaluating the goals of the National Health Promotion Plan and developing health promotion programs. Data for a span of 10 years were used: 2007–2013, 2015, 2017, and 2019. The 2014, 2016, and 2018 surveys did not include adult suicidal ideation, so they were excluded. All participants in KHANES provided written consent prior to the investigation so that their personal information could be used. This study included 45,386 adults aged 20 years or older who had been working for at least one year out of 10 years of survey data. Among them, a total of 43,095 people were analyzed, excluding 1391 people who did not answer their work type and 919 people who did not respond to questions related to suicidal ideation (Fig. 1). The Institutional Review Board of the Korea Disease Control and Prevention Agency approved this study (2018-01-03-P-A). ## 2.2. Measurements ### 2.2.1. Assessment of work patterns We divided work types into day work and shift work. Shift work included evening work (14:00–24:00), night shift (21:00–08:00), regular day and night shift work, 24-h shift work, split work (more than two working hours per day), irregular shift work, and other forms of shift work. ### 2.2.2. Assessment for suicide Suicide was evaluated by asking questions about suicidal ideation over the past year. The evaluative question presented to study participants asked, “*During the past year, have you ever felt that you were willing to die?*” They were classified as having suicidal ideation if they answered yes, and if they answered no, they were classified as having no suicidal ideation. ### 2.2.3. Assessment for quality of life Quality of life can be divided into health-related quality of life (HRQOL) and non-health-related quality of life (NHRQOL) (Spilker, 1996). Health-related quality of life refers to areas of life that are directly affected by changes in health. Health, as defined by the WHO, is not simply the absence of disease, but complete physical, mental, and social well-being. In this study, EuroQol-5 Dimension (EQ-5D) was used as an HRQOL measurement tool. EQ-5D is a tool that can measure HRQOL as a utility and consists of five items which include mobility, self-care, normal activities, pain/discomfort, and anxiety/depression. The higher the total score, the higher the quality of life. ### 2.2.4. Assessment for stress The stress level is evaluated with close-ended questions on a four points Likert scale (How much stress do you feel in your daily life?). The participants answered four type of stress level; extremely, stressful, moderately and minimally. ## 2.3. Statistical analysis In this study, 19 analyzable variables thought to be related to suicidal ideation were selected and used. Missing values in some data were filled in using Predictive Mean Matching (PMM) from the Multiple Imputation by Chained Equations (MICE) package of R statistical software. Discussion In this study, suicidal ideation was predicted according to daytime or shift work using machine learning techniques. To predict this, variables such as depressive symptoms, quality of life scores, and stress perception, all of which are known risk factors for suicide, were used. We used RF for establish higher explanatory power to evaluate the model suitability, followed by DT to present the explanatory power of variables relative to suicidal ideation. The RF technique was found to select suicidal ideation with high specificity in both shift workers and daytime workers. In the DT model, it was confirmed that depressive symptoms, quality of life, and stress level were variables affecting suicidal ideation in both shift workers and daytime workers. When all three risk factors were present, the model results confirmed that there was a suicide risk of 54.0% for daytime workers and 82.7% for shift workers. These findings indicate that more delicate emotional management is required because shift workers who have all three risk factors may have a higher suicide risk. On the other hand, in the case of daytime workers, the research also suggests that other risk factors are affecting suicide risk in addition to the three risk factors. The next predictor variable was BMI, and a lower BMI was found to be a better predictor of suicidal ideation. This is consistent with the results of previous studies that low BMI is correlated with high suicide risk (Magnusson et al., 2006; Perera et al., 2010). Also, the low SES as a predictor is consistent with the results of previous studies (Daley et al., 2009; Taylor et al., 2005). This seems to be because SES is a factor that is mainly related to a person's living environment and quality of life. Machine learning methods for suicide research are useful for identifying risk factors using large-scale data (Fazel and O'Reilly, 2020). This research method is useful for identifying new risk factors from existing data, as well as known risk factors (de la Garza et al., 2021; Kim et al., 2021). In this study, it was confirmed that known variables act differently according to the characteristics of the group through the machine learning technique, and it was confirmed that the risk of suicide can be greatly increased by the group. A major risk factor for suicide is depression (Isometsa et al., 1994). In both types of work analyzed in this study, depression was the biggest risk factor for suicide. Shift workers have more emotional problems such as depression, suicidal ideation, and stress than daytime workers (Park et al., 2016). In addition, shift workers work at times that do not match with the physiological and social circadian rhythms, so their quality of sleep is poor. Among machine learning algorithms, RF is a method used to identify an optimal result by randomly combining the results by constructing multiple decision trees; RF is widely used because it is more accurate than decision trees. However, RF also has the disadvantage of losing the explanatory power of the variables included in the decision trees. A decision tree (DT) is one of the most widely used machine learning techniques for the purpose of classifying high-risk subjects. A decision tree is composed of decision nodes, branches, and leaves. It is divided into yes and no from the first question (Root Node), and the variable area is divided into two for each node, leading to the last terminal node. Finally, each divided tree is a set with the same tendency. Separation at each node can be said to have the highest explanatory, predictive power.
