General statistics Of the total 43,095 subjects, 22,604 daytime workers and 20,491 shift workers were enrolled. Age, sex, household income, education level, marital status, occupational classification, subjective health status, hypertension, stroke history, myocardial infarction or angina history, diabetes, drinking, smoking, stress level in daily life, depressive symptom and EQ-5D score was associated with suicidal ideation for both daytime workers and shift workers. Dyslipidemia was only associated with suicidal ideation in daytime workers, and cancer history was only associated with suicidal ideation in shift workers, and body mass index was not associated with suicidal ideation in both daytime workers and shift workers. Among the daytime workers, 1795 (7.9%) reported suicidal ideation and 3397 (16.6%) shift workers reported suicidal ideation during the past year. The older they were, the higher the rate of suicidal ideation ($p < 0.001$) in daytime workers and shift workers also had a higher rate of suicidal ideation as they got older ($p < 0.001$). Additionally, among daytime workers, the rate of suicidal ideation was higher among women (10.2%, $p < 0.001$) and females (21.0%) were nearly twice as likely to have suicidal ideation as males (10.9%, $p < 0.001$) in shift workers. Both daytime workers and shift workers had a higher rate of suicidal ideation when their household income ($p < 0.001$) and education level were lower ($p < 0.001$). work was identified as a risk factor for workplace suicide (Stack, 2001; Tiesman et al., 2015). In our previous study, we confirmed that major emotional problems like depression, anxiety, and suicidal ideation were common among shift workers (Park et al., 2020). Another study reported that shift work increased work stress and that the risk of suicide was significantly increased when the quality of sleep was poor (Son and Lee, 2021). These results considered shift work as one of the major risk factors, but the question of which of the various factors affects the risk of suicide was not adequately addressed. ## 1.3. Purpose of this study With the continued development of machine learning, research using it is diversifying. Machine learning is useful when analyzing multiple predictors when there are nonlinear observation and interaction terms that are difficult to conceptualize theoretically and model in practice. This study attempted to predict suicidal ideation based on shift work patterns using machine learning techniques. For this purpose, a variety of variables from national health surveys conducted over several years were used as predictive variables. # 2. Methods ## 2.1. Participants This study used data from KHANES. The KHANES is a nationwide health and nutrition survey based on Article 16 of the National Health Promotion Act enacted in 1995. The health level, health behavior, and food and nutritional intake are representative and reliable statistics at the national level and through these data, help to establish health policy, such as setting and evaluating the goals of the National Health Promotion Plan and developing health promotion programs. Data for a span of 10 years were used: 2007–2013, 2015, 2017, and 2019. The 2014, 2016, and 2018 surveys did not include adult suicidal ideation, so they were excluded. All participants in KHANES provided written consent prior to the investigation so that their personal information could be used. This study included 45,386 adults aged 20 years or older who had been working for at least one year out of 10 years of survey data. Among them, a total of 43,095 people were analyzed, excluding 1391 people who did not answer their work type and 919 people who did not respond to questions related to suicidal ideation (Fig. 1). The Institutional Review Board of the Korea Disease Control and Prevention Agency approved this study (2018-01-03-P-A). ## 2.2. Measurements ### 2.2.1. Assessment of work patterns We divided work types into day work and shift work. Shift work included evening work (14:00–24:00), night shift (21:00–08:00), regular day and night shift work, 24-h shift work, split work (more than two working hours per day), irregular shift work, and other forms of shift work. ### 2.2.2. Assessment for suicide Suicide was evaluated by asking questions about suicidal ideation over the past year. The evaluative question presented to study participants asked, “*During the past year, have you ever felt that you were willing to die?*” They were classified as having suicidal ideation if they answered yes, and if they answered no, they were classified as having no suicidal ideation. ### 2.2.3. Assessment for quality of life Quality of life can be divided into health-related quality of life (HRQOL) and non-health-related quality of life (NHRQOL) (Spilker, 1996). Health-related quality of life refers to areas of life that are directly affected by changes in health. Health, as defined by the WHO, is not simply the absence of disease, but complete physical, mental, and social well-being. In this study, EuroQol-5 Dimension (EQ-5D) was used as an HRQOL measurement tool. EQ-5D is a tool that can measure HRQOL as a utility and consists of five items which include mobility, self-care, normal activities, pain/discomfort, and anxiety/depression. The higher the total score, the higher the quality of life. ### 2.2.4. Assessment for stress The stress level is evaluated with close-ended questions on a four points Likert scale (How much stress do you feel in your daily life?). The participants answered four type of stress level; extremely, stressful, moderately and minimally. ## 2.3. Statistical analysis In this study, 19 analyzable variables thought to be related to suicidal ideation were selected and used. Missing values in some data were filled in using Predictive Mean Matching (PMM) from the Multiple Imputation by Chained Equations (MICE) package of R statistical software. Discussion In this study, suicidal ideation was predicted according to daytime or shift work using machine learning techniques. To predict this, variables such as depressive symptoms, quality of life scores, and stress perception, all of which are known risk factors for suicide, were used. We used RF for establish higher explanatory power to evaluate the model suitability, followed by DT to present the explanatory power of variables relative to suicidal ideation. The RF technique was found to select suicidal ideation with high specificity in both shift workers and daytime workers. In the DT model, it was confirmed that depressive symptoms, quality of life, and stress level were variables affecting suicidal ideation in both shift workers and daytime workers. When all three risk factors were present, the model results confirmed that there was a suicide risk of 54.0% for daytime workers and 82.7% for shift workers. These findings indicate that more delicate emotional management is required because shift workers who have all three risk factors may have a higher suicide risk. On the other hand, in the case of daytime workers, the research also suggests that other risk factors are affecting suicide risk in addition to the three risk factors. The next predictor variable was BMI, and a lower BMI was found to be a better predictor of suicidal ideation. Assessment of work patterns We divided work types into day work and shift work. Shift work included evening work (14:00–24:00), night shift (21:00–08:00), regular day and night shift work, 24-h shift work, split work (more than two working hours per day), irregular shift work, and other forms of shift work. ### 2.2.2. Assessment for suicide Suicide was evaluated by asking questions about suicidal ideation over the past year. The evaluative question presented to study participants asked, “*During the past year, have you ever felt that you were willing to die?*” They were classified as having suicidal ideation if they answered yes, and if they answered no, they were classified as having no suicidal ideation. ### 2.2.3. Assessment for quality of life Quality of life can be divided into health-related quality of life (HRQOL) and non-health-related quality of life (NHRQOL) (Spilker, 1996). Health-related quality of life refers to areas of life that are directly affected by changes in health. Health, as defined by the WHO, is not simply the absence of disease, but complete physical, mental, and social well-being. In this study, EuroQol-5 Dimension (EQ-5D) was used as an HRQOL measurement tool. EQ-5D is a tool that can measure HRQOL as a utility and consists of five items which include mobility, self-care, normal activities, pain/discomfort, and anxiety/depression. The higher the total score, the higher the quality of life. ### 2.2.4. Assessment for stress The stress level is evaluated with close-ended questions on a four points Likert scale (How much stress do you feel in your daily life?). The participants answered four type of stress level; extremely, stressful, moderately and minimally. ## 2.3. Among machine learning algorithms, RF is a method used to identify an optimal result by randomly combining the results by constructing multiple decision trees; RF is widely used because it is more accurate than decision trees. However, RF also has the disadvantage of losing the explanatory power of the variables included in the decision trees. A decision tree (DT) is one of the most widely used machine learning techniques for the purpose of classifying high-risk subjects. A decision tree is composed of decision nodes, branches, and leaves. It is divided into yes and no from the first question (Root Node), and the variable area is divided into two for each node, leading to the last terminal node. Finally, each divided tree is a set with the same tendency. Separation at each node can be said to have the highest explanatory, predictive power. Therefore, in this study, RF, a method with higher explanatory power, was performed first to evaluate the model suitability, followed by DT to present the explanatory power of each variable relative to suicidal ideation. Discussion In this study, suicidal ideation was predicted according to daytime or shift work using machine learning techniques. To predict this, variables such as depressive symptoms, quality of life scores, and stress perception, all of which are known risk factors for suicide, were used. We used RF for establish higher explanatory power to evaluate the model suitability, followed by DT to present the explanatory power of variables relative to suicidal ideation. The RF technique was found to select suicidal ideation with high specificity in both shift workers and daytime workers. In the DT model, it was confirmed that depressive symptoms, quality of life, and stress level were variables affecting suicidal ideation in both shift workers and daytime workers. When all three risk factors were present, the model results confirmed that there was a suicide risk of 54.0% for daytime workers and 82.7% for shift workers. These findings indicate that more delicate emotional management is required because shift workers who have all three risk factors may have a higher suicide risk. On the other hand, in the case of daytime workers, the research also suggests that other risk factors are affecting suicide risk in addition to the three risk factors. The next predictor variable was BMI, and a lower BMI was found to be a better predictor of suicidal ideation. Journal of Affective Disorders 307 (2022) 125–132 Contents lists available at ScienceDirect Journal of Affective Disorders journal homepage: www.elsevier.com/locate/jad ## Research paper # Prediction of suicidal ideation in shift workers compared to non-shift workers using machine learning techniques Hwanjin Park^a, Kounseok Lee^b,* ^a Department of Occupational & Environmental Medicine, Kangbuk Samsung Hospital, Sungkyunkwan University School of Medicine, Seoul, Republic of Korea ^b Department of Psychiatry, Hanyang University Medical Center, Seoul, Republic of Korea --- ## ARTICLE INFO Keywords: - Shift workers - Daytime workers - Suicide - Depression - Machine learning ## ABSTRACT Background: Shift work can affect sleep and increase the risk of suicide. This study attempted to predict suicidal ideation according to shift work by using machine learning techniques. Methods: We analyzed a total of 43,095 data conducted by using the 10-year Korean National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey (KHANES). Shift workers and daytime workers were categorized and analyzed using random forest (RF) and decision tree (DT) techniques of machine learning techniques. Results: Shift workers were more than twice as likely to have suicidal ideation as daytime workers. The RF model showed an accuracy of 91.6% for shift workers and 98% for daytime workers. In the DT technique, the rate of suicidal ideation was the highest among shift workers (82.7%) when they were depressed and had an EuroQol-5 Dimension (EQ-5D) score of less than 0.71. Limitations: Shift work type was evaluated questionnaire and based on screening data, it was not possible to reflect recent changes in the work type and we evaluated for only suicidal ideation for suicide risk factors. Conclusion: The variables influencing the suicide risk of shift workers and daytime workers differ. In the case of shift workers, negative factors such as depression and low quality of life are risk factors for suicide. Efforts are needed to reduce risk factors through administrative and policy interventions to manage workers' health by early screening. --- ## 1. Introduction ### 1.1. Shift work and health Shift work is defined as working outside the normal working hours of 7:00 am to 6:00 pm, with 15–25% of global workers working in shifts (Wickwire et al., 2017). Shift workers are exposed to artificial light at night, which causes their circadian rhythm to be disturbed (Fonken et al., 2013; Stevens et al., 2007). Light exposure at night can impair learning and memory abilities (Fonken et al., 2012) and may lead to neurodegeneration associated with Alzheimer's disease (Kim et al., 2018). Shift workers often complain of sleep disturbances or drowsiness during waking hours due to disturbances of the normal sleep-wake cycle. According to the Korean National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey (KHANES), 37.6% of workers get less than seven hours of sleep. Among them, sleep deprivation impacts 61.8% of shift workers (Yong et al., 2017). In addition, light pollution negatively impacts overall human health, including aging, metabolic processes, heart disease, diabetes, and mood disorders (Gangwisch, 2014; Hood et al., 2004; Stevens et al., 2007). Sleep is essential for humans to maintain physical and mental homeostasis by providing rest and stability. However, shift workers have no choice but to sleep at a different time than the body's circadian rhythm, resulting in poor sleep quality and sleep deprivation (Niu et al., 2011). Workers who complained of sleep disturbance were 2.8 times more likely to receive treatment (Daley et al., 2009) or prescription drugs for various health problems, including mental health problems, compared to those who did not (Haus and Smolensky, 2013; Kecklund and Axelsson, 2016). In the case of nurses, it can impact patient safety by reducing concentration and increasing fatigue during work, thus increasing the risk of various in-hospital accidents such as medication errors or malfunctions of medical devices (Wickwire et al., 2017; Yuan et al., 2011). As chronic circadian misalignment occurs, this social jet lag is known to have a negative effect on individual health, such as unhealthy eating habits, personality changes, metabolic disorders, and increased depression (Roenneberg et al., 2019). --- * Corresponding author at: Department of Psychiatry, Hanyang University Medical Center, 222-1, Wangsimni-ro, Seongdong-gu, Seoul 04763, Republic of Korea. The RF technique was found to select suicidal ideation with high specificity in both shift workers and daytime workers. Purpose of this study With the continued development of machine learning, research using it is diversifying. Machine learning is useful when analyzing multiple predictors when there are nonlinear observation and interaction terms that are difficult to conceptualize theoretically and model in practice. This study attempted to predict suicidal ideation based on shift work patterns using machine learning techniques. For this purpose, a variety of variables from national health surveys conducted over several years were used as predictive variables. # 2. Methods ## 2.1. Participants This study used data from KHANES. The KHANES is a nationwide health and nutrition survey based on Article 16 of the National Health Promotion Act enacted in 1995. The health level, health behavior, and food and nutritional intake are representative and reliable statistics at the national level and through these data, help to establish health policy, such as setting and evaluating the goals of the National Health Promotion Plan and developing health promotion programs. Data for a span of 10 years were used: 2007–2013, 2015, 2017, and 2019. The 2014, 2016, and 2018 surveys did not include adult suicidal ideation, so they were excluded. All participants in KHANES provided written consent prior to the investigation so that their personal information could be used. This study included 45,386 adults aged 20 years or older who had been working for at least one year out of 10 years of survey data. Among them, a total of 43,095 people were analyzed, excluding 1391 people who did not answer their work type and 919 people who did not respond to questions related to suicidal ideation (Fig. 1). The Institutional Review Board of the Korea Disease Control and Prevention Agency approved this study (2018-01-03-P-A). ## 2.2. Measurements ### 2.2.1. Assessment of work patterns We divided work types into day work and shift work. Shift work included evening work (14:00–24:00), night shift (21:00–08:00), regular day and night shift work, 24-h shift work, split work (more than two working hours per day), irregular shift work, and other forms of shift work. ### 2.2.2. Assessment for suicide Suicide was evaluated by asking questions about suicidal ideation over the past year. The evaluative question presented to study participants asked, “*During the past year, have you ever felt that you were willing to die?*” They were classified as having suicidal ideation if they answered yes, and if they answered no, they were classified as having no suicidal ideation. ### 2.2.3. Assessment for quality of life Quality of life can be divided into health-related quality of life (HRQOL) and non-health-related quality of life (NHRQOL) (Spilker, 1996). Health-related quality of life refers to areas of life that are directly affected by changes in health. Health, as defined by the WHO, is not simply the absence of disease, but complete physical, mental, and social well-being. In this study, EuroQol-5 Dimension (EQ-5D) was used as an HRQOL measurement tool. EQ-5D is a tool that can measure HRQOL as a utility and consists of five items which include mobility, self-care, normal activities, pain/discomfort, and anxiety/depression. The higher the total score, the higher the quality of life. ### 2.2.4. Assessment for stress The stress level is evaluated with close-ended questions on a four points Likert scale (How much stress do you feel in your daily life?). The participants answered four type of stress level; extremely, stressful, moderately and minimally. ## 2.3. Among machine learning algorithms, RF is a method used to identify an optimal result by randomly combining the results by constructing multiple decision trees; RF is widely used because it is more accurate than decision trees. However, RF also has the disadvantage of losing the explanatory power of the variables included in the decision trees. A decision tree (DT) is one of the most widely used machine learning techniques for the purpose of classifying high-risk subjects. A decision tree is composed of decision nodes, branches, and leaves. It is divided into yes and no from the first question (Root Node), and the variable area is divided into two for each node, leading to the last terminal node. Finally, each divided tree is a set with the same tendency. Separation at each node can be said to have the highest explanatory, predictive power. Therefore, in this study, RF, a method with higher explanatory power, was performed first to evaluate the model suitability, followed by DT to present the explanatory power of each variable relative to suicidal ideation. Discussion In this study, suicidal ideation was predicted according to daytime or shift work using machine learning techniques. To predict this, variables such as depressive symptoms, quality of life scores, and stress perception, all of which are known risk factors for suicide, were used. We used RF for establish higher explanatory power to evaluate the model suitability, followed by DT to present the explanatory power of variables relative to suicidal ideation. The RF technique was found to select suicidal ideation with high specificity in both shift workers and daytime workers. In the DT model, it was confirmed that depressive symptoms, quality of life, and stress level were variables affecting suicidal ideation in both shift workers and daytime workers. When all three risk factors were present, the model results confirmed that there was a suicide risk of 54.0% for daytime workers and 82.7% for shift workers. These findings indicate that more delicate emotional management is required because shift workers who have all three risk factors may have a higher suicide risk. On the other hand, in the case of daytime workers, the research also suggests that other risk factors are affecting suicide risk in addition to the three risk factors. The next predictor variable was BMI, and a lower BMI was found to be a better predictor of suicidal ideation. General statistics Of the total 43,095 subjects, 22,604 daytime workers and 20,491 shift workers were enrolled. Age, sex, household income, education level, marital status, occupational classification, subjective health status, hypertension, stroke history, myocardial infarction or angina history, diabetes, drinking, smoking, stress level in daily life, depressive symptom and EQ-5D score was associated with suicidal ideation for both daytime workers and shift workers. Dyslipidemia was only associated with suicidal ideation in daytime workers, and cancer history was only associated with suicidal ideation in shift workers, and body mass index was not associated with suicidal ideation in both daytime workers and shift workers. Among the daytime workers, 1795 (7.9%) reported suicidal ideation and 3397 (16.6%) shift workers reported suicidal ideation during the past year. The older they were, the higher the rate of suicidal ideation ($p < 0.001$) in daytime workers and shift workers also had a higher rate of suicidal ideation as they got older ($p < 0.001$). Additionally, among daytime workers, the rate of suicidal ideation was higher among women (10.2%, $p < 0.001$) and females (21.0%) were nearly twice as likely to have suicidal ideation as males (10.9%, $p < 0.001$) in shift workers. Both daytime workers and shift workers had a higher rate of suicidal ideation when their household income ($p < 0.001$) and education level were lower ($p < 0.001$). Among machine learning algorithms, RF is a method used to identify an optimal result by randomly combining the results by constructing multiple decision trees; RF is widely used because it is more accurate than decision trees. However, RF also has the disadvantage of losing the explanatory power of the variables included in the decision trees. A decision tree (DT) is one of the most widely used machine learning techniques for the purpose of classifying high-risk subjects. A decision tree is composed of decision nodes, branches, and leaves. It is divided into yes and no from the first question (Root Node), and the variable area is divided into two for each node, leading to the last terminal node. Finally, each divided tree is a set with the same tendency. Separation at each node can be said to have the highest explanatory, predictive power. Therefore, in this study, RF, a method with higher explanatory power, was performed first to evaluate the model suitability, followed by DT to present the explanatory power of each variable relative to suicidal ideation. All ML analyses were conducted including all variables in Table 1. Daytime workers and shift workers were analyzed by dividing the sample into training data and test data by 70% and 30%, respectively. Those who experienced depressive symptoms for 2 weeks or more and had an EQ-5D score of less than 0.71 had the highest rate of suicidal ideation (82.7%). If they experienced depressive symptoms for 2 weeks or more, had an EQ-5D score of 0.91 or higher, their daily life stress perception was stressed or extremely stressed, their BMI was less than 22, and their household income is low, the rate of suicidal ideation was 69.4%. If they experienced depressive symptoms and their EQ-5D score was 0.71-0.91, and their daily life stress perception was stressed or extremely stressed, the rate of suicidal ideation was the third highest at 66.8%. If they experienced depressive symptoms, had an EQ-5D score that was 0.91 or higher, had daily life stress perception that was stressed or extremely stressed, and had a BMI that was 30 or higher, the rate of suicidal ideation was the fourth highest at 66.7%. The rate of suicidal ideation was the lowest among those who had not experienced depressive symptoms for more than 2 weeks, at 10.1% (Fig. 4). ## 4. Discussion In this study, suicidal ideation was predicted according to daytime or shift work using machine learning techniques. To predict this, variables such as depressive symptoms, quality of life scores, and stress perception, all of which are known risk factors for suicide, were used. We used RF for establish higher explanatory power to evaluate the model suitability, followed by DT to present the explanatory power of variables relative to suicidal ideation. The RF technique was found to select suicidal ideation with high specificity in both shift workers and daytime workers. In the DT model, it was confirmed that depressive symptoms, quality of life, and stress level were variables affecting suicidal ideation in both shift workers and daytime workers. When all three risk factors were present, the model results confirmed that there was a suicide risk of 54.0% for daytime workers and 82.7% for shift workers. These findings indicate that more delicate emotional management is required because shift workers who have all three risk factors may have a higher suicide risk. On the other hand, in the case of daytime workers, the research also suggests that other risk factors are affecting suicide risk in addition to the three risk factors. The next predictor variable was BMI, and a lower BMI was found to be a better predictor of suicidal ideation. This is consistent with the results of previous studies that low BMI is correlated with high suicide risk (Magnusson et al., 2006; Perera et al., 2010). Also, the low SES as a predictor is consistent with the results of previous studies (Daley et al., 2009; Taylor et al., 2005). This seems to be because SES is a factor that is mainly related to a person's living environment and quality of life. Machine learning methods for suicide research are useful for identifying risk factors using large-scale data (Fazel and O'Reilly, 2020). This research method is useful for identifying new risk factors from existing data, as well as known risk factors (de la Garza et al., 2021; Kim et al., 2021). In this study, it was confirmed that known variables act differently according to the characteristics of the group through the machine learning technique, and it was confirmed that the risk of suicide can be greatly increased by the group. A major risk factor for suicide is depression (Isometsa et al., 1994). In both types of work analyzed in this study, depression was the biggest risk factor for suicide. Shift workers have more emotional problems such as depression, suicidal ideation, and stress than daytime workers (Park et al., 2016). In addition, shift workers work at times that do not match with the physiological and social circadian rhythms, so their quality of sleep is poor. Discussion In this study, suicidal ideation was predicted according to daytime or shift work using machine learning techniques. To predict this, variables such as depressive symptoms, quality of life scores, and stress perception, all of which are known risk factors for suicide, were used. We used RF for establish higher explanatory power to evaluate the model suitability, followed by DT to present the explanatory power of variables relative to suicidal ideation. The RF technique was found to select suicidal ideation with high specificity in both shift workers and daytime workers. In the DT model, it was confirmed that depressive symptoms, quality of life, and stress level were variables affecting suicidal ideation in both shift workers and daytime workers. When all three risk factors were present, the model results confirmed that there was a suicide risk of 54.0% for daytime workers and 82.7% for shift workers. On the other hand, in the case of daytime workers, the research also suggests that other risk factors are affecting suicide risk in addition to the three risk factors. The next predictor variable was BMI, and a lower BMI was found to be a better predictor of suicidal ideation. It is divided into yes and no from the first question (Root Node), and the variable area is divided into two for each node, leading to the last terminal node. Finally, each divided tree is a set with the same tendency. Separation at each node can be said to have the highest explanatory, predictive power. the National Health Promotion Plan and developing health promotion programs. Data for a span of 10 years were used: 2007–2013, 2015, 2017, and 2019. The 2014, 2016, and 2018 surveys did not include adult suicidal ideation, so they were excluded. All participants in KHANES provided written consent prior to the investigation so that their personal information could be used. This study included 45,386 adults aged 20 years or older who had been working for at least one year out of 10 years of survey data. Among them, a total of 43,095 people were analyzed, excluding 1391 people who did not answer their work type and 919 people who did not respond to questions related to suicidal ideation (Fig. 1). The Institutional Review Board of the Korea Disease Control and Prevention Agency approved this study (2018-01-03-P-A). ## 2.2. Measurements ### 2.2.1. Assessment of work patterns We divided work types into day work and shift work. Shift work included evening work (14:00–24:00), night shift (21:00–08:00), regular day and night shift work, 24-h shift work, split work (more than two working hours per day), irregular shift work, and other forms of shift work. ### 2.2.2. Assessment for suicide Suicide was evaluated by asking questions about suicidal ideation over the past year. The evaluative question presented to study participants asked, “*During the past year, have you ever felt that you were willing to die?*” They were classified as having suicidal ideation if they answered yes, and if they answered no, they were classified as having no suicidal ideation. ### 2.2.3. Assessment for quality of life Quality of life can be divided into health-related quality of life (HRQOL) and non-health-related quality of life (NHRQOL) (Spilker, 1996). Health-related quality of life refers to areas of life that are directly affected by changes in health. Health, as defined by the WHO, is not simply the absence of disease, but complete physical, mental, and social well-being. In this study, EuroQol-5 Dimension (EQ-5D) was used as an HRQOL measurement tool. EQ-5D is a tool that can measure HRQOL as a utility and consists of five items which include mobility, self-care, normal activities, pain/discomfort, and anxiety/depression. The higher the total score, the higher the quality of life. ### 2.2.4. Assessment for stress The stress level is evaluated with close-ended questions on a four points Likert scale (How much stress do you feel in your daily life?). The participants answered four type of stress level; extremely, stressful, moderately and minimally. ## 2.3. To predict this, variables such as depressive symptoms, quality of life scores, and stress perception, all of which are known risk factors for suicide, were used. We used RF for establish higher explanatory power to evaluate the model suitability, followed by DT to present the explanatory power of variables relative to suicidal ideation. The RF technique was found to select suicidal ideation with high specificity in both shift workers and daytime workers. In the DT model, it was confirmed that depressive symptoms, quality of life, and stress level were variables affecting suicidal ideation in both shift workers and daytime workers. Among machine learning algorithms, RF is a method used to identify an optimal result by randomly combining the results by constructing multiple decision trees; RF is widely used because it is more accurate than decision trees. However, RF also has the disadvantage of losing the explanatory power of the variables included in the decision trees. A decision tree (DT) is one of the most widely used machine learning techniques for the purpose of classifying high-risk subjects. A decision tree is composed of decision nodes, branches, and leaves. It is divided into yes and no from the first question (Root Node), and the variable area is divided into two for each node, leading to the last terminal node. Finally, each divided tree is a set with the same tendency. Separation at each node can be said to have the highest explanatory, predictive power. Another study reported that shift work increased work stress and that the risk of suicide was significantly increased when the quality of sleep was poor (Son and Lee, 2021). Purpose of this study With the continued development of machine learning, research using it is diversifying. Machine learning is useful when analyzing multiple predictors when there are nonlinear observation and interaction terms that are difficult to conceptualize theoretically and model in practice. This study attempted to predict suicidal ideation based on shift work patterns using machine learning techniques. For this purpose, a variety of variables from national health surveys conducted over several years were used as predictive variables. # 2. Methods ## 2.1. Participants This study used data from KHANES. The KHANES is a nationwide health and nutrition survey based on Article 16 of the National Health Promotion Act enacted in 1995. The health level, health behavior, and food and nutritional intake are representative and reliable statistics at the national level and through these data, help to establish health policy, such as setting and evaluating the goals of the National Health Promotion Plan and developing health promotion programs. Data for a span of 10 years were used: 2007–2013, 2015, 2017, and 2019. The 2014, 2016, and 2018 surveys did not include adult suicidal ideation, so they were excluded. All participants in KHANES provided written consent prior to the investigation so that their personal information could be used. This study included 45,386 adults aged 20 years or older who had been working for at least one year out of 10 years of survey data. Among them, a total of 43,095 people were analyzed, excluding 1391 people who did not answer their work type and 919 people who did not respond to questions related to suicidal ideation (Fig. 1). The Institutional Review Board of the Korea Disease Control and Prevention Agency approved this study (2018-01-03-P-A). ## 2.2. Measurements ### 2.2.1. Assessment of work patterns We divided work types into day work and shift work. Shift work included evening work (14:00–24:00), night shift (21:00–08:00), regular day and night shift work, 24-h shift work, split work (more than two working hours per day), irregular shift work, and other forms of shift work. ### 2.2.2. Assessment for suicide Suicide was evaluated by asking questions about suicidal ideation over the past year. The evaluative question presented to study participants asked, “*During the past year, have you ever felt that you were willing to die?*” They were classified as having suicidal ideation if they answered yes, and if they answered no, they were classified as having no suicidal ideation. ### 2.2.3. Assessment for quality of life Quality of life can be divided into health-related quality of life (HRQOL) and non-health-related quality of life (NHRQOL) (Spilker, 1996). Health-related quality of life refers to areas of life that are directly affected by changes in health. Health, as defined by the WHO, is not simply the absence of disease, but complete physical, mental, and social well-being. In this study, EuroQol-5 Dimension (EQ-5D) was used as an HRQOL measurement tool. EQ-5D is a tool that can measure HRQOL as a utility and consists of five items which include mobility, self-care, normal activities, pain/discomfort, and anxiety/depression. The higher the total score, the higher the quality of life. ### 2.2.4. Assessment for stress The stress level is evaluated with close-ended questions on a four points Likert scale (How much stress do you feel in your daily life?). The participants answered four type of stress level; extremely, stressful, moderately and minimally. ## 2.3. Among machine learning algorithms, RF is a method used to identify an optimal result by randomly combining the results by constructing multiple decision trees; RF is widely used because it is more accurate than decision trees. However, RF also has the disadvantage of losing the explanatory power of the variables included in the decision trees. A decision tree (DT) is one of the most widely used machine learning techniques for the purpose of classifying high-risk subjects. A decision tree is composed of decision nodes, branches, and leaves. It is divided into yes and no from the first question (Root Node), and the variable area is divided into two for each node, leading to the last terminal node. Finally, each divided tree is a set with the same tendency. Separation at each node can be said to have the highest explanatory, predictive power. Therefore, in this study, RF, a method with higher explanatory power, was performed first to evaluate the model suitability, followed by DT to present the explanatory power of each variable relative to suicidal ideation. A major risk factor for suicide is depression (Isometsa et al., 1994). In both types of work analyzed in this study, depression was the biggest risk factor for suicide. Suicide is a phenomenon in which not only depressive symptoms, but also various emotional factors interact in a complex manner. According to the interpersonal theory of suicide, thwarted belongingness and perceived burdensomeness are the most influential factors in suicidal ideation that cause the desire to commit suicide (Joiner, 2007). For workers, the workplace has many meanings, including a means of livelihood, a place to take responsibility for their work and feel a sense of accomplishment, as well as a sense of belonging as a member of an organization. In the shift worker group, their quality of life and the level of stress: the variables affecting suicidal ideation had a greater effect compared with daytime workers. Since these factors can cause emotional difficulties, they can act as direct or indirect risk factors for suicide. As the satisfaction gained while working affects not only work life but also daily life, work satisfaction in an individual's life is important (Kwon and Lee, 2015). However, in the case of shift workers, results confirmed that emotional difficulties had a greater impact than on daytime workers. This type of work, itself, causes stress and can become a risk factor for suicide through processes such as decreased work satisfaction. Adjustment problems of shift workers may vary depending on individual characteristics. In general, women have more difficulty sleeping than men as they get older, and there are also differences in shift work adaptation based on chronotype (Booker et al., 2018; Wickwire et al., 2017). One example, the circadian type, is an individual's sleep-wake preference with a 24-h cycle, that is classified into morning type, intermediate type, and evening type (Booker et al., 2018). In addition, when we divide our circadian preferences into younger, male, morning, and evening types, the evening type can adapt relatively well (Saksvik et al., 2011). In the case of shift worker, active environmental control measures, such as using blackout curtains to improve sleep or earplugs to reduce noise, can also be helpful. Interventions such as light therapy before a night shift and wearing sunglasses after work to limit light are beneficial for workers with fast rotational shifts, especially those in the evening type (Olson et al., 2020). The RF technique was found to select suicidal ideation with high specificity in both shift workers and daytime workers. Shift work and suicide A study of police officers discovered that depression, PTSD symptoms, and the type of work all increased suicidal ideation in female police officers (Violanti et al., 2008). Shift work was identified as a risk factor for workplace suicide (Stack, 2001; Tiesman et al., 2015). In our previous study, we confirmed that major emotional problems like depression, anxiety, and suicidal ideation were common among shift workers (Park et al., 2020). Another study reported that shift work increased work stress and that the risk of suicide was significantly increased when the quality of sleep was poor (Son and Lee, 2021). These results considered shift work as one of the major risk factors, but the question of which of the various factors affects the risk of suicide was not adequately addressed. ## 1.3. Purpose of this study With the continued development of machine learning, research using it is diversifying. Machine learning is useful when analyzing multiple predictors when there are nonlinear observation and interaction terms that are difficult to conceptualize theoretically and model in practice. Data for a span of 10 years were used: 2007–2013, 2015, 2017, and 2019. The 2014, 2016, and 2018 surveys did not include adult suicidal ideation, so they were excluded. Data Characteristics For the proposed analysis, data drawn from patients with PD interacting with the "Fishing Game" and iMAT are used. These data corresponded to the clinical motor assessment data of patients with PD, performed by neurologists from the three different European medical centers (i.e., Greece, Germany, and the UK). The main characteristics embedded in the clinical dataset correspond to patients’ username, ID, demographics, whether on medication or not, Hoehn and Yahr (H&Y) clinical rating scale, and their score in MDS-UPDRS Part III items 18, 23, 24, 25, 26, and 28. The H&Y is a standard clinical rating scale that stages the functional disability associated with PD. The original H&Y scale consists of five stages, where Stage 1 has unilateral involvement, Stage 2 bilateral without impairment of balance, Stage 3 bilateral with impairment of posture, Stage 4 represents the severity of the disease associated with lack of physical independence, and finally, Stage 5 is for patients bounded by a bed or wheelchair (Goetz et al., 2004). The patients in this study enrolled from three different countries, i.e., Greece, Germany, and the UK. The gender distribution was a ratio of 1 to 2, having 9 women and 18 men patients with PD, where the majority were male patients with PD. All patients were under PD medication except one participant. The data acquisition took place from September 2019 to January 2020, during periodic sessions (1 per month) of the iMAT within a controlled environment at the three medical centers. PD Rehabilitation and SGs Multiple pieces of evidence revealed that patients with PD suffer from progressive deterioration in their disability, despite following the recommended medical prescriptions (Ellis et al., 2008; Abbruzzese et al., 2016). Exercise and physical activity were found to be directly correlated with enhancing the health and well-being of patients with PD. Rehabilitation therapies for PD primarily focus on improving patients' overall quality of life, maximizing their level of mobility and activity (Soh et al., 2012). In spite of several proves of adopting physical activities in rehabilitation programs is powerful means for reducing the risk of causing PD, the current conventional programs have been discovered to be heterogeneous, sub-optimal, and lack common consensus (Abbruzzese et al., 2016). In addition, supporting exercise-based rehabilitation programs continues to face challenges in cost, accessibility, patient adherence, and acceptability (Barry et al., 2014). Abbruzzese et al. (2016), proposed an innovative substitute by introducing therapeutic techniques, such as Motor Imagery (MI) and Action Observation Therapy (AOT) (Abbruzzese et al., 2016). Through matching the internal representations with the imagined and observed actions from these methods, patients' motor skills are enhanced and new learning tasks are built. (2017), considered the use of Motion Capture Systems (MCS), such as the Microsoft Kinect® sensor, for patients with neurological disorders like PD. PD Rehabilitation and SGs Multiple pieces of evidence revealed that patients with PD suffer from progressive deterioration in their disability, despite following the recommended medical prescriptions (Ellis et al., 2008; Abbruzzese et al., 2016). Exercise and physical activity were found to be directly correlated with enhancing the health and well-being of patients with PD. Rehabilitation therapies for PD primarily focus on improving patients' overall quality of life, maximizing their level of mobility and activity (Soh et al., 2012). In spite of several proves of adopting physical activities in rehabilitation programs is powerful means for reducing the risk of causing PD, the current conventional programs have been discovered to be heterogeneous, sub-optimal, and lack common consensus (Abbruzzese et al., 2016). In addition, supporting exercise-based rehabilitation programs continues to face challenges in cost, accessibility, patient adherence, and acceptability (Barry et al., 2014). Abbruzzese et al. (2016), proposed an innovative substitute by introducing therapeutic techniques, such as Motor Imagery (MI) and Action Observation Therapy (AOT) (Abbruzzese et al., 2016). Through matching the internal representations with the imagined and observed actions from these methods, patients' motor skills are enhanced and new learning tasks are built. Nevertheless, some practical limitations occur with its adoption as an intervention for PD rehabilitation (Abbruzzese et al., 2016). Knippenberg et al. (2017), considered the use of Motion Capture Systems (MCS), such as the Microsoft Kinect® sensor, for patients with neurological disorders like PD. Assessment results from its use at rehabilitation centers showed its potential to assess patients in body balance and fall prevention (Stone and Skubic, 2014; Yang et al., 2014), during their clinical measurement of motor functions and gait assessments (Galna et al., 2014; Rocha et al., 2015), body balance, hand tracking, and analyzing their posture and limb tasks (Ferraris et al., 2014, 2019; Rocha et al., 2015; Otte et al., 2016; Yang et al., 2016). # Machine Learning for PD Staging **FIGURE 1** | The overview of the i-PROGNOSIS PGS environment. is depicted in Figure 3. RESULTS AND DISCUSSION ## 4.1. Demographics Impact To study the impact of patients’ demographics, i.e., age and gender, on the corresponding FVs (i.e., 2, 4, and 6) across the two classes (H&Y stage 1 and stage 2), a linear regression analysis was initially performed. Table 2 lists the estimated statistical significance level (*p*-value) for age and gender with the features related to the PGS and iMAT; boldface values denote statistically significant difference, i.e., *p* < 0.05. From the results presented in Table 2, age impacts only some of the iMAT score-related features, such as T1med, T3med, T5med, and T6med, and has no impact on the PGS score-related features. Moreover, gender shows no significant impact on all features; i.e., both from the PGS and iMAT. ## 4.2. FVs Update Based on the findings of Table 2, the initial versions of the FVs considered (1–6) are updated to the ones tabulated in Table 3, creating five scenarios for the classification process. In this way, the impact of age is only considered in the construction of the different FVs that include impactful demographics. ## 4.3. Classification Results The classification performance for all scenarios of Table 3 and for the KNN, SVM, and RF classifiers is depicted in Figure 6 (FV scenarios 1–3) and Figure 7 (FV scenarios 4, 5), respectively. Both figures present the related confusion matrices, which include the accuracy, precision, and recall metrics (Table 1), accordingly. Moreover, Table 4 tabulates the accuracy for each FV scenario (Table 3), combined with the corresponding F1 score and the MCC (Table 1). Based on the results reported in Figures 6, 7, and Table 4, it is clear that in most cases, the information that is provided by the PGS/iMAT scores and their FV results has quite a satisfactory classification performance, in terms of the resulted metrics. More specifically, the FV scenario 1, which is solely based on the iMAT-related features, achieves a classification accuracy that ranges from 81.5% (RF) up to 92.6% (KNN, SVM). This performance is improved when the iMAT-related FVs are combined with the age information (FV scenario 2), extending the accuracy range from 88.9% (RF, SVM) up to 96.3% (KNN). When the PGS-related FVs are solely employed (FV scenario 3), the classification accuracy is increased in all classifiers’ output, ranging from 95.2% (KNN, SVM) up to 100% (RF). When there is a combination of the PGS/iMAT-related FVs (FV scenario 4), the classification accuracy is still sustained high, ranging from 90.5% (KNN) up to 95.2% (SVM, RF). Finally, when the age is also combined (FV scenario 5), all classifiers converge to a 95.2% accuracy. Considering the performance of the three classifiers, KNN sustains values greater than 90% accuracy across all FV scenarios, whereas SVM and RF have a wider range of performance, depending on the different FV scenarios, ranging from 88.9 up to 95.2% and from 81.5 up to 100%, respectively. This performance is also reflected in the corresponding values of F1 score/MCC (Table 4), with the RF exhibiting the lowest (0.737/0.596; FV scenario 1) and the highest (1/1; FV scenario 3) estimated values across the three classifiers. PD Rehabilitation and SGs Multiple pieces of evidence revealed that patients with PD suffer from progressive deterioration in their disability, despite following the recommended medical prescriptions (Ellis et al., 2008; Abbruzzese et al., 2016). Exercise and physical activity were found to be directly correlated with enhancing the health and well-being of patients with PD. Rehabilitation therapies for PD primarily focus on improving patients' overall quality of life, maximizing their level of mobility and activity (Soh et al., 2012). In spite of several proves of adopting physical activities in rehabilitation programs is powerful means for reducing the risk of causing PD, the current conventional programs have been discovered to be heterogeneous, sub-optimal, and lack common consensus (Abbruzzese et al., 2016). In addition, supporting exercise-based rehabilitation programs continues to face challenges in cost, accessibility, patient adherence, and acceptability (Barry et al., 2014). Abbruzzese et al. (2016), proposed an innovative substitute by introducing therapeutic techniques, such as Motor Imagery (MI) and Action Observation Therapy (AOT) (Abbruzzese et al., 2016). Through matching the internal representations with the imagined and observed actions from these methods, patients' motor skills are enhanced and new learning tasks are built. Nevertheless, some practical limitations occur with its adoption as an intervention for PD rehabilitation (Abbruzzese et al., 2016). Knippenberg et al. (2017), considered the use of Motion Capture Systems (MCS), such as the Microsoft Kinect® sensor, for patients with neurological disorders like PD. Assessment results from its use at rehabilitation centers showed its potential to assess patients in body balance and fall prevention (Stone and Skubic, 2014; Yang et al., 2014), during their clinical measurement of motor functions and gait assessments (Galna et al., 2014; Rocha et al., 2015), body balance, hand tracking, and analyzing their posture and limb tasks (Ferraris et al., 2014, 2019; Rocha et al., 2015; Otte et al., 2016; Yang et al., 2016). # Machine Learning for PD Staging **FIGURE 1** | The overview of the i-PROGNOSIS PGS environment. is depicted in Figure 3. Clearly, the combination of both information sources, as seen by the employed classifiers, reveals their importance to arrive at an efficient classification of the stage of patients with PD (early or more advanced). This is further supported by the fact that the PGS/iMAT were designed following a co-creation approach, trying to gamify clinical assessment processes and quantify the PD symptoms in a more intuitive and naturalistic way. Hence, patients from their premises can have an intermediate use (e.g., every 10–15 days) of iMAT between periodic sessions of PGSs (e.g., daily or every 2 days per week), providing data that the proposed classification pipeline would use to infer for the improvement/deterioration of patients’ PD motor skills in a longitudinal fashion. In this way, constructive feedback could be provided, both to the patient and his/her attending doctor, guiding more personalized and targeted interventions. Classification Results The classification performance for all scenarios of Table 3 and for the KNN, SVM, and RF classifiers is depicted in Figure 6 (FV scenarios 1–3) and Figure 7 (FV scenarios 4, 5), respectively. Both figures present the related confusion matrices, which include the accuracy, precision, and recall metrics (Table 1), accordingly. Moreover, Table 4 tabulates the accuracy for each FV scenario (Table 3), combined with the corresponding F1 score and the MCC (Table 1). Based on the results reported in Figures 6, 7, and Table 4, it is clear that in most cases, the information that is provided by the PGS/iMAT scores and their FV results has quite a satisfactory classification performance, in terms of the resulted metrics. More specifically, the FV scenario 1, which is solely based on the iMAT-related features, achieves a classification accuracy that ranges from 81.5% (RF) up to 92.6% (KNN, SVM). This performance is improved when the iMAT-related FVs are combined with the age information (FV scenario 2), extending the accuracy range from 88.9% (RF, SVM) up to 96.3% (KNN). When the PGS-related FVs are solely employed (FV scenario 3), the classification accuracy is increased in all classifiers’ output, ranging from 95.2% (KNN, SVM) up to 100% (RF). When there is a combination of the PGS/iMAT-related FVs (FV scenario 4), the classification accuracy is still sustained high, ranging from 90.5% (KNN) up to 95.2% (SVM, RF). Finally, when the age is also combined (FV scenario 5), all classifiers converge to a 95.2% accuracy. Considering the performance of the three classifiers, KNN sustains values greater than 90% accuracy across all FV scenarios, whereas SVM and RF have a wider range of performance, depending on the different FV scenarios, ranging from 88.9 up to 95.2% and from 81.5 up to 100%, respectively. Based on the aforementioned, the present study extends the study presented in Dias et al. (2020b), by identifying the potentiality to correctly estimate the severity of the PD, as measured by clinical metrics, via machine learning analysis of the iMAT and PGS scores. In this endeavor, the data reported in Dias et al. (2020b), drawn from 27 patients with early PD, are further analyzed under various testing scenarios employing machine learning, leading to encouraging results regarding the potentiality to combine iMAT with PGS, in order to efficiently estimate the severity of patients with PD. PD Rehabilitation and SGs Multiple pieces of evidence revealed that patients with PD suffer from progressive deterioration in their disability, despite following the recommended medical prescriptions (Ellis et al., 2008; Abbruzzese et al., 2016). Exercise and physical activity were found to be directly correlated with enhancing the health and well-being of patients with PD. Rehabilitation therapies for PD primarily focus on improving patients' overall quality of life, maximizing their level of mobility and activity (Soh et al., 2012). In spite of several proves of adopting physical activities in rehabilitation programs is powerful means for reducing the risk of causing PD, the current conventional programs have been discovered to be heterogeneous, sub-optimal, and lack common consensus (Abbruzzese et al., 2016). In addition, supporting exercise-based rehabilitation programs continues to face challenges in cost, accessibility, patient adherence, and acceptability (Barry et al., 2014). Abbruzzese et al. (2016), proposed an innovative substitute by introducing therapeutic techniques, such as Motor Imagery (MI) and Action Observation Therapy (AOT) (Abbruzzese et al., 2016). Through matching the internal representations with the imagined and observed actions from these methods, patients' motor skills are enhanced and new learning tasks are built. Nevertheless, some practical limitations occur with its adoption as an intervention for PD rehabilitation (Abbruzzese et al., 2016). Knippenberg et al. (2017), considered the use of Motion Capture Systems (MCS), such as the Microsoft Kinect® sensor, for patients with neurological disorders like PD. Assessment results from its use at rehabilitation centers showed its potential to assess patients in body balance and fall prevention (Stone and Skubic, 2014; Yang et al., 2014), during their clinical measurement of motor functions and gait assessments (Galna et al., 2014; Rocha et al., 2015), body balance, hand tracking, and analyzing their posture and limb tasks (Ferraris et al., 2014, 2019; Rocha et al., 2015; Otte et al., 2016; Yang et al., 2016). # Machine Learning for PD Staging **FIGURE 1** | The overview of the i-PROGNOSIS PGS environment. is depicted in Figure 3. PD Rehabilitation and SGs Multiple pieces of evidence revealed that patients with PD suffer from progressive deterioration in their disability, despite following the recommended medical prescriptions (Ellis et al., 2008; Abbruzzese et al., 2016). Rehabilitation therapies for PD primarily focus on improving patients' overall quality of life, maximizing their level of mobility and activity (Soh et al., 2012). (2016), proposed an innovative substitute by introducing therapeutic techniques, such as Motor Imagery (MI) and Action Observation Therapy (AOT) (Abbruzzese et al., 2016). Demographics Impact To study the impact of patients’ demographics, i.e., age and gender, on the corresponding FVs (i.e., 2, 4, and 6) across the two classes (H&Y stage 1 and stage 2), a linear regression analysis was initially performed. Table 2 lists the estimated statistical significance level (*p*-value) for age and gender with the features related to the PGS and iMAT; boldface values denote statistically significant difference, i.e., *p* < 0.05. From the results presented in Table 2, age impacts only some of the iMAT score-related features, such as T1med, T3med, T5med, and T6med, and has no impact on the PGS score-related features. Moreover, gender shows no significant impact on all features; i.e., both from the PGS and iMAT. ## 4.2. FVs Update Based on the findings of Table 2, the initial versions of the FVs considered (1–6) are updated to the ones tabulated in Table 3, creating five scenarios for the classification process. In this way, the impact of age is only considered in the construction of the different FVs that include impactful demographics. ## 4.3. Classification Results The classification performance for all scenarios of Table 3 and for the KNN, SVM, and RF classifiers is depicted in Figure 6 (FV scenarios 1–3) and Figure 7 (FV scenarios 4, 5), respectively. Both figures present the related confusion matrices, which include the accuracy, precision, and recall metrics (Table 1), accordingly. Moreover, Table 4 tabulates the accuracy for each FV scenario (Table 3), combined with the corresponding F1 score and the MCC (Table 1). Based on the results reported in Figures 6, 7, and Table 4, it is clear that in most cases, the information that is provided by the PGS/iMAT scores and their FV results has quite a satisfactory classification performance, in terms of the resulted metrics. More specifically, the FV scenario 1, which is solely based on the iMAT-related features, achieves a classification accuracy that ranges from 81.5% (RF) up to 92.6% (KNN, SVM). This performance is improved when the iMAT-related FVs are combined with the age information (FV scenario 2), extending the accuracy range from 88.9% (RF, SVM) up to 96.3% (KNN). When the PGS-related FVs are solely employed (FV scenario 3), the classification accuracy is increased in all classifiers’ output, ranging from 95.2% (KNN, SVM) up to 100% (RF). When there is a combination of the PGS/iMAT-related FVs (FV scenario 4), the classification accuracy is still sustained high, ranging from 90.5% (KNN) up to 95.2% (SVM, RF). Finally, when the age is also combined (FV scenario 5), all classifiers converge to a 95.2% accuracy. Considering the performance of the three classifiers, KNN sustains values greater than 90% accuracy across all FV scenarios, whereas SVM and RF have a wider range of performance, depending on the different FV scenarios, ranging from 88.9 up to 95.2% and from 81.5 up to 100%, respectively. This performance is also reflected in the corresponding values of F1 score/MCC (Table 4), with the RF exhibiting the lowest (0.737/0.596; FV scenario 1) and the highest (1/1; FV scenario 3) estimated values across the three classifiers. With the availability of new Natural User Interfaces (NUIs), combined with the concept of serious games, efforts were placed in creating personalized serious games (SGs), such as the PGS Dias et al. (2020c) from the i-PROGNOSIS project (www.i-prognosis.eu), as both intervention and/or motor assessment tool for monitoring and tracking the behavioral change of patients with PD in terms of gait, agility, balance, and coordination impairments, as well as assess patients in adhering to physical therapy through enrolling in a gamified environment (Anzivino et al., 2018). Moreover, one of the deployed intelligent tools that can be seen as an alternative solution for the standard rating scales, MDS-UPDRS Part III subscores, is the intelligent Motor Assessment Tests (iMAT) (Dias et al., 2020b) from the i-PROGNOSIS project. Although the diagnosis of PD commonly relies on motor symptoms, non-motor symptoms such as cognitive changes related to attention and other conditions have been studied as supportive means for early diagnosis (Postuma et al., 2015). A revolutionary substitute by several researchers studied the application of machine learning as measures for PD diagnosis and assessment with the help of analyzing motor symptoms, kinematics, and wearable sensor data (Ahlrichs and Lawo, 2013; Ramdhani et al., 2018; Belić et al., 2019). Based on the aforementioned, the present study extends the study presented in Dias et al. (2020b), by identifying the potentiality to correctly estimate the severity of the PD, as measured by clinical metrics, via machine learning analysis of the iMAT and PGS scores. In this endeavor, the data reported in Dias et al. (2020b), drawn from 27 patients with early PD, are further analyzed under various testing scenarios employing machine learning, leading to encouraging results regarding the potentiality to combine iMAT with PGS, in order to efficiently estimate the severity of patients with PD. The present study is structured as follows: In Section 2, a related background on the main topics addressing PD rehabilitation, SGs, and i-PROGNOSIS PGS/iMAT characteristics is presented. In Section 3, the dataset characteristics along with the proposed methodology are provided. Furthermore, Section 4 highlights and discusses the results and the efficiency of the proposed approach along with the related limitations, including future extensions. Finally, Section 5, concludes the article. # 2. BACKGROUND ## 2.1. PD Rehabilitation and SGs Multiple pieces of evidence revealed that patients with PD suffer from progressive deterioration in their disability, despite following the recommended medical prescriptions (Ellis et al., 2008; Abbruzzese et al., 2016). Exercise and physical activity were found to be directly correlated with enhancing the health and well-being of patients with PD. Rehabilitation therapies for PD primarily focus on improving patients' overall quality of life, maximizing their level of mobility and activity (Soh et al., 2012). In spite of several proves of adopting physical activities in rehabilitation programs is powerful means for reducing the risk of causing PD, the current conventional programs have been discovered to be heterogeneous, sub-optimal, and lack common consensus (Abbruzzese et al., 2016). In addition, supporting exercise-based rehabilitation programs continues to face challenges in cost, accessibility, patient adherence, and acceptability (Barry et al., 2014). Abbruzzese et al. (2016), proposed an innovative substitute by introducing therapeutic techniques, such as Motor Imagery (MI) and Action Observation Therapy (AOT) (Abbruzzese et al., 2016). Through matching the internal representations with the imagined and observed actions from these methods, patients' motor skills are enhanced and new learning tasks are built. Nevertheless, some practical limitations occur with its adoption as an intervention for PD rehabilitation (Abbruzzese et al., 2016). Knippenberg et al. (2017), considered the use of Motion Capture Systems (MCS), such as the Microsoft Kinect® sensor, for patients with neurological disorders like PD. Assessment results from its use at rehabilitation centers showed its potential to assess patients in body balance and fall prevention (Stone and Skubic, 2014; Yang et al., 2014), during their clinical measurement of motor functions and gait assessments (Galna et al., 2014; Rocha et al., 2015), body balance, hand tracking, and analyzing their posture and limb tasks (Ferraris et al., 2014, 2019; Rocha et al., 2015; Otte et al., 2016; Yang et al., 2016). # Machine Learning for PD Staging **FIGURE 1** | The overview of the i-PROGNOSIS PGS environment. is depicted in Figure 3. Classification Results The classification performance for all scenarios of Table 3 and for the KNN, SVM, and RF classifiers is depicted in Figure 6 (FV scenarios 1–3) and Figure 7 (FV scenarios 4, 5), respectively. Both figures present the related confusion matrices, which include the accuracy, precision, and recall metrics (Table 1), accordingly. Based on the results reported in Figures 6, 7, and Table 4, it is clear that in most cases, the information that is provided by the PGS/iMAT scores and their FV results has quite a satisfactory classification performance, in terms of the resulted metrics. More specifically, the FV scenario 1, which is solely based on the iMAT-related features, achieves a classification accuracy that ranges from 81.5% (RF) up to 92.6% (KNN, SVM). This performance is improved when the iMAT-related FVs are combined with the age information (FV scenario 2), extending the accuracy range from 88.9% (RF, SVM) up to 96.3% (KNN). When the PGS-related FVs are solely employed (FV scenario 3), the classification accuracy is increased in all classifiers’ output, ranging from 95.2% (KNN, SVM) up to 100% (RF). When there is a combination of the PGS/iMAT-related FVs (FV scenario 4), the classification accuracy is still sustained high, ranging from 90.5% (KNN) up to 95.2% (SVM, RF). Finally, when the age is also combined (FV scenario 5), all classifiers converge to a 95.2% accuracy. Considering the performance of the three classifiers, KNN sustains values greater than 90% accuracy across all FV scenarios, whereas SVM and RF have a wider range of performance, depending on the different FV scenarios, ranging from 88.9 up to 95.2% and from 81.5 up to 100%, respectively. In spite of several proves of adopting physical activities in rehabilitation programs is powerful means for reducing the risk of causing PD, the current conventional programs have been discovered to be heterogeneous, sub-optimal, and lack common consensus (Abbruzzese et al., 2016). In addition, supporting exercise-based rehabilitation programs continues to face challenges in cost, accessibility, patient adherence, and acceptability (Barry et al., 2014). Abbruzzese et al. (2016), proposed an innovative substitute by introducing therapeutic techniques, such as Motor Imagery (MI) and Action Observation Therapy (AOT) (Abbruzzese et al., 2016). Through matching the internal representations with the imagined and observed actions from these methods, patients' motor skills are enhanced and new learning tasks are built. Nevertheless, some practical limitations occur with its adoption as an intervention for PD rehabilitation (Abbruzzese et al., 2016). Knippenberg et al. (2017), considered the use of Motion Capture Systems (MCS), such as the Microsoft Kinect® sensor, for patients with neurological disorders like PD. Data Characteristics For the proposed analysis, data drawn from patients with PD interacting with the "Fishing Game" and iMAT are used. These data corresponded to the clinical motor assessment data of patients with PD, performed by neurologists from the three different European medical centers (i.e., Greece, Germany, and the UK). The main characteristics embedded in the clinical dataset correspond to patients’ username, ID, demographics, whether on medication or not, Hoehn and Yahr (H&Y) clinical rating scale, and their score in MDS-UPDRS Part III items 18, 23, 24, 25, 26, and 28. The H&Y is a standard clinical rating scale that stages the functional disability associated with PD. The original H&Y scale consists of five stages, where Stage 1 has unilateral involvement, Stage 2 bilateral without impairment of balance, Stage 3 bilateral with impairment of posture, Stage 4 represents the severity of the disease associated with lack of physical independence, and finally, Stage 5 is for patients bounded by a bed or wheelchair (Goetz et al., 2004). However, based on the present dataset, the H&Y stages in this study are limited to one and three, labeled here as class 1 (Stage 1) and class 2 (Stage 3), respectively. ### 3.1.2. Participants' Demographics The dataset of the present study involved a total of 27 PD patients with a distribution of class1/class2 as 9/18. Patients undergoing this study ranged between the age of 43 and 79 years, with 69 years old as the highest number of patients and 62 years as the mean age. The patients in this study enrolled from three different countries, i.e., Greece, Germany, and the UK. The gender distribution was a ratio of 1 to 2, having 9 women and 18 men patients with PD, where the majority were male patients with PD. All patients were under PD medication except one participant. The data acquisition took place from September 2019 to January 2020, during periodic sessions (1 per month) of the iMAT within a controlled environment at the three medical centers. Each patient with PD performed each Assessment Test up to four times per session. The H&Y is a standard clinical rating scale that stages the functional disability associated with PD. The original H&Y scale consists of five stages, where Stage 1 has unilateral involvement, Stage 2 bilateral without impairment of balance, Stage 3 bilateral with impairment of posture, Stage 4 represents the severity of the disease associated with lack of physical independence, and finally, Stage 5 is for patients bounded by a bed or wheelchair (Goetz et al., 2004). PD Rehabilitation and SGs Multiple pieces of evidence revealed that patients with PD suffer from progressive deterioration in their disability, despite following the recommended medical prescriptions (Ellis et al., 2008; Abbruzzese et al., 2016). Exercise and physical activity were found to be directly correlated with enhancing the health and well-being of patients with PD. Rehabilitation therapies for PD primarily focus on improving patients' overall quality of life, maximizing their level of mobility and activity (Soh et al., 2012). In spite of several proves of adopting physical activities in rehabilitation programs is powerful means for reducing the risk of causing PD, the current conventional programs have been discovered to be heterogeneous, sub-optimal, and lack common consensus (Abbruzzese et al., 2016). In addition, supporting exercise-based rehabilitation programs continues to face challenges in cost, accessibility, patient adherence, and acceptability (Barry et al., 2014). Abbruzzese et al. (2016), proposed an innovative substitute by introducing therapeutic techniques, such as Motor Imagery (MI) and Action Observation Therapy (AOT) (Abbruzzese et al., 2016). Through matching the internal representations with the imagined and observed actions from these methods, patients' motor skills are enhanced and new learning tasks are built. Nevertheless, some practical limitations occur with its adoption as an intervention for PD rehabilitation (Abbruzzese et al., 2016). Knippenberg et al. (2017), considered the use of Motion Capture Systems (MCS), such as the Microsoft Kinect® sensor, for patients with neurological disorders like PD. Data Characteristics For the proposed analysis, data drawn from patients with PD interacting with the "Fishing Game" and iMAT are used. These data corresponded to the clinical motor assessment data of patients with PD, performed by neurologists from the three different European medical centers (i.e., Greece, Germany, and the UK). The main characteristics embedded in the clinical dataset correspond to patients’ username, ID, demographics, whether on medication or not, Hoehn and Yahr (H&Y) clinical rating scale, and their score in MDS-UPDRS Part III items 18, 23, 24, 25, 26, and 28. The H&Y is a standard clinical rating scale that stages the functional disability associated with PD. The original H&Y scale consists of five stages, where Stage 1 has unilateral involvement, Stage 2 bilateral without impairment of balance, Stage 3 bilateral with impairment of posture, Stage 4 represents the severity of the disease associated with lack of physical independence, and finally, Stage 5 is for patients bounded by a bed or wheelchair (Goetz et al., 2004). However, based on the present dataset, the H&Y stages in this study are limited to one and three, labeled here as class 1 (Stage 1) and class 2 (Stage 3), respectively. ### 3.1.2. Participants' Demographics The dataset of the present study involved a total of 27 PD patients with a distribution of class1/class2 as 9/18. Patients undergoing this study ranged between the age of 43 and 79 years, with 69 years old as the highest number of patients and 62 years as the mean age. The patients in this study enrolled from three different countries, i.e., Greece, Germany, and the UK. The gender distribution was a ratio of 1 to 2, having 9 women and 18 men patients with PD, where the majority were male patients with PD. All patients were under PD medication except one participant. The data acquisition took place from September 2019 to January 2020, during periodic sessions (1 per month) of the iMAT within a controlled environment at the three medical centers. Each patient with PD performed each Assessment Test up to four times per session. Although the diagnosis of PD commonly relies on motor symptoms, non-motor symptoms such as cognitive changes related to attention and other conditions have been studied as supportive means for early diagnosis (Postuma et al., 2015). Based on the aforementioned, the present study extends the study presented in Dias et al. (2020b), by identifying the potentiality to correctly estimate the severity of the PD, as measured by clinical metrics, via machine learning analysis of the iMAT and PGS scores. In this endeavor, the data reported in Dias et al. (2020b), drawn from 27 patients with early PD, are further analyzed under various testing scenarios employing machine learning, leading to encouraging results regarding the potentiality to combine iMAT with PGS, in order to efficiently estimate the severity of patients with PD. PD Rehabilitation and SGs Multiple pieces of evidence revealed that patients with PD suffer from progressive deterioration in their disability, despite following the recommended medical prescriptions (Ellis et al., 2008; Abbruzzese et al., 2016). Exercise and physical activity were found to be directly correlated with enhancing the health and well-being of patients with PD. Rehabilitation therapies for PD primarily focus on improving patients' overall quality of life, maximizing their level of mobility and activity (Soh et al., 2012). In spite of several proves of adopting physical activities in rehabilitation programs is powerful means for reducing the risk of causing PD, the current conventional programs have been discovered to be heterogeneous, sub-optimal, and lack common consensus (Abbruzzese et al., 2016). In addition, supporting exercise-based rehabilitation programs continues to face challenges in cost, accessibility, patient adherence, and acceptability (Barry et al., 2014). Abbruzzese et al. (2016), proposed an innovative substitute by introducing therapeutic techniques, such as Motor Imagery (MI) and Action Observation Therapy (AOT) (Abbruzzese et al., 2016). Through matching the internal representations with the imagined and observed actions from these methods, patients' motor skills are enhanced and new learning tasks are built. Nevertheless, some practical limitations occur with its adoption as an intervention for PD rehabilitation (Abbruzzese et al., 2016). Knippenberg et al. (2017), considered the use of Motion Capture Systems (MCS), such as the Microsoft Kinect® sensor, for patients with neurological disorders like PD. Assessment results from its use at rehabilitation centers showed its potential to assess patients in body balance and fall prevention (Stone and Skubic, 2014; Yang et al., 2014), during their clinical measurement of motor functions and gait assessments (Galna et al., 2014; Rocha et al., 2015), body balance, hand tracking, and analyzing their posture and limb tasks (Ferraris et al., 2014, 2019; Rocha et al., 2015; Otte et al., 2016; Yang et al., 2016). # Machine Learning for PD Staging **FIGURE 1** | The overview of the i-PROGNOSIS PGS environment. is depicted in Figure 3.
