Discussion Early total symptom change in week five contributed substantially to outcome prediction for CBT. The baseline symptom score was also a significant predictor, which might at least partly be attributable to regression toward later outcome prediction. None of the other variables were predictive of treatment outcome in week 10. The prediction performance was far from clinically relevant; the best learner could only explain 51.2 % variance of CBT treatment outcome, which confirms the difficulty of predicting treatment outcomes. The external validation confirmed the findings, but with a slightly lower performance compared to the original results. Typically, external validations exhibit lower performance than reported in cross-validation due to over-calibration, resulting in somewhat reduced transferability to new datasets (Betancur et al., 2019). While other studies used machine learning methods, ours was the first to use it in a routine dataset and include information on early symptom change. Applying more sophisticated preprocessing and learning methods did not substantially improve performance. With the caveat that overall predictive performance was not extremely high with around 45 % of all variability in outcomes explained by the predictors, the significance of both baseline symptom scores and early total symptom change in predicting outcomes is apparent in various machine learning analysis pipelines. The differential importance of these variables across machine learning pipelines used different metrics including percent increase in mean squared error and total decrease in node impurities, but all pointed in the same direction. One explanation for the predictive power of early symptom change is that patients, who had positive early symptom change, experienced relief of some symptoms and developed hope and an alliance with the therapist. More specifically, our examination of subscale scores yielded findings indicating that changes in scores on subscales associated with depressed mood and anxiety occurred early on, and were predictive of treatment outcomes. Conversely, individuals who do not show early symptom improvement may potentially benefit from increasing the intensity or altering the type of intervention by clinicians. The advantage of early symptom change over pre-treatment demographics predictors seems quite substantial, which proved that individual demographics were not associated with reported accuracy (Sajjadian et al., 2021). These results were in line with previous studies (Santor and Segal, 2003; Stassen et al., 2007; Szegedi et al., 2003; Tadić et al., 2010). Findings were also consistent with studies on other psychiatric diseases like schizophrenia (Samara et al., 2015) and anxiety (Baldwin et al., 2012). Our findings suggest that a continuous measure of early symptom change is a more effective predictor of treatment outcome compared to a categorical change variable. Specifically, Schindler et al. (2013) reported that a model utilizing categorical early symptom change had an accuracy of 38.9 % in predicting treatment response, whereas in our current study it accounted for 47.1 %–51.2 % of the variance in outcomes. If these findings would indicate not only a predictive, but also causal relationship, therapists could focus on addressing target indicators such as readiness and intensity to potentially enhance early symptom change, which may lead to improved treatment outcomes later on. The large sample size of this study ensured a high level of statistical power. More importantly, our dataset from a large psychotherapy outpatient center provided information on real-world effectiveness. The study also has several limitations. First, selection bias may have occurred as excluded patients had higher baseline SQ48 scores compared to included patients. Second, we excluded patients who completed the treatment trajectory with fewer than ten sessions, which may have affected the performance of our machine learning algorithms. Third, limited predictors are available in real-world clinical practice; Hence our dataset had relatively few potential predictors. Identifying better ways to predict treatment outcome using additional routinely measured predictive variables is still necessary to ensure the accessibility of treatment by offering more tailored treatment durations. ## 5. Conclusion Early total symptom change during the first five weeks was a significant predictor of treatment outcome for CBT in a routine clinical setting, as demonstrated by both linear regression and machine learning pipelines. Interestingly, more sophisticated preprocessing and learning methods did not substantially improve performance. Analysis of changes in subscale scores revealed that improvement in symptoms related to depressed mood and anxiety predicted treatment response, indicating the potential clinical relevance of early symptom monitoring to identify patients who need increased intervention intensity or alteration of treatment type. These routinely measured predictive variables could support better-tailored CBT treatment. However, future research may need to explore alternative sources of information, as the currently available routinely collected data may only explain up to 51.2 % of the total variance in outcomes. ## Disclosure All authors have approved the final manuscript. ## CRediT authorship contribution statement FL, TL and FJ contributed to the design of the study and preparation of the manuscript. Machine learning analysis pipeline To investigate possible selection bias, independent *t*-tests and chi-square tests were applied to compare the complete cases with the patients whose symptom questionnaires were not completed at or within two weeks after baseline, the 5th and the 10th session. A two-sided test with a *p*-value of <0.05 was considered statistically significant. Four machine learning algorithms were trained: random forest, support vector machine (SVM), extreme gradient boosting (XGboost), and neural network. Different machine learners were compared to linear regression. ### Results Early symptom change and baseline symptom score were the only significant predictors. Models with early symptom change explained 22.0 % to 23.3 % more variance than those without early symptom change. Specifically, the baseline total symptom score, and the early symptom score changes of the subscales pertaining to depression and anxiety were the top three predictors of treatment outcome. ### Limitation Excluded patients with missing treatment outcomes had slightly higher symptom scores at baseline, indicating possible selection bias. ### Conclusion Early symptom change improved the prediction of treatment outcomes. The prediction performance achieved is far from clinical relevance; the best learner could only explain 51.2 % of the variance in outcomes. Compared to linear regression, more sophisticated preprocessing and learning methods did not substantially improve performance. ## 1. Introduction Cognitive behavior therapy (CBT) is an effective treatment for depression on average. While CBT has an overall evidence-based effectiveness rate of 57 % (Spinhoven et al., 2018), individual responses to the treatment do vary. Practitioners hence face the challenge to plan and adjust therapy for individual clients with potentially different needs and backgrounds. Developing a prediction algorithm to forecast treatment outcomes in early stages of treatment could help address this issue by allowing for timely adjustment of therapy and potentially improve the overall effectiveness of CBT (Sajjadian et al., 2021). Numerous potential predictors including patient characteristics, such as age, gender, education, socioeconomic status, childhood trauma, and age of onset, as well as clinical features, such as severity and chronicity, have been examined in the literature. Previous studies found that a combination of pre-treatment characteristics, including baseline total symptom score, Anxiety Symptom Index total score, and subscale scores such as depressed mood, extraversion, and psychological needs, can be potential predictors for CBT outcomes. However, these studies were limited by small sample sizes and could not produce robust results for clinical decision-making (Cohen et al., 2020; Huibers et al., 2015). Studies with relatively large samples have demonstrated that sub-scale scores can predict antidepressant treatment efficacy for individual patients (Chekroud et al., 2016; Kautzky et al., 2017). Study by (Chekroud, 2016) found that the Quick Inventory of Depressive Symptomatology-Self Report (QIDS-SR) subscales of psychomotor agitation, energy and sadness predicted treatment response to citalopram. Neuroimaging biomarkers are a third type of significant predictors (Dunlop et al., 2017). A barrier to using neuroimaging as a predictor in decision tools is the financial costs and cumbersome procedure, making it an unlikely routine test in clinical practice. In addition, symptom change over time, particularly early in treatment, has emerged as a promising predictor of treatment outcomes. According to (Santor and Segal, 2001), the degree of symptom improvement in the first 10 weeks of treatment emerged as a strong predictor of depression symptom return at both the 3-month and 6-month follow-up evaluations. Other trial-based studies confirmed this finding, but all suffered from small sample sizes (Lewis et al., 2012; Tadić et al., 2010). A study of 193 patients (Schindler et al., 2013) showed that early symptom change, as a categorical predictor of treatment outcome, could explain 27.7 % of the variance in symptomatic outcome. (Schilagert & Hiller, 2017) evaluated the predictive value of early response in routine practice with CBT as treatment for depression. They found that early response at the tenth session was a good predictor for final treatment outcome and remission regarding depressive symptoms (OR = 8.75 and OR = 5.32, respectively). These approaches used linear and logistic regression. Also, most studies categorized early symptom change into discrete groups and this may be less informative than the use of a continuous variable. The present study sought to extend previous work by exploring pretreatment predictors and early-treatment total symptom change as a continuous variable in a large routine dataset using machine learning approaches and comparing these to linear regression. Additionally, the role of early subscale symptom change was further detailed by investigating which subscale score changes were most significant for predicting treatment outcome. However, more severe patients (n = 1153) referred to specialist outpatient treatment could receive further treatment sessions (mean = 17.54). Predictors Available predictor variables included demographic characteristics, clinical characteristics, baseline diagnosis information, and therapy-related characteristics. Potential demographic predictors were gender, age, level of education, work status, and living situation. Therapists diagnosed depression according to the fourth edition of Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of mental disorders (DSM-IV) (Stein et al., 2010) using an automated and shorter version of the Schedules for Clinical Assessment in Neuropsychiatry (SCAN), the mini-SCAN, with proven reliability and validity (Nienhuis et al., 2010). Stage of the depression was based on a structured clinical interview for the DSM-IV. Therapy-related predictors were level of care (intensity of treatment), baseline severity (SQ48 score at t0), and early symptom change in either the total score or the subscale scores. ## 2.4. Discussion Early total symptom change in week five contributed substantially to outcome prediction for CBT. The baseline symptom score was also a significant predictor, which might at least partly be attributable to regression toward later outcome prediction. None of the other variables were predictive of treatment outcome in week 10. The prediction performance was far from clinically relevant; the best learner could only explain 51.2 % variance of CBT treatment outcome, which confirms the difficulty of predicting treatment outcomes. The external validation confirmed the findings, but with a slightly lower performance compared to the original results. Typically, external validations exhibit lower performance than reported in cross-validation due to over-calibration, resulting in somewhat reduced transferability to new datasets (Betancur et al., 2019). While other studies used machine learning methods, ours was the first to use it in a routine dataset and include information on early symptom change. Applying more sophisticated preprocessing and learning methods did not substantially improve performance. With the caveat that overall predictive performance was not extremely high with around 45 % of all variability in outcomes explained by the predictors, the significance of both baseline symptom scores and early total symptom change in predicting outcomes is apparent in various machine learning analysis pipelines. The differential importance of these variables across machine learning pipelines used different metrics including percent increase in mean squared error and total decrease in node impurities, but all pointed in the same direction. One explanation for the predictive power of early symptom change is that patients, who had positive early symptom change, experienced relief of some symptoms and developed hope and an alliance with the therapist. More specifically, our examination of subscale scores yielded findings indicating that changes in scores on subscales associated with depressed mood and anxiety occurred early on, and were predictive of treatment outcomes. Conversely, individuals who do not show early symptom improvement may potentially benefit from increasing the intensity or altering the type of intervention by clinicians. The advantage of early symptom change over pre-treatment demographics predictors seems quite substantial, which proved that individual demographics were not associated with reported accuracy (Sajjadian et al., 2021). These results were in line with previous studies (Santor and Segal, 2003; Stassen et al., 2007; Szegedi et al., 2003; Tadić et al., 2010). Findings were also consistent with studies on other psychiatric diseases like schizophrenia (Samara et al., 2015) and anxiety (Baldwin et al., 2012). Our findings suggest that a continuous measure of early symptom change is a more effective predictor of treatment outcome compared to a categorical change variable. Specifically, Schindler et al. (2013) reported that a model utilizing categorical early symptom change had an accuracy of 38.9 % in predicting treatment response, whereas in our current study it accounted for 47.1 %–51.2 % of the variance in outcomes. If these findings would indicate not only a predictive, but also causal relationship, therapists could focus on addressing target indicators such as readiness and intensity to potentially enhance early symptom change, which may lead to improved treatment outcomes later on. The large sample size of this study ensured a high level of statistical power. More importantly, our dataset from a large psychotherapy outpatient center provided information on real-world effectiveness. The study also has several limitations. Typically, external validations exhibit lower performance than reported in cross-validation due to over-calibration, resulting in somewhat reduced transferability to new datasets (Betancur et al., 2019). While other studies used machine learning methods, ours was the first to use it in a routine dataset and include information on early symptom change. Applying more sophisticated preprocessing and learning methods did not substantially improve performance. With the caveat that overall predictive performance was not extremely high with around 45 % of all variability in outcomes explained by the predictors, the significance of both baseline symptom scores and early total symptom change in predicting outcomes is apparent in various machine learning analysis pipelines. The differential importance of these variables across machine learning pipelines used different metrics including percent increase in mean squared error and total decrease in node impurities, but all pointed in the same direction. One explanation for the predictive power of early symptom change is that patients, who had positive early symptom change, experienced relief of some symptoms and developed hope and an alliance with the therapist. More specifically, our examination of subscale scores yielded findings indicating that changes in scores on subscales associated with depressed mood and anxiety occurred early on, and were predictive of treatment outcomes. Conversely, individuals who do not show early symptom improvement may potentially benefit from increasing the intensity or altering the type of intervention by clinicians. The advantage of early symptom change over pre-treatment demographics predictors seems quite substantial, which proved that individual demographics were not associated with reported accuracy (Sajjadian et al., 2021). These results were in line with previous studies (Santor and Segal, 2003; Stassen et al., 2007; Szegedi et al., 2003; Tadić et al., 2010). Findings were also consistent with studies on other psychiatric diseases like schizophrenia (Samara et al., 2015) and anxiety (Baldwin et al., 2012). Our findings suggest that a continuous measure of early symptom change is a more effective predictor of treatment outcome compared to a categorical change variable. Specifically, Schindler et al. (2013) reported that a model utilizing categorical early symptom change had an accuracy of 38.9 % in predicting treatment response, whereas in our current study it accounted for 47.1 %–51.2 % of the variance in outcomes. If these findings would indicate not only a predictive, but also causal relationship, therapists could focus on addressing target indicators such as readiness and intensity to potentially enhance early symptom change, which may lead to improved treatment outcomes later on. The large sample size of this study ensured a high level of statistical power. More importantly, our dataset from a large psychotherapy outpatient center provided information on real-world effectiveness. The study also has several limitations. First, selection bias may have occurred as excluded patients had higher baseline SQ48 scores compared to included patients. Second, we excluded patients who completed the treatment trajectory with fewer than ten sessions, which may have affected the performance of our machine learning algorithms. Third, limited predictors are available in real-world clinical practice; Hence our dataset had relatively few potential predictors. Identifying better ways to predict treatment outcome using additional routinely measured predictive variables is still necessary to ensure the accessibility of treatment by offering more tailored treatment durations. ## 5. Machine learning analysis pipeline To investigate possible selection bias, independent *t*-tests and chi-square tests were applied to compare the complete cases with the patients whose symptom questionnaires were not completed at or within two weeks after baseline, the 5th and the 10th session. Models with early symptom change explained 22.0 % to 23.3 % more variance than those without early symptom change. Specifically, the baseline total symptom score, and the early symptom score changes of the subscales pertaining to depression and anxiety were the top three predictors of treatment outcome. ### Limitation Excluded patients with missing treatment outcomes had slightly higher symptom scores at baseline, indicating possible selection bias. ### Conclusion Early symptom change improved the prediction of treatment outcomes. The prediction performance achieved is far from clinical relevance; the best learner could only explain 51.2 % of the variance in outcomes. Compared to linear regression, more sophisticated preprocessing and learning methods did not substantially improve performance. ## 1. Introduction Cognitive behavior therapy (CBT) is an effective treatment for depression on average. While CBT has an overall evidence-based effectiveness rate of 57 % (Spinhoven et al., 2018), individual responses to the treatment do vary. Practitioners hence face the challenge to plan and adjust therapy for individual clients with potentially different needs and backgrounds. Developing a prediction algorithm to forecast treatment outcomes in early stages of treatment could help address this issue by allowing for timely adjustment of therapy and potentially improve the overall effectiveness of CBT (Sajjadian et al., 2021). Numerous potential predictors including patient characteristics, such as age, gender, education, socioeconomic status, childhood trauma, and age of onset, as well as clinical features, such as severity and chronicity, have been examined in the literature. Previous studies found that a combination of pre-treatment characteristics, including baseline total symptom score, Anxiety Symptom Index total score, and subscale scores such as depressed mood, extraversion, and psychological needs, can be potential predictors for CBT outcomes. However, these studies were limited by small sample sizes and could not produce robust results for clinical decision-making (Cohen et al., 2020; Huibers et al., 2015). Studies with relatively large samples have demonstrated that sub-scale scores can predict antidepressant treatment efficacy for individual patients (Chekroud et al., 2016; Kautzky et al., 2017). A barrier to using neuroimaging as a predictor in decision tools is the financial costs and cumbersome procedure, making it an unlikely routine test in clinical practice. The external validation confirmed the findings, but with a slightly lower performance compared to the original results. Typically, external validations exhibit lower performance than reported in cross-validation due to over-calibration, resulting in somewhat reduced transferability to new datasets (Betancur et al., 2019). While other studies used machine learning methods, ours was the first to use it in a routine dataset and include information on early symptom change. Applying more sophisticated preprocessing and learning methods did not substantially improve performance. With the caveat that overall predictive performance was not extremely high with around 45 % of all variability in outcomes explained by the predictors, the significance of both baseline symptom scores and early total symptom change in predicting outcomes is apparent in various machine learning analysis pipelines. The differential importance of these variables across machine learning pipelines used different metrics including percent increase in mean squared error and total decrease in node impurities, but all pointed in the same direction. One explanation for the predictive power of early symptom change is that patients, who had positive early symptom change, experienced relief of some symptoms and developed hope and an alliance with the therapist. More specifically, our examination of subscale scores yielded findings indicating that changes in scores on subscales associated with depressed mood and anxiety occurred early on, and were predictive of treatment outcomes. Conversely, individuals who do not show early symptom improvement may potentially benefit from increasing the intensity or altering the type of intervention by clinicians. The advantage of early symptom change over pre-treatment demographics predictors seems quite substantial, which proved that individual demographics were not associated with reported accuracy (Sajjadian et al., 2021). These results were in line with previous studies (Santor and Segal, 2003; Stassen et al., 2007; Szegedi et al., 2003; Tadić et al., 2010). Findings were also consistent with studies on other psychiatric diseases like schizophrenia (Samara et al., 2015) and anxiety (Baldwin et al., 2012). Our findings suggest that a continuous measure of early symptom change is a more effective predictor of treatment outcome compared to a categorical change variable. Specifically, Schindler et al. (2013) reported that a model utilizing categorical early symptom change had an accuracy of 38.9 % in predicting treatment response, whereas in our current study it accounted for 47.1 %–51.2 % of the variance in outcomes. If these findings would indicate not only a predictive, but also causal relationship, therapists could focus on addressing target indicators such as readiness and intensity to potentially enhance early symptom change, which may lead to improved treatment outcomes later on. The large sample size of this study ensured a high level of statistical power. More importantly, our dataset from a large psychotherapy outpatient center provided information on real-world effectiveness. The study also has several limitations. First, selection bias may have occurred as excluded patients had higher baseline SQ48 scores compared to included patients. Second, we excluded patients who completed the treatment trajectory with fewer than ten sessions, which may have affected the performance of our machine learning algorithms. Third, limited predictors are available in real-world clinical practice; Hence our dataset had relatively few potential predictors. Identifying better ways to predict treatment outcome using additional routinely measured predictive variables is still necessary to ensure the accessibility of treatment by offering more tailored treatment durations. ## 5. Conclusion Early total symptom change during the first five weeks was a significant predictor of treatment outcome for CBT in a routine clinical setting, as demonstrated by both linear regression and machine learning pipelines. Interestingly, more sophisticated preprocessing and learning methods did not substantially improve performance. Analysis of changes in subscale scores revealed that improvement in symptoms related to depressed mood and anxiety predicted treatment response, indicating the potential clinical relevance of early symptom monitoring to identify patients who need increased intervention intensity or alteration of treatment type. These routinely measured predictive variables could support better-tailored CBT treatment. However, future research may need to explore alternative sources of information, as the currently available routinely collected data may only explain up to 51.2 % of the total variance in outcomes. ## Disclosure All authors have approved the final manuscript. ## CRediT authorship contribution statement FL, TL and FJ contributed to the design of the study and preparation of the manuscript. In addition, symptom change over time, particularly early in treatment, has emerged as a promising predictor of treatment outcomes. According to (Santor and Segal, 2001), the degree of symptom improvement in the first 10 weeks of treatment emerged as a strong predictor of depression symptom return at both the 3-month and 6-month follow-up evaluations. Other trial-based studies confirmed this finding, but all suffered from small sample sizes (Lewis et al., 2012; Tadić et al., 2010). A study of 193 patients (Schindler et al., 2013) showed that early symptom change, as a categorical predictor of treatment outcome, could explain 27.7 % of the variance in symptomatic outcome. (Schilagert & Hiller, 2017) evaluated the predictive value of early response in routine practice with CBT as treatment for depression. They found that early response at the tenth session was a good predictor for final treatment outcome and remission regarding depressive symptoms (OR = 8.75 and OR = 5.32, respectively). These approaches used linear and logistic regression. Also, most studies categorized early symptom change into discrete groups and this may be less informative than the use of a continuous variable. The present study sought to extend previous work by exploring pretreatment predictors and early-treatment total symptom change as a continuous variable in a large routine dataset using machine learning approaches and comparing these to linear regression. Additionally, the role of early subscale symptom change was further detailed by investigating which subscale score changes were most significant for predicting treatment outcome. Models with early symptom change explained 22.0 % to 23.3 % more variance than those without early symptom change. Specifically, the baseline total symptom score, and the early symptom score changes of the subscales pertaining to depression and anxiety were the top three predictors of treatment outcome. ### Limitation Excluded patients with missing treatment outcomes had slightly higher symptom scores at baseline, indicating possible selection bias. ### Conclusion Early symptom change improved the prediction of treatment outcomes. The prediction performance achieved is far from clinical relevance; the best learner could only explain 51.2 % of the variance in outcomes. Compared to linear regression, more sophisticated preprocessing and learning methods did not substantially improve performance. ## 1. Introduction Cognitive behavior therapy (CBT) is an effective treatment for depression on average. While CBT has an overall evidence-based effectiveness rate of 57 % (Spinhoven et al., 2018), individual responses to the treatment do vary. Practitioners hence face the challenge to plan and adjust therapy for individual clients with potentially different needs and backgrounds. Developing a prediction algorithm to forecast treatment outcomes in early stages of treatment could help address this issue by allowing for timely adjustment of therapy and potentially improve the overall effectiveness of CBT (Sajjadian et al., 2021). Numerous potential predictors including patient characteristics, such as age, gender, education, socioeconomic status, childhood trauma, and age of onset, as well as clinical features, such as severity and chronicity, have been examined in the literature. Previous studies found that a combination of pre-treatment characteristics, including baseline total symptom score, Anxiety Symptom Index total score, and subscale scores such as depressed mood, extraversion, and psychological needs, can be potential predictors for CBT outcomes. However, these studies were limited by small sample sizes and could not produce robust results for clinical decision-making (Cohen et al., 2020; Huibers et al., 2015). Studies with relatively large samples have demonstrated that sub-scale scores can predict antidepressant treatment efficacy for individual patients (Chekroud et al., 2016; Kautzky et al., 2017). Typically, external validations exhibit lower performance than reported in cross-validation due to over-calibration, resulting in somewhat reduced transferability to new datasets (Betancur et al., 2019). While other studies used machine learning methods, ours was the first to use it in a routine dataset and include information on early symptom change. Applying more sophisticated preprocessing and learning methods did not substantially improve performance. With the caveat that overall predictive performance was not extremely high with around 45 % of all variability in outcomes explained by the predictors, the significance of both baseline symptom scores and early total symptom change in predicting outcomes is apparent in various machine learning analysis pipelines. The differential importance of these variables across machine learning pipelines used different metrics including percent increase in mean squared error and total decrease in node impurities, but all pointed in the same direction. One explanation for the predictive power of early symptom change is that patients, who had positive early symptom change, experienced relief of some symptoms and developed hope and an alliance with the therapist. More specifically, our examination of subscale scores yielded findings indicating that changes in scores on subscales associated with depressed mood and anxiety occurred early on, and were predictive of treatment outcomes. Conversely, individuals who do not show early symptom improvement may potentially benefit from increasing the intensity or altering the type of intervention by clinicians. The advantage of early symptom change over pre-treatment demographics predictors seems quite substantial, which proved that individual demographics were not associated with reported accuracy (Sajjadian et al., 2021). These results were in line with previous studies (Santor and Segal, 2003; Stassen et al., 2007; Szegedi et al., 2003; Tadić et al., 2010). Findings were also consistent with studies on other psychiatric diseases like schizophrenia (Samara et al., 2015) and anxiety (Baldwin et al., 2012). Our findings suggest that a continuous measure of early symptom change is a more effective predictor of treatment outcome compared to a categorical change variable. Specifically, Schindler et al. (2013) reported that a model utilizing categorical early symptom change had an accuracy of 38.9 % in predicting treatment response, whereas in our current study it accounted for 47.1 %–51.2 % of the variance in outcomes. If these findings would indicate not only a predictive, but also causal relationship, therapists could focus on addressing target indicators such as readiness and intensity to potentially enhance early symptom change, which may lead to improved treatment outcomes later on. The large sample size of this study ensured a high level of statistical power. More importantly, our dataset from a large psychotherapy outpatient center provided information on real-world effectiveness. The study also has several limitations. First, selection bias may have occurred as excluded patients had higher baseline SQ48 scores compared to included patients. Second, we excluded patients who completed the treatment trajectory with fewer than ten sessions, which may have affected the performance of our machine learning algorithms. Third, limited predictors are available in real-world clinical practice; Hence our dataset had relatively few potential predictors. Identifying better ways to predict treatment outcome using additional routinely measured predictive variables is still necessary to ensure the accessibility of treatment by offering more tailored treatment durations. ## 5. Conclusion Early total symptom change during the first five weeks was a significant predictor of treatment outcome for CBT in a routine clinical setting, as demonstrated by both linear regression and machine learning pipelines. Interestingly, more sophisticated preprocessing and learning methods did not substantially improve performance. Analysis of changes in subscale scores revealed that improvement in symptoms related to depressed mood and anxiety predicted treatment response, indicating the potential clinical relevance of early symptom monitoring to identify patients who need increased intervention intensity or alteration of treatment type. These routinely measured predictive variables could support better-tailored CBT treatment. However, future research may need to explore alternative sources of information, as the currently available routinely collected data may only explain up to 51.2 % of the total variance in outcomes. ## Disclosure All authors have approved the final manuscript. ## CRediT authorship contribution statement FL, TL and FJ contributed to the design of the study and preparation of the manuscript. Method This study first applied various prediction models and learning algorithms to predict continuous treatment outcome at session ten, considering both pretreatment symptoms and early symptom change, that is, change over the first five sessions. Additionally, the predictive power of early symptom change in treatment outcome prediction of CBT was quantified by considering parameter importance in the resulting models. ## 2.1. Study sample and design CBT treatment typically entails weekly sessions lasting between 30 and 60 min, with a duration of 10 to 18 weeks. Data came from a large mental health outpatient clinic in the Netherlands, in which CBT is primarily offered as a treatment to adults suffering from depression. The dataset consisted of *n* = 4610 depression patients for whom treatment was initiated between March 2017 and April 2019. The dataset contained routinely collected data before, during and after treatment and was anonymized. We followed the principles of the Declaration of Helsinki and the research code of the University Medical Center Groningen. All patients were asked to provide their written informed consent for data collection and analyses to support CBT research and quality control. Nineteen patients in the dataset did not give consent and had been excluded from the dataset. ## 2.2. Outcome Outcomes were measured with the 48 items self-report symptom questionnaire (SQ-48), which includes seven scales measuring psychological distress: Depression (Mood), Anxiety (ANXI), Somatization (SOMA), Agoraphobia (AGOR), Aggression (AGGR) Cognitive problem (COGN), Social Phobia (SOPH). Outcome data were gathered at baseline ## 2.5. Machine learning analysis pipeline To investigate possible selection bias, independent *t*-tests and chi-square tests were applied to compare the complete cases with the patients whose symptom questionnaires were not completed at or within two weeks after baseline, the 5th and the 10th session. A two-sided test with a *p*-value of <0.05 was considered statistically significant. Four machine learning algorithms were trained: random forest, support vector machine (SVM), extreme gradient boosting (XGboost), and neural network. Algorithms were trained by tuning hyper-parameters with repeated five-fold cross-validation (ten repeats) on the training dataset. The performance of each algorithm was measured by the predictive R² (*R*²pred) on the testing dataset. Model performance metrics were averaged across test folds during the ten repeats to avoid opportune data splits. As a benchmark model, linear regression was applied to the complete cases, including all predictors. The model gain of each machine learning algorithm indicates the prediction variance not already explained by the benchmark model and is the difference in *R*²pred. Furthermore, to confirm the model's external generalizability, we conducted external validation of all the machine learning algorithms on a new, independent cohort (*N* = 486). A detailed summary of the characteristics of the patients is presented in table S4 in the supplementary. All analyses were implemented in R (version 3.4.1) and the code is available on GitHub. ## 2.6. Calculation of variable importance Variable importance was calculated for each of the machine learning algorithms separately, using the specific usual method to quantify variable importance. Second, the Lasso method to select significant pre dictors was also performed as a double-check for variable importance with $\lambda$ of 0.0025. Finally, plots were produced for the partial dependence (PD) on an overall average and the equivalent to a partial dependence analysis for each patient (Goldstein et al., 2015), called individual conditional expectation (ICE), was calculated. These plots offer insight into the functional relationship between predictors and the treatment outcome. (Table 2). The machine learning approaches had values ranging between 48.8 % and 51.2 %, offering an additional explained variance of up to 4.1 %. The best performing algorithm was the random forest (51.2 % explained variance). The most important predictors in all models were early symptom change (Delta) and SQ-48 at baseline (Fig. S1 in supplementary material). All models showed an increase in R$^2$ after the inclusion of early symptom change as a predictor, ranging from 22.0% to 23.3 % (see Fig. 1). The results obtained from the external validation, as shown in Table 1, indicate conformity with the original findings, although exhibiting a slightly inferior level of performance. Plots of PD and ICE indicated a relatively linear relationship between early symptom change and treatment outcome (Fig. 2). Specifically, when the early symptom change was less than zero, i.e., a worsening situation, the treatment outcome was relatively stable. Similarly, when the early symptom change was over 50, patients’ treatment outcomes continued to change in a relatively stable manner. Treatment outcome ## 2.7. Analysis of early symptom change in subscale scores Additionally, we applied a Lasso regression model to determine which changes in subscale symptom scores predicted the outcome of CBT treatment. The optimal penalty tuning parameter ($\lambda$) of the Lasso was selected through repeated five-fold cross-validation on the training dataset. This process was repeated ten times for each penalty value, and the mean squared error (MSE) was computed and averaged. In addition, symptom change over time, particularly early in treatment, has emerged as a promising predictor of treatment outcomes. According to (Santor and Segal, 2001), the degree of symptom improvement in the first 10 weeks of treatment emerged as a strong predictor of depression symptom return at both the 3-month and 6-month follow-up evaluations. Other trial-based studies confirmed this finding, but all suffered from small sample sizes (Lewis et al., 2012; Tadić et al., 2010). A study of 193 patients (Schindler et al., 2013) showed that early symptom change, as a categorical predictor of treatment outcome, could explain 27.7 % of the variance in symptomatic outcome. (Schilagert & Hiller, 2017) evaluated the predictive value of early response in routine practice with CBT as treatment for depression. They found that early response at the tenth session was a good predictor for final treatment outcome and remission regarding depressive symptoms (OR = 8.75 and OR = 5.32, respectively). These approaches used linear and logistic regression. Also, most studies categorized early symptom change into discrete groups and this may be less informative than the use of a continuous variable. The present study sought to extend previous work by exploring pretreatment predictors and early-treatment total symptom change as a continuous variable in a large routine dataset using machine learning approaches and comparing these to linear regression. Additionally, the role of early subscale symptom change was further detailed by investigating which subscale score changes were most significant for predicting treatment outcome. Introduction Cognitive behavior therapy (CBT) is an effective treatment for depression on average. While CBT has an overall evidence-based effectiveness rate of 57 % (Spinhoven et al., 2018), individual responses to the treatment do vary. Practitioners hence face the challenge to plan and adjust therapy for individual clients with potentially different needs and backgrounds. Developing a prediction algorithm to forecast treatment outcomes in early stages of treatment could help address this issue by allowing for timely adjustment of therapy and potentially improve the overall effectiveness of CBT (Sajjadian et al., 2021). Numerous potential predictors including patient characteristics, such as age, gender, education, socioeconomic status, childhood trauma, and age of onset, as well as clinical features, such as severity and chronicity, have been examined in the literature. Previous studies found that a combination of pre-treatment characteristics, including baseline total symptom score, Anxiety Symptom Index total score, and subscale scores such as depressed mood, extraversion, and psychological needs, can be potential predictors for CBT outcomes. However, these studies were limited by small sample sizes and could not produce robust results for clinical decision-making (Cohen et al., 2020; Huibers et al., 2015). Studies with relatively large samples have demonstrated that sub-scale scores can predict antidepressant treatment efficacy for individual patients (Chekroud et al., 2016; Kautzky et al., 2017). Study by (Chekroud, 2016) found that the Quick Inventory of Depressive Symptomatology-Self Report (QIDS-SR) subscales of psychomotor agitation, energy and sadness predicted treatment response to citalopram. Neuroimaging biomarkers are a third type of significant predictors (Dunlop et al., 2017). A barrier to using neuroimaging as a predictor in decision tools is the financial costs and cumbersome procedure, making it an unlikely routine test in clinical practice. In addition, symptom change over time, particularly early in treatment, has emerged as a promising predictor of treatment outcomes. According to (Santor and Segal, 2001), the degree of symptom improvement in the first 10 weeks of treatment emerged as a strong predictor of depression symptom return at both the 3-month and 6-month follow-up evaluations. Other trial-based studies confirmed this finding, but all suffered from small sample sizes (Lewis et al., 2012; Tadić et al., 2010). A study of 193 patients (Schindler et al., 2013) showed that early symptom change, as a categorical predictor of treatment outcome, could explain 27.7 % of the variance in symptomatic outcome. (Schilagert & Hiller, 2017) evaluated the predictive value of early response in routine practice with CBT as treatment for depression. They found that early response at the tenth session was a good predictor for final treatment outcome and remission regarding depressive symptoms (OR = 8.75 and OR = 5.32, respectively). These approaches used linear and logistic regression. Also, most studies categorized early symptom change into discrete groups and this may be less informative than the use of a continuous variable. The present study sought to extend previous work by exploring pretreatment predictors and early-treatment total symptom change as a continuous variable in a large routine dataset using machine learning approaches and comparing these to linear regression. Additionally, the role of early subscale symptom change was further detailed by investigating which subscale score changes were most significant for predicting treatment outcome. However, more severe patients (n = 1153) referred to specialist outpatient treatment could receive further treatment sessions (mean = 17.54). Predictors Available predictor variables included demographic characteristics, clinical characteristics, baseline diagnosis information, and therapy-related characteristics. Potential demographic predictors were gender, age, level of education, work status, and living situation. Therapists diagnosed depression according to the fourth edition of Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of mental disorders (DSM-IV) (Stein et al., 2010) using an automated and shorter version of the Schedules for Clinical Assessment in Neuropsychiatry (SCAN), the mini-SCAN, with proven reliability and validity (Nienhuis et al., 2010). Stage of the depression was based on a structured clinical interview for the DSM-IV. Therapy-related predictors were level of care (intensity of treatment), baseline severity (SQ48 score at t0), and early symptom change in either the total score or the subscale scores. ## 2.4. The external validation confirmed the findings, but with a slightly lower performance compared to the original results. Typically, external validations exhibit lower performance than reported in cross-validation due to over-calibration, resulting in somewhat reduced transferability to new datasets (Betancur et al., 2019). While other studies used machine learning methods, ours was the first to use it in a routine dataset and include information on early symptom change. Applying more sophisticated preprocessing and learning methods did not substantially improve performance. With the caveat that overall predictive performance was not extremely high with around 45 % of all variability in outcomes explained by the predictors, the significance of both baseline symptom scores and early total symptom change in predicting outcomes is apparent in various machine learning analysis pipelines. The differential importance of these variables across machine learning pipelines used different metrics including percent increase in mean squared error and total decrease in node impurities, but all pointed in the same direction. One explanation for the predictive power of early symptom change is that patients, who had positive early symptom change, experienced relief of some symptoms and developed hope and an alliance with the therapist. More specifically, our examination of subscale scores yielded findings indicating that changes in scores on subscales associated with depressed mood and anxiety occurred early on, and were predictive of treatment outcomes. Conversely, individuals who do not show early symptom improvement may potentially benefit from increasing the intensity or altering the type of intervention by clinicians. The advantage of early symptom change over pre-treatment demographics predictors seems quite substantial, which proved that individual demographics were not associated with reported accuracy (Sajjadian et al., 2021). These results were in line with previous studies (Santor and Segal, 2003; Stassen et al., 2007; Szegedi et al., 2003; Tadić et al., 2010). Findings were also consistent with studies on other psychiatric diseases like schizophrenia (Samara et al., 2015) and anxiety (Baldwin et al., 2012). Our findings suggest that a continuous measure of early symptom change is a more effective predictor of treatment outcome compared to a categorical change variable. Specifically, Schindler et al. (2013) reported that a model utilizing categorical early symptom change had an accuracy of 38.9 % in predicting treatment response, whereas in our current study it accounted for 47.1 %–51.2 % of the variance in outcomes. If these findings would indicate not only a predictive, but also causal relationship, therapists could focus on addressing target indicators such as readiness and intensity to potentially enhance early symptom change, which may lead to improved treatment outcomes later on. The large sample size of this study ensured a high level of statistical power. More importantly, our dataset from a large psychotherapy outpatient center provided information on real-world effectiveness. The study also has several limitations. First, selection bias may have occurred as excluded patients had higher baseline SQ48 scores compared to included patients. Second, we excluded patients who completed the treatment trajectory with fewer than ten sessions, which may have affected the performance of our machine learning algorithms. Third, limited predictors are available in real-world clinical practice; Hence our dataset had relatively few potential predictors. Identifying better ways to predict treatment outcome using additional routinely measured predictive variables is still necessary to ensure the accessibility of treatment by offering more tailored treatment durations. ## 5. Conclusion Early total symptom change during the first five weeks was a significant predictor of treatment outcome for CBT in a routine clinical setting, as demonstrated by both linear regression and machine learning pipelines. Interestingly, more sophisticated preprocessing and learning methods did not substantially improve performance. Analysis of changes in subscale scores revealed that improvement in symptoms related to depressed mood and anxiety predicted treatment response, indicating the potential clinical relevance of early symptom monitoring to identify patients who need increased intervention intensity or alteration of treatment type. These routinely measured predictive variables could support better-tailored CBT treatment. Numerous potential predictors including patient characteristics, such as age, gender, education, socioeconomic status, childhood trauma, and age of onset, as well as clinical features, such as severity and chronicity, have been examined in the literature. Previous studies found that a combination of pre-treatment characteristics, including baseline total symptom score, Anxiety Symptom Index total score, and subscale scores such as depressed mood, extraversion, and psychological needs, can be potential predictors for CBT outcomes. However, these studies were limited by small sample sizes and could not produce robust results for clinical decision-making (Cohen et al., 2020; Huibers et al., 2015). Studies with relatively large samples have demonstrated that sub-scale scores can predict antidepressant treatment efficacy for individual patients (Chekroud et al., 2016; Kautzky et al., 2017). A barrier to using neuroimaging as a predictor in decision tools is the financial costs and cumbersome procedure, making it an unlikely routine test in clinical practice. In addition, symptom change over time, particularly early in treatment, has emerged as a promising predictor of treatment outcomes. Predictors Available predictor variables included demographic characteristics, clinical characteristics, baseline diagnosis information, and therapy-related characteristics. Discussion Early total symptom change in week five contributed substantially to outcome prediction for CBT. The baseline symptom score was also a significant predictor, which might at least partly be attributable to regression toward later outcome prediction. None of the other variables were predictive of treatment outcome in week 10. The prediction performance was far from clinically relevant; the best learner could only explain 51.2 % variance of CBT treatment outcome, which confirms the difficulty of predicting treatment outcomes. The external validation confirmed the findings, but with a slightly lower performance compared to the original results. Typically, external validations exhibit lower performance than reported in cross-validation due to over-calibration, resulting in somewhat reduced transferability to new datasets (Betancur et al., 2019). While other studies used machine learning methods, ours was the first to use it in a routine dataset and include information on early symptom change. Applying more sophisticated preprocessing and learning methods did not substantially improve performance. With the caveat that overall predictive performance was not extremely high with around 45 % of all variability in outcomes explained by the predictors, the significance of both baseline symptom scores and early total symptom change in predicting outcomes is apparent in various machine learning analysis pipelines. The differential importance of these variables across machine learning pipelines used different metrics including percent increase in mean squared error and total decrease in node impurities, but all pointed in the same direction. One explanation for the predictive power of early symptom change is that patients, who had positive early symptom change, experienced relief of some symptoms and developed hope and an alliance with the therapist. More specifically, our examination of subscale scores yielded findings indicating that changes in scores on subscales associated with depressed mood and anxiety occurred early on, and were predictive of treatment outcomes. Conversely, individuals who do not show early symptom improvement may potentially benefit from increasing the intensity or altering the type of intervention by clinicians. The advantage of early symptom change over pre-treatment demographics predictors seems quite substantial, which proved that individual demographics were not associated with reported accuracy (Sajjadian et al., 2021). These results were in line with previous studies (Santor and Segal, 2003; Stassen et al., 2007; Szegedi et al., 2003; Tadić et al., 2010). Findings were also consistent with studies on other psychiatric diseases like schizophrenia (Samara et al., 2015) and anxiety (Baldwin et al., 2012). Our findings suggest that a continuous measure of early symptom change is a more effective predictor of treatment outcome compared to a categorical change variable. Specifically, Schindler et al. (2013) reported that a model utilizing categorical early symptom change had an accuracy of 38.9 % in predicting treatment response, whereas in our current study it accounted for 47.1 %–51.2 % of the variance in outcomes. If these findings would indicate not only a predictive, but also causal relationship, therapists could focus on addressing target indicators such as readiness and intensity to potentially enhance early symptom change, which may lead to improved treatment outcomes later on. Conclusion Early total symptom change during the first five weeks was a significant predictor of treatment outcome for CBT in a routine clinical setting, as demonstrated by both linear regression and machine learning pipelines. Interestingly, more sophisticated preprocessing and learning methods did not substantially improve performance. Analysis of changes in subscale scores revealed that improvement in symptoms related to depressed mood and anxiety predicted treatment response, indicating the potential clinical relevance of early symptom monitoring to identify patients who need increased intervention intensity or alteration of treatment type. These routinely measured predictive variables could support better-tailored CBT treatment. Machine learning analysis pipeline To investigate possible selection bias, independent *t*-tests and chi-square tests were applied to compare the complete cases with the patients whose symptom questionnaires were not completed at or within two weeks after baseline, the 5th and the 10th session. A two-sided test with a *p*-value of <0.05 was considered statistically significant. Four machine learning algorithms were trained: random forest, support vector machine (SVM), extreme gradient boosting (XGboost), and neural network. Algorithms were trained by tuning hyper-parameters with repeated five-fold cross-validation (ten repeats) on the training dataset. The performance of each algorithm was measured by the predictive R² (*R*²pred) on the testing dataset. Model performance metrics were averaged across test folds during the ten repeats to avoid opportune data splits. As a benchmark model, linear regression was applied to the complete cases, including all predictors. The model gain of each machine learning algorithm indicates the prediction variance not already explained by the benchmark model and is the difference in *R*²pred. Furthermore, to confirm the model's external generalizability, we conducted external validation of all the machine learning algorithms on a new, independent cohort (*N* = 486). A detailed summary of the characteristics of the patients is presented in table S4 in the supplementary. Typically, external validations exhibit lower performance than reported in cross-validation due to over-calibration, resulting in somewhat reduced transferability to new datasets (Betancur et al., 2019). While other studies used machine learning methods, ours was the first to use it in a routine dataset and include information on early symptom change. Applying more sophisticated preprocessing and learning methods did not substantially improve performance. With the caveat that overall predictive performance was not extremely high with around 45 % of all variability in outcomes explained by the predictors, the significance of both baseline symptom scores and early total symptom change in predicting outcomes is apparent in various machine learning analysis pipelines. The differential importance of these variables across machine learning pipelines used different metrics including percent increase in mean squared error and total decrease in node impurities, but all pointed in the same direction. One explanation for the predictive power of early symptom change is that patients, who had positive early symptom change, experienced relief of some symptoms and developed hope and an alliance with the therapist. More specifically, our examination of subscale scores yielded findings indicating that changes in scores on subscales associated with depressed mood and anxiety occurred early on, and were predictive of treatment outcomes. Conversely, individuals who do not show early symptom improvement may potentially benefit from increasing the intensity or altering the type of intervention by clinicians. The advantage of early symptom change over pre-treatment demographics predictors seems quite substantial, which proved that individual demographics were not associated with reported accuracy (Sajjadian et al., 2021). These results were in line with previous studies (Santor and Segal, 2003; Stassen et al., 2007; Szegedi et al., 2003; Tadić et al., 2010). Findings were also consistent with studies on other psychiatric diseases like schizophrenia (Samara et al., 2015) and anxiety (Baldwin et al., 2012). Our findings suggest that a continuous measure of early symptom change is a more effective predictor of treatment outcome compared to a categorical change variable. Specifically, Schindler et al. (2013) reported that a model utilizing categorical early symptom change had an accuracy of 38.9 % in predicting treatment response, whereas in our current study it accounted for 47.1 %–51.2 % of the variance in outcomes. If these findings would indicate not only a predictive, but also causal relationship, therapists could focus on addressing target indicators such as readiness and intensity to potentially enhance early symptom change, which may lead to improved treatment outcomes later on. The large sample size of this study ensured a high level of statistical power. More importantly, our dataset from a large psychotherapy outpatient center provided information on real-world effectiveness. The study also has several limitations. First, selection bias may have occurred as excluded patients had higher baseline SQ48 scores compared to included patients. Second, we excluded patients who completed the treatment trajectory with fewer than ten sessions, which may have affected the performance of our machine learning algorithms. Third, limited predictors are available in real-world clinical practice; Hence our dataset had relatively few potential predictors. Identifying better ways to predict treatment outcome using additional routinely measured predictive variables is still necessary to ensure the accessibility of treatment by offering more tailored treatment durations. ## 5. Conclusion Early total symptom change during the first five weeks was a significant predictor of treatment outcome for CBT in a routine clinical setting, as demonstrated by both linear regression and machine learning pipelines. Interestingly, more sophisticated preprocessing and learning methods did not substantially improve performance. Analysis of changes in subscale scores revealed that improvement in symptoms related to depressed mood and anxiety predicted treatment response, indicating the potential clinical relevance of early symptom monitoring to identify patients who need increased intervention intensity or alteration of treatment type. These routinely measured predictive variables could support better-tailored CBT treatment. However, future research may need to explore alternative sources of information, as the currently available routinely collected data may only explain up to 51.2 % of the total variance in outcomes. ## Disclosure All authors have approved the final manuscript. ## CRediT authorship contribution statement FL, TL and FJ contributed to the design of the study and preparation of the manuscript. Method This study first applied various prediction models and learning algorithms to predict continuous treatment outcome at session ten, considering both pretreatment symptoms and early symptom change, that is, change over the first five sessions. Additionally, the predictive power of early symptom change in treatment outcome prediction of CBT was quantified by considering parameter importance in the resulting models. ## 2.1. Study sample and design CBT treatment typically entails weekly sessions lasting between 30 and 60 min, with a duration of 10 to 18 weeks. Data came from a large mental health outpatient clinic in the Netherlands, in which CBT is primarily offered as a treatment to adults suffering from depression. The dataset consisted of *n* = 4610 depression patients for whom treatment was initiated between March 2017 and April 2019. The dataset contained routinely collected data before, during and after treatment and was anonymized. We followed the principles of the Declaration of Helsinki and the research code of the University Medical Center Groningen. All patients were asked to provide their written informed consent for data collection and analyses to support CBT research and quality control. Nineteen patients in the dataset did not give consent and had been excluded from the dataset. ## 2.2. Outcome Outcomes were measured with the 48 items self-report symptom questionnaire (SQ-48), which includes seven scales measuring psychological distress: Depression (Mood), Anxiety (ANXI), Somatization (SOMA), Agoraphobia (AGOR), Aggression (AGGR) Cognitive problem (COGN), Social Phobia (SOPH). Outcome data were gathered at baseline ## 2.5. Machine learning analysis pipeline To investigate possible selection bias, independent *t*-tests and chi-square tests were applied to compare the complete cases with the patients whose symptom questionnaires were not completed at or within two weeks after baseline, the 5th and the 10th session. A two-sided test with a *p*-value of <0.05 was considered statistically significant. Four machine learning algorithms were trained: random forest, support vector machine (SVM), extreme gradient boosting (XGboost), and neural network. Algorithms were trained by tuning hyper-parameters with repeated five-fold cross-validation (ten repeats) on the training dataset. The performance of each algorithm was measured by the predictive R² (*R*²pred) on the testing dataset. Model performance metrics were averaged across test folds during the ten repeats to avoid opportune data splits. As a benchmark model, linear regression was applied to the complete cases, including all predictors. The model gain of each machine learning algorithm indicates the prediction variance not already explained by the benchmark model and is the difference in *R*²pred. Furthermore, to confirm the model's external generalizability, we conducted external validation of all the machine learning algorithms on a new, independent cohort (*N* = 486). A detailed summary of the characteristics of the patients is presented in table S4 in the supplementary. All analyses were implemented in R (version 3.4.1) and the code is available on GitHub. ## 2.6. Calculation of variable importance Variable importance was calculated for each of the machine learning algorithms separately, using the specific usual method to quantify variable importance. Second, the Lasso method to select significant pre dictors was also performed as a double-check for variable importance with $\lambda$ of 0.0025. Finally, plots were produced for the partial dependence (PD) on an overall average and the equivalent to a partial dependence analysis for each patient (Goldstein et al., 2015), called individual conditional expectation (ICE), was calculated. These plots offer insight into the functional relationship between predictors and the treatment outcome. (Table 2). The machine learning approaches had values ranging between 48.8 % and 51.2 %, offering an additional explained variance of up to 4.1 %. The best performing algorithm was the random forest (51.2 % explained variance). The most important predictors in all models were early symptom change (Delta) and SQ-48 at baseline (Fig. S1 in supplementary material). All models showed an increase in R$^2$ after the inclusion of early symptom change as a predictor, ranging from 22.0% to 23.3 % (see Fig. 1). The results obtained from the external validation, as shown in Table 1, indicate conformity with the original findings, although exhibiting a slightly inferior level of performance. Plots of PD and ICE indicated a relatively linear relationship between early symptom change and treatment outcome (Fig. 2). Specifically, when the early symptom change was less than zero, i.e., a worsening situation, the treatment outcome was relatively stable. Similarly, when the early symptom change was over 50, patients’ treatment outcomes continued to change in a relatively stable manner. Treatment outcome ## 2.7. Analysis of early symptom change in subscale scores Additionally, we applied a Lasso regression model to determine which changes in subscale symptom scores predicted the outcome of CBT treatment. The optimal penalty tuning parameter ($\lambda$) of the Lasso was selected through repeated five-fold cross-validation on the training dataset. This process was repeated ten times for each penalty value, and the mean squared error (MSE) was computed and averaged. Then, the tuning parameter value that produced the most regularized model, while still satisfying the criterion of cross-validated error being within one standard error of the minimum was selected. ## 3. Different machine learners were compared to linear regression. ### Results Early symptom change and baseline symptom score were the only significant predictors. Models with early symptom change explained 22.0 % to 23.3 % more variance than those without early symptom change. Specifically, the baseline total symptom score, and the early symptom score changes of the subscales pertaining to depression and anxiety were the top three predictors of treatment outcome. ### Limitation Excluded patients with missing treatment outcomes had slightly higher symptom scores at baseline, indicating possible selection bias. ### Conclusion Early symptom change improved the prediction of treatment outcomes. The prediction performance achieved is far from clinical relevance; the best learner could only explain 51.2 % of the variance in outcomes. Compared to linear regression, more sophisticated preprocessing and learning methods did not substantially improve performance. ## 1. Introduction Cognitive behavior therapy (CBT) is an effective treatment for depression on average. While CBT has an overall evidence-based effectiveness rate of 57 % (Spinhoven et al., 2018), individual responses to the treatment do vary. Practitioners hence face the challenge to plan and adjust therapy for individual clients with potentially different needs and backgrounds. Developing a prediction algorithm to forecast treatment outcomes in early stages of treatment could help address this issue by allowing for timely adjustment of therapy and potentially improve the overall effectiveness of CBT (Sajjadian et al., 2021). Numerous potential predictors including patient characteristics, such as age, gender, education, socioeconomic status, childhood trauma, and age of onset, as well as clinical features, such as severity and chronicity, have been examined in the literature. Previous studies found that a combination of pre-treatment characteristics, including baseline total symptom score, Anxiety Symptom Index total score, and subscale scores such as depressed mood, extraversion, and psychological needs, can be potential predictors for CBT outcomes. However, these studies were limited by small sample sizes and could not produce robust results for clinical decision-making (Cohen et al., 2020; Huibers et al., 2015). Studies with relatively large samples have demonstrated that sub-scale scores can predict antidepressant treatment efficacy for individual patients (Chekroud et al., 2016; Kautzky et al., 2017). Neuroimaging biomarkers are a third type of significant predictors (Dunlop et al., 2017). A barrier to using neuroimaging as a predictor in decision tools is the financial costs and cumbersome procedure, making it an unlikely routine test in clinical practice. In addition, symptom change over time, particularly early in treatment, has emerged as a promising predictor of treatment outcomes. According to (Santor and Segal, 2001), the degree of symptom improvement in the first 10 weeks of treatment emerged as a strong predictor of depression symptom return at both the 3-month and 6-month follow-up evaluations. Other trial-based studies confirmed this finding, but all suffered from small sample sizes (Lewis et al., 2012; Tadić et al., 2010). A study of 193 patients (Schindler et al., 2013) showed that early symptom change, as a categorical predictor of treatment outcome, could explain 27.7 % of the variance in symptomatic outcome. (Schilagert & Hiller, 2017) evaluated the predictive value of early response in routine practice with CBT as treatment for depression. They found that early response at the tenth session was a good predictor for final treatment outcome and remission regarding depressive symptoms (OR = 8.75 and OR = 5.32, respectively). These approaches used linear and logistic regression. Also, most studies categorized early symptom change into discrete groups and this may be less informative than the use of a continuous variable. The present study sought to extend previous work by exploring pretreatment predictors and early-treatment total symptom change as a continuous variable in a large routine dataset using machine learning approaches and comparing these to linear regression. Additionally, the role of early subscale symptom change was further detailed by investigating which subscale score changes were most significant for predicting treatment outcome. Discussion Early total symptom change in week five contributed substantially to outcome prediction for CBT. The baseline symptom score was also a significant predictor, which might at least partly be attributable to regression toward later outcome prediction. None of the other variables were predictive of treatment outcome in week 10. The prediction performance was far from clinically relevant; the best learner could only explain 51.2 % variance of CBT treatment outcome, which confirms the difficulty of predicting treatment outcomes. The external validation confirmed the findings, but with a slightly lower performance compared to the original results. Typically, external validations exhibit lower performance than reported in cross-validation due to over-calibration, resulting in somewhat reduced transferability to new datasets (Betancur et al., 2019). While other studies used machine learning methods, ours was the first to use it in a routine dataset and include information on early symptom change. Applying more sophisticated preprocessing and learning methods did not substantially improve performance. With the caveat that overall predictive performance was not extremely high with around 45 % of all variability in outcomes explained by the predictors, the significance of both baseline symptom scores and early total symptom change in predicting outcomes is apparent in various machine learning analysis pipelines. The differential importance of these variables across machine learning pipelines used different metrics including percent increase in mean squared error and total decrease in node impurities, but all pointed in the same direction. One explanation for the predictive power of early symptom change is that patients, who had positive early symptom change, experienced relief of some symptoms and developed hope and an alliance with the therapist. More specifically, our examination of subscale scores yielded findings indicating that changes in scores on subscales associated with depressed mood and anxiety occurred early on, and were predictive of treatment outcomes. Conversely, individuals who do not show early symptom improvement may potentially benefit from increasing the intensity or altering the type of intervention by clinicians. The advantage of early symptom change over pre-treatment demographics predictors seems quite substantial, which proved that individual demographics were not associated with reported accuracy (Sajjadian et al., 2021). These results were in line with previous studies (Santor and Segal, 2003; Stassen et al., 2007; Szegedi et al., 2003; Tadić et al., 2010). Findings were also consistent with studies on other psychiatric diseases like schizophrenia (Samara et al., 2015) and anxiety (Baldwin et al., 2012). Our findings suggest that a continuous measure of early symptom change is a more effective predictor of treatment outcome compared to a categorical change variable. Specifically, Schindler et al. (2013) reported that a model utilizing categorical early symptom change had an accuracy of 38.9 % in predicting treatment response, whereas in our current study it accounted for 47.1 %–51.2 % of the variance in outcomes. Conclusion Early total symptom change during the first five weeks was a significant predictor of treatment outcome for CBT in a routine clinical setting, as demonstrated by both linear regression and machine learning pipelines. Interestingly, more sophisticated preprocessing and learning methods did not substantially improve performance. Analysis of changes in subscale scores revealed that improvement in symptoms related to depressed mood and anxiety predicted treatment response, indicating the potential clinical relevance of early symptom monitoring to identify patients who need increased intervention intensity or alteration of treatment type. These routinely measured predictive variables could support better-tailored CBT treatment. In addition, symptom change over time, particularly early in treatment, has emerged as a promising predictor of treatment outcomes. According to (Santor and Segal, 2001), the degree of symptom improvement in the first 10 weeks of treatment emerged as a strong predictor of depression symptom return at both the 3-month and 6-month follow-up evaluations. Other trial-based studies confirmed this finding, but all suffered from small sample sizes (Lewis et al., 2012; Tadić et al., 2010). A study of 193 patients (Schindler et al., 2013) showed that early symptom change, as a categorical predictor of treatment outcome, could explain 27.7 % of the variance in symptomatic outcome. (Schilagert & Hiller, 2017) evaluated the predictive value of early response in routine practice with CBT as treatment for depression. They found that early response at the tenth session was a good predictor for final treatment outcome and remission regarding depressive symptoms (OR = 8.75 and OR = 5.32, respectively). These approaches used linear and logistic regression. Also, most studies categorized early symptom change into discrete groups and this may be less informative than the use of a continuous variable. The present study sought to extend previous work by exploring pretreatment predictors and early-treatment total symptom change as a continuous variable in a large routine dataset using machine learning approaches and comparing these to linear regression. Additionally, the role of early subscale symptom change was further detailed by investigating which subscale score changes were most significant for predicting treatment outcome.
