For patients with mild to moderate depression, in short-term general outpatient treatment, the outcome measurement after session 10 is the end of the treatment measurement. However, more severe patients (n = 1153) referred to specialist outpatient treatment could receive further treatment sessions (mean = 17.54). Early symptom change, in both total score and subscale scores, was defined as the difference between SQ(t0) and SQ(t1) (Delta- SQ(t0) – SQ(t1)). Treatment outcome was defined as SQ(t2). ## 2.3. Predictors Available predictor variables included demographic characteristics, clinical characteristics, baseline diagnosis information, and therapy-related characteristics. Potential demographic predictors were gender, age, level of education, work status, and living situation. Therapists diagnosed depression according to the fourth edition of Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of mental disorders (DSM-IV) (Stein et al., 2010) using an automated and shorter version of the Schedules for Clinical Assessment in Neuropsychiatry (SCAN), the mini-SCAN, with proven reliability and validity (Nienhuis et al., 2010). Stage of the depression was based on a structured clinical interview for the DSM-IV. Therapy-related predictors were level of care (intensity of treatment), baseline severity (SQ48 score at t0), and early symptom change in either the total score or the subscale scores. ## 2.4. Data preparation Missing data for predictors was <20 % for all variables, and Little's test indicated most missingness was missing completely at random. Hence, the baseline analysis was a complete case approach, using the SMOGN approach (Branco et al., 2017) to deal with imbalanced data. Sensitivity analyses were performed regarding balancing, handling of missing data and inclusion of different subtypes of depression. ## 2. Method This study first applied various prediction models and learning algorithms to predict continuous treatment outcome at session ten, considering both pretreatment symptoms and early symptom change, that is, change over the first five sessions. Additionally, the predictive power of early symptom change in treatment outcome prediction of CBT was quantified by considering parameter importance in the resulting models. ## 2.1. Study sample and design CBT treatment typically entails weekly sessions lasting between 30 and 60 min, with a duration of 10 to 18 weeks. Data came from a large mental health outpatient clinic in the Netherlands, in which CBT is primarily offered as a treatment to adults suffering from depression. The dataset consisted of *n* = 4610 depression patients for whom treatment was initiated between March 2017 and April 2019. The dataset contained routinely collected data before, during and after treatment and was anonymized. We followed the principles of the Declaration of Helsinki and the research code of the University Medical Center Groningen. All patients were asked to provide their written informed consent for data collection and analyses to support CBT research and quality control. Nineteen patients in the dataset did not give consent and had been excluded from the dataset. ## 2.2. Outcome Outcomes were measured with the 48 items self-report symptom questionnaire (SQ-48), which includes seven scales measuring psychological distress: Depression (Mood), Anxiety (ANXI), Somatization (SOMA), Agoraphobia (AGOR), Aggression (AGGR) Cognitive problem (COGN), Social Phobia (SOPH). Outcome data were gathered at baseline ## 2.5. Machine learning analysis pipeline To investigate possible selection bias, independent *t*-tests and chi-square tests were applied to compare the complete cases with the patients whose symptom questionnaires were not completed at or within two weeks after baseline, the 5th and the 10th session. A two-sided test with a *p*-value of <0.05 was considered statistically significant. Four machine learning algorithms were trained: random forest, support vector machine (SVM), extreme gradient boosting (XGboost), and neural network. Algorithms were trained by tuning hyper-parameters with repeated five-fold cross-validation (ten repeats) on the training dataset. The performance of each algorithm was measured by the predictive R² (*R*²pred) on the testing dataset. Model performance metrics were averaged across test folds during the ten repeats to avoid opportune data splits. As a benchmark model, linear regression was applied to the complete cases, including all predictors. The model gain of each machine learning algorithm indicates the prediction variance not already explained by the benchmark model and is the difference in *R*²pred. Furthermore, to confirm the model's external generalizability, we conducted external validation of all the machine learning algorithms on a new, independent cohort (*N* = 486). A detailed summary of the characteristics of the patients is presented in table S4 in the supplementary. There was no deception involved. All participants who volunteered to participate in the experiment signed an informed consent form and were debriefed after the experiment. Figure 6 provides a brief overview of the entire experimental process, which comprises three phases. Detailed experimental tasks and procedures can be found in Online Resource 4. experiences were suggested to offer restoration effects comparable to those of physical forest experiences, aiding in stress reduction and well-being recovery (Reese et al., 2022). Compared to traditional experimental methods, virtual experiments offer enhanced safety for participants, eliminating the risk of physical harm (Hamilton et al., 2021). Additionally, they are more accessible, cost-effective, and conducive to repetition. Both domestically and internationally, significant academic efforts have been devoted to examining the characteristics of psychophysiological changes in unconventional states through simulated experiments. These efforts encompass a wide range of contexts, from accidents in transportation, construction, and coal mines to earthquakes and fires. VR technology enables the near-realistic reproduction of complex scenarios in these contexts. Overall, the unusual stimuli (including material, organic, and social) activate, to varying degrees, the individual’s mental activities (including cognition, emotion, and volition), which induce corresponding decision-making behaviors, as well as diverse patterns of physiological reactions such as electrocardiogram (ECG) and EDA. Nevertheless, to our knowledge, there remain some limitations, which are outlined below. Firstly, the existing literature has primarily focused on the construction industry rather than the coal mining industry. Secondly, the emergencies simulated using VR technology mostly involved single-fire accidents in buildings, which differed from the gas explosion accidents underground in coal mines, characterized by their suddenness and catastrophic nature. Furthermore, more literature has examined the relationship with behavioral responses only from a single perspective, either psychologically or physiologically. These weaknesses formulate the research gaps in understanding the neurobiological mechanisms of emergency reactions to coal mine accidents, which impedes coal miners from accurately recognizing their emergency behaviors and prevents managers from developing strategies to enhance their emergency response capabilities. Following the research clues and gaps, our study is focused on the psychophysiological characteristics of emergency reactions to coal mine accidents. From there, it further aims to explore the potential of significant indicators as predictors for emergency reactions. In other words, this study is an attempt to answer the following research questions: What characterizes emergency reactions to coal mine accidents and how can such characteristics be utilized to predict emergency reactions? The research objectives can be facilitated by utilizing VR technology to simulate a virtual scenario of a gas explosion accident triggered by a coal mine fire in the whole process. This endeavor holds the potential to prevent coal mine accidents and mitigate injuries. ## Materials and Methods ### Questionnaire Survey In this experiment, questionnaire surveys were conducted to gauge subjects’ personality traits and assess their mental activities during emergency reactions. The Psychometric Questionnaire was developed to test the personality traits and safety literacy levels of the subjects, drawing from the Revised Neuroticism Extraversion Openness Personality Inventory (Costa Jr & McCrae, 2008) and the Eysenck Personality Questionnaire-Revised (Eysenck & Eysenck, 1993). It comprised six sections: basic personal information, personality, emotion, cognition, awareness, and experience, as detailed in Online Resource 1. The Risk Perception Inventory (RPI) (Online Resource 1) was developed based on the available well-established scales by Li (2019) and Mao (2021). It was intended to assess subjects’ perceived and cognitive abilities regarding the risks of coal mine accidents by utilizing 10 items. Specifically, the first three questions were worth 2 or 1 points for selecting whether or not a particular risk had been perceived. The other seven items pertained to subjective judgments about the objectivity, unpredictability, calamitability, and variability of the risks of coal mine accidents. A five-point Likert scale was adopted, ranging from “Strongly Disagree” to “Strongly Agree” with values of 1, 2, 3, 4, and 5, respectively. All items were positively scored, with a total score of 41 on the scale. The State-trait Anxiety Inventory (SAI) (Spielberger et al., 2017), a widely recognized tool in psychology, was adapted to assess the state anxiety of subjects during emergencies in coal mine accidents (Online Resource 1). It consisted of 20 items, representing the influences of transitory situational stress. Each item offered four options: 1 point for ‘very slight’, 2 points for ‘slight’, 3 points for ‘pronounced’, and 4 points for ‘very strong’, allowing subjects to indicate the intensity of their perceived anxiety in the situations. Of these, the items with reverse scoring served to validate the scale’s measurement accuracy. Accounting for all question items, the scale was scored with a maximum of 80 and a minimum of 20 points. ### Simulation Experiment on Emergency Response to Coal Mine Accidents ### Experimental Subject To minimize the influence of individual differences on emergency reactions to coal mine accidents, homogeneous groups of similar age and education were deemed as appropriate subjects for this experiment. The following criteria were adhered to in the process of subject selection: subjects were required to be male following national regulations, as female workers are prohibited from working underground in mines; subjects were expected to be in good health, free from motion sickness and claustrophobia, and not under the influence of psychoactive drugs; participants should either have normal vision or myopia of fewer than 350 degrees with corrected visual acuity and should not have astigmatism; individuals who had experienced a late night were discouraged from participating in the experiment the following day; participation in the experiment was voluntary and not coerced. The sample size was determined by referencing previous experimental studies (Online Resource 2) on emergency evacuation from virtual building fires (Crescentini et al., 2016; Deng et al., 2022) and subway fire (Chen et al., 2021); stress reactions to coal mining accidents (Nie et al., 2016) and metro fire (Lin et al., 2020); the effects on behavioral capacity from fatigue (Zhang et al., 2023), coal mine noise (Fu et al., 2022), and underground low-light conditions (Li et al., 2022); as well as machine learning algorithms for stress detection (Siam et al., 2023), emotion recognition (Doma & Pirouz, 2020), and driving behavior identification (Bejani & Ghatee, 2018; Darzi et al., 2018; Wang et al., 2020; Yang et al., 2018). Should this be accompanied by intense state anxiety, however, the seeking process would be severely impeded. Not only does this manifest itself in a prolongation of the seeking duration, but also in the increasing likelihood of unsuccessful avoidance. Such negative impact can be substantiated by a correlation analysis between mental activities and behavioral performances, the results of which are available in Online Resource 6. Furthermore, the RF classifier demonstrated superior performance over other well-known classifiers, such as KN, SVM, and neural network, for the identification of driving style by utilizing motoring data from 11 male truck drivers in Baiyinhua No.2 open-pit mine (Wang et al., 2020). The overall classification accuracy for identifying driving styles was 95.39% when the mining truck was operating under heavy load and 90.74% when operating with no load. Integrating successful experiences in stress detection, emotion recognition, and behavior prediction, the KN, DT, and RF algorithms were intentionally selected for this study. The aim was to identify emergency behavioral patterns (EBP) by utilizing psychophysiological characteristics. The behavioral reactions triggered by mental activities are accompanied by consistent and regular physiological changes, which can be further analyzed for more profound insights using machine learning algorithms. In recent years, this research paradigm has been extensively adopted to study psychophysiology and behavior across various high-risk industries such as transportation, construction, and coal mining. One particularly noteworthy example is the performance of the decision tree (DT) classifier, which achieved an accuracy of 97.6% in classifying the unsafe behaviors of a random sample of 80 workers who took part in a mass rapid transit tunnelling project in Singapore (Goh et al., 2018). This accuracy surpassed that of the other five widely-used machine learning algorithms, as well as logistic regression (LR). Besides, classic machine learning techniques have proven capable of identifying different emotional states using the DEAP Dataset, an EEG signal repository containing data from 32 participants at distinct locations: Geneva, Switzerland; Twente, Netherlands; London, United Kingdom (Doma & Pirouz, 2020). The highest accuracy for emotion recognition achieved by multiple classification algorithms was in the following descending order: k-nearest neighbor (KN), support vector machine (SVM), DT, and LR. Moreover, stress assessment studies have been conducted to develop machine-learning models for classifying stress and relaxation (Siam et al., 2023). The approach to detecting mental stress utilized the DRIVEDB Dataset, which contains physiological signal data from 17 automotive drivers and is publicly available on PhysioNet (Healey & Picard, 2008). It was reported that the random forest (RF) classifier outperformed other techniques, namely KN, SVM, DT, and LR, achieving a classification accuracy of 98.2% for automatic stress detection. Initially, the psychophysiological indicators exhibiting significant changes were taken as input features and fed into the three classifiers integrated into the Scikit-learn library. Subsequently, the experiment samples were divided into a training set, which comprised 80% of the data, and a validation set, which encompassed the remaining 20%. This partitioning was achieved using the ‘train_test_split’ function, with a ‘random_state’ parameter in the range of (1, 10). The optimization process of k-nearest neighbor classification (KNC) models is outlined below. Initially, the algorithm for the KN classifier was set as “kd_tree”, considering that the dimensionality and sample size of the input features were not excessively large. Subsequently, the remaining hyperparameters were automatically tuned by employing the grid search technique. The “GridSearchCV” function exhaustively generated candidates for the “n_neighbors” from the range of (2, 10), and for the “weights” from the range of (uniform, distance). Each combination of parameter values was independently utilized to fit the training set, resulting in trained models. The “accuracy_score” on the whole data- set served as a metric to evaluate the performance of each trained model. Ultimately, the optimal KNC models were selected based on achieving the maximum accuracies with different input features. Following a process similar to the optimization of KNC models, the DT and RF classifiers were employed to develop the decision tree classification (DTC) and random forest classification (RFC) models of EBP, respectively. The hyperparameters were automatically tuned by the "GridSearchCV" function, along with the repartitioning of the training sets by the updated values of "random_state" in the "train_test_split" function. In particular, "criterion" was traversed by a loop in the range of (gini, entropy, log_loss); "max_depth" in the range of (2, 10); "min_samples_leaf" in the range of (1, 6); "min_samples_split" in the range of (2, 6); "random_state" in the range of (1, 10). The hyperparameters values for all KNC, DTC, and RFC models under various sample splitting conditions are detailed in Online Resource 7. The performances of different classification models depend on their classifiers and input features. Figure 17 illustrates both the average and maximum accuracies of all unimodal-based classification models. Concerning input features, the classification models based on SKT, EMG, SCL, SCR, RANGE, IBI, SDNN, PNN50, and LF/HF demonstrated higher average accuracies under various sample splitting conditions (Online Resource 7). Additionally, the optimal unimodal-based models exhibited superior performance on the input features of SC, SCR, SCL-SCR, RANGE, IBI, SDNN, and LF/HF (Online Resource 7), thereby validating the discriminative role of these metrics in identifying EBP. Consequently, indicators such as SCR, RANGE, IBI, SDNN, and LF/HF, which excel in both average and maximum accuracies, serve as justifiable discriminative attributes for EBP. Out of these, LF/HF stands out as a critical indicator, achieving the highest average accuracy of 87.4% among all classification models. This

They achieve this by stimulating α/β receptors, increasing capillary permeability, and enhancing muscle contractility (Barreiro Arcos, 2022; Hu et al., 2018). The heightened metabolism associated with these processes can be observed through increased sweat production and elevated cardiac output. Integrating successful experiences in stress detection, emotion recognition, and behavior prediction, the KN, DT, and RF algorithms were intentionally selected for this study. The aim was to identify emergency behavioral patterns (EBP) by utilizing psychophysiological characteristics. The behavioral reactions triggered by mental activities are accompanied by consistent and regular physiological changes, which can be further analyzed for more profound insights using machine learning algorithms. In recent years, this research paradigm has been extensively adopted to study psychophysiology and behavior across various high-risk industries such as transportation, construction, and coal mining. One particularly noteworthy example is the performance of the decision tree (DT) classifier, which achieved an accuracy of 97.6% in classifying the unsafe behaviors of a random sample of 80 workers who took part in a mass rapid transit tunnelling project in Singapore (Goh et al., 2018). This accuracy surpassed that of the other five widely-used machine learning algorithms, as well as logistic regression (LR). Besides, classic machine learning techniques have proven capable of identifying different emotional states using the DEAP Dataset, an EEG signal repository containing data from 32 participants at distinct locations: Geneva, Switzerland; Twente, Netherlands; London, United Kingdom (Doma & Pirouz, 2020). The highest accuracy for emotion recognition achieved by multiple classification algorithms was in the following descending order: k-nearest neighbor (KN), support vector machine (SVM), DT, and LR. Moreover, stress assessment studies have been conducted to develop machine-learning models for classifying stress and relaxation (Siam et al., 2023). The approach to detecting mental stress utilized the DRIVEDB Dataset, which contains physiological signal data from 17 automotive drivers and is publicly available on PhysioNet (Healey & Picard, 2008). It was reported that the random forest (RF) classifier outperformed other techniques, namely KN, SVM, DT, and LR, achieving a classification accuracy of 98.2% for automatic stress detection. What’s more, machine learning algorithms. The process of identification was implemented using PyCharm, a Python IDE (Integrated Development Environment). Initially, the psychophysiological indicators exhibiting significant changes were taken as input features and fed into the three classifiers integrated into the Scikit-learn library. Subsequently, the experiment samples were divided into a training set, which comprised 80% of the data, and a validation set, which encompassed the remaining 20%. This partitioning was achieved using the ‘train_test_split’ function, with a ‘random_state’ parameter in the range of (1, 10). The optimization process of k-nearest neighbor classification (KNC) models is outlined below. Initially, the algorithm for the KN classifier was set as “kd_tree”, considering that the dimensionality and sample size of the input features were not excessively large. Subsequently, the remaining hyperparameters were automatically tuned by employing the grid search technique. The “GridSearchCV” function exhaustively generated candidates for the “n_neighbors” from the range of (2, 10), and for the “weights” from the range of (uniform, distance). Each combination of parameter values was independently utilized to fit the training set, resulting in trained models. The “accuracy_score” on the whole data- set served as a metric to evaluate the performance of each trained model. Ultimately, the optimal KNC models were selected based on achieving the maximum accuracies with different input features. Following a process similar to the optimization of KNC models, the DT and RF classifiers were employed to develop the decision tree classification (DTC) and random forest classification (RFC) models of EBP, respectively. The hyperparameters were automatically tuned by the "GridSearchCV" function, along with the repartitioning of the training sets by the updated values of "random_state" in the "train_test_split" function. In particular, "criterion" was traversed by a loop in the range of (gini, entropy, log_loss); "max_depth" in the range of (2, 10); "min_samples_leaf" in the range of (1, 6); "min_samples_split" in the range of (2, 6); "random_state" in the range of (1, 10). The hyperparameters values for all KNC, DTC, and RFC models under various sample splitting conditions are detailed in Online Resource 7. The performances of different classification models depend on their classifiers and input features. Figure 17 illustrates both the average and maximum accuracies of all unimodal-based classification models. Concerning input features, the classification models based on SKT, EMG, SCL, SCR, RANGE, IBI, SDNN, PNN50, and LF/HF demonstrated higher average accuracies under various sample splitting conditions (Online Resource 7). Additionally, the optimal unimodal-based models exhibited superior performance on the input features of SC, SCR, SCL-SCR, RANGE, IBI, SDNN, and LF/HF (Online Resource 7), thereby validating the discriminative role of these metrics in identifying EBP. Consequently, indicators such as SCR, RANGE, IBI, SDNN, and LF/HF, which excel in both average and maximum accuracies, serve as justifiable discriminative attributes for EBP. Out of these, LF/HF stands out as a critical indicator, achieving the highest average accuracy of 87.4% among all classification models. This

Compared to traditional experimental methods, virtual experiments offer enhanced safety for participants, eliminating the risk of physical harm (Hamilton et al., 2021). Additionally, they are more accessible, cost-effective, and conducive to repetition. Both domestically and internationally, significant academic efforts have been devoted to examining the characteristics of psychophysiological changes in unconventional states through simulated experiments. These efforts encompass a wide range of contexts, from accidents in transportation, construction, and coal mines to earthquakes and fires. VR technology enables the near-realistic reproduction of complex scenarios in these contexts. Overall, the unusual stimuli (including material, organic, and social) activate, to varying degrees, the individual’s mental activities (including cognition, emotion, and volition), which induce corresponding decision-making behaviors, as well as diverse patterns of physiological reactions such as electrocardiogram (ECG) and EDA. Nevertheless, to our knowledge, there remain some limitations, which are outlined below. Firstly, the existing literature has primarily focused on the construction industry rather than the coal mining industry. Secondly, the emergencies simulated using VR technology mostly involved single-fire accidents in buildings, which differed from the gas explosion accidents underground in coal mines, characterized by their suddenness and catastrophic nature. Furthermore, more literature has examined the relationship with behavioral responses only from a single perspective, either psychologically or physiologically. These weaknesses formulate the research gaps in understanding the neurobiological mechanisms of emergency reactions to coal mine accidents, which impedes coal miners from accurately recognizing their emergency behaviors and prevents managers from developing strategies to enhance their emergency response capabilities. Following the research clues and gaps, our study is focused on the psychophysiological characteristics of emergency reactions to coal mine accidents. From there, it further aims to explore the potential of significant indicators as predictors for emergency reactions. In other words, this study is an attempt to answer the following research questions: What characterizes emergency reactions to coal mine accidents and how can such characteristics be utilized to predict emergency reactions? The research objectives can be facilitated by utilizing VR technology to simulate a virtual scenario of a gas explosion accident triggered by a coal mine fire in the whole process. This endeavor holds the potential to prevent coal mine accidents and mitigate injuries. ## Materials and Methods ### Questionnaire Survey In this experiment, questionnaire surveys were conducted to gauge subjects’ personality traits and assess their mental activities during emergency reactions. The Psychometric Questionnaire was developed to test the personality traits and safety literacy levels of the subjects, drawing from the Revised Neuroticism Extraversion Openness Personality Inventory (Costa Jr & McCrae, 2008) and the Eysenck Personality Questionnaire-Revised (Eysenck & Eysenck, 1993). It comprised six sections: basic personal information, personality, emotion, cognition, awareness, and experience, as detailed in Online Resource 1. The Risk Perception Inventory (RPI) (Online Resource 1) was developed based on the available well-established scales by Li (2019) and Mao (2021). It was intended to assess subjects’ perceived and cognitive abilities regarding the risks of coal mine accidents by utilizing 10 items. Specifically, the first three questions were worth 2 or 1 points for selecting whether or not a particular risk had been perceived. The other seven items pertained to subjective judgments about the objectivity, unpredictability, calamitability, and variability of the risks of coal mine accidents. A five-point Likert scale was adopted, ranging from “Strongly Disagree” to “Strongly Agree” with values of 1, 2, 3, 4, and 5, respectively. All items were positively scored, with a total score of 41 on the scale. The State-trait Anxiety Inventory (SAI) (Spielberger et al., 2017), a widely recognized tool in psychology, was adapted to assess the state anxiety of subjects during emergencies in coal mine accidents (Online Resource 1). It consisted of 20 items, representing the influences of transitory situational stress. Each item offered four options: 1 point for ‘very slight’, 2 points for ‘slight’, 3 points for ‘pronounced’, and 4 points for ‘very strong’, allowing subjects to indicate the intensity of their perceived anxiety in the situations. Of these, the items with reverse scoring served to validate the scale’s measurement accuracy. Accounting for all question items, the scale was scored with a maximum of 80 and a minimum of 20 points. ### Simulation Experiment on Emergency Response to Coal Mine Accidents ### Experimental Subject To minimize the influence of individual differences on emergency reactions to coal mine accidents, homogeneous groups of similar age and education were deemed as appropriate subjects for this experiment. The following criteria were adhered to in the process of subject selection: subjects were required to be male following national regulations, as female workers are prohibited from working underground in mines; subjects were expected to be in good health, free from motion sickness and claustrophobia, and not under the influence of psychoactive drugs; participants should either have normal vision or myopia of fewer than 350 degrees with corrected visual acuity and should not have astigmatism; individuals who had experienced a late night were discouraged from participating in the experiment the following day; participation in the experiment was voluntary and not coerced. The sample size was determined by referencing previous experimental studies (Online Resource 2) on emergency evacuation from virtual building fires (Crescentini et al., 2016; Deng et al., 2022) and subway fire (Chen et al., 2021); stress reactions to coal mining accidents (Nie et al., 2016) and metro fire (Lin et al., 2020); the effects on behavioral capacity from fatigue (Zhang et al., 2023), coal mine noise (Fu et al., 2022), and underground low-light conditions (Li et al., 2022); as well as machine learning algorithms for stress detection (Siam et al., 2023), emotion recognition (Doma & Pirouz, 2020), and driving behavior identification (Bejani & Ghatee, 2018; Darzi et al., 2018; Wang et al., 2020; Yang et al., 2018). In addition, objective conditions were also taken into account. A total of 50 male students from the China University of Mining & Technology-Beijing were recruited as subjects for

The correct escape route was the tunnel with the shortest distance and devoid of any risks. If a subject reached the refuge along the correct route within 60 s, it was recognized as a successful escape. Otherwise, the escape was deemed unsuccessful if the chosen route was incorrect or if the allocated time was exceeded. Within the virtual scenarios, participants were entirely free to autonomously decide whether and how to behave according to their desires, without any interference from the experimenters. Part of the experiment process of the virtual emergency escape is shown in Fig. 7. What's next, participants were required to complete the SAI and the RPI to provide as accurate feedback as possible on their mental activities during the emergency escape. Last but not least, a forest intervention was conducted after the escape to reduce the potential impacts of participating in the high-stress VR simulated emergency scenarios. The participants were prompted to take as much time as they needed to be exposed to the virtual natural environment. All participants reported a shift away from negative affect and restoration of subjective vitality following the virtual nature experience. Finally, the experiment concluded by rewarding the participants. The complete physiological record of each subject was divided into two segments: the baseline segment, which captured the roaming period during which the subject's physiological signals were monitored in their natural state without any induced stressors; and the emergency segment, which encompassed the period from the start to the end of the virtual emergency escape, during which physiological stress were measured. Physiological data for different segments are available in Online Resource 5. It was inevitable that the monitoring data of physiological signals would be noisy and distorted. The noise and distortion may be attributed to continuous body movement and hair on the skin reducing the adhesion between the skin and the physiological sensors (Iqbal et al., 2021). To address this issue, the raw physiological data were pre-processed to restore their intrinsic features as much as possible. On one hand, the data noise was eliminated using a sequence of steps: filtering, smoothing, scaling, and down-sampling. Different signals lend themselves to different techniques. For example, EDA was subjected to low-pass and Gaussian filtering for its extremely low frequency; HRV, Fig. 7 Emergency escape in virtual scenes which was highly susceptible to external noise, underwent low-pass, high-pass, and band-stop filtering; SKT, which was slightly affected by the external environment, was subjected to the system’s default sliding mean filtering; the RESP with frequencies below 10HZ underwent low-pass, band-stop, and sliding mean filtering. On the other hand, outliers and missing values were further processed with statistical methods. Specifically, the outliers with too large absolute values were replaced with the mean values, following the principle of $M − 3SD \le X \le M + 3SD$, where $X$ represents the data of physiological signal, $M$ represents the mean value, and SD represents the standard deviation (Zhang, 2007). The missing values between interval values were filled in by utilizing linear interpolation, a straightforward and widely used method (Liu et al., 2020). emergency mental activities and the psychological factors that could influence them. The natural environment featured scenic forestry scenes, embracing a wide variety of plants and animals as well as streams and birdsong, as presented in Online Resource 3. ## Experimental Procedure The experiment was designed and conducted following the ethical standards of the Chinese Psychological Society and with the 1964 Helsinki Declaration and its later amendments or comparable ethical standards. There was no deception involved. All participants who volunteered to participate in the experiment signed an informed consent form and were debriefed after the experiment. Figure 6 provides a brief overview of the entire experimental process, which comprises three phases. Detailed experimental tasks and procedures can be found in Online Resource 4. Initially, participants were informed of the privacy policy, potential consequences, and their right to withdraw at any time. If voluntarily choosing to participate in the experiment, they were required to sign the informed consent form and complete the Psychometric Questionnaire. The aim was to identify emergency behavioral patterns (EBP) by utilizing psychophysiological characteristics. Moreover, stress assessment studies have been conducted to develop machine-learning models for classifying stress and relaxation (Siam et al., 2023). The approach to detecting mental stress utilized the DRIVEDB Dataset, which contains physiological signal data from 17 automotive drivers and is publicly available on PhysioNet (Healey & Picard, 2008). Psychologically, the highly destructive virtual accident scenarios induced anxiety in the subjects. This anxiety potentially threw them into a state of fear that the catastrophe would occur in the real world. To ensure the psychological well-being of the subjects, forest interventions were applied to mitigate the potential negative impacts induced by the high-stress scenarios. The natural environment serves as a potential buffer for poor mental health (van den Berg et al., 2010). On one hand, nature experience provides a “soft fascination” that allows a person to pay attention effortlessly (Bratman et al., 2012). On the other hand, the presence of nature evokes an evolutionary response to safety and survival, which produces positive emotions (Berto, 2014). In other words, the subjects experienced lower physiological and psychological stress when observing images of forests, which represent a natural environment necessary for our evolutionary history. It is expected to explore the micro-mechanisms of physiological changes in emergency reactions, focusing on aspects such as the waveforms of ERPs and potential distribution patterns. This exploration will be based on psychophysiological theories to deepen our understanding of how the body responds during emergencies. In addition to personality, cognition, and awareness, it is essential to investigate the effects of mental activities such as attention, emotional potency (Yang et al., 2021), safety attitude (Li et al., 2019), and safety motivation (Xia et al., 2020) on emergency response, as well as the interactions between them. Further exploration is warranted into the physiological basis of mental activities that influence an individual's decision-making during accident emergency response. This includes studying the neural mechanisms of brain activation, which can be grounded in biopsychology theories. Besides, human behavioral performance in emergencies can be judged more accurately using motion-capture technology (Ahmed & Onan Demirel, 2019). Last but not least, advanced machine learning algorithms such as artificial neural networks (Dastres & Soori, 2021) and deep learning (Hu et al., 2023), known for their strong robustness and high accuracy, can be combined with data mining techniques to facilitate the accurate prediction and precise recognition of behavioral performance at coal mine accident scenes. This is particularly important due to the complexity and variability of factors involved in such scenarios. (2) Excessive anxiety can induce vegetative dysfunction, leading to endocrine disorders that cause mental hyperarousal or debilitating physical fatigue beyond voluntary control. The performances of multimodal-based models demonstrate enhancement compared to the unimodal-based models for identifying EBP by utilizing psychophysiological indicators with significant changes. Among unimodal-based models, LF/HF stands out as a critical indicator, achieving the highest average accuracy of 87.4%. However, the multimodal-RFC model, outperforming all other models with accuracies of up to 92%, holds promise as an optimal predictor for early warning systems of EBP during coal mine accident emergencies. ## Conclusions As research into accident causation progresses, scholars are placing increasing emphasis on behavioral safety. Driven by psychological factors, there exists an intricate relationship between the mental activities induced by accident stimuli and the resulting physiological changes and behavioral performances. This paper represents a preliminary exploration of the psychophysiological and behavioral reaction mechanisms underlying coal mine accident emergencies, leading to the following conclusions. (1) During accident emergencies, certain personality traits such as extraversion and openness, along with a high level of cognitive ability, facilitate an individual’s perception of risk in the surrounding environment. Both domestically and internationally, significant academic efforts have been devoted to examining the characteristics of psychophysiological changes in unconventional states through simulated experiments. These efforts encompass a wide range of contexts, from accidents in transportation, construction, and coal mines to earthquakes and fires. VR technology enables the near-realistic reproduction of complex scenarios in these contexts. Overall, the unusual stimuli (including material, organic, and social) activate, to varying degrees, the individual’s mental activities (including cognition, emotion, and volition), which induce corresponding decision-making behaviors, as well as diverse patterns of physiological reactions such as electrocardiogram (ECG) and EDA. Nevertheless, to our knowledge, there remain some limitations, which are outlined below. Firstly, the existing literature has primarily focused on the construction industry rather than the coal mining industry. Secondly, the emergencies simulated using VR technology mostly involved single-fire accidents in buildings, which differed from the gas explosion accidents underground in coal mines, characterized by their suddenness and catastrophic nature. Furthermore, more literature has examined the relationship with behavioral responses only from a single perspective, either psychologically or physiologically. These weaknesses formulate the research gaps in understanding the neurobiological mechanisms of emergency reactions to coal mine accidents, which impedes coal miners from accurately recognizing their emergency behaviors and prevents managers from developing strategies to enhance their emergency response capabilities. Following the research clues and gaps, our study is focused on the psychophysiological characteristics of emergency reactions to coal mine accidents. From there, it further aims to explore the potential of significant indicators as predictors for emergency reactions. In other words, this study is an attempt to answer the following research questions: What characterizes emergency reactions to coal mine accidents and how can such characteristics be utilized to predict emergency reactions? The research objectives can be facilitated by utilizing VR technology to simulate a virtual scenario of a gas explosion accident triggered by a coal mine fire in the whole process. The Risk Perception Inventory (RPI) (Online Resource 1) was developed based on the available well-established scales by Li (2019) and Mao (2021). It was intended to assess subjects’ perceived and cognitive abilities regarding the risks of coal mine accidents by utilizing 10 items. Specifically, the first three questions were worth 2 or 1 points for selecting whether or not a particular risk had been perceived. The other seven items pertained to subjective judgments about the objectivity, unpredictability, calamitability, and variability of the risks of coal mine accidents. A five-point Likert scale was adopted, ranging from “Strongly Disagree” to “Strongly Agree” with values of 1, 2, 3, 4, and 5, respectively. All items were positively scored, with a total score of 41 on the scale. The State-trait Anxiety Inventory (SAI) (Spielberger et al., 2017), a widely recognized tool in psychology, was adapted to assess the state anxiety of subjects during emergencies in coal mine accidents (Online Resource 1). It consisted of 20 items, representing the influences of transitory situational stress. Each item offered four options: 1 point for ‘very slight’, 2 points for ‘slight’, 3 points for ‘pronounced’, and 4 points for ‘very strong’, allowing subjects to indicate the intensity of their perceived anxiety in the situations. Of these, the items with reverse scoring served to validate the scale’s measurement accuracy. Crowds of real human subjects were observed to move and interact in an immersive three-dimensional virtual environment, mimicking the typical patterns of crowds in real-life crowded situations (Moussasid et al., 2016). VR exposures have proven to be highly effective in creating a sense of experimental realism, eliciting and modulating psychophysiological reactions such as anxiety and fear measured by EDA (Crescentini et al., 2016). Furthermore, VR has been demonstrated to influence attitudes and behaviors related to personal safety, such as in aircraft evacuations (Chittaro, 2014a, b). The changes in subjects’ emotions, in terms of both emotional potency and arousal, triggered by the immersive virtual environment created using VR technology, proved to be feasible to assess the sense of presence experienced by subjects during virtual building fire emergency evacuation tasks (Zou et al., 2017). During the virtual fire escape, individuals’ emergency escape capabilities were found to be significantly positively correlated with changes in skin conductance (SC), skin conductance level (SCL), and HR, while being significantly negatively correlated with changes in low frequency (LF) and low frequency/ high frequency (LF/HF) (Chen et al., 2021; Liu et al., 2021; Wang & Li, 2023). This pattern suggests that excessive stress may be a contributing factor to emergency behavior. The evacuation scenarios created using two VR technologies, namely cave automatic virtual environment and mobile-driven helmet-mounted display (HMD), consistently demonstrated their impacts on personnel behavior (Ronchi et al., 2019). In addition, immersive VR nature experiences were suggested to offer restoration effects comparable to those of physical forest experiences, aiding in stress reduction and well-being recovery (Reese et al., 2022). Compared to traditional experimental methods, virtual experiments offer enhanced safety for participants, eliminating the risk of physical harm (Hamilton et al., 2021). Additionally, they are more accessible, cost-effective, and conducive to repetition. Both domestically and internationally, significant academic efforts have been devoted to examining the characteristics of psychophysiological changes in unconventional states through simulated experiments. These efforts encompass a wide range of contexts, from accidents in transportation, construction, and coal mines to earthquakes and fires. VR technology enables the near-realistic reproduction of complex scenarios in these contexts. Overall, the unusual stimuli (including material, organic, and social) activate, to varying degrees, the individual’s mental activities (including cognition, emotion, and volition), which induce corresponding decision-making behaviors, as well as diverse patterns of physiological reactions such as electrocardiogram (ECG) and EDA. Nevertheless, to our knowledge, there remain some limitations, which are outlined below. Firstly, the existing literature has primarily focused on the construction industry rather than the coal mining industry. Secondly, the emergencies simulated using VR technology mostly involved single-fire accidents in buildings, which differed from the gas explosion accidents underground in coal mines, characterized by their suddenness and catastrophic nature. Furthermore, more literature has examined the relationship with behavioral responses only from a single perspective, either psychologically or physiologically. These weaknesses formulate the research gaps in understanding the neurobiological mechanisms of emergency reactions to coal mine accidents, which impedes coal miners from accurately recognizing their emergency behaviors and prevents managers from developing strategies to enhance their emergency response capabilities. Following the research clues and gaps, our study is focused on the psychophysiological characteristics of emergency reactions to coal mine accidents. From there, it further aims to explore the potential of significant indicators as predictors for emergency reactions. In other words, this study is an attempt to answer the following research questions: What characterizes emergency reactions to coal mine accidents and how can such characteristics be utilized to predict emergency reactions? The research objectives can be facilitated by utilizing VR technology to simulate a virtual scenario of a gas explosion accident triggered by a coal mine fire in the whole process. This endeavor holds the potential to prevent coal mine accidents and mitigate injuries. ## Materials and Methods ### Questionnaire Survey In this experiment, questionnaire surveys were conducted to gauge subjects’ personality traits and assess their mental activities during emergency reactions. The Psychometric Questionnaire was developed to test the personality traits and safety literacy levels of the subjects, drawing from the Revised Neuroticism Extraversion Openness Personality Inventory (Costa Jr & McCrae, 2008) and the Eysenck Personality Questionnaire-Revised (Eysenck & Eysenck, 1993). It comprised six sections: basic personal information, personality, emotion, cognition, awareness, and experience, as detailed in Online Resource 1. The Risk Perception Inventory (RPI) (Online Resource 1) was developed based on the available well-established scales by Li (2019) and Mao (2021). It was intended to assess subjects’ perceived and cognitive abilities regarding the risks of coal mine accidents by utilizing 10 items. Specifically, the first three questions were worth 2 or 1 points for selecting whether or not a particular risk had been perceived. The other seven items pertained to subjective judgments about the objectivity, unpredictability, calamitability, and variability of the risks of coal mine accidents. A five-point Likert scale was adopted, ranging from “Strongly Disagree” to “Strongly Agree” with values of 1, 2, 3, 4, and 5, respectively. All items were positively scored, with a total score of 41 on the scale. The State-trait Anxiety Inventory (SAI) (Spielberger et al., 2017), a widely recognized tool in psychology, was adapted to assess the state anxiety of subjects during emergencies in coal mine accidents (Online Resource 1). It consisted of 20 items, representing the influences of transitory situational stress. Each item offered four options: 1 point for ‘very slight’, 2 points for ‘slight’, 3 points for ‘pronounced’, and 4 points for ‘very strong’, allowing subjects to indicate the intensity of their perceived anxiety in the situations. Of these, the items with reverse scoring served to validate the scale’s measurement accuracy. Accounting for all question items, the scale was scored with a maximum of 80 and a minimum of 20 points. ### Simulation Experiment on Emergency Response to Coal Mine Accidents ### Experimental Subject To minimize the influence of individual differences on emergency reactions to coal mine accidents, homogeneous groups of similar age and education were deemed as appropriate

The Psychometric Questionnaire was developed to test the personality traits and safety literacy levels of the subjects, drawing from the Revised Neuroticism Extraversion Openness Personality Inventory (Costa Jr & McCrae, 2008) and the Eysenck Personality Questionnaire-Revised (Eysenck & Eysenck, 1993). It comprised six sections: basic personal information, personality, emotion, cognition, awareness, and experience, as detailed in Online Resource 1. The Risk Perception Inventory (RPI) (Online Resource 1) was developed based on the available well-established scales by Li (2019) and Mao (2021). It was intended to assess subjects’ perceived and cognitive abilities regarding the risks of coal mine accidents by utilizing 10 items. Specifically, the first three questions were worth 2 or 1 points for selecting whether or not a particular risk had been perceived. The other seven items pertained to subjective judgments about the objectivity, unpredictability, calamitability, and variability of the risks of coal mine accidents. A five-point Likert scale was adopted, ranging from “Strongly Disagree” to “Strongly Agree” with values of 1, 2, 3, 4, and 5, respectively. All items were positively scored, with a total score of 41 on the scale. The State-trait Anxiety Inventory (SAI) (Spielberger et al., 2017), a widely recognized tool in psychology, was adapted to assess the state anxiety of subjects during emergencies in coal mine accidents (Online Resource 1). It consisted of 20 items, representing the influences of transitory situational stress. Each item offered four options: 1 point for ‘very slight’, 2 points for ‘slight’, 3 points for ‘pronounced’, and 4 points for ‘very strong’, allowing subjects to indicate the intensity of their perceived anxiety in the situations. Of these, the items with reverse scoring served to validate the scale’s measurement accuracy. Accounting for all question items, the scale was scored with a maximum of 80 and a minimum of 20 points. ### Simulation Experiment on Emergency Response to Coal Mine Accidents ### Experimental Subject To minimize the influence of individual differences on emergency reactions to coal mine accidents, homogeneous groups of similar age and education were deemed as appropriate subjects for this experiment. There was no deception involved. All participants who volunteered to participate in the experiment signed an informed consent form and were debriefed after the experiment. Figure 6 provides a brief overview of the entire experimental process, which comprises three phases. Detailed experimental tasks and procedures can be found in Online Resource 4. Initially, participants were informed of the privacy policy, potential consequences, and their right to withdraw at any time. If voluntarily choosing to participate in the experiment, they were required to sign the informed consent form and complete the Psychometric Questionnaire. Meanwhile, the laboratory's environmental parameters were regulated as temperature to 20 °C, wind speed to 0.7 m/s, and humidity to 55%. Wearing of the wireless physiological sensors and calibration of the eye tracker were also performed during this phase. Then, they roamed the virtual coal mines for 3 min in a natural state without being exposed to any stimuli. This roaming period allowed participants to familiarize themselves with the virtual environment and provided a baseline of physiological signals for the subsequent stimuli. Following the baseline (roaming) period, participants experienced a simulation of an emergency escape from coal mine accidents. In these simulated scenarios, participants witnessed specific warning signs of coal and gas outbursts occurring at the coal mining face, such as the outward bulging or sheet ganging of the coal wall. As the scene switched, they arrived at the belt conveyor, where a pile of coal dust had accumulated underneath the conveyor, and sparks were visible. Immediately, they encountered a gas explosion accident a few seconds later and were instructed to equip self-rescuer in preparation for an emergency escape. Following that, the virtual system initiated a countdown as the emergency escape began. Should this be accompanied by intense state anxiety, however, the seeking process would be severely impeded. Not only does this manifest itself in a prolongation of the seeking duration, but also in the increasing likelihood of unsuccessful avoidance. The overall classification accuracy for identifying driving styles was 95.39% when the mining truck was operating under heavy load and 90.74% when operating with no load. Integrating successful experiences in stress detection, emotion recognition, and behavior prediction, the KN, DT, and RF algorithms were intentionally selected for this study. The aim was to identify emergency behavioral patterns (EBP) by utilizing psychophysiological characteristics. The behavioral reactions triggered by mental activities are accompanied by consistent and regular physiological changes, which can be further analyzed for more profound insights using machine learning algorithms. In recent years, this research paradigm has been extensively adopted to study psychophysiology and behavior across various high-risk industries such as transportation, construction, and coal mining. One particularly noteworthy example is the performance of the decision tree (DT) classifier, which achieved an accuracy of 97.6% in classifying the unsafe behaviors of a random sample of 80 workers who took part in a mass rapid transit tunnelling project in Singapore (Goh et al., 2018). This accuracy surpassed that of the other five widely-used machine learning algorithms, as well as logistic regression (LR). Besides, classic machine learning techniques have proven capable of identifying different emotional states using the DEAP Dataset, an EEG signal repository containing data from 32 participants at distinct locations: Geneva, Switzerland; Twente, Netherlands; London, United Kingdom (Doma & Pirouz, 2020). The highest accuracy for emotion recognition achieved by multiple classification algorithms was in the following descending order: k-nearest neighbor (KN), support vector machine (SVM), DT, and LR. Moreover, stress assessment studies have been conducted to develop machine-learning models for classifying stress and relaxation (Siam et al., 2023). The approach to detecting mental stress utilized the DRIVEDB Dataset, which contains physiological signal data from 17 automotive drivers and is publicly available on PhysioNet (Healey & Picard, 2008). It was reported that the random forest (RF) classifier outperformed other techniques, namely KN, SVM, DT, and LR, achieving a classification accuracy of 98.2% for automatic stress detection. Initially, the psychophysiological indicators exhibiting significant changes were taken as input features and fed into the three classifiers integrated into the Scikit-learn library. Subsequently, the experiment samples were divided into a training set, which comprised 80% of the data, and a validation set, which encompassed the remaining 20%. This partitioning was achieved using the ‘train_test_split’ function, with a ‘random_state’ parameter in the range of (1, 10). The optimization process of k-nearest neighbor classification (KNC) models is outlined below. Initially, the algorithm for the KN classifier was set as “kd_tree”, considering that the dimensionality and sample size of the input features were not excessively large. Subsequently, the remaining hyperparameters were automatically tuned by employing the grid search technique. The “GridSearchCV” function exhaustively generated candidates for the “n_neighbors” from the range of (2, 10), and for the “weights” from the range of (uniform, distance). Each combination of parameter values was independently utilized to fit the training set, resulting in trained models. The “accuracy_score” on the whole data- set served as a metric to evaluate the performance of each trained model. Ultimately, the optimal KNC models were selected based on achieving the maximum accuracies with different input features. Following a process similar to the optimization of KNC models, the DT and RF classifiers were employed to develop the decision tree classification (DTC) and random forest classification (RFC) models of EBP, respectively. The hyperparameters were automatically tuned by the "GridSearchCV" function, along with the repartitioning of the training sets by the updated values of "random_state" in the "train_test_split" function. In particular, "criterion" was traversed by a loop in the range of (gini, entropy, log_loss); "max_depth" in the range of (2, 10); "min_samples_leaf" in the range of (1, 6); "min_samples_split" in the range of (2, 6); "random_state" in the range of (1, 10). The hyperparameters values for all KNC, DTC, and RFC models under various sample splitting conditions are detailed in Online Resource 7. The performances of different classification models depend on their classifiers and input features. Figure 17 illustrates both the average and maximum accuracies of all unimodal-based classification models. Concerning input features, the classification models based on SKT, EMG, SCL, SCR, RANGE, IBI, SDNN, PNN50, and LF/HF demonstrated higher average accuracies under various sample splitting conditions (Online Resource 7). Additionally, the optimal unimodal-based models exhibited superior performance on the input features of SC, SCR, SCL-SCR, RANGE, IBI, SDNN, and LF/HF (Online Resource 7), thereby validating the discriminative role of these metrics in identifying EBP. Consequently, indicators such as SCR, RANGE, IBI, SDNN, and LF/HF, which excel in both average and maximum accuracies, serve as justifiable discriminative attributes for EBP. Out of these, LF/HF stands out as a critical indicator, achieving the highest average accuracy of 87.4% among all classification models. This

In recent years, this research paradigm has been extensively adopted to study psychophysiology and behavior across various high-risk industries such as transportation, construction, and coal mining. One particularly noteworthy example is the performance of the decision tree (DT) classifier, which achieved an accuracy of 97.6% in classifying the unsafe behaviors of a random sample of 80 workers who took part in a mass rapid transit tunnelling project in Singapore (Goh et al., 2018). This accuracy surpassed that of the other five widely-used machine learning algorithms, as well as logistic regression (LR). Besides, classic machine learning techniques have proven capable of identifying different emotional states using the DEAP Dataset, an EEG signal repository containing data from 32 participants at distinct locations: Geneva, Switzerland; Twente, Netherlands; London, United Kingdom (Doma & Pirouz, 2020). The highest accuracy for emotion recognition achieved by multiple classification algorithms was in the following descending order: k-nearest neighbor (KN), support vector machine (SVM), DT, and LR. Moreover, stress assessment studies have been conducted to develop machine-learning models for classifying stress and relaxation (Siam et al., 2023). The approach to detecting mental stress utilized the DRIVEDB Dataset, which contains physiological signal data from 17 automotive drivers and is publicly available on PhysioNet (Healey & Picard, 2008). Ultimately, the optimal KNC models were selected based on achieving the maximum accuracies with different input features. Compared to traditional experimental methods, virtual experiments offer enhanced safety for participants, eliminating the risk of physical harm (Hamilton et al., 2021). Additionally, they are more accessible, cost-effective, and conducive to repetition. Both domestically and internationally, significant academic efforts have been devoted to examining the characteristics of psychophysiological changes in unconventional states through simulated experiments. These efforts encompass a wide range of contexts, from accidents in transportation, construction, and coal mines to earthquakes and fires. VR technology enables the near-realistic reproduction of complex scenarios in these contexts. Overall, the unusual stimuli (including material, organic, and social) activate, to varying degrees, the individual’s mental activities (including cognition, emotion, and volition), which induce corresponding decision-making behaviors, as well as diverse patterns of physiological reactions such as electrocardiogram (ECG) and EDA. Nevertheless, to our knowledge, there remain some limitations, which are outlined below. Firstly, the existing literature has primarily focused on the construction industry rather than the coal mining industry. Secondly, the emergencies simulated using VR technology mostly involved single-fire accidents in buildings, which differed from the gas explosion accidents underground in coal mines, characterized by their suddenness and catastrophic nature. Furthermore, more literature has examined the relationship with behavioral responses only from a single perspective, either psychologically or physiologically. These weaknesses formulate the research gaps in understanding the neurobiological mechanisms of emergency reactions to coal mine accidents, which impedes coal miners from accurately recognizing their emergency behaviors and prevents managers from developing strategies to enhance their emergency response capabilities. Following the research clues and gaps, our study is focused on the psychophysiological characteristics of emergency reactions to coal mine accidents. From there, it further aims to explore the potential of significant indicators as predictors for emergency reactions. In other words, this study is an attempt to answer the following research questions: What characterizes emergency reactions to coal mine accidents and how can such characteristics be utilized to predict emergency reactions? The research objectives can be facilitated by utilizing VR technology to simulate a virtual scenario of a gas explosion accident triggered by a coal mine fire in the whole process. This endeavor holds the potential to prevent coal mine accidents and mitigate injuries. ## Materials and Methods ### Questionnaire Survey In this experiment, questionnaire surveys were conducted to gauge subjects’ personality traits and assess their mental activities during emergency reactions. The Psychometric Questionnaire was developed to test the personality traits and safety literacy levels of the subjects, drawing from the Revised Neuroticism Extraversion Openness Personality Inventory (Costa Jr & McCrae, 2008) and the Eysenck Personality Questionnaire-Revised (Eysenck & Eysenck, 1993). It comprised six sections: basic personal information, personality, emotion, cognition, awareness, and experience, as detailed in Online Resource 1. The Risk Perception Inventory (RPI) (Online Resource 1) was developed based on the available well-established scales by Li (2019) and Mao (2021). It was intended to assess subjects’ perceived and cognitive abilities regarding the risks of coal mine accidents by utilizing 10 items. Specifically, the first three questions were worth 2 or 1 points for selecting whether or not a particular risk had been perceived. The other seven items pertained to subjective judgments about the objectivity, unpredictability, calamitability, and variability of the risks of coal mine accidents. A five-point Likert scale was adopted, ranging from “Strongly Disagree” to “Strongly Agree” with values of 1, 2, 3, 4, and 5, respectively. All items were positively scored, with a total score of 41 on the scale. The State-trait Anxiety Inventory (SAI) (Spielberger et al., 2017), a widely recognized tool in psychology, was adapted to assess the state anxiety of subjects during emergencies in coal mine accidents (Online Resource 1). It consisted of 20 items, representing the influences of transitory situational stress. Each item offered four options: 1 point for ‘very slight’, 2 points for ‘slight’, 3 points for ‘pronounced’, and 4 points for ‘very strong’, allowing subjects to indicate the intensity of their perceived anxiety in the situations. Of these, the items with reverse scoring served to validate the scale’s measurement accuracy. Accounting for all question items, the scale was scored with a maximum of 80 and a minimum of 20 points. ### Simulation Experiment on Emergency Response to Coal Mine Accidents ### Experimental Subject To minimize the influence of individual differences on emergency reactions to coal mine accidents, homogeneous groups of similar age and education were deemed as appropriate subjects for this experiment. The following criteria were adhered to in the process of subject selection: subjects were required to be male following national regulations, as female workers are prohibited from working underground in mines; subjects were expected to be in good health, free from motion sickness and claustrophobia, and not under the influence of psychoactive drugs; participants should either have normal vision or myopia of fewer than 350 degrees with corrected visual acuity and should not have astigmatism; individuals who had experienced a late night were discouraged from participating in the experiment the following day; participation in the experiment was voluntary and not coerced. The sample size was determined by referencing previous experimental studies (Online Resource 2) on emergency evacuation from virtual building fires (Crescentini et al., 2016; Deng et al., 2022) and subway fire (Chen et al., 2021); stress reactions to coal mining accidents (Nie et al., 2016) and metro fire (Lin et al., 2020); the effects on behavioral capacity from fatigue (Zhang et al., 2023), coal mine noise (Fu et al., 2022), and underground low-light conditions (Li et al., 2022); as well as machine learning algorithms for stress detection (Siam et al., 2023), emotion recognition (Doma & Pirouz, 2020), and driving behavior identification (Bejani & Ghatee, 2018; Darzi et al., 2018; Wang et al., 2020; Yang et al., 2018). In addition, objective conditions were also taken into account. A total of 50 male students from the China University of Mining & Technology-Beijing were recruited as subjects for

The correct escape route was the tunnel with the shortest distance and devoid of any risks. If a subject reached the refuge along the correct route within 60 s, it was recognized as a successful escape. Otherwise, the escape was deemed unsuccessful if the chosen route was incorrect or if the allocated time was exceeded. Within the virtual scenarios, participants were entirely free to autonomously decide whether and how to behave according to their desires, without any interference from the experimenters. Part of the experiment process of the virtual emergency escape is shown in Fig. 7. What's next, participants were required to complete the SAI and the RPI to provide as accurate feedback as possible on their mental activities during the emergency escape. Last but not least, a forest intervention was conducted after the escape to reduce the potential impacts of participating in the high-stress VR simulated emergency scenarios. The participants were prompted to take as much time as they needed to be exposed to the virtual natural environment. All participants reported a shift away from negative affect and restoration of subjective vitality following the virtual nature experience. Finally, the experiment concluded by rewarding the participants. The complete physiological record of each subject was divided into two segments: the baseline segment, which captured the roaming period during which the subject's physiological signals were monitored in their natural state without any induced stressors; and the emergency segment, which encompassed the period from the start to the end of the virtual emergency escape, during which physiological stress were measured. Physiological data for different segments are available in Online Resource 5. It was inevitable that the monitoring data of physiological signals would be noisy and distorted. The noise and distortion may be attributed to continuous body movement and hair on the skin reducing the adhesion between the skin and the physiological sensors (Iqbal et al., 2021). To address this issue, the raw physiological data were pre-processed to restore their intrinsic features as much as possible. On one hand, the data noise was eliminated using a sequence of steps: filtering, smoothing, scaling, and down-sampling. Different signals lend themselves to different techniques. For example, EDA was subjected to low-pass and Gaussian filtering for its extremely low frequency; HRV, Fig. 7 Emergency escape in virtual scenes which was highly susceptible to external noise, underwent low-pass, high-pass, and band-stop filtering; SKT, which was slightly affected by the external environment, was subjected to the system’s default sliding mean filtering; the RESP with frequencies below 10HZ underwent low-pass, band-stop, and sliding mean filtering. On the other hand, outliers and missing values were further processed with statistical methods. Specifically, the outliers with too large absolute values were replaced with the mean values, following the principle of $M − 3SD \le X \le M + 3SD$, where $X$ represents the data of physiological signal, $M$ represents the mean value, and SD represents the standard deviation (Zhang, 2007). Next, a formula is proposed to calculate the capacity of emergency reaction based on the psychophysiological characteristics. Finally, the implications of emergency psychophysiological reactions were explored, along with the potential utilization of machine learning methods for identifying the patterns of emergency behaviors based on these reaction characteristics. ## Statistical Analysis Following data pre-processing, the physiological signals were initially subjected to a preliminary linear analysis, primarily consisting of time-domain and frequency-domain analyses. The time-domain analysis took place by treating the physiological signal as a function of time. In contrast, the frequency-domain analysis performed a power spectral density analysis of the signal by utilizing the Fast Fourier Transform. The two analysis methods extracted statistically characterized indicators from the physiological signals based on different dimensions. Compared to traditional experimental methods, virtual experiments offer enhanced safety for participants, eliminating the risk of physical harm (Hamilton et al., 2021). Additionally, they are more accessible, cost-effective, and conducive to repetition. Both domestically and internationally, significant academic efforts have been devoted to examining the characteristics of psychophysiological changes in unconventional states through simulated experiments. These efforts encompass a wide range of contexts, from accidents in transportation, construction, and coal mines to earthquakes and fires. VR technology enables the near-realistic reproduction of complex scenarios in these contexts. Overall, the unusual stimuli (including material, organic, and social) activate, to varying degrees, the individual’s mental activities (including cognition, emotion, and volition), which induce corresponding decision-making behaviors, as well as diverse patterns of physiological reactions such as electrocardiogram (ECG) and EDA. Nevertheless, to our knowledge, there remain some limitations, which are outlined below. Firstly, the existing literature has primarily focused on the construction industry rather than the coal mining industry. Secondly, the emergencies simulated using VR technology mostly involved single-fire accidents in buildings, which differed from the gas explosion accidents underground in coal mines, characterized by their suddenness and catastrophic nature. Furthermore, more literature has examined the relationship with behavioral responses only from a single perspective, either psychologically or physiologically. These weaknesses formulate the research gaps in understanding the neurobiological mechanisms of emergency reactions to coal mine accidents, which impedes coal miners from accurately recognizing their emergency behaviors and prevents managers from developing strategies to enhance their emergency response capabilities. Following the research clues and gaps, our study is focused on the psychophysiological characteristics of emergency reactions to coal mine accidents. From there, it further aims to explore the potential of significant indicators as predictors for emergency reactions. In other words, this study is an attempt to answer the following research questions: What characterizes emergency reactions to coal mine accidents and how can such characteristics be utilized to predict emergency reactions? The research objectives can be facilitated by utilizing VR technology to simulate a virtual scenario of a gas explosion accident triggered by a coal mine fire in the whole process. This endeavor holds the potential to prevent coal mine accidents and mitigate injuries. ## Materials and Methods ### Questionnaire Survey In this experiment, questionnaire surveys were conducted to gauge subjects’ personality traits and assess their mental activities during emergency reactions. The Psychometric Questionnaire was developed to test the personality traits and safety literacy levels of the subjects, drawing from the Revised Neuroticism Extraversion Openness Personality Inventory (Costa Jr & McCrae, 2008) and the Eysenck Personality Questionnaire-Revised (Eysenck & Eysenck, 1993). It comprised six sections: basic personal information, personality, emotion, cognition, awareness, and experience, as detailed in Online Resource 1. The Risk Perception Inventory (RPI) (Online Resource 1) was developed based on the available well-established scales by Li (2019) and Mao (2021). It was intended to assess subjects’ perceived and cognitive abilities regarding the risks of coal mine accidents by utilizing 10 items. Specifically, the first three questions were worth 2 or 1 points for selecting whether or not a particular risk had been perceived. The other seven items pertained to subjective judgments about the objectivity, unpredictability, calamitability, and variability of the risks of coal mine accidents. A five-point Likert scale was adopted, ranging from “Strongly Disagree” to “Strongly Agree” with values of 1, 2, 3, 4, and 5, respectively. All items were positively scored, with a total score of 41 on the scale. The State-trait Anxiety Inventory (SAI) (Spielberger et al., 2017), a widely recognized tool in psychology, was adapted to assess the state anxiety of subjects during emergencies in coal mine accidents (Online Resource 1). It consisted of 20 items, representing the influences of transitory situational stress. Each item offered four options: 1 point for ‘very slight’, 2 points for ‘slight’, 3 points for ‘pronounced’, and 4 points for ‘very strong’, allowing subjects to indicate the intensity of their perceived anxiety in the situations. Of these, the items with reverse scoring served to validate the scale’s measurement accuracy. Accounting for all question items, the scale was scored with a maximum of 80 and a minimum of 20 points. ### Simulation Experiment on Emergency Response to Coal Mine Accidents ### Experimental Subject To minimize the influence of individual differences on emergency reactions to coal mine accidents, homogeneous groups of similar age and education were deemed as appropriate subjects for this experiment. The following criteria were adhered to in the process of subject selection: subjects were required to be male following national regulations, as female workers are prohibited from working underground in mines; subjects were expected to be in good health, free from motion sickness and claustrophobia, and not under the influence of psychoactive drugs; participants should either have normal vision or myopia of fewer than 350 degrees with corrected visual acuity and should not have astigmatism; individuals who had experienced a late night were discouraged from participating in the experiment the following day; participation in the experiment was voluntary and not coerced. The sample size was determined by referencing previous experimental studies (Online Resource 2) on emergency evacuation from virtual building fires (Crescentini et al., 2016; Deng et al., 2022) and subway fire (Chen et al., 2021); stress reactions to coal mining accidents (Nie et al., 2016) and metro fire (Lin et al., 2020); the effects on behavioral capacity from fatigue (Zhang et al., 2023), coal mine noise (Fu et al., 2022), and underground low-light conditions (Li et al., 2022); as well as machine learning algorithms for stress detection (Siam et al., 2023), emotion recognition (Doma & Pirouz, 2020), and driving behavior identification (Bejani & Ghatee, 2018; Darzi et al., 2018; Wang et al., 2020; Yang et al., 2018). In addition, objective conditions were also taken into account. A total of 50 male students from the China University of Mining & Technology-Beijing were recruited as subjects for
