The aim was to identify emergency behavioral patterns (EBP) by utilizing psychophysiological characteristics. The behavioral reactions triggered by mental activities are accompanied by consistent and regular physiological changes, which can be further analyzed for more profound insights using machine learning algorithms. In recent years, this research paradigm has been extensively adopted to study psychophysiology and behavior across various high-risk industries such as transportation, construction, and coal mining. One particularly noteworthy example is the performance of the decision tree (DT) classifier, which achieved an accuracy of 97.6% in classifying the unsafe behaviors of a random sample of 80 workers who took part in a mass rapid transit tunnelling project in Singapore (Goh et al., 2018). This accuracy surpassed that of the other five widely-used machine learning algorithms, as well as logistic regression (LR). Besides, classic machine learning techniques have proven capable of identifying different emotional states using the DEAP Dataset, an EEG signal repository containing data from 32 participants at distinct locations: Geneva, Switzerland; Twente, Netherlands; London, United Kingdom (Doma & Pirouz, 2020). The highest accuracy for emotion recognition achieved by multiple classification algorithms was in the following descending order: k-nearest neighbor (KN), support vector machine (SVM), DT, and LR. Moreover, stress assessment studies have been conducted to develop machine-learning models for classifying stress and relaxation (Siam et al., 2023). The approach to detecting mental stress utilized the DRIVEDB Dataset, which contains physiological signal data from 17 automotive drivers and is publicly available on PhysioNet (Healey & Picard, 2008). A 3D video was employed to immerse participants in a virtual natural environment, aiming to alleviate the potential negative effects of high stress. The natural environment featured scenic forestry scenes, embracing a wide variety of plants and animals as well as streams and birdsong, as presented in Online Resource 3. ## Experimental Procedure The experiment was designed and conducted following the ethical standards of the Chinese Psychological Society and with the 1964 Helsinki Declaration and its later amendments or comparable ethical standards. There was no deception involved. All participants who volunteered to participate in the experiment signed an informed consent form and were debriefed after the experiment. Figure 6 provides a brief overview of the entire experimental process, which comprises three phases. Detailed experimental tasks and procedures can be found in Online Resource 4. Initially, participants were informed of the privacy policy, potential consequences, and their right to withdraw at any time. If voluntarily choosing to participate in the experiment, they were required to sign the informed consent form and complete the Psychometric Questionnaire. Meanwhile, the laboratory's environmental parameters were regulated as temperature to 20 °C, wind speed to 0.7 m/s, and humidity to 55%. Wearing of the wireless physiological sensors and calibration of the eye tracker were also performed during this phase. Then, they roamed the virtual coal mines for 3 min in a natural state without being exposed to any stimuli. This roaming period allowed participants to familiarize themselves with the virtual environment and provided a baseline of physiological signals for the subsequent stimuli. Following the baseline (roaming) period, participants experienced a simulation of an emergency escape from coal mine accidents. In these simulated scenarios, participants witnessed specific warning signs of coal and gas outbursts occurring at the coal mining face, such as the outward bulging or sheet ganging of the coal wall. As the scene switched, they arrived at the belt conveyor, where a pile of coal dust had accumulated underneath the conveyor, and sparks were visible. Immediately, they encountered a gas explosion accident a few seconds later and were instructed to equip self-rescuer in preparation for an emergency escape. Following that, the virtual system initiated a countdown as the emergency escape began. The correct escape route was the tunnel with the shortest distance and devoid of any risks. If a subject reached the refuge along the correct route within 60 s, it was recognized as a successful escape. Otherwise, the escape was deemed unsuccessful if the chosen route was incorrect or if the allocated time was exceeded. Within the virtual scenarios, participants were entirely free to autonomously decide whether and how to behave according to their desires, without any interference from the experimenters. Part of the experiment process of the virtual emergency escape is shown in Fig. 7. What's next, participants were required to complete the SAI and the RPI to provide as accurate feedback as possible on their mental activities during the emergency escape. Last but not least, a forest intervention was conducted after the escape to reduce the potential impacts of participating in the high-stress VR simulated emergency scenarios. The participants were prompted to take as much time as they needed to be exposed to the virtual natural environment. All participants reported a shift away from negative affect and restoration of subjective vitality following the virtual nature experience. Finally, the experiment concluded by rewarding the participants. The complete physiological record of each subject was divided into two segments: the baseline segment, which captured the roaming period during which the subject's physiological signals were monitored in their natural state without any induced stressors; and the emergency segment, which encompassed the period from the start to the end of the virtual emergency escape, during which physiological stress were measured. Physiological data for different segments are available in Online Resource 5. It was inevitable that the monitoring data of physiological signals would be noisy and distorted. The noise and distortion may be attributed to continuous body movement and hair on the skin reducing the adhesion between the skin and the physiological sensors (Iqbal et al., 2021). To address this issue, the raw physiological data were pre-processed to restore their intrinsic features as much as possible. On one hand, the data noise was eliminated using a sequence of steps: filtering, smoothing, scaling, and down-sampling. Different signals lend themselves to different techniques. For example, EDA was subjected to low-pass and Gaussian filtering for its extremely low frequency; HRV, Fig. 7 Emergency escape in virtual scenes which was highly susceptible to external noise, underwent low-pass, high-pass, and band-stop filtering; SKT, which was slightly affected by the external environment, was subjected to the system’s default sliding mean filtering; the RESP with frequencies below 10HZ underwent low-pass, band-stop, and sliding mean filtering. On the other hand, outliers and missing values were further processed with statistical methods. Specifically, the outliers with too large absolute values were replaced with the mean values, following the principle of $M − 3SD \le X \le M + 3SD$, where $X$ represents the data of physiological

signal, $M$ represents the mean value, and SD represents the standard deviation (Zhang, 2007). The time-domain analysis took place by treating the physiological signal as a function of time. In contrast, the frequency-domain analysis performed a power spectral density analysis of the signal by utilizing the Fast Fourier Transform. The two analysis methods extracted statistically characterized indicators from the physiological signals based on different dimensions. Figure 8 depicts the indicators extracted from different physiological signals in this study along with a brief explanation of each. ## Results and Analysis ### Characteristics of Emergency Reaction to Coal Mine Accident ### Emergency Mental Activities Then, the characteristics of emergency reactions to coal mine accidents were analyzed with statistical methods. Specifically, a correlation analysis was conducted between Pearson correlation analysis was conducted between emergency mental activities, including risk perception and state anxiety, and the psychological factors affecting these mental activities. The correlations between the variables are shown in Fig. 9. Detailed correlation coefficients and their significance levels are provided in Online Resource 6. Figure 8: Brief explanation of physiological indicators. The results reported significant positive correlations between risk perception and extraversion, agreeableness, openness, and cognition, respectively. State anxiety exhibited a significant positive correlation with neuroticism and a significant negative correlation with emotional stability, conscientiousness, awareness, and experience. Moreover, there are correlations between different personality traits, as well as between personality traits and psychological processes. Particularly striking were the significant negative correlations between neuroticism and extraversion & conscientiousness, while significant positive correlations were found between agreeableness and extraversion & openness, and between extraversion and openness. Neuroticism exerted a significant negative effect on emotional stability, whereas conscientiousness exerted a significant positive effect on both emotional stability and emergency awareness. Additionally, a significant positive correlation was also observed between risk perception and state anxiety. ## Emergency Physiological Changes EDA EDA refers to the physiological activity in the organism that results in changes in skin resistance or conductance due to secretion by sweat glands. The normality of EDA indicators was evaluated by the Shapiro-Wilk test. The p-values for each indicator were all found to be less than 0.05, indicating that none followed a normal distribution. Accordingly, the Wilcoxon signed rank test was utilized to assess the significance of their differences, and the results are presented in Table 1. Integrating successful experiences in stress detection, emotion recognition, and behavior prediction, the KN, DT, and RF algorithms were intentionally selected for this study. The aim was to identify emergency behavioral patterns (EBP) by utilizing psychophysiological characteristics. The behavioral reactions triggered by mental activities are accompanied by consistent and regular physiological changes, which can be further analyzed for more profound insights using machine learning algorithms. In recent years, this research paradigm has been extensively adopted to study psychophysiology and behavior across various high-risk industries such as transportation, construction, and coal mining. One particularly noteworthy example is the performance of the decision tree (DT) classifier, which achieved an accuracy of 97.6% in classifying the unsafe behaviors of a random sample of 80 workers who took part in a mass rapid transit tunnelling project in Singapore (Goh et al., 2018). This accuracy surpassed that of the other five widely-used machine learning algorithms, as well as logistic regression (LR). Besides, classic machine learning techniques have proven capable of identifying different emotional states using the DEAP Dataset, an EEG signal repository containing data from 32 participants at distinct locations: Geneva, Switzerland; Twente, Netherlands; London, United Kingdom (Doma & Pirouz, 2020). The highest accuracy for emotion recognition achieved by multiple classification algorithms was in the following descending order: k-nearest neighbor (KN), support vector machine (SVM), DT, and LR. Moreover, stress assessment studies have been conducted to develop machine-learning models for classifying stress and relaxation (Siam et al., 2023). The approach to detecting mental stress utilized the DRIVEDB Dataset, which contains physiological signal data from 17 automotive drivers and is publicly available on PhysioNet (Healey & Picard, 2008). It was reported that the random forest (RF) classifier outperformed other techniques, namely KN, SVM, DT, and LR, achieving a classification accuracy of 98.2% for automatic stress detection. Initially, the psychophysiological indicators exhibiting significant changes were taken as input features and fed into the three classifiers integrated into the Scikit-learn library. Subsequently, the experiment samples were divided into a training set, which comprised 80% of the data, and a validation set, which encompassed the remaining 20%. This partitioning was achieved using the ‘train_test_split’ function, with a ‘random_state’ parameter in the range of (1, 10). The optimization process of k-nearest neighbor classification (KNC) models is outlined below. Initially, the algorithm for the KN classifier was set as “kd_tree”, considering that the dimensionality and sample size of the input features were not excessively large. Subsequently, the remaining hyperparameters were automatically tuned by employing the grid search technique. The “GridSearchCV” function exhaustively generated candidates for the “n_neighbors” from the range of (2, 10), and for the “weights” from the range of (uniform, distance). Each combination of parameter values was independently utilized to fit the training set, resulting in trained models. The “accuracy_score” on the whole data- set served as a metric to evaluate the performance of each trained model. Ultimately, the optimal KNC models were selected based on achieving the maximum accuracies with different input features. Following a process similar to the optimization of KNC models, the DT and RF classifiers were employed to develop the decision tree classification (DTC) and random forest classification (RFC) models of EBP, respectively. The hyperparameters were automatically tuned by the "GridSearchCV" function, along with the repartitioning of the training sets by the updated values of "random_state" in the "train_test_split" function. In particular, "criterion" was traversed by a loop in the range of (gini, entropy, log_loss); "max_depth" in the range of (2, 10); "min_samples_leaf" in the range of (1, 6); "min_samples_split" in the range of (2, 6); "random_state" in the range of (1, 10). The hyperparameters values for all KNC, DTC, and RFC models under various sample splitting conditions are detailed in Online Resource 7. The performances of different classification models depend on their classifiers and input features. Figure 17 illustrates both the average and maximum accuracies of all unimodal-based classification models. Concerning input features, the classification models based on SKT, EMG, SCL, SCR, RANGE, IBI, SDNN, PNN50, and LF/HF demonstrated higher average accuracies under various sample splitting conditions (Online Resource 7). Additionally, the optimal unimodal-based models exhibited superior performance on the input features of SC, SCR, SCL-SCR, RANGE, IBI, SDNN, and LF/HF (Online Resource 7), thereby validating the discriminative role of these metrics in identifying EBP. Consequently, indicators such as SCR, RANGE, IBI, SDNN, and LF/HF, which excel in both average and maximum accuracies, serve as justifiable discriminative attributes for EBP. Out of these, LF/HF stands out as a critical indicator, achieving the highest average accuracy of 87.4% among all classification models. This

They achieve this by stimulating α/β receptors, increasing capillary permeability, and enhancing muscle contractility (Barreiro Arcos, 2022; Hu et al., 2018). By leveraging knowledge of emergency response procedures, drawing from similar past experiences, and having a general understanding of how to manage stressful situations, individuals can make more informed decisions and take appropriate actions promptly. This indicates a greater ability to prepare themselves to respond effectively to emergencies (Kyung Hui & Og Cheol, 2017). Regarding physiological changes, regularity is mainly characterized by the enhancements of EDA, EMG, and HRV, alongside the significant reductions in RESP and SKT. These changes reflect an imbalance between the sympathetic and parasympathetic nervous systems, which may result from abnormalities in endocrine activities (hormonal) and autonomic responses (involuntary) through the hyper-activation of the hypothalamus-hypophysis neuroendocrine axis (Ulrich-Lai & Herman, 2009). During emergency reactions, the hypothalamus signals the anterior pituitary gland to release adrenocorticotropic hormone, which stimulates the adrenal cortex to release adrenal cortical hormones, such as cortisol (Hinds & Sanchez, 2022). The hypothalamus also signals the release of thyroid-stimulating hormone, which stimulates the thyroid gland to release thyroid hormones (Shiota & Kalat, 2017). All of these hormones play critical roles in regulating metabolism and preparing the body to respond to stressors. They achieve this by stimulating α/β receptors, increasing capillary permeability, and enhancing muscle contractility (Barreiro Arcos, 2022; Hu et al., 2018). The heightened metabolism associated with these processes can be observed through increased sweat production and elevated cardiac output. This heightened metabolic activity is further reflected in enhanced EDA, EMG, and HRV activity. Moreover, the accelerated oxidative breakdown of energy substrates and the expedited thermal dissipation from the skin surface are primarily responsible for reductions in RESP and SKT. These physiological responses collectively optimize energy production and muscle function, ensuring the body can effectively manage and respond to stressors during emergency situations. These reaction patterns, which provide optimal adaptation for specific stages of imminent danger (Schauer & Elbert, 2010), have been extensively documented in studies on practitioners in the transportation and aviation sectors. For example, cognitive arousal levels increased earlier in drivers who avoided a collision compared to those who did not, even before the actual hazard was visually detected (Ba et al., 2016). This was evidenced by a significant elevation in SC. Similar changes can also be observed in pilots under specific conditions, such as turbulence, indicating comparable levels of cognitive arousal (Borghini et al., 2014). Additionally, there is a consistent decline in IBI with extended exposure to adventurous flight conditions (Wang & Gao, 2020). Moreover, the characteristics of mental activities and physiological changes in simulated coal mine accident emergencies were coherent with those observed in other situations, such as a subway fire (Lin, 2020). There was no deception involved. All participants who volunteered to participate in the experiment signed an informed consent form and were debriefed after the experiment. Figure 6 provides a brief overview of the entire experimental process, which comprises three phases. Detailed experimental tasks and procedures can be found in Online Resource 4. Initially, participants were informed of the privacy policy, potential consequences, and their right to withdraw at any time. If voluntarily choosing to participate in the experiment, they were required to sign the informed consent form and complete the Psychometric Questionnaire. Meanwhile, the laboratory's environmental parameters were regulated as temperature to 20 °C, wind speed to 0.7 m/s, and humidity to 55%. Wearing of the wireless physiological sensors and calibration of the eye tracker were also performed during this phase. Then, they roamed the virtual coal mines for 3 min in a natural state without being exposed to any stimuli. This roaming period allowed participants to familiarize themselves with the virtual environment and provided a baseline of physiological signals for the subsequent stimuli. Following the baseline (roaming) period, participants experienced a simulation of an emergency escape from coal mine accidents. In these simulated scenarios, participants witnessed specific warning signs of coal and gas outbursts occurring at the coal mining face, such as the outward bulging or sheet ganging of the coal wall. As the scene switched, they arrived at the belt conveyor, where a pile of coal dust had accumulated underneath the conveyor, and sparks were visible. Immediately, they encountered a gas explosion accident a few seconds later and were instructed to equip self-rescuer in preparation for an emergency escape. Following that, the virtual system initiated a countdown as the emergency escape began. The correct escape route was the tunnel with the shortest distance and devoid of any risks. If a subject reached the refuge along the correct route within 60 s, it was recognized as a successful escape. Otherwise, the escape was deemed unsuccessful if the chosen route was incorrect or if the allocated time was exceeded. Within the virtual scenarios, participants were entirely free to autonomously decide whether and how to behave according to their desires, without any interference from the experimenters. The participants were prompted to take as much time as they needed to be exposed to the virtual natural environment. Finally, the experiment concluded by rewarding the participants. Integrating successful experiences in stress detection, emotion recognition, and behavior prediction, the KN, DT, and RF algorithms were intentionally selected for this study. The aim was to identify emergency behavioral patterns (EBP) by utilizing psychophysiological characteristics. The behavioral reactions triggered by mental activities are accompanied by consistent and regular physiological changes, which can be further analyzed for more profound insights using machine learning algorithms. In recent years, this research paradigm has been extensively adopted to study psychophysiology and behavior across various high-risk industries such as transportation, construction, and coal mining. One particularly noteworthy example is the performance of the decision tree (DT) classifier, which achieved an accuracy of 97.6% in classifying the unsafe behaviors of a random sample of 80 workers who took part in a mass rapid transit tunnelling project in Singapore (Goh et al., 2018). This accuracy surpassed that of the other five widely-used machine learning algorithms, as well as logistic regression (LR). Besides, classic machine learning techniques have proven capable of identifying different emotional states using the DEAP Dataset, an EEG signal repository containing data from 32 participants at distinct locations: Geneva, Switzerland; Twente, Netherlands; London, United Kingdom (Doma & Pirouz, 2020). The highest accuracy for emotion recognition achieved by multiple classification algorithms was in the following descending order: k-nearest neighbor (KN), support vector machine (SVM), DT, and LR. Moreover, stress assessment studies have been conducted to develop machine-learning models for classifying stress and relaxation (Siam et al., 2023). The approach to detecting mental stress utilized the DRIVEDB Dataset, which contains physiological signal data from 17 automotive drivers and is publicly available on PhysioNet (Healey & Picard, 2008). It was reported that the random forest (RF) classifier outperformed other techniques, namely KN, SVM, DT, and LR, achieving a classification accuracy of 98.2% for automatic stress detection. Initially, the psychophysiological indicators exhibiting significant changes were taken as input features and fed into the three classifiers integrated into the Scikit-learn library. Subsequently, the experiment samples were divided into a training set, which comprised 80% of the data, and a validation set, which encompassed the remaining 20%. This partitioning was achieved using the ‘train_test_split’ function, with a ‘random_state’ parameter in the range of (1, 10). The optimization process of k-nearest neighbor classification (KNC) models is outlined below. Initially, the algorithm for the KN classifier was set as “kd_tree”, considering that the dimensionality and sample size of the input features were not excessively large. Subsequently, the remaining hyperparameters were automatically tuned by employing the grid search technique. The “GridSearchCV” function exhaustively generated candidates for the “n_neighbors” from the range of (2, 10), and for the “weights” from the range of (uniform, distance). Each combination of parameter values was independently utilized to fit the training set, resulting in trained models. The “accuracy_score” on the whole data- set served as a metric to evaluate the performance of each trained model. Ultimately, the optimal KNC models were selected based on achieving the maximum accuracies with different input features. Following a process similar to the optimization of KNC models, the DT and RF classifiers were employed to develop the decision tree classification (DTC) and random forest classification (RFC) models of EBP, respectively. The hyperparameters were automatically tuned by the "GridSearchCV" function, along with the repartitioning of the training sets by the updated values of "random_state" in the "train_test_split" function. In particular, "criterion" was traversed by a loop in the range of (gini, entropy, log_loss); "max_depth" in the range of (2, 10); "min_samples_leaf" in the range of (1, 6); "min_samples_split" in the range of (2, 6); "random_state" in the range of (1, 10). The hyperparameters values for all KNC, DTC, and RFC models under various sample splitting conditions are detailed in Online Resource 7. The performances of different classification models depend on their classifiers and input features. Figure 17 illustrates both the average and maximum accuracies of all unimodal-based classification models. Concerning input features, the classification models based on SKT, EMG, SCL, SCR, RANGE, IBI, SDNN, PNN50, and LF/HF demonstrated higher average accuracies under various sample splitting conditions (Online Resource 7). Additionally, the optimal unimodal-based models exhibited superior performance on the input features of SC, SCR, SCL-SCR, RANGE, IBI, SDNN, and LF/HF (Online Resource 7), thereby validating the discriminative role of these metrics in identifying EBP. Consequently, indicators such as SCR, RANGE, IBI, SDNN, and LF/HF, which excel in both average and maximum accuracies, serve as justifiable discriminative attributes for EBP. Out of these, LF/HF stands out as a critical indicator, achieving the highest average accuracy of 87.4% among all classification models. This

Subjects had to rely on overhead miner's lamps to illuminate their escape routes. The intermittent explosive sounds, coupled with the thick smoke, created a realistic and immersive emergency scenario simulating a coal mine accident disaster. The virtual emergency scenarios were meticulously designed to recreate the tension and desperation experienced by miners during accident emergencies, aiming to elicit more authentic psychophysiological reactions from the subjects. However, this high-stress VR immersion experience may have induced negative effects such as anxiety and even fear in the subjects, potentially leading to temporary impairments in their mental health. A 3D video was employed to immerse participants in a virtual natural environment, aiming to alleviate the potential negative effects of high stress. The natural environment featured scenic forestry scenes, embracing a wide variety of plants and animals as well as streams and birdsong, as presented in Online Resource 3. ## Experimental Procedure The experiment was designed and conducted following the ethical standards of the Chinese Psychological Society and with the 1964 Helsinki Declaration and its later amendments or comparable ethical standards. There was no deception involved. All participants who volunteered to participate in the experiment signed an informed consent form and were debriefed after the experiment. Figure 6 provides a brief overview of the entire experimental process, which comprises three phases. Detailed experimental tasks and procedures can be found in Online Resource 4. Initially, participants were informed of the privacy policy, potential consequences, and their right to withdraw at any time. If voluntarily choosing to participate in the experiment, they were required to sign the informed consent form and complete the Psychometric Questionnaire. Meanwhile, the laboratory's environmental parameters were regulated as temperature to 20 °C, wind speed to 0.7 m/s, and humidity to 55%. Wearing of the wireless physiological sensors and calibration of the eye tracker were also performed during this phase. Then, they roamed the virtual coal mines for 3 min in a natural state without being exposed to any stimuli. This roaming period allowed participants to familiarize themselves with the virtual environment and provided a baseline of physiological signals for the subsequent stimuli. Following the baseline (roaming) period, participants experienced a simulation of an emergency escape from coal mine accidents. In these simulated scenarios, participants witnessed specific warning signs of coal and gas outbursts occurring at the coal mining face, such as the outward bulging or sheet ganging of the coal wall. As the scene switched, they arrived at the belt conveyor, where a pile of coal dust had accumulated underneath the conveyor, and sparks were visible. Immediately, they encountered a gas explosion accident a few seconds later and were instructed to equip self-rescuer in preparation for an emergency escape. Following that, the virtual system initiated a countdown as the emergency escape began. They achieve this by stimulating α/β receptors, increasing capillary permeability, and enhancing muscle contractility (Barreiro Arcos, 2022; Hu et al., 2018). The heightened metabolism associated with these processes can be observed through increased sweat production and elevated cardiac output. This heightened metabolic activity is further reflected in enhanced EDA, EMG, and HRV activity. Moreover, the accelerated oxidative breakdown of energy substrates and the expedited thermal dissipation from the skin surface are primarily responsible for reductions in RESP and SKT. These physiological responses collectively optimize energy production and muscle function, ensuring the body can effectively manage and respond to stressors during emergency situations. These reaction patterns, which provide optimal adaptation for specific stages of imminent danger (Schauer & Elbert, 2010), have been extensively documented in studies on practitioners in the transportation and aviation sectors. For example, cognitive arousal levels increased earlier in drivers who avoided a collision compared to those who did not, even before the actual hazard was visually detected (Ba et al., 2016). This was evidenced by a significant elevation in SC. Similar changes can also be observed in pilots under specific conditions, such as turbulence, indicating comparable levels of cognitive arousal (Borghini et al., 2014). Additionally, there is a consistent decline in IBI with extended exposure to adventurous flight conditions (Wang & Gao, 2020). Moreover, the characteristics of mental activities and physiological changes in simulated coal mine accident emergencies were coherent with those observed in other situations, such as a subway fire (Lin, 2020). This underscores that emergency physiological changes are provoked by external stimuli inducing mental activities, even if the form of such external stimuli is not identical. Acute stimulation promotes the close connection between the brain regions responsible for perception, memories, thoughts, and feelings, and the areas that control and represent changes in our internal bodily states, which are part of the autonomic nervous system (Quadt et al., 2022). This interconnectedness allows our brain to process information from the external stimulus while simultaneously regulating our body's reactions to that information through endocrine (Quadt et al., 2022). For example, the DT classifier achieved accuracies greater than 98% for the recognition of dangerous driving behaviors, such as no-event, change-lane, turn, and U-turn, by utilizing motoring data from 27 drivers with different cars in 7 min of driving periods (Bejani & Ghatee, 2018). As well, it performed a comparatively high accuracy of 98.8% for the detection of hazardous driver states, including alert and drowsy, by utilizing psychological data collected from 21 healthy participants taking part in four 45-minute sessions of simulated driving (Darzi et al., 2018). Additionally, the KN classifier showed promising results, with an average accuracy of 69.5% and a highest accuracy of 83.5% for the prediction of base driving features (i.e. aggressive versus unaggressive, stable versus unstable), utilizing EEG data collected from 52 healthy participants with an average driving experience of 9.64 years (Yang et al., 2018). ## Identification of Emergency Behavior Pattern Upon accurately perceiving risk, individuals tend to immediately engage in behavioral reactions to seek avoidance. Should this be accompanied by intense state anxiety, however, the seeking process would be severely impeded. Not only does this manifest itself in a prolongation of the seeking duration, but also in the increasing likelihood of unsuccessful avoidance. Such negative impact can be substantiated by a correlation analysis between mental activities and behavioral performances, the results of which are available in Online Resource 6. Furthermore, the RF classifier demonstrated superior performance over other well-known classifiers, such as KN, SVM, and neural network, for the identification of driving style by utilizing motoring data from 11 male truck drivers in Baiyinhua No.2 open-pit mine (Wang et al., 2020). The overall classification accuracy for identifying driving styles was 95.39% when the mining truck was operating under heavy load and 90.74% when operating with no load. Integrating successful experiences in stress detection, emotion recognition, and behavior prediction, the KN, DT, and RF algorithms were intentionally selected for this study. The aim was to identify emergency behavioral patterns (EBP) by utilizing psychophysiological characteristics. The behavioral reactions triggered by mental activities are accompanied by consistent and regular physiological changes, which can be further analyzed for more profound insights using machine learning algorithms. In recent years, this research paradigm has been extensively adopted to study psychophysiology and behavior across various high-risk industries such as transportation, construction, and coal mining. One particularly noteworthy example is the performance of the decision tree (DT) classifier, which achieved an accuracy of 97.6% in classifying the unsafe behaviors of a random sample of 80 workers who took part in a mass rapid transit tunnelling project in Singapore (Goh et al., 2018). This accuracy surpassed that of the other five widely-used machine learning algorithms, as well as logistic regression (LR). Besides, classic machine learning techniques have proven capable of identifying different emotional states using the DEAP Dataset, an EEG signal repository containing data from 32 participants at distinct locations: Geneva, Switzerland; Twente, Netherlands; London, United Kingdom (Doma & Pirouz, 2020). The highest accuracy for emotion recognition achieved by multiple classification algorithms was in the following descending order: k-nearest neighbor (KN), support vector machine (SVM), DT, and LR. Moreover, stress assessment studies have been conducted to develop machine-learning models for classifying stress and relaxation (Siam et al., 2023). The approach to detecting mental stress utilized the DRIVEDB Dataset, which contains physiological signal data from 17 automotive drivers and is publicly available on PhysioNet (Healey & Picard, 2008). There was no deception involved. All participants who volunteered to participate in the experiment signed an informed consent form and were debriefed after the experiment. Figure 6 provides a brief overview of the entire experimental process, which comprises three phases. Detailed experimental tasks and procedures can be found in Online Resource 4. Initially, participants were informed of the privacy policy, potential consequences, and their right to withdraw at any time. If voluntarily choosing to participate in the experiment, they were required to sign the informed consent form and complete the Psychometric Questionnaire. Meanwhile, the laboratory's environmental parameters were regulated as temperature to 20 °C, wind speed to 0.7 m/s, and humidity to 55%. Wearing of the wireless physiological sensors and calibration of the eye tracker were also performed during this phase. Then, they roamed the virtual coal mines for 3 min in a natural state without being exposed to any stimuli. This roaming period allowed participants to familiarize themselves with the virtual environment and provided a baseline of physiological signals for the subsequent stimuli. Following the baseline (roaming) period, participants experienced a simulation of an emergency escape from coal mine accidents. In these simulated scenarios, participants witnessed specific warning signs of coal and gas outbursts occurring at the coal mining face, such as the outward bulging or sheet ganging of the coal wall. As the scene switched, they arrived at the belt conveyor, where a pile of coal dust had accumulated underneath the conveyor, and sparks were visible. Immediately, they encountered a gas explosion accident a few seconds later and were instructed to equip self-rescuer in preparation for an emergency escape. Following that, the virtual system initiated a countdown as the emergency escape began. Additionally, the KN classifier showed promising results, with an average accuracy of 69.5% and a highest accuracy of 83.5% for the prediction of base driving features (i.e. aggressive versus unaggressive, stable versus unstable), utilizing EEG data collected from 52 healthy participants with an average driving experience of 9.64 years (Yang et al., 2018). ## Identification of Emergency Behavior Pattern Upon accurately perceiving risk, individuals tend to immediately engage in behavioral reactions to seek avoidance. Should this be accompanied by intense state anxiety, however, the seeking process would be severely impeded. Not only does this manifest itself in a prolongation of the seeking duration, but also in the increasing likelihood of unsuccessful avoidance. Such negative impact can be substantiated by a correlation analysis between mental activities and behavioral performances, the results of which are available in Online Resource 6. Furthermore, the RF classifier demonstrated superior performance over other well-known classifiers, such as KN, SVM, and neural network, for the identification of driving style by utilizing motoring data from 11 male truck drivers in Baiyinhua No.2 open-pit mine (Wang et al., 2020). The overall classification accuracy for identifying driving styles was 95.39% when the mining truck was operating under heavy load and 90.74% when operating with no load. Integrating successful experiences in stress detection, emotion recognition, and behavior prediction, the KN, DT, and RF algorithms were intentionally selected for this study. The aim was to identify emergency behavioral patterns (EBP) by utilizing psychophysiological characteristics. The behavioral reactions triggered by mental activities are accompanied by consistent and regular physiological changes, which can be further analyzed for more profound insights using machine learning algorithms. In recent years, this research paradigm has been extensively adopted to study psychophysiology and behavior across various high-risk industries such as transportation, construction, and coal mining. One particularly noteworthy example is the performance of the decision tree (DT) classifier, which achieved an accuracy of 97.6% in classifying the unsafe behaviors of a random sample of 80 workers who took part in a mass rapid transit tunnelling project in Singapore (Goh et al., 2018). This accuracy surpassed that of the other five widely-used machine learning algorithms, as well as logistic regression (LR). Besides, classic machine learning techniques have proven capable of identifying different emotional states using the DEAP Dataset, an EEG signal repository containing data from 32 participants at distinct locations: Geneva, Switzerland; Twente, Netherlands; London, United Kingdom (Doma & Pirouz, 2020). The highest accuracy for emotion recognition achieved by multiple classification algorithms was in the following descending order: k-nearest neighbor (KN), support vector machine (SVM), DT, and LR. Moreover, stress assessment studies have been conducted to develop machine-learning models for classifying stress and relaxation (Siam et al., 2023). The approach to detecting mental stress utilized the DRIVEDB Dataset, which contains physiological signal data from 17 automotive drivers and is publicly available on PhysioNet (Healey & Picard, 2008). It was reported that the random forest (RF) classifier outperformed other techniques, namely KN, SVM, DT, and LR, achieving a classification accuracy of 98.2% for automatic stress detection. What’s more, machine learning algorithms. The process of identification was implemented using PyCharm, a Python IDE (Integrated Development Environment). Initially, the psychophysiological indicators exhibiting significant changes were taken as input features and fed into the three classifiers integrated into the Scikit-learn library. Subsequently, the experiment samples were divided into a training set, which comprised 80% of the data, and a validation set, which encompassed the remaining 20%. This partitioning was achieved using the ‘train_test_split’ function, with a ‘random_state’ parameter in the range of (1, 10). The optimization process of k-nearest neighbor classification (KNC) models is outlined below. Initially, the algorithm for the KN classifier was set as “kd_tree”, considering that the dimensionality and sample size of the input features were not excessively large. Subsequently, the remaining hyperparameters were automatically tuned by employing the grid search technique. The “GridSearchCV” function exhaustively generated candidates for the “n_neighbors” from the range of (2, 10), and for the “weights” from the range of (uniform, distance). Each combination of parameter values was independently utilized to fit the training set, resulting in trained models. The “accuracy_score” on the whole data- set served as a metric to evaluate the performance of each trained model. Ultimately, the optimal KNC models were selected based on achieving the maximum accuracies with different input features. Following a process similar to the optimization of KNC models, the DT and RF classifiers were employed to develop the decision tree classification (DTC) and random forest classification (RFC) models of EBP, respectively. The hyperparameters were automatically tuned by the "GridSearchCV" function, along with the repartitioning of the training sets by the updated values of "random_state" in the "train_test_split" function. In particular, "criterion" was traversed by a loop in the range of (gini, entropy, log_loss); "max_depth" in the range of (2, 10); "min_samples_leaf" in the range of (1, 6); "min_samples_split" in the range of (2, 6); "random_state" in the range of (1, 10). The hyperparameters values for all KNC, DTC, and RFC models under various sample splitting conditions are detailed in Online Resource 7. The performances of different classification models depend on their classifiers and input features. Figure 17 illustrates both the average and maximum accuracies of all unimodal-based classification models. Concerning input features, the classification models based on SKT, EMG, SCL, SCR, RANGE, IBI, SDNN, PNN50, and LF/HF demonstrated higher average accuracies under various sample splitting conditions (Online Resource 7). Additionally, the optimal unimodal-based models exhibited superior performance on the input features of SC, SCR, SCL-SCR, RANGE, IBI, SDNN, and LF/HF (Online Resource 7), thereby validating the discriminative role of these metrics in identifying EBP. Consequently, indicators such as SCR, RANGE, IBI, SDNN, and LF/HF, which excel in both average and maximum accuracies, serve as justifiable discriminative attributes for EBP. Out of these, LF/HF stands out as a critical indicator, achieving the highest average accuracy of 87.4% among all classification models. This

Ultimately, the optimal KNC models were selected based on achieving the maximum accuracies with different input features. Following a process similar to the optimization of KNC models, the DT and RF classifiers were employed to develop the decision tree classification (DTC) and random forest classification (RFC) models of EBP, respectively. The hyperparameters were automatically tuned by the "GridSearchCV" function, along with the repartitioning of the training sets by the updated values of "random_state" in the "train_test_split" function. In particular, "criterion" was traversed by a loop in the range of (gini, entropy, log_loss); "max_depth" in the range of (2, 10); "min_samples_leaf" in the range of (1, 6); "min_samples_split" in the range of (2, 6); "random_state" in the range of (1, 10). Concerning input features, the classification models based on SKT, EMG, SCL, SCR, RANGE, IBI, SDNN, PNN50, and LF/HF demonstrated higher average accuracies under various sample splitting conditions (Online Resource 7). Additionally, the optimal unimodal-based models exhibited superior performance on the input features of SC, SCR, SCL-SCR, RANGE, IBI, SDNN, and LF/HF (Online Resource 7), thereby validating the discriminative role of these metrics in identifying EBP. Consequently, indicators such as SCR, RANGE, IBI, SDNN, and LF/HF, which excel in both average and maximum accuracies, serve as justifiable discriminative attributes for EBP. The natural environment featured scenic forestry scenes, embracing a wide variety of plants and animals as well as streams and birdsong, as presented in Online Resource 3. ## Experimental Procedure The experiment was designed and conducted following the ethical standards of the Chinese Psychological Society and with the 1964 Helsinki Declaration and its later amendments or comparable ethical standards. There was no deception involved. All participants who volunteered to participate in the experiment signed an informed consent form and were debriefed after the experiment. Figure 6 provides a brief overview of the entire experimental process, which comprises three phases. Detailed experimental tasks and procedures can be found in Online Resource 4. Initially, participants were informed of the privacy policy, potential consequences, and their right to withdraw at any time. If voluntarily choosing to participate in the experiment, they were required to sign the informed consent form and complete the Psychometric Questionnaire. Meanwhile, the laboratory's environmental parameters were regulated as temperature to 20 °C, wind speed to 0.7 m/s, and humidity to 55%. Wearing of the wireless physiological sensors and calibration of the eye tracker were also performed during this phase. Then, they roamed the virtual coal mines for 3 min in a natural state without being exposed to any stimuli. This roaming period allowed participants to familiarize themselves with the virtual environment and provided a baseline of physiological signals for the subsequent stimuli. Following the baseline (roaming) period, participants experienced a simulation of an emergency escape from coal mine accidents. In these simulated scenarios, participants witnessed specific warning signs of coal and gas outbursts occurring at the coal mining face, such as the outward bulging or sheet ganging of the coal wall. As the scene switched, they arrived at the belt conveyor, where a pile of coal dust had accumulated underneath the conveyor, and sparks were visible. Immediately, they encountered a gas explosion accident a few seconds later and were instructed to equip self-rescuer in preparation for an emergency escape. Following that, the virtual system initiated a countdown as the emergency escape began. The correct escape route was the tunnel with the shortest distance and devoid of any risks. If a subject reached the refuge along the correct route within 60 s, it was recognized as a successful escape. Within the virtual scenarios, participants were entirely free to autonomously decide whether and how to behave according to their desires, without any interference from the experimenters. Last but not least, a forest intervention was conducted after the escape to reduce the potential impacts of participating in the high-stress VR simulated emergency scenarios. The participants were prompted to take as much time as they needed to be exposed to the virtual natural environment. All participants reported a shift away from negative affect and restoration of subjective vitality following the virtual nature experience. Finally, the experiment concluded by rewarding the participants. The complete physiological record of each subject was divided into two segments: the baseline segment, which captured the roaming period during which the subject's physiological signals were monitored in their natural state without any induced stressors; and the emergency segment, which encompassed the period from the start to the end of the virtual emergency escape, during which physiological stress were measured. To address this issue, the raw physiological data were pre-processed to restore their intrinsic features as much as possible. The natural environment featured scenic forestry scenes, embracing a wide variety of plants and animals as well as streams and birdsong, as presented in Online Resource 3. ## Experimental Procedure The experiment was designed and conducted following the ethical standards of the Chinese Psychological Society and with the 1964 Helsinki Declaration and its later amendments or comparable ethical standards. There was no deception involved. All participants who volunteered to participate in the experiment signed an informed consent form and were debriefed after the experiment. Figure 6 provides a brief overview of the entire experimental process, which comprises three phases. Detailed experimental tasks and procedures can be found in Online Resource 4. Initially, participants were informed of the privacy policy, potential consequences, and their right to withdraw at any time. Meanwhile, the laboratory's environmental parameters were regulated as temperature to 20 °C, wind speed to 0.7 m/s, and humidity to 55%. Wearing of the wireless physiological sensors and calibration of the eye tracker were also performed during this phase. Then, they roamed the virtual coal mines for 3 min in a natural state without being exposed to any stimuli. This roaming period allowed participants to familiarize themselves with the virtual environment and provided a baseline of physiological signals for the subsequent stimuli. Following the baseline (roaming) period, participants experienced a simulation of an emergency escape from coal mine accidents. In these simulated scenarios, participants witnessed specific warning signs of coal and gas outbursts occurring at the coal mining face, such as the outward bulging or sheet ganging of the coal wall. As the scene switched, they arrived at the belt conveyor, where a pile of coal dust had accumulated underneath the conveyor, and sparks were visible. Immediately, they encountered a gas explosion accident a few seconds later and were instructed to equip self-rescuer in preparation for an emergency escape. Following that, the virtual system initiated a countdown as the emergency escape began. Should this be accompanied by intense state anxiety, however, the seeking process would be severely impeded. Not only does this manifest itself in a prolongation of the seeking duration, but also in the increasing likelihood of unsuccessful avoidance. Integrating successful experiences in stress detection, emotion recognition, and behavior prediction, the KN, DT, and RF algorithms were intentionally selected for this study. The aim was to identify emergency behavioral patterns (EBP) by utilizing psychophysiological characteristics. The behavioral reactions triggered by mental activities are accompanied by consistent and regular physiological changes, which can be further analyzed for more profound insights using machine learning algorithms. In recent years, this research paradigm has been extensively adopted to study psychophysiology and behavior across various high-risk industries such as transportation, construction, and coal mining. One particularly noteworthy example is the performance of the decision tree (DT) classifier, which achieved an accuracy of 97.6% in classifying the unsafe behaviors of a random sample of 80 workers who took part in a mass rapid transit tunnelling project in Singapore (Goh et al., 2018). This accuracy surpassed that of the other five widely-used machine learning algorithms, as well as logistic regression (LR). Besides, classic machine learning techniques have proven capable of identifying different emotional states using the DEAP Dataset, an EEG signal repository containing data from 32 participants at distinct locations: Geneva, Switzerland; Twente, Netherlands; London, United Kingdom (Doma & Pirouz, 2020). The highest accuracy for emotion recognition achieved by multiple classification algorithms was in the following descending order: k-nearest neighbor (KN), support vector machine (SVM), DT, and LR. Moreover, stress assessment studies have been conducted to develop machine-learning models for classifying stress and relaxation (Siam et al., 2023). The approach to detecting mental stress utilized the DRIVEDB Dataset, which contains physiological signal data from 17 automotive drivers and is publicly available on PhysioNet (Healey & Picard, 2008). It was reported that the random forest (RF) classifier outperformed other techniques, namely KN, SVM, DT, and LR, achieving a classification accuracy of 98.2% for automatic stress detection. What’s more, machine learning algorithms. The process of identification was implemented using PyCharm, a Python IDE (Integrated Development Environment). Initially, the psychophysiological indicators exhibiting significant changes were taken as input features and fed into the three classifiers integrated into the Scikit-learn library. Subsequently, the experiment samples were divided into a training set, which comprised 80% of the data, and a validation set, which encompassed the remaining 20%. This partitioning was achieved using the ‘train_test_split’ function, with a ‘random_state’ parameter in the range of (1, 10). The optimization process of k-nearest neighbor classification (KNC) models is outlined below. Initially, the algorithm for the KN classifier was set as “kd_tree”, considering that the dimensionality and sample size of the input features were not excessively large. Subsequently, the remaining hyperparameters were automatically tuned by employing the grid search technique. The “GridSearchCV” function exhaustively generated candidates for the “n_neighbors” from the range of (2, 10), and for the “weights” from the range of (uniform, distance). Each combination of parameter values was independently utilized to fit the training set, resulting in trained models. The “accuracy_score” on the whole data- set served as a metric to evaluate the performance of each trained model. Ultimately, the optimal KNC models were selected based on achieving the maximum accuracies with different input features. Following a process similar to the optimization of KNC models, the DT and RF classifiers were employed to develop the decision tree classification (DTC) and random forest classification (RFC) models of EBP, respectively. The hyperparameters were automatically tuned by the "GridSearchCV" function, along with the repartitioning of the training sets by the updated values of "random_state" in the "train_test_split" function. In particular, "criterion" was traversed by a loop in the range of (gini, entropy, log_loss); "max_depth" in the range of (2, 10); "min_samples_leaf" in the range of (1, 6); "min_samples_split" in the range of (2, 6); "random_state" in the range of (1, 10). The hyperparameters values for all KNC, DTC, and RFC models under various sample splitting conditions are detailed in Online Resource 7. The performances of different classification models depend on their classifiers and input features. Figure 17 illustrates both the average and maximum accuracies of all unimodal-based classification models. Concerning input features, the classification models based on SKT, EMG, SCL, SCR, RANGE, IBI, SDNN, PNN50, and LF/HF demonstrated higher average accuracies under various sample splitting conditions (Online Resource 7). Additionally, the optimal unimodal-based models exhibited superior performance on the input features of SC, SCR, SCL-SCR, RANGE, IBI, SDNN, and LF/HF (Online Resource 7), thereby validating the discriminative role of these metrics in identifying EBP. Consequently, indicators such as SCR, RANGE, IBI, SDNN, and LF/HF, which excel in both average and maximum accuracies, serve as justifiable discriminative attributes for EBP. Out of these, LF/HF stands out as a critical indicator, achieving the highest average accuracy of 87.4% among all classification models. This

Compared to traditional experimental methods, virtual experiments offer enhanced safety for participants, eliminating the risk of physical harm (Hamilton et al., 2021). Additionally, they are more accessible, cost-effective, and conducive to repetition. Both domestically and internationally, significant academic efforts have been devoted to examining the characteristics of psychophysiological changes in unconventional states through simulated experiments. These efforts encompass a wide range of contexts, from accidents in transportation, construction, and coal mines to earthquakes and fires. VR technology enables the near-realistic reproduction of complex scenarios in these contexts. Overall, the unusual stimuli (including material, organic, and social) activate, to varying degrees, the individual’s mental activities (including cognition, emotion, and volition), which induce corresponding decision-making behaviors, as well as diverse patterns of physiological reactions such as electrocardiogram (ECG) and EDA. Nevertheless, to our knowledge, there remain some limitations, which are outlined below. Firstly, the existing literature has primarily focused on the construction industry rather than the coal mining industry. Secondly, the emergencies simulated using VR technology mostly involved single-fire accidents in buildings, which differed from the gas explosion accidents underground in coal mines, characterized by their suddenness and catastrophic nature. Furthermore, more literature has examined the relationship with behavioral responses only from a single perspective, either psychologically or physiologically. These weaknesses formulate the research gaps in understanding the neurobiological mechanisms of emergency reactions to coal mine accidents, which impedes coal miners from accurately recognizing their emergency behaviors and prevents managers from developing strategies to enhance their emergency response capabilities. Following the research clues and gaps, our study is focused on the psychophysiological characteristics of emergency reactions to coal mine accidents. From there, it further aims to explore the potential of significant indicators as predictors for emergency reactions. In other words, this study is an attempt to answer the following research questions: What characterizes emergency reactions to coal mine accidents and how can such characteristics be utilized to predict emergency reactions? The research objectives can be facilitated by utilizing VR technology to simulate a virtual scenario of a gas explosion accident triggered by a coal mine fire in the whole process. This endeavor holds the potential to prevent coal mine accidents and mitigate injuries. ## Materials and Methods ### Questionnaire Survey In this experiment, questionnaire surveys were conducted to gauge subjects’ personality traits and assess their mental activities during emergency reactions. The Psychometric Questionnaire was developed to test the personality traits and safety literacy levels of the subjects, drawing from the Revised Neuroticism Extraversion Openness Personality Inventory (Costa Jr & McCrae, 2008) and the Eysenck Personality Questionnaire-Revised (Eysenck & Eysenck, 1993). It comprised six sections: basic personal information, personality, emotion, cognition, awareness, and experience, as detailed in Online Resource 1. The Risk Perception Inventory (RPI) (Online Resource 1) was developed based on the available well-established scales by Li (2019) and Mao (2021). It was intended to assess subjects’ perceived and cognitive abilities regarding the risks of coal mine accidents by utilizing 10 items. Specifically, the first three questions were worth 2 or 1 points for selecting whether or not a particular risk had been perceived. The other seven items pertained to subjective judgments about the objectivity, unpredictability, calamitability, and variability of the risks of coal mine accidents. A five-point Likert scale was adopted, ranging from “Strongly Disagree” to “Strongly Agree” with values of 1, 2, 3, 4, and 5, respectively. All items were positively scored, with a total score of 41 on the scale. The State-trait Anxiety Inventory (SAI) (Spielberger et al., 2017), a widely recognized tool in psychology, was adapted to assess the state anxiety of subjects during emergencies in coal mine accidents (Online Resource 1). It consisted of 20 items, representing the influences of transitory situational stress. Each item offered four options: 1 point for ‘very slight’, 2 points for ‘slight’, 3 points for ‘pronounced’, and 4 points for ‘very strong’, allowing subjects to indicate the intensity of their perceived anxiety in the situations. Of these, the items with reverse scoring served to validate the scale’s measurement accuracy. Accounting for all question items, the scale was scored with a maximum of 80 and a minimum of 20 points. ### Simulation Experiment on Emergency Response to Coal Mine Accidents ### Experimental Subject To minimize the influence of individual differences on emergency reactions to coal mine accidents, homogeneous groups of similar age and education were deemed as appropriate subjects for this experiment. The following criteria were adhered to in the process of subject selection: subjects were required to be male following national regulations, as female workers are prohibited from working underground in mines; subjects were expected to be in good health, free from motion sickness and claustrophobia, and not under the influence of psychoactive drugs; participants should either have normal vision or myopia of fewer than 350 degrees with corrected visual acuity and should not have astigmatism; individuals who had experienced a late night were discouraged from participating in the experiment the following day; participation in the experiment was voluntary and not coerced. The sample size was determined by referencing previous experimental studies (Online Resource 2) on emergency evacuation from virtual building fires (Crescentini et al., 2016; Deng et al., 2022) and subway fire (Chen et al., 2021); stress reactions to coal mining accidents (Nie et al., 2016) and metro fire (Lin et al., 2020); the effects on behavioral capacity from fatigue (Zhang et al., 2023), coal mine noise (Fu et al., 2022), and underground low-light conditions (Li et al., 2022); as well as machine learning algorithms for stress detection (Siam et al., 2023), emotion recognition (Doma & Pirouz, 2020), and driving behavior identification (Bejani & Ghatee, 2018; Darzi et al., 2018; Wang et al., 2020; Yang et al., 2018). Stable emotion fosters organizational ability and structured perception, which contribute to the development of reality-oriented thinking, judgment, and evaluative capacity under stressful circumstances (Hmm, 2020). Second only to emotional stability, similar past experiences are conducive to early familiarity with emergencies and response processes, thereby facilitating the enhancement of emergency handling ability. Last but not least, a heightened sense of crisis motivates individuals to proactively focus on and prioritize the impending emergencies, formulating a plan of action accordingly. By leveraging knowledge of emergency response procedures, drawing from similar past experiences, and having a general understanding of how to manage stressful situations, individuals can make more informed decisions and take appropriate actions promptly. This indicates a greater ability to prepare themselves to respond effectively to emergencies (Kyung Hui & Og Cheol, 2017). Regarding physiological changes, regularity is mainly characterized by the enhancements of EDA, EMG, and HRV, alongside the significant reductions in RESP and SKT. These changes reflect an imbalance between the sympathetic and parasympathetic nervous systems, which may result from abnormalities in endocrine activities (hormonal) and autonomic responses (involuntary) through the hyper-activation of the hypothalamus-hypophysis neuroendocrine axis (Ulrich-Lai & Herman, 2009). During emergency reactions, the hypothalamus signals the anterior pituitary gland to release adrenocorticotropic hormone, which stimulates the adrenal cortex to release adrenal cortical hormones, such as cortisol (Hinds & Sanchez, 2022). The hypothalamus also signals the release of thyroid-stimulating hormone, which stimulates the thyroid gland to release thyroid hormones (Shiota & Kalat, 2017). All of these hormones play critical roles in regulating metabolism and preparing the body to respond to stressors. They achieve this by stimulating α/β receptors, increasing capillary permeability, and enhancing muscle contractility (Barreiro Arcos, 2022; Hu et al., 2018). The heightened metabolism associated with these processes can be observed through increased sweat production and elevated cardiac output. This heightened metabolic activity is further reflected in enhanced EDA, EMG, and HRV activity. Moreover, the accelerated oxidative breakdown of energy substrates and the expedited thermal dissipation from the skin surface are primarily responsible for reductions in RESP and SKT. These physiological responses collectively optimize energy production and muscle function, ensuring the body can effectively manage and respond to stressors during emergency situations. These reaction patterns, which provide optimal adaptation for specific stages of imminent danger (Schauer & Elbert, 2010), have been extensively documented in studies on practitioners in the transportation and aviation sectors. For example, cognitive arousal levels increased earlier in drivers who avoided a collision compared to those who did not, even before the actual hazard was visually detected (Ba et al., 2016). This was evidenced by a significant elevation in SC. Similar changes can also be observed in pilots under specific conditions, such as turbulence, indicating comparable levels of cognitive arousal (Borghini et al., 2014). Additionally, there is a consistent decline in IBI with extended exposure to adventurous flight conditions (Wang & Gao, 2020). Moreover, the characteristics of mental activities and physiological changes in simulated coal mine accident emergencies were coherent with those observed in other situations, such as a subway fire (Lin, 2020). This underscores that emergency physiological changes are provoked by external stimuli inducing mental activities, even if the form of such external stimuli is not identical. Ultimately, the optimal KNC models were selected based on achieving the maximum accuracies with different input features. Following a process similar to the optimization of KNC models, the DT and RF classifiers were employed to develop the decision tree classification (DTC) and random forest classification (RFC) models of EBP, respectively. The hyperparameters were automatically tuned by the "GridSearchCV" function, along with the repartitioning of the training sets by the updated values of "random_state" in the "train_test_split" function. In particular, "criterion" was traversed by a loop in the range of (gini, entropy, log_loss); "max_depth" in the range of (2, 10); "min_samples_leaf" in the range of (1, 6); "min_samples_split" in the range of (2, 6); "random_state" in the range of (1, 10). The hyperparameters values for all KNC, DTC, and RFC models under various sample splitting conditions are detailed in Online Resource 7. The performances of different classification models depend on their classifiers and input features. Figure 17 illustrates both the average and maximum accuracies of all unimodal-based classification models. Concerning input features, the classification models based on SKT, EMG, SCL, SCR, RANGE, IBI, SDNN, PNN50, and LF/HF demonstrated higher average accuracies under various sample splitting conditions (Online Resource 7). Additionally, the optimal unimodal-based models exhibited superior performance on the input features of SC, SCR, SCL-SCR, RANGE, IBI, SDNN, and LF/HF (Online Resource 7), thereby validating the discriminative role of these metrics in identifying EBP. Consequently, indicators such as SCR, RANGE, IBI, SDNN, and LF/HF, which excel in both average and maximum accuracies, serve as justifiable discriminative attributes for EBP. The natural environment featured scenic forestry scenes, embracing a wide variety of plants and animals as well as streams and birdsong, as presented in Online Resource 3. ## Experimental Procedure The experiment was designed and conducted following the ethical standards of the Chinese Psychological Society and with the 1964 Helsinki Declaration and its later amendments or comparable ethical standards. There was no deception involved. All participants who volunteered to participate in the experiment signed an informed consent form and were debriefed after the experiment. Figure 6 provides a brief overview of the entire experimental process, which comprises three phases. Detailed experimental tasks and procedures can be found in Online Resource 4. Initially, participants were informed of the privacy policy, potential consequences, and their right to withdraw at any time. If voluntarily choosing to participate in the experiment, they were required to sign the informed consent form and complete the Psychometric Questionnaire. Meanwhile, the laboratory's environmental parameters were regulated as temperature to 20 °C, wind speed to 0.7 m/s, and humidity to 55%. Wearing of the wireless physiological sensors and calibration of the eye tracker were also performed during this phase. Then, they roamed the virtual coal mines for 3 min in a natural state without being exposed to any stimuli. This roaming period allowed participants to familiarize themselves with the virtual environment and provided a baseline of physiological signals for the subsequent stimuli. Following the baseline (roaming) period, participants experienced a simulation of an emergency escape from coal mine accidents. In these simulated scenarios, participants witnessed specific warning signs of coal and gas outbursts occurring at the coal mining face, such as the outward bulging or sheet ganging of the coal wall. As the scene switched, they arrived at the belt conveyor, where a pile of coal dust had accumulated underneath the conveyor, and sparks were visible. Immediately, they encountered a gas explosion accident a few seconds later and were instructed to equip self-rescuer in preparation for an emergency escape. Following that, the virtual system initiated a countdown as the emergency escape began. Compared to traditional experimental methods, virtual experiments offer enhanced safety for participants, eliminating the risk of physical harm (Hamilton et al., 2021). Additionally, they are more accessible, cost-effective, and conducive to repetition. Both domestically and internationally, significant academic efforts have been devoted to examining the characteristics of psychophysiological changes in unconventional states through simulated experiments. These efforts encompass a wide range of contexts, from accidents in transportation, construction, and coal mines to earthquakes and fires. VR technology enables the near-realistic reproduction of complex scenarios in these contexts. Overall, the unusual stimuli (including material, organic, and social) activate, to varying degrees, the individual’s mental activities (including cognition, emotion, and volition), which induce corresponding decision-making behaviors, as well as diverse patterns of physiological reactions such as electrocardiogram (ECG) and EDA. Nevertheless, to our knowledge, there remain some limitations, which are outlined below. Firstly, the existing literature has primarily focused on the construction industry rather than the coal mining industry. Secondly, the emergencies simulated using VR technology mostly involved single-fire accidents in buildings, which differed from the gas explosion accidents underground in coal mines, characterized by their suddenness and catastrophic nature. Furthermore, more literature has examined the relationship with behavioral responses only from a single perspective, either psychologically or physiologically. These weaknesses formulate the research gaps in understanding the neurobiological mechanisms of emergency reactions to coal mine accidents, which impedes coal miners from accurately recognizing their emergency behaviors and prevents managers from developing strategies to enhance their emergency response capabilities. Following the research clues and gaps, our study is focused on the psychophysiological characteristics of emergency reactions to coal mine accidents. From there, it further aims to explore the potential of significant indicators as predictors for emergency reactions. In other words, this study is an attempt to answer the following research questions: What characterizes emergency reactions to coal mine accidents and how can such characteristics be utilized to predict emergency reactions? The research objectives can be facilitated by utilizing VR technology to simulate a virtual scenario of a gas explosion accident triggered by a coal mine fire in the whole process. This endeavor holds the potential to prevent coal mine accidents and mitigate injuries. ## Materials and Methods ### Questionnaire Survey In this experiment, questionnaire surveys were conducted to gauge subjects’ personality traits and assess their mental activities during emergency reactions. The Psychometric Questionnaire was developed to test the personality traits and safety literacy levels of the subjects, drawing from the Revised Neuroticism Extraversion Openness Personality Inventory (Costa Jr & McCrae, 2008) and the Eysenck Personality Questionnaire-Revised (Eysenck & Eysenck, 1993). It comprised six sections: basic personal information, personality, emotion, cognition, awareness, and experience, as detailed in Online Resource 1. The Risk Perception Inventory (RPI) (Online Resource 1) was developed based on the available well-established scales by Li (2019) and Mao (2021). It was intended to assess subjects’ perceived and cognitive abilities regarding the risks of coal mine accidents by utilizing 10 items. Specifically, the first three questions were worth 2 or 1 points for selecting whether or not a particular risk had been perceived. The other seven items pertained to subjective judgments about the objectivity, unpredictability, calamitability, and variability of the risks of coal mine accidents. A five-point Likert scale was adopted, ranging from “Strongly Disagree” to “Strongly Agree” with values of 1, 2, 3, 4, and 5, respectively. All items were positively scored, with a total score of 41 on the scale. The State-trait Anxiety Inventory (SAI) (Spielberger et al., 2017), a widely recognized tool in psychology, was adapted to assess the state anxiety of subjects during emergencies in coal mine accidents (Online Resource 1). It consisted of 20 items, representing the influences of transitory situational stress. Each item offered four options: 1 point for ‘very slight’, 2 points for ‘slight’, 3 points for ‘pronounced’, and 4 points for ‘very strong’, allowing subjects to indicate the intensity of their perceived anxiety in the situations. Of these, the items with reverse scoring served to validate the scale’s measurement accuracy. Accounting for all question items, the scale was scored with a maximum of 80 and a minimum of 20 points. ### Simulation Experiment on Emergency Response to Coal Mine Accidents ### Experimental Subject To minimize the influence of individual differences on emergency reactions to coal mine accidents, homogeneous groups of similar age and education were deemed as appropriate subjects for this experiment. The following criteria were adhered to in the process of subject selection: subjects were required to be male following national regulations, as female workers are prohibited from working underground in mines; subjects were expected to be in good health, free from motion sickness and claustrophobia, and not under the influence of psychoactive drugs; participants should either have normal vision or myopia of fewer than 350 degrees with corrected visual acuity and should not have astigmatism; individuals who had experienced a late night were discouraged from participating in the experiment the following day; participation in the experiment was voluntary and not coerced. The sample size was determined by referencing previous experimental studies (Online Resource 2) on emergency evacuation from virtual building fires (Crescentini et al., 2016; Deng et al., 2022) and subway fire (Chen et al., 2021); stress reactions to coal mining accidents (Nie et al., 2016) and metro fire (Lin et al., 2020); the effects on behavioral capacity from fatigue (Zhang et al., 2023), coal mine noise (Fu et al., 2022), and underground low-light conditions (Li et al., 2022); as well as machine learning algorithms for stress detection (Siam et al., 2023), emotion recognition (Doma & Pirouz, 2020), and driving behavior identification (Bejani & Ghatee, 2018; Darzi et al., 2018; Wang et al., 2020; Yang et al., 2018). The correct escape route was the tunnel with the shortest distance and devoid of any risks. If a subject reached the refuge along the correct route within 60 s, it was recognized as a successful escape. Otherwise, the escape was deemed unsuccessful if the chosen route was incorrect or if the allocated time was exceeded.
