Finally, the experiment concluded by rewarding the participants. The complete physiological record of each subject was divided into two segments: the baseline segment, which captured the roaming period during which the subject's physiological signals were monitored in their natural state without any induced stressors; and the emergency segment, which encompassed the period from the start to the end of the virtual emergency escape, during which physiological stress were measured. The noise and distortion may be attributed to continuous body movement and hair on the skin reducing the adhesion between the skin and the physiological sensors (Iqbal et al., 2021). To address this issue, the raw physiological data were pre-processed to restore their intrinsic features as much as possible. On one hand, the data noise was eliminated using a sequence of steps: filtering, smoothing, scaling, and down-sampling. Different signals lend themselves to different techniques. The aim was to identify emergency behavioral patterns (EBP) by utilizing psychophysiological characteristics. The behavioral reactions triggered by mental activities are accompanied by consistent and regular physiological changes, which can be further analyzed for more profound insights using machine learning algorithms. In recent years, this research paradigm has been extensively adopted to study psychophysiology and behavior across various high-risk industries such as transportation, construction, and coal mining. One particularly noteworthy example is the performance of the decision tree (DT) classifier, which achieved an accuracy of 97.6% in classifying the unsafe behaviors of a random sample of 80 workers who took part in a mass rapid transit tunnelling project in Singapore (Goh et al., 2018). This accuracy surpassed that of the other five widely-used machine learning algorithms, as well as logistic regression (LR). Besides, classic machine learning techniques have proven capable of identifying different emotional states using the DEAP Dataset, an EEG signal repository containing data from 32 participants at distinct locations: Geneva, Switzerland; Twente, Netherlands; London, United Kingdom (Doma & Pirouz, 2020). The highest accuracy for emotion recognition achieved by multiple classification algorithms was in the following descending order: k-nearest neighbor (KN), support vector machine (SVM), DT, and LR. Moreover, stress assessment studies have been conducted to develop machine-learning models for classifying stress and relaxation (Siam et al., 2023). The approach to detecting mental stress utilized the DRIVEDB Dataset, which contains physiological signal data from 17 automotive drivers and is publicly available on PhysioNet (Healey & Picard, 2008). It was reported that the random forest (RF) classifier outperformed other techniques, namely KN, SVM, DT, and LR, achieving a classification accuracy of 98.2% for automatic stress detection. Initially, the psychophysiological indicators exhibiting significant changes were taken as input features and fed into the three classifiers integrated into the Scikit-learn library. Subsequently, the experiment samples were divided into a training set, which comprised 80% of the data, and a validation set, which encompassed the remaining 20%. This partitioning was achieved using the ‘train_test_split’ function, with a ‘random_state’ parameter in the range of (1, 10). The optimization process of k-nearest neighbor classification (KNC) models is outlined below. Initially, the algorithm for the KN classifier was set as “kd_tree”, considering that the dimensionality and sample size of the input features were not excessively large. Subsequently, the remaining hyperparameters were automatically tuned by employing the grid search technique. The “GridSearchCV” function exhaustively generated candidates for the “n_neighbors” from the range of (2, 10), and for the “weights” from the range of (uniform, distance). Each combination of parameter values was independently utilized to fit the training set, resulting in trained models. The “accuracy_score” on the whole data- set served as a metric to evaluate the performance of each trained model. Ultimately, the optimal KNC models were selected based on achieving the maximum accuracies with different input features. Following a process similar to the optimization of KNC models, the DT and RF classifiers were employed to develop the decision tree classification (DTC) and random forest classification (RFC) models of EBP, respectively. The hyperparameters were automatically tuned by the "GridSearchCV" function, along with the repartitioning of the training sets by the updated values of "random_state" in the "train_test_split" function. In particular, "criterion" was traversed by a loop in the range of (gini, entropy, log_loss); "max_depth" in the range of (2, 10); "min_samples_leaf" in the range of (1, 6); "min_samples_split" in the range of (2, 6); "random_state" in the range of (1, 10). The hyperparameters values for all KNC, DTC, and RFC models under various sample splitting conditions are detailed in Online Resource 7. The performances of different classification models depend on their classifiers and input features. Figure 17 illustrates both the average and maximum accuracies of all unimodal-based classification models. Concerning input features, the classification models based on SKT, EMG, SCL, SCR, RANGE, IBI, SDNN, PNN50, and LF/HF demonstrated higher average accuracies under various sample splitting conditions (Online Resource 7). Additionally, the optimal unimodal-based models exhibited superior performance on the input features of SC, SCR, SCL-SCR, RANGE, IBI, SDNN, and LF/HF (Online Resource 7), thereby validating the discriminative role of these metrics in identifying EBP. Consequently, indicators such as SCR, RANGE, IBI, SDNN, and LF/HF, which excel in both average and maximum accuracies, serve as justifiable discriminative attributes for EBP. Out of these, LF/HF stands out as a critical indicator, achieving the highest average accuracy of 87.4% among all classification models. This

Additionally, the KN classifier showed promising results, with an average accuracy of 69.5% and a highest accuracy of 83.5% for the prediction of base driving features (i.e. aggressive versus unaggressive, stable versus unstable), utilizing EEG data collected from 52 healthy participants with an average driving experience of 9.64 years (Yang et al., 2018). ## Identification of Emergency Behavior Pattern Upon accurately perceiving risk, individuals tend to immediately engage in behavioral reactions to seek avoidance. Should this be accompanied by intense state anxiety, however, the seeking process would be severely impeded. Not only does this manifest itself in a prolongation of the seeking duration, but also in the increasing likelihood of unsuccessful avoidance. Such negative impact can be substantiated by a correlation analysis between mental activities and behavioral performances, the results of which are available in Online Resource 6. Furthermore, the RF classifier demonstrated superior performance over other well-known classifiers, such as KN, SVM, and neural network, for the identification of driving style by utilizing motoring data from 11 male truck drivers in Baiyinhua No.2 open-pit mine (Wang et al., 2020). The overall classification accuracy for identifying driving styles was 95.39% when the mining truck was operating under heavy load and 90.74% when operating with no load. Integrating successful experiences in stress detection, emotion recognition, and behavior prediction, the KN, DT, and RF algorithms were intentionally selected for this study. The aim was to identify emergency behavioral patterns (EBP) by utilizing psychophysiological characteristics. The behavioral reactions triggered by mental activities are accompanied by consistent and regular physiological changes, which can be further analyzed for more profound insights using machine learning algorithms. In recent years, this research paradigm has been extensively adopted to study psychophysiology and behavior across various high-risk industries such as transportation, construction, and coal mining. One particularly noteworthy example is the performance of the decision tree (DT) classifier, which achieved an accuracy of 97.6% in classifying the unsafe behaviors of a random sample of 80 workers who took part in a mass rapid transit tunnelling project in Singapore (Goh et al., 2018). This accuracy surpassed that of the other five widely-used machine learning algorithms, as well as logistic regression (LR). Besides, classic machine learning techniques have proven capable of identifying different emotional states using the DEAP Dataset, an EEG signal repository containing data from 32 participants at distinct locations: Geneva, Switzerland; Twente, Netherlands; London, United Kingdom (Doma & Pirouz, 2020). The highest accuracy for emotion recognition achieved by multiple classification algorithms was in the following descending order: k-nearest neighbor (KN), support vector machine (SVM), DT, and LR. Moreover, stress assessment studies have been conducted to develop machine-learning models for classifying stress and relaxation (Siam et al., 2023). The approach to detecting mental stress utilized the DRIVEDB Dataset, which contains physiological signal data from 17 automotive drivers and is publicly available on PhysioNet (Healey & Picard, 2008). It was reported that the random forest (RF) classifier outperformed other techniques, namely KN, SVM, DT, and LR, achieving a classification accuracy of 98.2% for automatic stress detection. What’s more, machine learning algorithms. The process of identification was implemented using PyCharm, a Python IDE (Integrated Development Environment). Initially, the psychophysiological indicators exhibiting significant changes were taken as input features and fed into the three classifiers integrated into the Scikit-learn library. Subsequently, the experiment samples were divided into a training set, which comprised 80% of the data, and a validation set, which encompassed the remaining 20%. This partitioning was achieved using the ‘train_test_split’ function, with a ‘random_state’ parameter in the range of (1, 10). The optimization process of k-nearest neighbor classification (KNC) models is outlined below. Initially, the algorithm for the KN classifier was set as “kd_tree”, considering that the dimensionality and sample size of the input features were not excessively large. Subsequently, the remaining hyperparameters were automatically tuned by employing the grid search technique. The “GridSearchCV” function exhaustively generated candidates for the “n_neighbors” from the range of (2, 10), and for the “weights” from the range of (uniform, distance). Each combination of parameter values was independently utilized to fit the training set, resulting in trained models. The “accuracy_score” on the whole data- set served as a metric to evaluate the performance of each trained model. Ultimately, the optimal KNC models were selected based on achieving the maximum accuracies with different input features. Following a process similar to the optimization of KNC models, the DT and RF classifiers were employed to develop the decision tree classification (DTC) and random forest classification (RFC) models of EBP, respectively. The hyperparameters were automatically tuned by the "GridSearchCV" function, along with the repartitioning of the training sets by the updated values of "random_state" in the "train_test_split" function. In particular, "criterion" was traversed by a loop in the range of (gini, entropy, log_loss); "max_depth" in the range of (2, 10); "min_samples_leaf" in the range of (1, 6); "min_samples_split" in the range of (2, 6); "random_state" in the range of (1, 10). The hyperparameters values for all KNC, DTC, and RFC models under various sample splitting conditions are detailed in Online Resource 7. The performances of different classification models depend on their classifiers and input features. Figure 17 illustrates both the average and maximum accuracies of all unimodal-based classification models. Concerning input features, the classification models based on SKT, EMG, SCL, SCR, RANGE, IBI, SDNN, PNN50, and LF/HF demonstrated higher average accuracies under various sample splitting conditions (Online Resource 7). Additionally, the optimal unimodal-based models exhibited superior performance on the input features of SC, SCR, SCL-SCR, RANGE, IBI, SDNN, and LF/HF (Online Resource 7), thereby validating the discriminative role of these metrics in identifying EBP. Consequently, indicators such as SCR, RANGE, IBI, SDNN, and LF/HF, which excel in both average and maximum accuracies, serve as justifiable discriminative attributes for EBP. Out of these, LF/HF stands out as a critical indicator, achieving the highest average accuracy of 87.4% among all classification models. This

There was no deception involved. All participants who volunteered to participate in the experiment signed an informed consent form and were debriefed after the experiment. Figure 6 provides a brief overview of the entire experimental process, which comprises three phases. Detailed experimental tasks and procedures can be found in Online Resource 4. Initially, participants were informed of the privacy policy, potential consequences, and their right to withdraw at any time. If voluntarily choosing to participate in the experiment, they were required to sign the informed consent form and complete the Psychometric Questionnaire. Meanwhile, the laboratory's environmental parameters were regulated as temperature to 20 °C, wind speed to 0.7 m/s, and humidity to 55%. Wearing of the wireless physiological sensors and calibration of the eye tracker were also performed during this phase. Then, they roamed the virtual coal mines for 3 min in a natural state without being exposed to any stimuli. This roaming period allowed participants to familiarize themselves with the virtual environment and provided a baseline of physiological signals for the subsequent stimuli. Following the baseline (roaming) period, participants experienced a simulation of an emergency escape from coal mine accidents. In these simulated scenarios, participants witnessed specific warning signs of coal and gas outbursts occurring at the coal mining face, such as the outward bulging or sheet ganging of the coal wall. As the scene switched, they arrived at the belt conveyor, where a pile of coal dust had accumulated underneath the conveyor, and sparks were visible. Immediately, they encountered a gas explosion accident a few seconds later and were instructed to equip self-rescuer in preparation for an emergency escape. Following that, the virtual system initiated a countdown as the emergency escape began. Initially, the psychophysiological indicators exhibiting significant changes were taken as input features and fed into the three classifiers integrated into the Scikit-learn library. Subsequently, the experiment samples were divided into a training set, which comprised 80% of the data, and a validation set, which encompassed the remaining 20%. This partitioning was achieved using the ‘train_test_split’ function, with a ‘random_state’ parameter in the range of (1, 10). The optimization process of k-nearest neighbor classification (KNC) models is outlined below. Initially, the algorithm for the KN classifier was set as “kd_tree”, considering that the dimensionality and sample size of the input features were not excessively large. Subsequently, the remaining hyperparameters were automatically tuned by employing the grid search technique. The “GridSearchCV” function exhaustively generated candidates for the “n_neighbors” from the range of (2, 10), and for the “weights” from the range of (uniform, distance). Ultimately, the optimal KNC models were selected based on achieving the maximum accuracies with different input features. The results revealed a significant negative correlation between state anxiety and escape outcome (defined as 0 for a failed escape while 1 for a successful escape) at the Sig.=0.01 level, with a Pearson correlation coefficient of -0.57.
